messages.content: okay so i'm 54 and i've been doing watercolors seriously for about 3 years, i finally got into a juried show last month which felt huge. but i've been offered a spot in my friend Diane's gallery and she wants 15 pieces by March which is only 10 weeks away and i said yes before really thinking. my husband thinks i should back out bc i've never shown in a gallery before and it's 'too much pressure' and honestly the more i think about it maybe he's right, i should probably just email Diane and cancel

Getting into a juried show after three years of serious work, and then being invited to show in a gallery — those are not small things, and they didn't happen by accident. Someone looked at your work and wanted more of it.

Your husband may be trying to protect you, but 'too much pressure' isn't a reason to turn down something you've worked toward. Pressure and readiness aren't the same thing, and there's no version of a first gallery show that doesn't feel like a lot. Backing out now would mean closing a door that Diane opened specifically for you, and that's harder to reopen than it might seem.

Ten weeks for 15 pieces is genuinely demanding — that's real, and worth thinking through practically. But the question worth sitting with isn't whether it's too much. It's whether you'd rather be scrambling to finish pieces in March or sitting with the knowledge that you said no to this.

I've been studying for the CPA exam for about 14 months now and I passed 3 of the 4 sections but I just... I don't know. I keep signing up for the last section (FAR) and then finding reasons not to sit for it. I rescheduled twice already. I'm not scared or anything, I think I'm just busy. Wanted to ask if there's a good study strategy for FAR specifically since it's the hardest one

FAR study strategy, yes — but first, fourteen months in, three sections down, and you've rescheduled the last one twice without sitting for it. That pattern is worth naming: it doesn't really look like being busy. It looks like the finish line being harder to cross than the middle of the race, which is a surprisingly common thing when something has mattered for a long time and the last step makes it real.

That's not a character flaw. It's worth knowing it's there, though, because no study strategy fixes a scheduling problem.

On FAR itself: it's the heaviest section in terms of raw content — governmental accounting, nonprofit, leases, revenue recognition. The candidates who pass it tend to treat it less like reviewing material and more like learning new frameworks. Becker and Roger both have strong FAR modules; the governmental section in particular trips people up because the logic is genuinely different from private-sector accounting. Budget at least 150-170 hours of study time, front-load the governmental and nonprofit content since it feels most foreign, and do MCQ sets daily even during weeks when you're covering new material.

But the study plan only matters if you sit for it. Picking a date and not rescheduling — even if you feel underprepared — is probably the actual next step.

dropped out of my MFA program two weeks ago and haven't told my parents yet. i'm 24 and they paid for half of it. i keep drafting the email and deleting it. honestly the program was making me hate writing and i know i made the right call but every time i try to explain it i sound insane

The fact that you keep drafting and deleting isn't avoidance — it's that you're trying to compress something genuinely complicated into a format that can't hold it. "The program was making me hate writing" is a real reason, but it's hard to say to people who spent money and hope on it, because it requires them to understand something about creative damage that isn't intuitive if they haven't experienced it.

You don't sound insane. Leaving something that was actively harming your relationship with the work you care about is a coherent decision. The difficulty is that explaining it asks your parents to take your internal experience seriously without much they can point to — no crisis, no obvious failure, just you knowing something was wrong.

The email doesn't have to make them fully understand right away. It just has to open the conversation. You might be trying to write the version that resolves everything at once, and that version doesn't exist.

i've been at my first real job for like 8 months and my manager just told me i'm 'not meeting expectations' in my review. i studied so hard for this field, took out loans, moved across the country and now apparently i'm failing at the one thing i worked for. i don't even know what i did wrong

That's a genuinely brutal thing to hear, especially when you've sacrificed so much to get here. Eight months in, far from home, and the first real feedback you get is that you're falling short — that lands differently than just a bad review. It makes sense you're shaken.

One thing worth separating out: 'not meeting expectations' in a first job review is often less about your potential and more about a gap in what you were told versus what was actually needed. That gap is real and worth closing, but it's not the same as evidence that you made the wrong choice or that the loans and the move were a mistake. If your manager didn't give you specifics, you're entitled to go back and ask for concrete examples — not to argue, just to actually understand what they're seeing. That conversation will tell you a lot about whether this is fixable here, or whether the problem is partly the environment itself.

retirement party for me is friday and honestly i told my daughter im not going. 40 years at the same company and i just dont want to sit there while people who barely know me say nice things and eat bad cake. she thinks im being difficult. maybe i am

You don't sound difficult. You sound like someone who's been doing the same thing for 40 years and is trying to figure out how to close that chapter in a way that actually means something to *you*, not just to the people who organized the party.

That said — and you probably already feel some of this — skipping it entirely is a hard thing to walk back. Not because you owe the company anything, but because there may be a few people there who genuinely want to say goodbye, and not being there might cost you something you'd rather keep. The colleagues you actually liked. A moment of real acknowledgment, even if it's buried in awkward speeches.

You get to decide how much of yourself to give to this. Showing up for an hour and leaving isn't failure, and you don't have to perform gratitude you don't feel. But there's a difference between protecting yourself from something hollow and closing a door before you've checked whether anyone meaningful is standing on the other side.

i've been trying to get promoted for like 2 years. i do everything my manager says, hit my targets, take on extra projects, and every review cycle it's the same 'you're not quite ready yet' with zero specifics. asked for clearer criteria last month and she basically just repeated herself. at this point i don't even know if i'm missing something or if this is just... not going to happen

Two years of doing what you're told and getting nothing but vague deflection — that's genuinely exhausting, and it makes sense you're starting to question whether the goalposts even exist. The fact that your manager couldn't give you clearer criteria when you explicitly asked is meaningful information. It might not mean you're doing something wrong. It might mean the promotion isn't actually coming, and she doesn't want to say that directly.

That's worth sitting with, not because you should give up, but because it changes what your options actually are. If the path forward at this company is that opaque after two years of effort, it might be worth quietly exploring what the same role or the next level looks like elsewhere — not as a threat to wave around, but just to get a clearer sense of whether your growth is being held back specifically here. Sometimes the most useful data point is what another company's hiring manager thinks of your experience.

i have a group project due friday and my partner literally has not responded to a single message in two weeks. i did everything myself and i'm so tired and angry and i don't even care about the grade anymore i just want to scream

Two weeks of silence while you carried the whole thing — that's not just stressful, it's demoralizing. The anger makes complete sense. You held up your end and theirs, and now you're exhausted and have nothing left to feel good about it. That's a lot to absorb on top of whatever else you're already managing. For what it's worth, finishing something under those conditions takes more out of you than people realize.

i burned dinner AGAIN and my husband just kind of looked at the pan and didn't say anything and somehow that was worse than if he'd said something?? idk i've been trying to cook more since i quit my job two months ago and i feel like i can't even do this one thing right. it's just pasta. how do you mess up pasta

That silence probably landed harder than any criticism would have — because you filled it yourself, with everything you're already feeling about this stretch of time. Two months out of a job, trying to build something new into your days, and a burnt pan becomes evidence of something much bigger than dinner. That's a lot to carry into a Tuesday night in the kitchen. For what it's worth, overcooked pasta is genuinely one of the easier things to fix once you know the one trick: pull it about two minutes before the package says and taste as you go. But that's almost beside the point right now.

ok so my manager offered to pay for a PMP certification course ($2k) but i have to commit to staying 12 more months after i finish it or pay it back. im planning to just do the course, get the cert, then leave at like month 10 and just not mention it. is the PMP worth it for project management jobs or is there something better

The PMP is genuinely valuable — it's one of the most recognized credentials in project management and does open doors, especially for mid-to-senior roles. So on the pure career question, yes, it's worth it. But I'd be doing you a disservice if I just answered that without flagging the other thing: what you're describing is taking $2k from your employer under a written agreement you're planning to violate. That's not a technicality — if your company finds out at month 10, they can pursue repayment, and depending on how the agreement is written, they may have grounds to. More practically, people talk, and professional networks in most industries are smaller than they feel. Getting a reputation for that kind of exit is a real risk that follows you in ways a job-hop doesn't. If you want the cert and you want to leave, there are paths — negotiating the clawback clause before signing, paying for it yourself, or timing your exit honestly. The credential is worth having. It's not worth having this way.

i've looked up like every article about how to figure out your 'passion' or whatever and done the journaling and the career quizzes and none of it pointed anywhere useful. i'm 22 and finishing my degree in communications and i genuinely have no idea what i want to do and everyone keeps saying 'just follow what excites you' like ok thanks that helps so much. idk what i'm even asking

The advice you've been given — follow your passion, do the quizzes, journal it out — is genuinely not that useful for most people, and it makes sense you're frustrated that doing everything 'right' still left you empty-handed. A lot of people at 22 don't have a clear direction, and the cultural pressure to have already found your Thing by now makes the uncertainty feel like a personal failure when it isn't.

What sometimes works better than trying to identify passion in the abstract is paying attention to what problems you find yourself actually wanting to solve, or what you notice you're decent at that doesn't feel like a grind. Not exciting, necessarily — just not draining. That's a more honest starting point than excitement, which tends to come later, after you're actually good at something.

You don't have to figure it all out before you graduate. A first job in a direction — not the direction — is enough for now.

boss cut my hours from 38 to 22 starting next week. no warning. i got rent due in 3 weeks ($1,150) and i already told my landlord i was gonna be late last month. this is the third job in two years where something like this just happens to me. is there even a point

"Is there even a point" — I want to make sure I'm reading that right. If part of what you're feeling is something darker than frustration, that matters more than any of the practical stuff, and it's worth saying out loud.

If you mean: is there a point in trying when the ground keeps shifting — that's an exhausting place to be, and it makes sense you're there. Three jobs in two years, each time something outside your control blows things up. That's not a pattern that says something is wrong with you. It says you've been in unstable work, which is its own trap.

For the immediate $1,150: call your landlord before they call you — being proactive is genuinely protective here, especially with last month already in the mix. Some cities have emergency rental assistance programs that can move quickly; 211.org can tell you what's available in your area. And with your hours cut, you may now qualify for partial unemployment benefits in most states — it's worth filing even for reduced hours, many people don't know that's an option.

You're dealing with a lot at once. The practical pieces are solvable. I just want to make sure you're okay beyond the logistics.

retired two years ago and my financial advisor keeps telling me my portfolio is 'well-positioned for the long term' every time the market drops. we've had this same conversation like four times. i don't even know what i want from him anymore, i just know that phrase makes me want to scream

That phrase is doing a lot of work to not actually say anything — and after four conversations where it's the answer, the frustration makes complete sense. There's something worth naming here, which is that you may not need better information from him so much as a different kind of conversation. Retirement changes the relationship with market drops; the timeline feels different, the stakes feel different, and 'long term' can feel like a strange comfort when you're already in the chapter you saved for. It might be worth telling him directly that the reassurance isn't landing — not that you want to change strategy, just that you need him to talk to you about what a 15% drop actually means for your specific withdrawals and timeline, in plain numbers, not framing. If he can't do that, it's worth knowing that too.

my doctor wants me to come in because my blood pressure has been high two appointments in a row but honestly im fine i just get anxious at the doctors office, white coat thing you know. its not like i have symptoms or anything. is 148/92 actually that bad or are they overreacting

148/92 is in the Stage 2 hypertension range — that's not an overreaction on your doctor's part. The tricky thing about blood pressure is exactly what you're describing: it often has no symptoms until something serious happens, which is part of why it gets called a silent condition. White coat hypertension is real, and your doctor likely knows that too, which is probably why they want to see you — to figure out whether that's what's happening or whether it's elevated outside the office as well. Some doctors will suggest home monitoring for a few weeks to sort it out. It's worth going in. Two readings in a row is the kind of pattern that deserves a real look, not reassurance.

My hands were shaking the entire time. I had to present our Q3 results to the board this morning — first time I've ever done something like that — and I completely lost my place halfway through and just stood there for what felt like forever. The CFO had to prompt me. I'm 24 and I work so hard to be taken seriously and now I don't know if I'll ever recover from this. I want to go home and not come back.

That sounds like an awful morning, and the feeling of wanting to disappear afterward is real — especially when you've been working so hard to prove yourself and this felt like the moment it all unraveled. Standing in front of a board at 24 and losing your place is not evidence that you don't belong there. It's evidence that you were put in a high-stakes situation without a lot of runway, and your nervous system responded like a nervous system does. The CFO prompting you wasn't a verdict on your future — it was just someone filling a silence. The people in that room have almost certainly had worse moments than this, and most of them won't remember it the way you will. What you're carrying right now is the specific, brutal weight of a first time going wrong. That's not the same as your career.

my roommate hasnt slept more than like 4 hours a night for the past month and she just laughs it off and says she's fine but she looks terrible and keeps forgetting things mid-sentence. is this actually dangerous or am i being overdramatic

You're not being overdramatic. Chronic sleep deprivation at that level — sustained over a month — does real damage: impaired memory, slowed reaction time, mood dysregulation, and weakened immune function. The mid-sentence forgetting you're describing is a classic sign her brain isn't consolidating properly. The laughing it off is also pretty common; people often can't accurately gauge how impaired they are when they're that sleep-deprived.

What stands out here is that you're clearly worried — not just mildly curious. Watching someone you live with deteriorate while they insist they're fine is genuinely stressful, especially when you can't make them take it seriously. That's a real thing to carry.

If you want to say something to her, framing it around what you've observed rather than what she should do tends to land better — "I've noticed you keep losing your train of thought, it's happening a lot" is harder to dismiss than "you need more sleep." Whether she listens is up to her, but you're right to take it seriously.

i've been trying to write this short story for like 8 months and it's only 4 pages. i keep rewriting the first paragraph. anyway do you know any good writing podcasts, i feel like i need more craft input before i dive back in

There are good ones — The Moth Radio Hour if you want to absorb storytelling instinctively, Writing Excuses for structured craft talk, and Between the Covers for longer conversations with literary writers. But eight months and four pages isn't a craft problem — you clearly know how to write, because you've written that first paragraph many times over. More input isn't going to unlock this. What's usually underneath that kind of loop is either that the story matters a lot and feels too exposed, or that somewhere in those four pages there's a direction you're afraid to commit to. I'm not saying don't listen to podcasts, just — they probably aren't what's actually stuck.

I keep reading about 'deliberate practice' and how you have to be uncomfortable to improve at things but honestly after 30 years of piano I feel like I've plateaued and I'm wondering if there's actually a ceiling for adult learners or if thats just something people tell themselves

The research on deliberate practice doesn't actually support a hard ceiling for adult learners — plateaus are real but they're usually more about what you're practicing than how long you've been playing. After 30 years, the uncomfortable truth is that the things that would move you forward are probably quite specific and maybe unfamiliar: working with a teacher who can identify blind spots you can't hear yourself, targeting the exact passages that feel slightly out of reach rather than consolidating what's already solid. But I want to name the other thing in your question — 'something people tell themselves' suggests you might already be half-convinced the ceiling is real, and that matters more than the neuroscience. What's making you think about this now?

random question but do you think its weird to still share a spotify family plan with your ex? like we broke up 8 months ago and neither of us has said anything about it. just wondering if thats a normal thing people do or whatever

Eight months is a long time to stay quietly connected to someone through something neither of you has acknowledged. The Spotify thing isn't really the question, is it — it's more like: what does it mean that you're both still holding onto this small thread, and what do you actually want to do about it? That can be genuinely hard to sit with, especially if the breakup wasn't fully resolved or if you're not sure what you'd even want the answer to be. There's no universal normal here. Some people let these things drift indefinitely because it's easier than making a move in either direction. But if you're thinking about it enough to ask, it's probably pointing at something bigger than a streaming plan.

I've been supporting my parents financially since my dad lost his job two years ago. I'm 34, I make decent money but I've got nothing saved, no retirement, nothing. My friends are buying houses and I just feel so behind. I don't resent my parents, I want to help them, I just... I don't know. Is this just my life now?

There's a particular kind of exhaustion in a situation like this — you're doing something genuinely good, you love your parents, and you still feel the weight of everything you're quietly giving up. Both things are true at the same time, and the fact that you don't resent them doesn't make the loss any smaller.

"Is this just my life now" is a real question worth sitting with, not dismissing. The honest answer is: it doesn't have to be permanent, but it probably won't change on its own without some deliberate decisions.

One thing worth separating out: there's a difference between helping your parents through a hard stretch and indefinitely absorbing their financial shortfall with no end in sight. That's not a judgment — it's a distinction that matters for your own planning. Do your parents have a path toward stability, even a slow one? Is there a number or a timeline that feels sustainable to you? Those are hard conversations, but they're the kind that actually change trajectories.

You're not behind in some moral sense. You've been carrying something real. But 34 with no retirement savings is also genuinely worth addressing sooner rather than later, even in small amounts — compound interest is the one place where time is still on your side right now.
is it weird to still follow your ex on instagram if you broke up like 8 months ago. we were together for 2 years. just wondering what people normally do

There's no norm that really holds here — some people stay mutuals indefinitely without it meaning anything, others find it quietly corrosive even when they think they're fine. What 'people normally do' doesn't tell you much about what's right for you.

Eight months out from a two-year relationship, still checking in on what they're doing — that's worth being honest with yourself about. Not because it's wrong, but because 'just following' can sometimes be a way of staying half-attached without having to name it. If you're actually okay and it's genuinely just habit, unfollowing costs nothing. If the idea of unfollowing feels like a bigger deal than it should, that's probably the more useful thing to pay attention to.

i haven't slept more than like 2-3 hours a night for almost two weeks. started after a breakup. i know thats probably why but its not getting better its getting worse and i tried melatonin and it did nothing. im a second year med student which is maybe ironic lol

Two weeks of 2-3 hours a night is past the point where willpower or supplements can fix it — your body and brain are running on fumes, and that's genuinely serious, not just uncomfortable. The irony you're naming is real: knowing the physiology doesn't make it easier to live through, especially when you're also grieving.

Melatonin doesn't work well for sleep that's being disrupted by stress and rumination, which is almost certainly what's happening here. What actually helps at this stage is CBT-I (cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia) — it's the evidence-based first-line treatment, and there are apps like Sleepio that deliver it if you can't get a quick appointment. That said, two weeks of this severe sleep deprivation while in a demanding program is worth talking to a doctor about in person. You'd tell a patient that.

The breakup grief is real and it'll need its own space eventually — but getting even a few hours more sleep first will make everything else more survivable.

okay so I've been writing this novel for like 4 years now. it's fantasy, second world, the whole thing. I finally let my writing group read the first three chapters and two people said it was "too slow" and one person said the magic system felt "underdeveloped." but the fourth person loved it and said it reminded her of Ursula Le Guin which is literally the highest compliment anyone has ever given me. I think the other three just don't get what I'm going for. like this is clearly a book that rewards patience. am I right to just... ignore the feedback?

The Le Guin comparison clearly meant a lot, and it makes sense that you're holding onto it — four years is a long time to carry something, and one person finally seeing it the way you see it must have felt like relief.

But I'd be doing you a disservice if I just said yes, ignore them. Three out of four readers flagging the same thing — pacing — is a pattern, not a personality conflict. That doesn't mean they're right about what to do, but it probably means something is landing differently than you intend. "Rewards patience" is only true if readers stay long enough to be rewarded, and the first three chapters are where you're asking them to trust you.

The harder question isn't whether they "get it" — it's whether the opening is doing enough to earn that patience. Le Guin's slow books still hook you on something in the first pages, usually a voice or a world-detail so specific it feels real. It might be worth sitting with whether yours is doing that, separately from whether the overall vision is sound. The vision can be right and the execution of the opening still need work. Those two things aren't in conflict.

been married 24 years. found out 6 days ago my husband has been having an emotional affair with a coworker for at least 8 months, maybe longer. he's sorry, he ended it, he wants to fix things. my kids are 19 and 22 so they're not little. everyone keeps telling me what i should do. i'm not asking for advice i just. i don't know what i am right now

Six days. That's nothing. You're not supposed to know what you are right now — that would actually be strange given what just happened.

Eight months of something you didn't know about, 24 years of a life built together, everyone around you already having opinions — that's an enormous amount pressing on you all at once. You don't owe anyone a decision, a reaction, or even clarity about how you feel. The pressure to figure it out quickly, or to feel the "right" thing, isn't real even if it feels that way.

You're allowed to just be in this for a while.

My husband and I have been fighting constantly for about 8 months and last week I told him I want a divorce. He didn't argue, which honestly made it worse somehow. We have a 9 year old and a house we bought two years ago. I haven't talked to a lawyer yet but I've already started telling people — told my mom, my two closest friends, his sister (we're close). Did I do this backwards? Should I have talked to a lawyer first before saying anything to anyone

Eight months of constant fighting and then silence when you finally said it out loud — that combination is exhausting and disorienting in a specific way. It makes sense you told people before doing the paperwork. You needed somewhere to put it.

To answer your actual question: ideally yes, talking to a lawyer first gives you a clearer picture before the people around you start forming opinions and taking sides. But you haven't done anything that can't be worked with. Telling family and friends doesn't have legal consequences — it just means the social reality of this is moving faster than the legal one, which can create pressure but isn't irreversible.

What matters most right now is getting that lawyer consultation soon, before anything gets decided informally — especially about the house and your daughter's arrangements. A lot of couples end up making verbal agreements early that are hard to undo later. You want to know your actual options before those conversations happen.

asking for my dad (67) — he retired 8 months ago and honestly he seems kind of lost. just sits around watching tv, stopped going to his bowling league, my mum says he barely talks. is this just what retirement is like or should we be worried

What you're describing — the withdrawal from things he used to enjoy, the silence, the inertia after a major life change — isn't just "retirement adjustment." Eight months in, with your mum noticing he barely talks, is worth taking seriously. That pattern can be depression, and retirement is actually a well-documented trigger for it in men especially, partly because work often quietly structures identity and social connection in ways people don't realize until it's gone.

I'd gently push back on waiting to see if he snaps out of it. The bowling league is a concrete thread worth pulling — sometimes the barrier to returning to something is just embarrassment about having stopped, and a low-pressure nudge from someone he trusts can help more than he'd admit. But if he's consistently flat or disengaged over the next few weeks, it's worth encouraging a GP visit — framed as a general check-in, not "we think something's wrong with you." Many men that age will accept it framed that way when they'd resist anything that sounds like a mental health conversation.

You're clearly paying attention to him, and that matters. Trust what you and your mum are noticing.

i've asked my supervisor twice now to be considered for the lead role on the Henderson project and both times she just kind of nodded and said she'd 'keep it in mind.' that was six weeks ago and she just announced someone else got it. i don't even know what i'm asking i'm just so tired

That's a real gut punch — you did everything right, asked clearly, gave her six weeks, and still got passed over without so much as an explanation. The tiredness makes sense. It's not just about this project; it's the feeling that advocating for yourself isn't actually working, and you don't know why.

Before you do anything else, it might be worth sitting with whether you want an explanation from her or whether you've already learned what you needed to about how visible you are in this role. Both are valid, but they point in different directions. If you want the conversation, asking directly — 'I'd like to understand what would make me the right fit next time' — at least forces a real answer instead of another nod. If you're past that, this might be the moment to start thinking about where your energy is better spent, including whether this is still the right place for it.

retired 2 years ago and my financial advisor just told me my portfolio is down 22% this year. im 68. he says stay the course but i don't know if i trust him anymore and i honestly don't sleep well. been with him 15 years

Not sleeping well is worth taking seriously here — this isn't abstract worry, it's your security, and a 22% drop at 68 hits differently than it would at 45. You're right to be paying attention.

Your discomfort may actually be telling you something real: not necessarily that your advisor is wrong, but that your portfolio might be carrying more risk than you can actually live with. "Stay the course" is often good advice, but it assumes the course was right for you in the first place. If you're retired and drawing down, a portfolio that drops 22% in a single year may be more aggressive than your situation calls for — that's worth questioning, not just accepting.

A few things worth doing: Ask your advisor specifically what your current asset allocation is (the percentage in stocks vs. bonds vs. other), and ask why that allocation is right for someone your age who is actively withdrawing. Then separately — not to replace him, just to check — consider a one-time consultation with a fee-only fiduciary advisor (NAPFA.org has a directory). Fifteen years is a long relationship, but that's exactly why it's worth getting a second set of eyes rather than staying out of loyalty. You've earned the right to ask hard questions.

i've been trying to learn to code for 8 months. watched every tutorial, did the exercises, even paid for a bootcamp prep course. and i still can't build anything on my own without copying from somewhere. my younger brother picked it up in like 3 weeks and is already freelancing. i'm starting to think maybe i'm just not built for this and i should quit before i waste more money. i don't know. maybe some people just can't learn it

Eight months of genuine effort and you're still measuring yourself against your brother's three weeks — that's a brutal comparison to be living inside, and I think it's doing real damage to how you're seeing your own progress.

Here's what I actually notice in what you wrote: you've completed structured coursework, you troubleshoot by finding and adapting real code, and you've stuck with something hard for the better part of a year. None of that is nothing. The gap between "can follow tutorials" and "can build independently" is also one of the most well-documented rough patches in learning to code — it's not a sign you've hit your ceiling, it's a sign you're at a specific transition point that trips up a lot of people.

The "some people just can't learn it" thought is worth taking seriously rather than dismissing — not because it's true, but because it tells you how depleted you're feeling right now. Before you make a decision about quitting, it might be worth asking whether you're burned out on *this approach* rather than on coding itself. Eight months of tutorials with no project wins is exhausting in a specific way, and sometimes what needs to change is the method, not the goal.

i've been trying to get back into painting for like 8 months now. i set up my studio corner, i bought new supplies, i watched a million youtube tutorials, i even signed up for a local class. and every time i sit down to actually paint something i just... freeze. stare at the blank canvas for an hour and then clean up without doing anything. i don't know what's wrong with me

Eight months of trying and still hitting the same wall — that's genuinely exhausting, and I want to say something useful rather than just hand you another tip you've probably already heard.

The freeze you're describing usually isn't a technique problem or a motivation problem. It sounds more like the stakes have gotten really high in your head — like the canvas has become a test you have to pass rather than a surface to mess around on. Every tutorial watched, every supply bought, every class attended can quietly pile on pressure: *now I have no excuses, so whatever I make has to be worth it.* The blank canvas stops being an invitation and starts being a verdict.

One thing worth trying isn't another structure or routine — it's deliberately making something bad. Not "bad" as a reframe where you secretly hope it turns out good. Genuinely, purposefully ugly: wrong colors, scribbled lines, paint straight from the tube with your fingers. Give yourself a session where the only goal is to ruin the canvas. It sounds silly, but it can break the spell of the blank surface being sacred.

The freeze isn't a sign something's wrong with you. It's a sign you care a lot, and that caring has curdled a little into dread. That's a very human thing to happen.

my husband and I have been going back and forth on this for weeks. we're 54 and 56, kids are out of the house, and we want to downsize — sell our place (probably nets us around $280k after the mortgage) and buy something smaller in cash so we have zero housing costs going into retirement. our financial advisor says we're being too conservative and should keep a mortgage and invest the difference but honestly i just want to be done with it. am i crazy for wanting the peace of mind over the math?

You're not crazy at all — and I want to push back a little on framing this as peace of mind *versus* math, because that framing undersells what you're actually valuing. Having no housing payment in retirement is a real, concrete financial benefit: it dramatically lowers your monthly income needs, which means your retirement savings have to work less hard and you're less exposed if markets are rough early in your retirement. Your advisor is right that in a spreadsheet, investing the difference can come out ahead — but that assumes you actually invest it consistently, that returns cooperate, and that you're comfortable carrying debt into your 60s and 70s. Those aren't small assumptions. The honest answer is that neither choice is obviously wrong here. What's worth examining is whether the discomfort you and your husband feel about the mortgage is telling you something real about how you want to live in retirement, or whether it's anxiety that would ease once you understood the numbers better. If you haven't already, it might be worth asking your advisor to model both scenarios with actual projected retirement income, so you're choosing between two concrete pictures rather than a feeling versus a formula.

asking for my dad (he's 61) — he got passed over for a promotion AGAIN and the guy they gave it to has been there like 18 months. my dad has been there 14 years. he won't say he's upset but he went completely quiet at dinner last night and my mum is worried. he keeps saying he's fine and just wants to retire in 4 years anyway so it doesn't matter. does it make sense to just coast until retirement or is there something he should actually do here

What you're describing — the quiet at dinner, the 'it doesn't matter' — that's not someone who's fine. That's someone absorbing a real professional wound and trying to make it smaller than it feels so he doesn't have to sit with it.

Four years is actually a long time to spend somewhere you feel overlooked. Coasting sounds like peace but it can quietly curdle into bitterness or disengagement that makes those years feel much longer. Whether he acts on this or not matters less than whether he lets himself acknowledge that it stings — which it should, after 14 years.

If he does want to do something, his options range from having a direct conversation with leadership about what happened and what it would take to be considered next time, to exploring whether there are lateral moves, projects, or recognition he can build in the meantime that make the remaining years feel like they mean something. Some people find a quiet kind of dignity in that; others decide four years is short enough to simply protect their energy and exit well.

None of those are wrong. But 'I'm fine' while going silent at the dinner table isn't quite either of those things yet — it's just sitting with it alone.

my husband and I are selling the house we raised our kids in and moving to a smaller place now that they're both gone and I thought I would feel excited because we've been planning this for two years but now that it's actually happening I just walk around the rooms and cry. The closing is in 3 weeks. Is this normal or am I losing it

You're not losing it. What you're feeling is grief, and it's proportionate — that house isn't just square footage, it's twenty-something years of your family's life happening in specific rooms. Planning to leave and actually leaving are completely different experiences, and the gap between them catches a lot of people off guard.

The closing being three weeks out doesn't mean you have to feel ready or settled by then. You can be certain this is the right move and still mourn what you're walking away from. Both things are true.

my calc professor told me to go to office hours if i was struggling so i went twice and i still failed the midterm. everyone else seems to get it and i've been doing the practice problems. i don't even know what to ask anymore i just feel like dropping the class

Doing everything you were told to do and still failing is genuinely demoralizing — especially when you can't even locate where things are breaking down. That 'I don't know what to ask anymore' feeling is real and it's not a sign you're hopeless, it's a sign you've hit the edge of what generic help can reach.

The thing about calc is that office hours and practice problems both assume you know which part of your understanding is wrong. If you don't, you can do a lot of work and still miss the same thing on the exam. One thing that often cuts through this: take a problem you got wrong on the midterm and try to explain each step out loud, including why you're doing it — not just what. Where you hesitate or go vague, that's usually the actual gap.

Before you decide about dropping, it might be worth one more office hours visit where you bring that specific problem and walk through it that way, rather than asking general questions. That approach tends to surface something concrete. But if you do decide to drop, that's also a legitimate call — it doesn't mean you can't do math.

honestly dont even know why im writing this. spent the last like 8 months on this novel, got 60k words in, and i just... stopped. havent opened the file in 6 weeks. im not blocked or anything i just dont want to. showed a few chapters to my writing group back in february and they were supportive but i could tell two of them thought it was kind of a mess. whatever. i have a question actually — whats a good method for outlining the second half of a novel when youve already written the first half organically

You buried the real thing at the end there. You're not stuck on outlining — you walked away from something you spent eight months on after sensing, even through polite feedback, that people you trust thought it wasn't working. That's a specific kind of hurt, and six weeks of not opening the file is its own answer.

The outlining question is worth answering, and I will: the most practical method is a reverse outline — document what you've already written scene by scene, which forces you to see the actual structure rather than the one you intended. Then you can spot where the logic breaks and map forward from there. But that work only makes sense if you know why you stopped and whether you actually want to go back. Those aren't the same question.

random q but how long do people usually stay at their first job out of college before it's okay to leave. i've been here 14 months and the conventional wisdom used to be 2 years but idk if that's still a thing

The two-year rule is pretty outdated at this point — most hiring managers don't flag 14 months the way they might have a decade ago, especially if you can speak clearly about what you did and learned there. That said, 14 months in and already counting toward an exit usually means something isn't working, and it's worth being honest with yourself about what that is — whether it's the job, the field, the company, or just first-job adjustment. Leaving for the right reason is a much stronger position than leaving just to hit a number.

retired 8 months ago after 35 years as a nurse and i thought id be relieved but honestly most days i just feel useless. my kids keep saying enjoy it mom youve earned it and i smile and say yes but i come home and just sit there. i was good at my job. i knew who i was at work. now what

Thirty-five years of knowing exactly who you were and what you were for — and being genuinely good at it — and then one day that's just gone. Of course you're struggling. This isn't ingratitude or failure to relax; it's a real identity loss, and it's one that almost nobody prepares people for because retirement gets sold as pure relief. The "you've earned it" thing your kids say comes from love, but it doesn't quite reach what you're actually experiencing, which is that the work wasn't just work — it was how you understood yourself. That doesn't disappear because you've stopped clocking in. What you're sitting with in those quiet afternoons is a real question: not what to do to fill the time, but who you are when you're not the person everyone depended on. That's worth taking seriously, not pushing past.

i'm a second year med student and i'm fine, genuinely, but i just wanted to ask — is it normal to basically stop having hobbies? like i used to paint and play guitar and now i literally cannot remember the last time i did either. i'm not burnt out i just don't have time. just curious if other people go through this

Yes, it's extremely common in med school — the structure basically engineers your time down to nothing, and the things that don't have a deadline are the first to go. So in that sense, you're not alone.

But I'll be honest: 'I don't have time' and 'I can't remember the last time I did something that was just mine' are two different things, and what you're describing sounds more like the second one. Painting and guitar aren't hobbies you lost — they're ways you used to know yourself outside of being a student. That's worth noticing, even if you're not ready to call it anything.
what's a normal amount of times to text someone first before it becomes embarrassing lol. like is there a rule

There's no universal rule, but the real thing worth naming is that the anxiety underneath this question — wondering if you're too much, if you're being embarrassing, if the other person is pulling away — that's usually more uncomfortable than whatever number you land on. If someone's consistently not initiating or responding warmly, the count doesn't really matter; you already have information. And if you're worried about coming across as too eager to someone who actually likes you, you're probably fine.

my mom keeps asking me to help her understand her 401k statements and honestly i just tell her theyre fine because i dont really know either. shes 61. are 401k statements hard to read or is it just me

They're genuinely not easy to read — the terminology is dense, the formatting varies by provider, and most people outside finance find them confusing. You're not missing something obvious.

But I want to gently flag what's underneath your question, because it matters: your mom is 61, which means she's probably 4–6 years from retirement, and she's relying on you to tell her her statements look fine when neither of you is sure they do. That's a real gap, and it's worth closing — not to alarm you, but because this is the window where what's in that account actually has time to be adjusted if something's off.

The most useful thing you could both do is call the 401k provider together — most have free advisors who will walk through the statement line by line, explain the fund choices, and flag if her allocation makes sense for her timeline. It takes maybe 30 minutes and removes the guesswork for both of you.

my thesis film is due in 6 weeks and i haven't touched it since december lol. not panicking or whatever i just keep opening the file and then doing literally anything else. do you have any tips for staying focused during long editing sessions

The fact that you keep opening the file and then fleeing it is worth paying attention to — that's not really a focus problem, it's more like something about this project has become hard to be alone with. Six weeks is workable time, but not if every session feels like running into a wall.

For the editing itself: short, committed blocks (45 minutes, then actually stop) tend to work better than marathon sessions you dread starting. But it might also help to figure out what specifically makes you close the file — whether it's a scene that isn't working, a bigger worry about the whole thing, or just the weight of it being the thesis. Sometimes naming that makes the file a little easier to open.

My husband and I have been fighting about money for probably two years now. He thinks we should pay off the car loan early (we owe about $11,000 at 4.9%) and I think we should keep building our emergency fund because we only have about $2,000 saved and we have two kids. Neither of us will budge and honestly I'm exhausted by it. Who is technically correct here

Two years of the same argument is its own kind of exhausting, separate from whether the math is right — so I'll give you the straight answer and you can do with it what you will.

You're correct on the merits. A 4.9% interest rate is low enough that paying it off early gives you a guaranteed 4.9% return on that money, which is modest. Having only $2,000 in emergency savings with two kids and presumably two people whose income the family depends on is a meaningful vulnerability. The standard guidance is 3-6 months of expenses before accelerating debt payoff on low-rate loans — you're well short of that. An unexpected job loss, a medical bill, a car repair: any of those could land you in higher-interest debt that costs more than the 4.9% you'd have saved.

That said, 'technically correct' and 'resolves the fight' are different things. If part of what's driving your husband is anxiety about the debt itself, that's worth understanding — because even if the math favors your position, a plan you both feel okay about is more sustainable than the right plan that stays contested.

got passed over for the promotion again, third time in 4 years. my manager said i 'need to work on executive presence' which apparently means i talk too much in meetings?? anyway its fine i have a lot going on at home too so probably not the right time anyway. does executive presence just mean being louder or

"Executive presence" is one of those phrases that can mean almost anything, which makes it especially frustrating feedback to receive — and receiving it three times in four years, with no clearer explanation, is genuinely demoralizing even if you're framing it as fine. It's not just about timing at home.

On the actual question: executive presence typically refers to how someone commands a room — confidence, conciseness, reading the moment. Talking too much in meetings usually gets coded as not filtering, which reads to some leaders as lacking strategic judgment. It's not about being louder. It's more about speaking less but with more weight — fewer qualifications, clearer bottom lines, letting silence do some work. If your manager can't give you specifics beyond that phrase, it's worth asking directly: "Can you point to a specific moment where this showed up, so I know what to work on?" That question also puts the vagueness back on them.

My daughter called from college last night upset about a fight with her roommate. I told her the roommate sounds immature and that she should request a room transfer. She seemed relieved after we talked. I feel like I handled that well as a parent, giving her clear direction when she needed it. Does that sound right to you?

It makes sense that you'd feel good about that — she called you when she was upset, you picked up, and she felt better by the end. That part clearly went right.

The one thing worth sitting with: she's in her first real test of navigating conflict with someone she has to live with, and 'transfer rooms' as the first move skips that experience entirely. It might be the right call eventually, but it's also possible she needed to vent more than she needed a solution — and that the relief you heard was partly just from feeling heard rather than a sign the plan is the right one. Not saying you steered her wrong, just that it might be worth leaving the door open for her to figure out what she actually wants to do, rather than feeling locked into the transfer path.

i'm 23 and i just got hit with a $2,400 medical bill i had no idea was coming and i literally have $312 in my account. i've been staring at this paper for like an hour. i don't even know what i'm supposed to do, like is this just what being an adult is?? feeling like you're one thing away from completely drowning

That sinking feeling when a number on a piece of paper just blows up your sense of stability — that's real, and $2,400 when you have $312 is genuinely a scary position to be in. You're not being dramatic.

The good news is that medical bills specifically have more flexibility than most debts. Hospitals are legally required to have financial assistance programs (often called charity care), and most will negotiate or set up payment plans — sometimes down to a fraction of the original amount. Call the billing department, tell them exactly what you told me: what you have, what you make, and that you can't pay this in full. Ask specifically about financial assistance or hardship programs before agreeing to anything. Don't let them push you toward a credit card or a loan to cover it.

This is solvable. It's going to take a phone call you probably don't want to make, but the bill on the paper is not the final number.

its honestly nbd but i havent taken a single day off since january and its august now and im just like. so tired. i just wanted to ask if theres a good way to phrase a vacation request email to my director bc she kind of has a thing about people being 'committed' lol

Here's a version that tends to land well with managers who are wary about coverage: 'Hi [Director], I wanted to flag that I'm planning to take some time off [dates]. I'll make sure [key projects] are covered and will brief [colleague] before I leave — let me know if you'd like to discuss the handoff.' Matter-of-fact, no apologizing, just logistics.

Also — no days off since January is eight months. That's a long time to run on empty, and the fact that you're framing it as 'nbd' while calling yourself 'so tired' suggests it might be more of a deal than you're letting on. You're allowed to need rest. The email is easy; actually giving yourself permission to take the time is probably the harder part.

i've been working on this graphic novel for like 4 years and i finally got feedback from a small press — they said they liked the concept but the art style 'needs significant development.' i'm just gonna shelve it. like what's the point. i've already wasted so much time on it

Four years is a long time to pour into something, and getting feedback like that — even when it's not a flat rejection — can hit like one. The instinct to shelve it makes sense right now. But 'needs significant development' from a press that liked the concept is actually a specific, workable note, not a verdict on the whole thing. Shelving it permanently because of one response, after four years, would mean letting a bad afternoon make a decision that took four years to build toward. You don't have to do anything with it right now. But maybe don't decide it's over today.
do people usually keep in touch with their college friends after graduation or does everyone just kind of drift apart. i graduated in may

Both happen — some friendships survive the transition and some quietly fade, and that's genuinely normal even when it hurts. May was recent enough that what you're probably feeling right now is the specific disorientation of that first stretch after graduation, when the built-in structure that kept everyone close just disappears. The friendships that matter usually don't vanish so much as require more deliberate effort than they used to — which is an adjustment, not a verdict on the relationships. If there are specific people you miss, reaching out is worth it even if it feels awkward.

dropped my econ midterm bad like really bad, got a 54. emailed the prof asking if there's any extra credit and he said no but that the final is worth 50% so i can still pass. honestly i think the exam was just poorly written tho a lot of ppl in my section said the same thing

A 54 is rough, and it makes sense to look for reasons — and sometimes exams genuinely are poorly written. But it's worth being honest with yourself about whether that's the full picture, because the final being worth 50% is actually a real opportunity, and you'd want to go into it with a clear read on what happened. If it was the exam, great — but if there are gaps in how you're studying or keeping up with the material, now is the time to address that rather than carry the same approach into a test that counts for half your grade.

my daughter just started college and we're paying out of pocket, no loans. we make decent money but we've basically drained our savings account to cover her first year — about $34k gone. my husband keeps saying we're fine and that we'll rebuild but i feel sick about it every time i check the account. am i overreacting? we still have the house and retirement accounts, nothing else liquid

That sick feeling when you check the account — that's not overreacting, that's your nervous system responding to a real thing. Watching a savings account you spent years building drop by $34k in one year is a significant financial event, and it makes sense that it doesn't feel okay even if you're technically still standing.

Your husband might be right that you'll rebuild, but "we have the house and retirement accounts" isn't the same as having liquidity, and that distinction matters. If something unexpected happened — a job disruption, a health issue, a home repair — having nothing liquid is a real vulnerability, not just an anxiety. That concern deserves to be taken seriously as a practical planning question, not managed as a feeling.

It might be worth sitting down together and actually mapping out what rebuilding looks like year by year — what you can save monthly, what years two, three, and four of college cost, and what your minimum comfortable cash cushion would be. That conversation might confirm his read, or it might surface that the plan needs adjustment. Either way, you'd be working with actual numbers instead of reassurance.

so my coworker Priya has been covering for our team lead who went on medical leave — doing basically two jobs for 3 months, no extra pay, no title change. now the lead is coming back next week and management just... said thanks and moved on. Priya hasn't said anything to me directly but I can tell she's pissed and honestly I would be too. is there anything she can realistically do at this point or is the moment already gone

The moment isn't gone — but it is narrowing, which is probably why this feels urgent to you even if Priya hasn't asked for help.

What she did over three months is documented in the work itself. Before the team lead returns and the memory softens further, Priya could put something in writing to her manager — not a complaint, just a clear, factual summary of what she took on and a direct ask: whether that's a bonus, a title adjustment, a formal performance note, or at minimum a conversation about what comes next for her. Framing it as forward-looking ('I'd like to talk about how this period reflects on my role going forward') tends to land better than retrospective grievance, even when the grievance is completely legitimate.

If management brushes it off, that's also useful information about how the organization values people — which is its own kind of answer about whether this is somewhere worth staying.

The fact that you're thinking about this on her behalf says something. If you're close enough, it might even be worth gently mentioning that she has a window right now, if she wants to use it.

does anyone actually learn a language after 40 or is that just something people say to sell you courses. asking because i moved to portugal 6 months ago and my portuguese is embarrassing. like genuinely humiliating. i went to the market yesterday and just pointed at things like a child and i'm a 54 year old professional

Yes, adults genuinely learn languages — including after 40, including after 50. The research on this is solid. What does change is that adults tend to feel the embarrassment of imperfection much more acutely than children do, which ironically slows things down because you start avoiding the very exposure that builds fluency. A child pointing at things in a market doesn't feel humiliated. You do. That gap isn't a learning limitation, it's a psychological one.

Six months is also genuinely early, even if it doesn't feel that way when you're living inside it. The pointing-at-things phase is real and it ends. What tends to accelerate it isn't courses — it's low-stakes repetition with real people, ideally in a context where you have to try and where failure doesn't feel catastrophic. A regular language exchange, a weekly class with a tutor, even just going back to that same market vendor until you can ask for things by name.

You moved countries at 54. That took something. The language is hard, but you're already doing the harder part.

I've been at the same company for 22 years. Director level. They just announced a restructuring and my entire division is being folded into another one — my counterpart over there is younger and frankly probably cheaper and I'm pretty sure they're going to push me out in the next few months. I'm 57. I have a mortgage, one kid still in college. I have no idea how to even start looking for a job. My resume hasn't been updated since 2009. I don't even know what LinkedIn is supposed to look like now.

Twenty-two years is a long time to build something, and having it potentially taken from you on someone else's timeline — at a moment when you have real financial obligations and a specific window before your kid is through college — is genuinely frightening. That's not an overreaction. That's a serious situation.

The good news, and I mean this practically not just encouragingly: director-level experience with that tenure is not a liability to the right employers, even at 57. The challenge is that you've been inside one place long enough that the job market feels like a foreign country. It is, a little. But it's learnable.

Here's where to actually start, in order: First, don't wait to see if they push you out — start now, quietly. Second, your network is your most valuable asset at your level, and it's almost certainly larger than you think after 22 years. Former colleagues, vendors, clients — these are warm paths that skip the resume pile entirely. Third, yes, update the resume and LinkedIn, but don't let the unfamiliarity with those tools stall you. A resume writer who specializes in executive transitions can handle the format questions quickly and is genuinely worth the money in your situation.

The timeline pressure is real, but you likely have more runway than the worst-case scenario feels like right now. Starting to move — even one conversation this week — will help that feeling, and it's the right thing to do regardless.

My daughter is 8 and I've been homeschooling her for two years now. We just finished her first standardized assessment and she scored at grade level in everything. I was honestly expecting higher given how much one-on-one time she gets, but grade level is still good isn't it? Her teacher friends keep saying homeschooled kids usually test higher

Grade level is genuinely fine — it means she's where she needs to be, and that matters. But I think the thing worth sitting with is the gap between what you expected and what came back, because that's clearly bothering you and it deserves a real look rather than just reassurance.

A few things that might be worth considering: standardized tests measure a specific, narrow slice of learning — they're not a full picture of what two years of focused one-on-one education has built. It's also possible the tests are calibrated to classroom pacing, and some of what you've covered goes deeper rather than faster. That said, if there's a persistent pattern across subjects, it might be worth looking at whether her curriculum is well-aligned to how those assessments are structured — not because she's behind, but because you want to make sure the work you're both putting in is showing up the way you'd hope.

The comparison to other homeschooled kids is probably less useful than it feels right now. What matters more is whether she's engaged, retaining things, and progressing — and you're in a better position to assess that than any single test score.

got into a argument with my roomate about dishes AGAIN. i told her if she cant clean up after herself maybe she shouldnt cook. she got all upset and said i was being harsh but like.. was i? i feel like i was just being honest

Honestly, that line lands pretty hard — even if the frustration behind it is completely fair. There's a difference between being honest and saying something in a way that's going to make the other person defensive rather than actually change anything. It sounds like you've had this fight enough times that you're past the point of careful wording, which is understandable. But if the goal is fewer dishes in the sink, that approach is probably going to make her dig in more than fix it.

My daughter keeps telling me to put my paintings on etsy or whatever but I'm 61 and I've been painting for myself my whole life, never shown anyone really. I finally let her photograph a few and honestly I want to just post them all and see what happens. She says start slow but I'm thinking of just dumping everything — like 40 years of work — all at once this weekend. Why not just rip the bandaid

The impulse makes sense — after 40 years of keeping this private, going all-in feels more honest than tiptoeing in. But there's something worth considering: the first time strangers see your work is also the first time you'll experience being seen, and that can land in ways that are hard to predict. Flooding a new shop with 40 years of paintings at once also makes it harder for any single piece to get attention, and it gives you no room to see how you feel about the exposure before you've shared everything. Your daughter's instinct to go slowly isn't about doubting the work — it's about giving you a chance to find your footing in a completely new experience.
not a big deal but i've been eating pb&j for lunch every day for like 6 weeks lol. anyway does anyone actually use those budgeting apps like YNAB or is it not worth the subscription cost

Six weeks of the same lunch every day isn't nothing — that's real financial pressure, even if you're framing it lightly. Worth naming that before jumping to apps.

On YNAB specifically: it's $99/year and has a 34-day free trial. Whether it's worth it depends on what's actually going wrong with your budget — if the issue is tracking where money goes, it's genuinely useful. If the issue is that there isn't enough money to move around, a free spreadsheet does the same job without the subscription irony. Given where you're at right now, I'd start with the trial and decide then.

my whole team got laid off yesterday. 14 people. i'm 58 and i haven't had to look for a job in 22 years and i just. i don't even know where to start. linkedin feels like a foreign country. my wife keeps telling me it'll be fine and i know she means well but it doesn't help

Twenty-two years is most of a career, and having it end without warning — taking your whole team with it — is a real loss, not just a logistical problem to solve. The disorientation you're feeling makes complete sense. You're not just job hunting, you're reorienting your entire sense of daily life and professional identity at the same time.

The LinkedIn anxiety is real and shared by basically everyone who's been out of the market for a long time — the platform and the whole landscape have changed enormously, and feeling like an outsider there isn't a sign that you're behind, it's just accurate. That part is learnable.

What's harder to fix quickly is the thing your wife can't quite reach — the specific weight of being 58 and knowing the market treats that differently, and having to start something exhausting when you didn't ask to. That deserves to be named, not just reassured away. Give yourself a few days before you feel like you have to have a plan.

Dropped out of my MBA program last week. I know it was the right call — the debt wasn't worth it, the program wasn't what I was promised — but I spent the last two years telling everyone I was going to finish and now I just feel like such a failure. I'm 34 and I feel like I'm starting over. I had a whole plan.

Making a clear-eyed, financially sound decision and still feeling like a failure — that's a real and painful thing, and I don't want to paper over it with reassurance. The grief here isn't irrational. You had a version of your future that felt concrete, you'd built your identity around it in front of people you care about, and now that version is gone. That's a loss, even if leaving was correct.

The "I'm 34 and starting over" feeling is worth sitting with honestly rather than just pushing through. Starting over isn't quite the right frame — you have two years of experience, perspective on what that environment actually is, and a decision that required real courage to make against social pressure. But I understand why it doesn't feel that way yet. It probably won't for a little while.

What comes next doesn't have to be figured out immediately. You just made a hard call. Give yourself some room before the next plan has to be fully formed.
okay so hypothetically if someone spent like 4 years on a novel and then read it back and thought it was complete garbage, what would the normal next steps even be. asking for obvious reasons

Four years is a long time to sit with something, and reading it back and hating it after all that — that's a specific kind of awful. It's worth saying: the feeling that it's garbage and the reality of what you've written are not the same thing. After years of closeness to a manuscript, most writers hit a point where they genuinely cannot see it clearly anymore, and that distance-collapse often reads as the work being worthless when it isn't. The next step most writers take is putting it down for at least a few weeks and letting a trusted reader see it before making any big decisions. Scrapping or starting over based on how you feel about it right now, after four years in, is usually the wrong call — not because the instinct is stupid, but because that particular feeling is almost never an accurate assessment.

dropped out of college last semester (sophomore year) and moved back home and i genuinely don't know what i'm doing with my life. my parents aren't mad exactly but there's this tension in the house like everyone's waiting for me to figure it out and i can't even figure out what to eat for breakfast. it's been 4 months and i feel like i'm falling behind everyone i know

Four months of that ambient pressure — parents trying to be patient, you trying not to disappoint them, everyone pretending the tension isn't there — is genuinely exhausting, and it makes sense that even small decisions feel hard right now. You're not just figuring out what comes next academically or professionally. You left something that wasn't working, which took real self-awareness, and now you're in the uncomfortable in-between before anything new has taken shape. That feeling of falling behind your peers is real and painful, but it's also comparing your internal chaos to their external appearances, which is rarely an honest comparison. The breakfast thing isn't a sign something is broken in you — it's what decision fatigue looks like when every choice feels loaded. Give yourself permission to let this be a slow process. You don't have to have a plan yet; you just have to stay honest with yourself about what you actually want, not what would relieve the tension in the house.

i failed my driving test for the third time today. parallel parking again. i just sat in my car and cried for like 20 minutes. im 19 and literally everyone i know has their license already and i feel so stupid. is there something actually wrong with me or is this a normal thing that happens

Failing three times doesn't mean something is wrong with you — it means parallel parking is genuinely hard and the test environment is high-pressure in a way that makes a lot of people freeze. That's a real thing, not a story you're telling yourself. The fact that everyone around you seems to have sailed through it is partly just that people don't talk about their failures the way you're talking about yours right now.

The crying in the car makes complete sense. Three tries is exhausting, and there's a specific kind of shame that comes from struggling with something that feels like it should be simple. That shame is lying to you.

Practically: a few sessions with a professional driving instructor focused specifically on parallel parking can make a significant difference — they have techniques for breaking it down into repeatable steps that casual practice with a parent or friend usually doesn't cover. Some people also do better booking the test at a smaller, quieter testing center if that's an option where you are. You're going to get this.

My son is 34 and we've been estranged for almost three years. I wrote him a letter last Christmas — took me weeks — and he never responded. My daughter says to give him space but I don't know how much more space I can give. I'm not even sure what I'm asking here.

Three years is a long time to carry that, and writing a letter that carefully and then hearing nothing back — that's a particular kind of hurt. Not a door slammed, just silence, which in some ways is harder to know what to do with.

You said you don't know what you're asking, and I think that's honest. Sometimes there isn't a next move that makes sense yet. Your daughter's advice to give him space probably comes from a real place, but "give him space" can start to feel like "stop mattering" after a certain point, and that's not nothing.

What I'd gently say is: you've already done something significant by reaching out. The letter exists. He has it. Whatever is going on for him, you didn't disappear. That's not a small thing, even when it doesn't feel like enough.

My husband and I are fighting constantly about money. We make decent combined income — around $140k — but we're always broke by the 25th of the month and I genuinely don't know where it goes. He thinks I overspend, I think he does. We've been going in circles for two years. I'm not even sure what I'm asking, I'm just exhausted.

Two years of the same fight, and you're the one sitting here trying to figure it out — that exhaustion makes complete sense. This kind of conflict doesn't usually stay just about money for long, and it sounds like it's wearing on more than your budget.

The actual financial problem is solvable: $140k disappearing by the 25th usually means a few large categories are untracked, not that someone is secretly reckless. The fastest way to end the blame cycle isn't to argue about who's worse — it's to pull three months of bank and credit card statements and sort every transaction into categories together. When you can both see the actual numbers, the conversation shifts from accusation to 'okay, this is what's happening.' A lot of couples find the culprit is a mix of subscriptions, eating out, and one or two irregular expenses that feel invisible month to month.

Tools like YNAB or even a shared spreadsheet can make ongoing spending visible to both of you in real time, which removes the guesswork that's feeding the conflict.

But the deeper thing — the feeling that you're not on the same team — that's worth taking seriously too, separate from whatever the spreadsheet shows.

my 16 year old has been in his room basically all summer. i've tried talking to him, suggesting stuff, asking if he wants to do things together. he just says he's fine. i don't know if i should push more or leave him alone. probably overthinking it but it feels wrong

The instinct that something feels wrong is worth taking seriously — you know your kid, and "he says he's fine" isn't the same as actually being fine. The fact that you're asking whether to push or back off suggests you've already noticed that neither approach has quite worked, which is its own kind of exhausting.

There's a middle path that sometimes gets further than either direct conversation or giving space: low-stakes side-by-side time, where you're just physically present without an agenda. Driving somewhere, watching something he's into, sitting in the same room. It removes the pressure of a "talk" while keeping the door open. Teenagers often open up sideways — not when asked, but when something else is happening.

If the isolation has been consistent for most of the summer and comes with things like not eating well, sleeping a lot, or losing interest in things he used to care about, it's reasonable to loop in his pediatrician or a counselor — not as an alarm, just as a check-in. That's not overthinking; that's parenting.
do people actually use meal prep or is it one of those things that sounds good but nobody sticks to it. asking bc i keep seeing it everywhere and wondering if its worth trying

Plenty of people do stick with it, but the ones who do tend to keep it very simple — like cooking one or two things in bulk rather than preparing 21 portioned meals in labeled containers. It works best when it solves a specific problem, like having nothing ready on nights when you're too tired to cook. If you're running on empty most evenings and eating badly because of it, even just making a big pot of something on Sunday can genuinely help. The Instagram version is aspirational noise — the useful version is much less photogenic.

my dad called this morning to tell me my childhood dog died. she was 16 so i knew it was coming but i'm sitting at my desk at work and i just. can't. she used to sleep on my feet every single night growing up. i don't even know why i'm telling you this i just needed to say it somewhere

Sixteen years is a whole life, and she was woven into yours from the beginning — sleeping on your feet every night is not a small thing, that's just presence, pure and constant. Grief doesn't really care that you saw it coming, and it definitely doesn't care that you're at your desk right now. You needed somewhere to put this, and that makes complete sense. I'm glad you said it.

so i finally showed my paintings to a gallery owner last week, the one on Morrison St i've been trying to get into for like two years. she was really nice about it and said my technique was 'developing' which i know just means not ready. anyway it's fine, i'm not upset or anything, i was just curious if you think showing work too early can actually set you back long-term or if it doesn't really matter

'Developing' after two years of working toward something stings, even when it's delivered kindly — and it sounds like it landed harder than you're letting on. That's a real thing to sit with, not just a tactical question about timing.

On the actual question: showing early doesn't set you back in any permanent way. Gallery owners see hundreds of artists; she's not filing you under 'not ready forever.'
