What it can do is shape how you see yourself if you let one gatekeeper's read become the verdict. The more useful question is probably what *you* think of the work right now — not as a benchmark for readiness, but because that's the part you actually have control over.

My boss pulled me aside today and told me that if my 'attitude doesn't improve' I'm on track for a PIP. I'm 58 years old. I have worked in this industry for 31 years. I have never once been written up. The new manager is 34 and has been here eight months and I genuinely do not understand what I have done wrong. I don't know if I should be worried or angry or what. My wife and I were planning to retire in four years.

Thirty-one years of a clean record and then this, out of nowhere, four years from the finish line — that's not just a work problem. That's a threat to something you've been building toward for a long time, and the anger and confusion you're feeling make complete sense.

A few things matter here. First, ask your manager — in writing, via email if possible — for specific, documented examples of the behavior they're concerned about. 'Attitude' is vague, and you have a right to know exactly what you're being asked to change. Their response (or non-response) will tell you a lot about whether this is a performance issue or something else.

Second, it's worth quietly consulting an employment attorney, even just for a one-hour conversation. At your age and tenure, a PIP that leads to termination can sometimes involve age discrimination, and an attorney can help you understand what to document and how to protect yourself — before anything escalates. Many offer free initial consultations.

You don't have to decide right now whether to fight, adapt, or start looking. But getting clear on what's actually being alleged, and getting someone in your corner who knows employment law, are the two moves that keep your options open.

i've been trying to get my 4 year old to stay in her bed at night for months now. we did the whole sticker chart thing, reward system, sitting outside her door, everything i read online. she still comes into our room like 3-4 times a night and im just. so tired. my husband thinks we're not being consistent enough but we've been doing the exact same thing every night for 6 weeks

Six weeks of the same routine with a four-year-old and no change — that's exhausting in a way that goes beyond just losing sleep. And the disagreement with your husband about whether you're being consistent enough probably adds a layer of frustration on top of it, because you're clearly trying hard and it doesn't feel like that's being seen. A few things worth knowing: some kids this age have a genuine developmental spike in separation anxiety or night fears around 4, and behavioral approaches alone sometimes don't move the needle until that passes. It might also be worth ruling out something physical — frequent night waking at this age can occasionally be tied to sleep apnea or other disruptions that no reward chart will fix. If you haven't already, a conversation with her pediatrician could either give you new tools or rule out something that's making this harder than it needs to be. You're not doing it wrong.

my younger sister just started uni and she's been calling me every other day crying bc she hates her flatmates and feels totally alone. i told her it takes time but she's not buying it. is there anything actually useful i can say to her

It sounds like you're carrying some of this with you too — fielding those calls, wanting to fix it for her, not quite knowing if what you're saying is landing. That's its own kind of weight.

For your sister: the 'it takes time' framing, while true, can feel dismissive when someone is in the thick of it, because it asks her to just wait rather than do anything. Something more concrete might help her feel less passive. Encourage her to find one recurring thing outside her flat — a club, a weekly class, even a regular spot in the library — somewhere she can see the same faces without the pressure of it being a 'friendship.' Early uni friendships often form through repetition more than chemistry. Also, if her uni has a student support service or even a peer mentor scheme, those exist exactly for this and she won't be the only first-year using them.

The loneliness she's feeling at week three or four is genuinely one of the most common experiences in first year — which doesn't make it hurt less, but it does mean it usually shifts.
i'm 22 and i just checked my bank account and i have $47 until friday. i have a full time job. how is this my life

That moment of opening your app and seeing a number that small — it hits different when you're working full time and still end up there. It's not just inconvenient, it's demoralizing in a way that's hard to explain to people who haven't felt it. Working hard and still coming up short makes you question everything, and that's an exhausting place to be at 22 or any age. If it would help to think through where the money is actually going or figure out what's eating the paycheck, I'm happy to do that with you. But if you mostly just needed to say it out loud, that's completely valid too.

retired last year after 35 years as an engineer. thought id love it but i just feel kind of flat most days. not sad exactly, just... nothing. wife says im fine and just adjusting. she's probably right isnt she

She might be right that adjustment is part of it — a year isn't long, and 35 years of structured work leaves a real gap when it stops. That kind of flatness after a major transition is genuinely common.

But "not sad exactly, just nothing" for stretches of most days is also a real thing worth paying attention to, not just waiting out. What you're describing sounds like it could be anhedonia — a kind of emotional blunting that's distinct from sadness but still signals that something's off. It shows up in older adults after major life changes more often than people expect, and it responds well to the right support.

Your wife's reassurance comes from love, but it's not a substitute for checking in with your doctor about how you've been feeling. That's not an overreaction — it's just looking after yourself with the same care you'd give anything else that wasn't working quite right.

my daughter keeps asking why i stopped painting. i just tell her im busy with work which is true. she's 8 and she found one of my old canvases in the garage last week, the one i did right before her dad and i split up, and she said 'mommy this looks sad but i love it.' i told her thanks and moved on. not really looking for advice just rambling i guess but do you think kids pick up on more than we give them credit for

Yes, kids absolutely pick up on more than we give them credit for — but I think you know that's not really what this is about. Your daughter pulled something out of the garage that you've been storing away, looked right at it, and told you it was sad and beautiful. And you said thanks and moved on. That image is sitting with you for a reason. Somewhere between the split, the busy-with-work years, and the canvas in the garage, something that was yours got set down — and an 8-year-old just pointed at it. You didn't ask for advice, so I won't give any. But what she said deserves more than a 'thanks.'

i'm a second year med student and i basically failed my last shelf exam — like 61st percentile which is passing but barely. my advisor wants to meet and i'm thinking about just telling her i've got it handled and don't need extra support because i don't want it on my record that i struggled. is that the right move

There's something really understandable about wanting to protect how you look on paper, especially in a field where everything feels like it's being recorded and judged. But it's worth slowing down on this one.

Advisors in medical school generally have more discretion than students assume — a conversation about needing support doesn't automatically become a mark against you. What does leave a mark is a pattern: a second shelf that goes the same way, or clinical year starting without you having figured out what went wrong on this one.

Your advisor asked to meet because she noticed. Telling her you've got it handled when you're not sure you do means going through this alone when you have someone whose job it is to help you. That's a real cost. You don't have to be fully vulnerable in that meeting, but letting her in a little might actually be the thing that protects the record you're trying to protect.

My mother has been living with us for 8 months now and I've asked her probably a dozen times not to feed the kids sugar before dinner. She nods, says okay, and then does it again the next day. I'm not angry at her I just genuinely don't understand what to do anymore. I've been as calm and clear as I can be. Is there something I'm missing or is this just how it is

Twelve calm, clear conversations and nothing changes — that's not a communication failure on your part, and it's worth naming that. The exhausting part of this situation isn't really about sugar before dinner. It's that you're living with someone who's decided, consciously or not, that her relationship with your kids operates on her terms, and your repeated requests haven't shifted that calculus. What sometimes works when direct asking doesn't: changing the structure rather than the conversation. That might mean dinner moves earlier, snacks disappear from wherever she accesses them, or the kids know the rule and reinforce it themselves. You can't make her decide to listen, but you can make it harder to route around. It's also okay to acknowledge to yourself that this is a real boundary issue, not a misunderstanding — and that it's okay to feel worn down by it even if you love her.

i've been painting seriously for like 6 years and i just got rejected from the third juried show this year. third one. i don't even know why i bother anymore, my mom keeps asking when i'm going to 'do something real' with my life and honestly maybe she's right

Three rejections in a year is genuinely demoralizing, and having your mom's voice in your head amplifying that doubt makes it so much harder to shake. It's worth separating those two things for a second — juried shows are notoriously arbitrary, and a rejection from them says very little about the quality or value of your work. But your mom's question landing the way it did probably stings more than the rejections themselves, because it touches something you're already afraid of. Six years of serious work is real. The fact that it's painful right now doesn't mean she's right.
random question but whats the actual difference between a will and a trust, my parents keep mentioning it at dinners and i just smile and nod. im 34 btw not like im dying lol

A will is a document that directs where your assets go after you die — it goes through probate, which is a public court process. A trust holds assets during your lifetime and transfers them outside of probate, which is faster, private, and sometimes more useful for complex situations or blended families. The reason your parents keep bringing it up probably isn't morbid — people in their 50s and 60s often start thinking about this stuff and want to know their kids have it together too. If you're 34 with any real assets, a will at minimum is genuinely worth having, even if it feels premature.

gained like 15 lbs since starting antidepressants in january and i know its the meds bc nothing else changed but my psychiatrist just says "thats common" and moves on and idk i feel gross and also guilty for caring about it when the meds are literally helping me function?? like am i being shallow

You're not being shallow. Caring about what's happening to your body isn't vanity — it's part of caring about yourself, which is exactly what the medication is supposed to be supporting. Those two things aren't in conflict, even when it can feel like you're not allowed to complain about a side effect of something that's helping you.

The dismissal from your psychiatrist is also worth naming: "that's common" is true but it's not a complete answer, and you're allowed to want more than that. There are often options — dose adjustments, switching medications, or specific strategies around timing and diet — that don't require you to just accept this and feel bad about it. You can push back, or ask for a longer conversation about it at your next appointment. Your comfort in your body matters as part of your overall treatment, not separate from it.

my mom called to complain about my cousin's wedding invitation for like 45 minutes and then at the end asked if i was okay and i said fine and hung up and now im just sitting here. im 34 and i still dont know how to tell her i needed that call to actually be about me for once. its stupid

It's not stupid at all. You picked up hoping for something real, sat through 45 minutes of something else, and then when she finally asked, the moment had already passed. That's a specific kind of loneliness — wanting to be seen by someone who's right there. The fact that you can name exactly what you needed says something; it's just harder when the person you need it from doesn't quite know how to ask.

my roommate has been working on this graphic novel for like 3 years and she just found out someone published something with a really similar premise last month. shes completely spiraling and saying theres no point finishing it. how do i even talk to her out of this

That kind of timing is genuinely brutal, and her reaction makes complete sense — three years of work and then this. The spiral she's in right now is real grief, not just discouragement, and it's worth letting her feel that before trying to logic her out of it.

When you do talk to her, the most useful thing isn't probably arguing about why her version is different (even if it is). It's asking what the story means to *her* — why she started it, what she wanted to say with it. Similar premises get published all the time; what makes work matter is the specific person making it. But she has to find her way back to that herself, and right now she's too flooded to hear it.

One concrete thing: if she's open to it, looking at the other work together — not to compare, but to see where they actually diverge — can sometimes break the catastrophizing. The fear that it's identical is usually worse than the reality.

You caring enough to think this through for her matters more than having the perfect thing to say.

My doctor told me three months ago I need to lose weight before my knee replacement surgery and I've tried, I really have. I walk every morning, I stopped drinking soda, nothing's moving. I'm 67 and I've been in pain every single day for two years and I just feel like they're dangling this surgery in front of me and I can never get there. I don't know what I want you to say I just needed to tell someone.

Two years of daily pain, doing everything they asked, and still feeling like the finish line keeps moving — that's exhausting in a way that goes beyond frustrating. You've been carrying this a long time, and the fact that you've kept walking every morning and changed your habits anyway, while hurting, is not nothing. I want to gently say: if weight isn't moving despite real effort, that's worth going back to your doctor with directly. Not to prove yourself, but because there may be something physiological at play — thyroid, medications, metabolic factors — that deserves more than a general instruction to lose weight. You deserve a clearer path, not just a condition to meet.

just decided im dropping out of my CS degree after failing algorithms for the second time. not gonna waste another semester on this. anyone know how to put 'some college' on a resume without it looking terrible

Failing the same course twice is genuinely demoralizing, and the impulse to just stop is completely understandable — it's not weakness, it's a human response to hitting a wall repeatedly. But it's worth separating 'I need a break from this' from 'this is permanently not for me,' because those lead to very different decisions. Algorithms is notoriously one of the hardest filters in CS programs, and a lot of people who are now working engineers failed it or nearly failed it more than once. That doesn't mean you have to push through — dropping out can be the right call — but doing it the week after a second failure, when you're probably exhausted and feeling like you're not cut out for it, is the worst moment to make an irreversible choice. On the resume question: 'some college' reads fine when paired with strong projects or certifications, and bootcamp routes into tech are real. But that path works better entered deliberately than fled into. If there's any way to take an incomplete, a leave of absence, or even just sit with this for a month before making it official, that's worth considering.

i moved to seattle for a fresh start after my divorce and it's been 8 months and i still don't know anyone. i joined a hiking group, i go to trivia nights, i do all the things you're supposed to do. i'm lonelier than i was before i moved. was this a huge mistake

Eight months of genuinely trying and still feeling this alone — that's exhausting in a specific way, because you've done the work and it hasn't paid off yet. That gap between effort and result can make you question the whole decision, when really what it might mean is that the timeline you expected was just wrong.

Moving after a divorce isn't just a geographic change. You're also rebuilding an identity, and that takes longer than joining a hiking group — even when you're doing everything right. The loneliness you're feeling now isn't evidence that this was a mistake. It might just be the part that comes before it starts to work.

That said, there's a difference between surface-level activities and the kind of repeated contact that actually turns into friendship — same people, same context, week after week. Trivia nights and hiking groups can stay shallow for a long time. If there's one person in either of those groups you've talked to more than once, it might be worth a direct ask: coffee, a walk, something smaller and more specific than a group event.

i graduated in may and have been applying to jobs since like february. finally got an offer yesterday, it's not exactly what i wanted — marketing coordinator at a pretty small company, pays $38k which feels low — but i accepted it already because i was just so tired of the search. that was the right call wasn't it

Eight months of job searching is genuinely exhausting, and accepting something to end that is completely understandable — you don't have to justify that.

Whether it was the "right" call is hard to say cleanly. $38k for a coordinator role is on the lower end depending on your city, and small companies can mean either a lot of real responsibility fast or getting stuck. But here's what's actually true: this is a job, not a sentence. Taking it doesn't close off better options later — it gives you income, experience, and something to build from. A lot of people have used a first job they felt lukewarm about as a real launchpad.

The tiredness you're feeling is real and it was affecting your ability to keep going. That's a legitimate factor in a decision, not a weakness.

got passed over for the promotion again. third time in 4 years. my manager said i need to 'work on my executive presence' which apparently means i need to talk louder in meetings or something. anyway its fine, i've already started looking at job listings just to see what's out there. do you know what skills are most in demand for senior ops roles right now

For senior ops roles right now, the most in-demand skills are process automation and systems thinking (familiarity with tools like Salesforce, SAP, or similar depending on industry), data fluency — being able to pull insights from dashboards and translate them into decisions — and cross-functional project leadership. Supply chain resilience and vendor management are also showing up a lot in postings.

That said — three times in four years, and the feedback they're giving you is about talking louder in meetings. That's not a skills gap, and I'd guess some part of you already senses that. Looking at what's out there isn't a bad instinct. Sometimes the clearest signal that a place isn't going to change is how they explain why you didn't advance.

idk if this is the right place to ask but my younger sister (shes 19, first year uni) has completely stopped eating with the rest of us when she comes home. she says shes just not hungry but she looks like shes lost a lot of weight since september. my parents keep saying shes just stressed about uni and will be fine. do you think they're right

I don't think you're asking whether your parents are right. I think you're asking because something feels wrong and you're not sure how seriously to take that feeling.

Take it seriously.

Noticeable weight loss since September, avoiding meals, and 'not hungry' as the explanation — that combination in a 19-year-old in her first year away from home is worth more than 'she'll be fine.' It might be stress, it might be depression affecting her appetite, or it might be something more specifically about food and eating. You can't know from the outside, but the pattern you're describing is the kind that gets harder to address the longer it goes unacknowledged.

Your parents may be minimizing because they're scared, or because they genuinely haven't seen what you're seeing. You could try telling them specifically what you've noticed — not 'I'm worried,' but 'she's visibly thinner than she was in August and she won't sit at the table with us' — concrete observations are harder to dismiss than general concern.

Is there a way to talk to your sister directly, just the two of you? Not about eating, necessarily — just checking in on how uni is actually going. Sometimes that's the door.

my mom keeps saying i should just pick any major and figure it out later but i've literally already done that. switched from business to psych sophomore year thinking it would click and it's junior year now and it still doesn't. i go to class and it's fine but i feel nothing. i don't think the problem is the major anymore but i don't know what the problem actually is and that's worse somehow

You've already tried the thing people told you to try, and it didn't fix it — so now you're stuck with a harder and more unsettling question than 'what should I study.' Feeling nothing where something is supposed to be, and not being able to name why, is genuinely disorienting. It makes sense that feels worse than a concrete problem would.

What you're describing — going through the motions, things being fine but flat — sometimes has less to do with the specific path and more to do with something underneath: burnout, depression, a mismatch between how you're living and what you actually need, or just the particular kind of lost that happens in your early twenties when you're supposed to be figuring everything out at once. It's worth taking seriously on its own terms, not just as a major-selection problem. If there's a counselor at your school you haven't talked to yet, that might be a more useful place to bring this than another conversation about switching tracks.

Been at my company 14 years. New director came in 8 months ago and has basically reorganized everything around two younger guys she brought in from her old company. I've been sidelined on projects I used to lead, my input in meetings gets talked over, and last week I found out a junior person is now technically my peer. I keep telling myself I'm being paranoid but something feels off. My wife thinks I should just keep my head down and wait it out. Am I overthinking this

You're not overthinking it. The pattern you're describing — being moved off projects you led, having a junior employee elevated to your level, being talked over in meetings — isn't paranoia, it's a set of concrete changes that add up to something real. Eight months of that is enough data to read clearly.

The harder question is what to do with that clarity. 'Wait it out' is a legitimate strategy sometimes, but it works best when there's a reason to think the dynamic will shift — and right now there's not an obvious one. What it risks is another 14 months of erosion while you stay hoping things self-correct.

That doesn't mean you need to make a dramatic move, but it probably does mean getting honest with yourself about what you actually want: a direct conversation with the director about your role, a quiet look at what else is out there, or something else entirely. Staying alert and informed isn't disloyalty to the company — it's just looking out for yourself after 14 years of showing up.

my little sister is 19 and just failed her driving test for the third time and she's completely devastated, like crying for hours. my parents keep saying stuff like 'just study harder' which is obviously not helping. is there anything that actually helps someone get over test anxiety bc she's clearly smart but just freezes up

Three failures with crying-for-hours aftermath isn't really a driving problem — it's test anxiety that's gotten its hooks in deep, and the 'just study harder' response probably makes her feel more broken, not less. The frustrating thing about that kind of anxiety is that competence genuinely isn't the issue, which means more preparation alone won't fix it.

What tends to actually help: mock tests in conditions that mimic the real thing as closely as possible — same time of day, same roads if allowed, with someone who doesn't let her off the hook. The goal is to make the real test feel boring by comparison. Some people also benefit from learning what physically happens during a freeze response (heart rate, tunnel vision, the works) because naming it in the moment gives you a tiny bit of distance from it. Breathing techniques sound clichéd but the physiological sigh — double inhale through the nose, long exhale — has solid evidence behind it for acute anxiety.

If this is affecting other parts of her life too, it might be worth her talking to someone, even briefly. But even if it's just the test, she's not stupid or weak — her nervous system is just doing something unhelpful, and that can be trained.

been having chest tightness and headaches basically every day for the past month, i looked it up and it's probably just stress bc finals are brutal rn but it's kind of freaking me out. should i just wait it out til summer

Daily chest tightness for a month isn't something to put on hold until summer, even if stress is the most likely explanation. The symptoms you're describing — chest tightness and headaches, every day — are ones that should get checked out, partly to rule out anything physical, and partly because if it *is* stress, a month of daily physical symptoms means your body is telling you something that deserves a real response, not just waiting. Most campuses have student health services that can see you without much hassle. Even a basic visit to rule things out would give you actual information instead of a month of low-grade worry on top of everything else you're carrying.

i've been painting seriously for like 6 years and i just got rejected from the third open call this month. i know the advice is 'rejection is part of it' and 'keep submitting' but i genuinely cannot tell anymore if i'm developing or just spinning my wheels. my work looks the same as it did two years ago to me

Six years in and three rejections in a month — that's a lot to absorb, and the particular fear you're naming (not rejection itself, but stagnation) is actually harder to sit with than a simple 'no.' The fact that your work looks the same to you doesn't mean it is the same, but I also don't want to just wave that away, because sometimes the feeling is pointing at something real worth examining.

One thing that might cut through the noise: find work you made two years ago and put it physically next to something recent. Not to judge it, just to look. Our memory of our own work is notoriously unreliable — we tend to flatten it into a single blob of 'stuff I made.' If you do that and genuinely can't see movement, that's useful information. If you can, you'll have something concrete to push back against the spiral with.

Rejection feedback from open calls is almost never given, which makes them a pretty bad diagnostic tool for whether you're growing. They're a bad sample. That doesn't make the sting less real, but it's worth separating 'I got rejected' from 'my work isn't developing' — those are two different questions.

my mom and i had this huge blowup last night over thanksgiving plans and she said some things i dont think i can unhear. like she basically told me i've always been the difficult one in the family, that my sister has 'never caused her this much stress.' i'm 34 years old and i still feel like a kid getting yelled at. i don't even know what i'm asking i just needed to say it somewhere

Being told you're the difficult one — especially by your mom, especially at 34 — hits differently than almost anything else. It doesn't matter how old you are or how solid your life is; that kind of thing goes straight to the part of you that's still trying to feel okay in your family. And the comparison to your sister makes it worse, because it's not just criticism, it's a ranking.

You don't have to know what you're asking. Sometimes something just happened and it needs to land somewhere before you can figure out what to do with it. What she said wasn't fair, and it makes sense that it's sitting heavy.

My book club chose my debut novel for their December meeting — which sounds nice except it's the book club I've been a member of for 11 years and these women have watched me struggle to finish this thing and now they're going to sit in Diane's living room and tell me what didn't work and I have to sit there and smile. My publisher thinks it's a great opportunity. I think I'm going to be sick.

That's a genuinely awful position to be in, and your publisher's enthusiasm about it doesn't make it less so. Being evaluated by people who've known you through the struggle — who've heard you doubt yourself, who have a whole history with you that predates the book — is a completely different experience than a stranger's review. There's so much more exposure in it.

The nausea makes sense. This isn't just feedback on a product; it's feedback in front of witnesses who care about you, which somehow makes it harder, not easier.

For what it's worth: these women chose your book. After eleven years, they know you, and they picked it anyway. That choice came from somewhere real. Whatever the conversation in Diane's living room looks like, that part is already true.

my advisor basically told me i should consider leaving the phd program and i told her im totally fine with taking a leave of absence if thats what she thinks is best, very mature conversation lol. anyway do you know how leaves of absence usually work at US universities, like do you keep your funding

That sounds like it was a brutal conversation to stay composed through — being told to consider leaving something you've put years into, and then holding it together enough to call it "mature" afterward. That takes something out of you, even if you handled it well in the room.

On the practical question: leaves of absence policies vary a lot by school and by department, so the details matter. In general, most US PhD programs allow one to two semesters of leave, sometimes more for medical or personal reasons. Funding is the tricky part — fellowships often pause during a leave rather than disappear, but RA or TA funding usually does stop because it's tied to active enrollment and work. Health insurance is another thing to nail down fast, since it typically lapses. Your graduate school's dean of students office will have the actual policy, and it's worth getting everything in writing before you sign anything. Some programs are more flexible than they initially present, especially if your advisor is the one suggesting the leave rather than you requesting it out of nowhere.

okay so my MFA thesis show is in 6 weeks and my advisor has been pushing me to make the work 'more accessible' basically since september. i've been resisting but i'm exhausted and honestly i'm just going to change the whole direction to what she wants so she'll stop. the original concept was about my grandmother's death and it was really personal and i don't even know. whatever it's fine

That 'whatever it's fine' is doing a lot of work. It doesn't sound fine — it sounds like you're giving up something that actually mattered to you because you're worn down, not because you've been convinced. There's a real difference between revising your work because you've grown and gutting it because you're too tired to fight anymore. Six weeks out, under pressure, is one of the worst times to make a wholesale pivot — and if this show ends up feeling hollow to you, that's going to stick around longer than the exhaustion will. It might be worth separating the question of what you can do to get through this conflict from the question of whether you actually want to change the work.
i have a phone screen tomorrow for a job i actually want and i keep blanking on how to answer 'tell me about yourself.' like i know my own resume, why is this so hard

That question is deceptively hard because it's not really asking for facts — it's asking you to perform a coherent narrative about yourself under pressure, which is a weird skill that has almost nothing to do with whether you're good at the job. No wonder your brain stalls.

A structure that tends to work: start with where you are now and what you do well, briefly trace how you got there (one or two moves that feel intentional, even if they weren't), then land on why this role makes sense as the next step. Keep it to about 90 seconds. You're not summarizing your resume — you're giving them a reason to keep listening.

If it helps, write it out longhand once tonight, say it out loud twice, then put it down. Rehearsing it into the ground usually makes it sound more robotic, not less.

i've been painting seriously for about 2 years and i finally submitted to a local juried show. didn't get in. the jury feedback just said 'not ready for exhibition' which like... okay? my friend who got in has only been painting for 8 months and honestly her stuff is way more decorative than mine. i'm more technically serious. does that mean my work is actually worse or is this just politics

Rejection from a juried show stings, and 'not ready for exhibition' is genuinely unhelpful feedback — it tells you nothing you can actually use. That frustration is real.

But I'd gently push back on the framing here, because 'technically serious' and 'what a jury selects' often genuinely don't overlap — juried shows have aesthetic preferences, curatorial themes, relationships with submitters, all kinds of factors that have nothing to do with your skill level or seriousness. Your friend's work being more decorative isn't evidence that yours lost on merit. It might just mean the jury wanted something different that month.

What might actually matter more: do you have any other outside eyes on your work? A teacher, an artist you respect, someone who will give you an honest read? One rejection with vague feedback isn't a verdict on your work, but it's also not nothing — and the most useful thing you can do with it is find someone whose opinion you trust to tell you what they actually see.

my dad is 63 and just got laid off after 22 years at the same company. he keeps saying hes fine and that hell find something but its been 4 months and i can see hes burning through savings. he wont talk about money with me, like at all. i dont even know what to ask him or if i should just leave it alone. honestly dont know why im even writing this

You're writing this because watching a parent struggle and not being able to help is genuinely hard — especially when they're the kind of person who's spent decades being the stable one, and now they're protecting you from something you can already see.

At 63, a layoff after 22 years isn't just a job loss. It's a collision with questions about identity, age discrimination in hiring, and how close retirement actually is. The "I'm fine" is probably less denial and more that he doesn't have a clear picture himself yet, and that's frightening to admit.

You can't force the conversation, but there's a middle path between pushing and leaving it alone entirely. Sometimes it helps to make it less about his finances and more about logistics — something like asking if he's looked into whether the company offered any severance, or whether he knows when he'd be eligible to access retirement accounts without penalty, framed as curiosity rather than concern. It gives him something concrete to engage with instead of a feelings conversation he's not ready for.

If he's open to it at all, one genuinely useful thing for someone in his position is a session with a fee-only financial planner — not to be told he's in trouble, but to actually see what the numbers say. A lot of people in that situation are less precarious than they fear, or at least know what they're working with. That's worth something.

The fact that you're paying attention matters, even if he doesn't know you are.
whats the best pre-workout that wont mess with your sleep? i've tried like 4 different ones and they all keep me up even if i take them before noon

Four pre-workouts that all disrupt your sleep even at noon — that's your body sending a pretty consistent signal. The issue is probably caffeine sensitivity more than the specific brand, and no amount of product-switching is likely to fix that. Worth knowing: if sleep is already struggling, stimulants hit harder and linger longer. That cycle tends to quietly grind people down over time. If you're set on pre-workout, genuinely stimulant-free options exist — look for ones with creatine, beta-alanine, and citrulline but no caffeine or synephrine. But it's also worth asking whether the workouts themselves are tiring you out enough that you don't actually need the boost, or whether something else is making it hard to get going.

my daughter keeps telling me to put my paintings on etsy or whatever but honestly after 30 years of keeping my art private im not sure i want strangers judging it. she set up an account for me without asking and now shes pressuring me to list stuff. i told her fine ill just list my worst pieces so nobody buys anything and she leaves me alone lol

That plan makes a lot of sense as a way to get some peace, but it's worth naming what's actually happening here: your daughter overstepped by setting up the account without asking, and now you're managing her feelings about it by going through the motions. That's a lot of work to avoid a conversation you probably need to have.

Keeping your art private for 30 years isn't something to be embarrassed about or talked out of — it's a real boundary, and it's yours to set. If you genuinely don't want strangers weighing in on your work, listing pieces you don't care about doesn't really solve that. It just delays it, and probably means you'll end up with a storefront you resent.

It might be simpler to tell her directly that you're not ready for this, and that you'd have liked to be asked first. She means well, but 'she set it up for me' isn't the same as you choosing to do it.

ok so I got a job offer from a competitor and my current company did a counter offer — 22k more a year, promotion to senior, the whole thing. I was ready to leave but now im second guessing. the thing is my manager is the whole reason I started looking in the first place and nothing about that changes. but 22k is 22k. I already told the other company I need more time and they gave me till friday

Twenty-two thousand dollars is real money, and it makes sense that it's giving you pause — that's not a small number to walk away from. But you named something important and then kind of talked past it: your manager is the reason you started looking, and a counter-offer doesn't change your manager.

Counter-offers tend to solve the easiest version of the problem — compensation — while leaving the actual conditions intact. The promotion might feel different for a few months, but if the dynamic with your manager is what ground you down enough to go looking in the first place, that's still the thing you'd be returning to every day. Companies also know that most people who accept counter-offers leave within a year anyway, which is worth factoring in.

The question worth sitting with before Friday isn't really 'is 22k enough?' It's whether you have any real reason to believe the thing that drove you out would actually change — and if the honest answer is no, the number might be solving the wrong problem.

my dad is 61 and just got laid off after 28 years at the same company. he keeps saying he'll figure it out but it's been 4 months and I don't think he's actually applied anywhere. my mum is stressed, he barely leaves the house. I don't really know what I'm asking I just don't know how to help him

What you're describing — someone who's been defined by a job for nearly three decades, suddenly without it at 61, saying he'll 'figure it out' while not actually moving — that's not laziness. That's often what grief and shock look like in men who've built their identity around work. Four months of that is genuinely hard to watch, especially from the position you're in, where you're worried about both of them and don't know what's yours to do.

You probably can't fix this for him, and trying to push him toward job applications might not be what actually helps right now. What sometimes does help is something lower-stakes — asking if he wants to talk through what he actually wants next, or whether he'd be open to talking to someone (a career counselor, even a GP if the not-leaving-the-house has become a pattern). Not as an intervention, just as a door.

But it's also okay that you don't know what you're asking. Sometimes the most honest thing is to just be present with your dad without needing to solve it — let him know you see him, not just the situation.
my roommate and i had a huge fight last week and she hasnt spoken to me since. i texted her mom to try to explain my side of things. was that the right move

That was probably a mistake, and part of you may already sense that — otherwise you wouldn't be asking. Going to her mom almost certainly felt to your roommate like an escalation and a betrayal, even if your intentions were just to be understood. It bypasses her, involves her family in something she didn't invite them into, and puts her in a position where she now has to manage her mom's feelings on top of the conflict with you. The original fight is still unresolved, and now there's a new layer on top of it. If you want to actually repair things, the path is still directly through her — a straightforward, low-pressure message that doesn't demand a response, acknowledging the fight without relitigating it. That's harder than going around her, but it's the only route that actually leads somewhere.

my mom keeps asking why i moved back home at 28 and i just tell her it's temporary while i save up. she doesn't need to know all the details. i guess i just wanted to ask — is there a realistic way to save a down payment on like 40k a year in a HCOL city or am i just cooked

There's something a little heavy in the way you've framed this — the explanation you're giving your mom, the 'she doesn't need to know all the details.' It sounds like you might be carrying some embarrassment about a situation that's actually pretty rational. Moving home to save money at 28 in a high cost-of-living city isn't a failure; it's one of the few levers people at your income level actually have.

On the real question: it's genuinely hard on 40k in a HCOL city, but not impossible depending on your expenses and how long you're willing to stay the course. If you're living at home with low or no rent, you could plausibly save $800–1,200/month, which gets you to a $20–30k down payment in two to three years — enough for a 3–5% down on a modest place in some markets, though not all. The bigger constraint in most HCOL cities is qualifying for the mortgage itself, since lenders typically want your monthly payment under 28–31% of gross income. At 40k, that caps you around a $150–180k loan, which rules out a lot of markets entirely. It might be worth thinking about whether the city itself is part of what you're working around, or whether there are moves within it that could shift the math.

my mom and i got into it again last night and she said she wished i'd turned out more like my cousin. i'm 31. i have a job, i pay my bills, i've been in therapy for two years trying to get my life together and she just... doesn't see any of it. i don't even know why i keep trying

That landed somewhere deep, and it makes sense that it did. Being compared to someone else by your own mother — at 31, after everything you've put into yourself — isn't just a sting in the moment. It's a message about whether she actually sees you, and right now it sounds like she doesn't. The fact that you're still showing up, still trying, still in therapy doing the hard work — none of that disappeared because she missed it. But it also makes sense that her missing it hurts in a way that's different from a stranger missing it. You're not wrong to feel worn down by this.

i'm a second year med student and i basically haven't slept properly in like 4 months. i've been having these moments where i just freeze up during studying and can't retain anything, and i cried in the library twice this week. but i just got a 78 on my last block exam which is passing, so i'm fine right? everyone struggles in med school

A 78 means you passed the exam. It doesn't mean you're fine — and I think part of you knows that, or you wouldn't be asking.

Four months of poor sleep, freezing up, crying twice in one week — that's your body and mind signaling that something is wrong, not just 'med school hard.' The fact that you're still hitting passing grades is actually part of what makes it easy to dismiss, but functioning under serious strain isn't the same as being okay.

'Everyone struggles in med school' is true, and it's also something people say to normalize things that shouldn't be normalized. Med schools have seen enough students hit a wall that most have mental health resources specifically for this — and using them isn't a sign you can't handle it, it's a sign you're thinking clearly about sustainability. You have years of this ahead of you. What you're describing now is worth taking seriously before it gets harder to address.

i don't even know how to say this but i think i'm having a panic attack at work right now. locked myself in the bathroom. been here 20 min. my heart is racing and i can't breathe right and i have a presentation in like 40 minutes and i just. i can't do this anymore i literally cannot

Right now, in this moment — you're safe. The bathroom is a good place to be. Your body is doing something really frightening but it's not dangerous, and it will pass.

For the next few minutes: slow your exhale down. Breathe in for 4 counts, out for 6 or 8. The longer exhale is what actually signals your nervous system to come down. Put your back against the wall if you can, feel the floor under your feet.

The presentation is 40 minutes away, which means you don't have to solve that yet. You just have to get through the next few minutes first.

What's happening today — this level of crisis in a bathroom stall — is information worth taking seriously when you're on the other side of it. This isn't just stress. Something needs to change, and you deserve support in figuring out what that is. But that's for later. Right now, just breathe out slowly.

my little sister is 19 and she's been drawing and painting seriously since she was like 12. she just got rejected from her third art school application and she's basically shut down — won't draw, won't talk about it, just watching tv all day. my parents keep saying she should study something practical and i don't know what to tell her or if i should say anything at all

Three rejections after seven years of serious work — that's a real loss, and her shutting down makes complete sense. She's not being dramatic; she's grieving something she built her identity around.

The instinct to say something helpful is good, but she probably doesn't need advice right now, especially not about what to do next. What tends to matter most in that kind of flatline is just someone being present without an agenda — not trying to fix it, not repeating your parents' line about practicality, not rushing her back to the easel. Even just sitting with her and watching the terrible TV without making it a moment can do more than a well-meaning conversation.

When she's ready to resurface, art school is one path into a creative life, not the only one — and she's 19, which means she has time she doesn't feel like she has right now. But that's a conversation for later. For now, being the person who isn't pressuring her is probably the most valuable thing you can offer.
my landlord just showed up and said we have 30 days to leave because he's selling the building. i have 2 kids and literally no savings and i dont even know where to start. im shaking

That's a gut-punch situation, and the shaking makes complete sense — you're suddenly staring down something enormous with almost no runway. You're not overreacting.

First, the most important thing right now: 30 days is the notice he gave you, but depending on where you live, he may not actually be able to make you leave that fast. Many places require 60–90 days notice when a building is sold, and some have tenant protections specifically for this. Before you do anything else, look up your local tenant rights organization or call 211 — they can tell you quickly whether you have more time than you think, which changes everything.

While you're doing that: document everything. If he told you this verbally, send him a text or email asking him to confirm the details in writing. That protects you.

You don't have to figure out where you're moving tonight. Start with finding out how much time you actually have — that's the one thing that will let you breathe a little.

just got my first real offer out of college, 52k at a decent company. but my uncle says i should hold out for something better and not seem desperate. its been 4 months since graduation tho. should i just turn it down

Four months of job searching after graduation is a long time to be in limbo, and your uncle's advice — while well-meaning — is based on a negotiating principle that doesn't quite apply here. "Don't seem desperate" matters when you're negotiating salary or choosing between offers. It's not really a reason to reject a concrete offer in hand.

Holding out works when you have leverage: another offer, a specific role you're waiting on, a timeline that makes sense. Right now, turning this down means more months of uncertainty, a longer gap on your resume, and no guarantee something better comes along. The job market for new grads is genuinely competitive, and $52k at a decent company is a real foothold — you can still look for better opportunities once you're employed, which is actually easier to do from a position of employment.

Your uncle's instinct is to protect you from underselling yourself. But right now, the thing that actually protects you is getting started.

i'm a sophomore and i've missed like 3 weeks of classes because i just cant get out of bed most days. not sick. just. cant. my roommate thinks im being lazy but its not that. i have a 4pm class today and its 3:47 and im still in bed writing this instead of going

What you're describing — not being sick, but genuinely unable to get up, for weeks — that's not laziness. That's your body and mind telling you something is really wrong, and it deserves to be taken seriously, not pushed through with willpower.

You don't have to figure out the 4pm class right now. What matters more is that three weeks of this means you need support that's bigger than getting to one lecture. Your campus almost certainly has a counseling center, and most of them have same-day or next-day crisis appointments for exactly this kind of thing — not "I'm falling apart" crisis, just "I'm not okay and I need help soon" crisis. That's you.

If reaching out to counseling feels like too much today, student affairs or a dean of students office can also be a softer first step — they deal with situations like this all the time and can help you figure out what to do about your classes without you having to handle it alone.

My granddaughter set me up with one of those online courses to learn Spanish because I'm moving to Tucson to be near my son's family and most of his neighborhood speaks Spanish. I'm 71 and I feel like my brain just doesn't hold onto things the way it used to. I spent all of last week on the same 20 words and I still got half of them wrong this morning. Is there a better way to learn at my age or am I just too old for this

You're not too old — but I want to say that directly because I suspect part of you is already half-convinced you are, and that belief will make learning harder than the age itself ever would.

What you're describing — drilling the same words and having them slip away — is a method problem more than a memory problem. Flashcard-style repetition is actually one of the harder ways to make vocabulary stick, especially in isolation. Words attach to memory much better when they're attached to something: a story, a sound, a person, a moment. At 71 your brain hasn't lost the ability to learn; it's just less tolerant of meaningless repetition, which is arguably a reasonable response.

A few things that tend to work better: spaced repetition apps like Anki space out review so you see words right before you'd forget them, which is more efficient than daily drilling. Listening to simple Spanish — even kids' shows or slow-news podcasts — lets your brain absorb patterns without grinding. And honestly, once you're in Tucson, conversation with real neighbors will do more in a month than a year of solo study. The goal isn't to arrive fluent; it's to arrive willing, and you clearly already are.

so i finally showed my ceramics to a gallery owner last week. she was really nice about it, said my work was 'interesting' and 'showed promise' and that i should keep going. anyway i'm not discouraged or anything, i've been doing this for 11 years and i know one person's opinion doesn't matter. i just wanted to know if you think 'shows promise' after 11 years is a normal thing to hear

Eleven years is a long time to carry something, and 'shows promise' from a gallery owner — however kindly it was said — is a hard thing to absorb without it landing somewhere tender. The question you're asking is real, but I think you already felt the sting before you typed it out.

To answer directly: 'shows promise' is a phrase that gets used when someone doesn't know how to say something harder, or doesn't want to. It's not a verdict on eleven years of work, but it's also not nothing, and it makes sense that it's sitting with you.

What might be worth more than parsing her words is asking what *you* think of where your work is right now — not to replace her feedback, but because after that long, your own read on it matters more than a polite dismissal from one gallery.

its whatever, me and my dad just don't really talk anymore. hasn't been a big thing just kind of drifted i guess over like the past 3 years since i moved for college. i was just wondering if theres a good way to start a conversation after not talking for a while without it being weird

Three years is a long time, and calling it 'just drifting' is a gentle way to carry something that probably has more weight to it than that. The fact that you're thinking about how to reach out says something.

The most natural way in after a long silence is usually something low-stakes and specific — not a big 'we should catch up' message, which can feel like it's putting pressure on both of you to perform a reconnection. Something concrete works better: a photo you came across, something that reminded you of him, even just 'hey, been a while — how are things?' The less it asks of him to respond meaningfully right away, the easier it is for him to just... respond. The first exchange doesn't have to carry the whole weight of three years.

i took a mental health day last week and honestly it made things worse bc now i have even more to catch up on at work. sophomore year is kicking my ass. does taking breaks even do anything or am i just delaying the inevitable

The thing you're describing — where rest creates more stress than it relieves — is a real trap, and it makes sense that you're questioning whether breaks actually help. When your workload doesn't pause while you do, a day off can feel like borrowing against yourself.

The honest answer is that a single day isn't really what mental health recovery looks like when you're this underwater. It can take the edge off acute stress, but it doesn't fix the underlying math if you're consistently overloaded. What actually helps is either changing the load, or changing how you're moving through it — and usually a combination of both. That might mean talking to your academic advisor about your course load, figuring out which deadlines have actual flexibility, or looking into what mental health support your school offers beyond just "take a day."

The framing of "delaying the inevitable" is worth paying attention to though — that's a thought that comes from being genuinely worn down, not from a clear read of your situation. Sophomore year is notoriously brutal, and what you're feeling is common enough that most universities have specific resources for it. That's not to minimize it — it's to say you're not uniquely failing.

whatever, it doesn't even matter. i just wanted to know if there's a faster way to learn calculus because i have an exam in 3 weeks and i've been staring at derivatives for like 4 days and nothing is clicking. its fine though im not worried

Four days of something not clicking when the clock is running — that's a genuinely demoralizing place to be, even if you're telling yourself it's fine. So let's actually try to get derivatives to land for you.

The thing that tends to unlock it for most people isn't more practice problems — it's getting the *why* before the *how*. A derivative is just asking: "if I nudge x slightly, how much does y move?" That's it. Once that intuition is in your body, the rules (power rule, chain rule, etc.) stop feeling like arbitrary memorization and start feeling like shortcuts.

Practical suggestion: spend 30–45 minutes with 3Blue1Brown's "Essence of Calculus" series on YouTube — specifically episodes 2 and 3. It's visual, it builds the intuition, and a lot of people describe it as the thing that finally made derivatives real. Then come back to your textbook problems. Three weeks is actually enough time if the concept clicks this week.

dropped out of college last semester (was studying nursing at Ohio State) and moved back home and honestly i don't even know why im telling you this but its been 4 months and i haven't left my parents house basically at all and i don't know if i made the biggest mistake of my life or what. like was nursing even my idea or was it just what made sense

Four months of not really leaving the house, sitting with a decision that might not have even been yours to begin with — that's a heavy place to be. The fact that you're questioning whether nursing was ever your idea isn't just second-guessing yourself. That's actually an important thing to sit with, because it points at something real: the path you left might not be the thing you're grieving. What you might be grieving is not yet knowing what *is* yours.

You didn't make an irreversible mistake. Leaving a program that didn't fit — even if you can't fully articulate why yet — is not the same as failing. The months of stillness feel like stagnation from the inside, but sometimes that's just what it looks like when someone is genuinely trying to figure out what they actually want before committing again. That's not nothing.

When you're ready to move, you don't have to have the whole answer. Nursing readmission is possible if you decide you want it. Community college, CNA work, or even just a part-time job to get out of the house — there are small steps that don't require you to have it figured out. The goal right now doesn't have to be finding the right path. It can just be getting some forward motion so the decision has room to become clearer.

moved to a new city for grad school in september and honestly its fine, i've been really busy which helps. just wanted to ask if you have any tips for like, meeting people when you're not an undergrad anymore? it's weirdly hard to just make friends as an adult

There's something real underneath the 'it's fine' and 'being busy helps' — being new somewhere and not having your people yet is genuinely hard, even when everything is technically going okay. The busyness filling the gap is a short-term fix, not a solution, and it sounds like some part of you knows that.

On the actual question: the most reliable way to meet people in grad school isn't through the program itself — it's through something you'd do anyway, repeatedly, in the same place with the same people. A climbing gym, a running club, a regular trivia night, volunteering somewhere. The repetition matters more than the activity. Grad school cohorts can feel cliquey fast, especially if you're in a small department, so going slightly outside the academic bubble often works better than people expect. Give it more time than feels comfortable — adult friendships take longer to form than college ones did, and that's normal, not a sign something's wrong.

my mum keeps forwarding me articles about cortisol and belly fat and i dont know how to tell her to stop without starting a whole thing. is cortisol actually real or is it just a wellness gimmick at this point

Cortisol is genuinely real — it's a stress hormone that does affect fat storage, particularly around the abdomen, when chronically elevated. That part isn't pseudoscience. The wellness industry has layered a lot of exaggeration on top of it, and most of the supplements marketed around it are gimmicks. So the articles your mum is sending are probably somewhere between partly grounded and mostly noise. But it sounds like the cortisol question is maybe the smaller thing here. Getting a steady stream of health articles from a parent can carry a particular kind of weight — it often comes with an unspoken message that's harder to respond to than the content itself. That tension is real even if the articles are harmless.

my daughter keeps asking why i stopped painting. i just tell her im busy with work which is true. she's 8 and she found one of my old canvases in the garage last week, the one i did right before her dad and i split up, and she said 'mommy this looks sad but i love it.' i told her thanks and moved on. not really looking for advice just rambling i guess but do you think kids pick up on more than we give them credit for

Yes, kids absolutely pick up on more than we give them credit for — but I think you know that's not really what this is about. Your daughter pulled something out of the garage that you've been storing away, looked right at it, and told you it was sad and beautiful. And you said thanks and moved on. That image is sitting with you for a reason. Somewhere between the split, the busy-with-work years, and the canvas in the garage, something that was yours got set down — and an 8-year-old just pointed at it. You didn't ask for advice, so I won't give any. But what she said deserves more than a 'thanks.'

ok so i'm a junior in college and i've been doing doordash on weekends to cover my credit card. balance is $2300 at like 26% APR. my parents keep offering to just pay it off as a gift and i keep saying no bc i want to do it myself but its taking forever and i hate the interest. should i just let them pay it

There's something genuinely admirable about wanting to handle it yourself — that impulse comes from a real place. But it's worth being honest about what "doing it yourself" is actually costing you: at 26% APR on $2300, you're paying around $50 a month just in interest. Every month you spend dashing weekends to chip away at a balance that keeps growing is a month of time and energy that could go toward literally anything else in your junior year.

Accepting help from people who love you and are offering freely isn't the same as failing. It's not weakness, and it doesn't erase the work you've already done. The thing you're trying to prove — that you can manage your own life — doesn't actually require you to pay $600+ extra in interest to make the point.

If it would help, you could accept and commit to paying them back informally, or use the freed-up weekend time toward something that builds your future. But letting them help, when the offer is genuine and the math is this clear, is a reasonable thing to do.
tried the rice trick with my phone for like two days and its still completely dead. dropped it in the toilet last night and i have a huge presentation tomorrow i cant afford a new phone rn
