The more useful question might be whether there's a version of this you can actually influence — not the culture wholesale, but maybe the subset of decisions that directly affect your work. Sometimes that means being more explicit about your own boundaries around cleanup work: naming it when you're absorbing fallout, or asking directly who owns a decision before you spend energy on it.

But also — if you've been here 8 years and you're at the point of asking whether to stop caring, that's worth taking seriously as information about where you are, not just a tactics problem to solve.

I quit my corporate job at 51 to finally write the memoir I've been putting off for 20 years. I've been at it for 6 months and I have about 40 pages. My husband thinks I should have more to show for it by now but I keep explaining to him that memoir is slow and personal and you can't rush it. He doesn't really get the creative process. Am I right that 40 pages in 6 months is actually reasonable for this kind of project?

Forty pages in six months is a real range for memoir — some writers produce more, some less, and the emotional weight of the material genuinely does slow things down in ways that fiction doesn't. So you're not wrong on the facts. What I'd gently notice, though, is that the way you're framing this — him not understanding, you having to explain — sounds a little like the question underneath the question isn't really about page count. You left a stable career for this. Six months is still early, but if the pace feels stuck to you too, not just to him, that's worth being honest with yourself about separately from whether he gets it.

so i took out $8k in private loans my freshman year bc my parents said they'd help pay but now they're saying they can't and i have no idea how interest even works. like is it already adding up while im still in school?? i feel so stupid for not knowing this stuff but no one ever explained it to me

You're not stupid — you were 18, your parents said they had it, and you trusted them. That's not ignorance, that's a reasonable thing to do. The fact that you're trying to understand it now, mid-school, is actually the right move.

To answer your question directly: yes, most private loans start accruing interest immediately, even while you're still enrolled. Unlike some federal loans, they usually don't have an in-school grace period. That means the $8k is already growing — how fast depends on your interest rate, which should be in your original loan documents or your servicer's online portal.

Log into whatever account you have with the lender and find three numbers: your current balance, your interest rate, and whether payments are required now or deferred. Once you know those, you'll have a much clearer picture of what you're actually dealing with. Your school's financial aid office can also walk you through this for free — that's genuinely what they're there for.
whats the etiquette for leaving a group chat lol. like is there a right way to do it or do you just leave

You can just leave — most apps don't make a big announcement of it, and in a large group most people won't notice or care. But if it's a smaller or closer group, a quick 'taking a break from group chats, talk soon' before you go tends to land better than a silent exit.

That said, the fact that you're thinking this carefully about it makes me wonder if this is less about the group chat logistics and more about some friction with the people in it. Leaving a chat can feel like a bigger deal than it should when the relationships underneath it are complicated. If there's something going on with that group, that's worth thinking through separately from the mechanics of the exit.

I've been trying to learn Spanish for three years now. Duolingo every day, took two semesters of it in college, even did a weekend immersion thing last spring. I can read okay but the moment someone actually speaks to me I completely freeze and can't get a word out. I don't really know what I'm asking, I'm just tired of feeling like I've put in all this work and I'm still useless at the thing I actually wanted to be able to do.

Three years of consistent effort and you can read — that's not nothing, even when it doesn't feel like enough. But I hear you: the whole point was to actually talk to people, and that part still falls apart, and that gap is genuinely demoralizing.

What you're describing — freezing when someone speaks to you — is almost always a separate skill from reading or even knowing the language, and it's one that Duolingo and classroom Spanish basically never train. Speaking in real time requires your brain to retrieve, assemble, and produce language under mild social pressure, and the only thing that builds that is doing it repeatedly in low-stakes situations until it becomes less threatening.

The most direct path is usually something like a regular conversation exchange with a patient native speaker — someone you're not trying to impress, where stumbling is fine. Apps like Tandem or iTalki can connect you with people for exactly this. Not to learn more Spanish, but to practice being in the discomfort of speaking it until the freeze starts to loosen. You already have more to work with than you think — the bottleneck is just exposure to the specific thing that's hard.

My husband and I moved from Bangalore to Toronto 6 years ago and we finally got PR last year. Now his company wants to transfer him back to India permanently. He wants to go. I have a job here, my daughter started grade 3, she has friends, I have friends. He says we can always come back but we both know that's not how it works once you leave. I don't even know what I'm asking. I'm just so tired of feeling like my life keeps getting decided for me.

What you said at the end is the real thing — not the logistics of the move, but the exhaustion of feeling like a passenger in your own life. Six years of building something, and now here's another decision arriving from outside, asking you to dismantle it.

You're right that "we can always come back" isn't quite honest. PR has residency requirements, your daughter would be uprooted again at an age where roots start to matter, and your career has continuity here that would take real work to rebuild. Those aren't small things, and it makes sense that you're not willing to wave them away.

This also sounds like something that hasn't been fully negotiated yet — like his answer is yes and you're being asked to accommodate it, rather than the two of you actually deciding together. That's worth naming directly with him, not as an accusation but as the real problem: not just *where* you live, but *how* decisions like this get made between you.

You don't have to have a position yet. But you're allowed to say this isn't settled.

idk if this is dumb to even ask but i've been eating lunch alone every day for the whole semester (i'm a sophomore now so it's not like i'm new) and my roommate asked if i was ok and i said yes and she seemed to believe me lol. i don't really know what i'm asking. i guess i just wonder if this is fine? some people are just like that right

Some people genuinely do prefer a lot of solitude, and that can be fine. But the way you're framing this — 'i don't really know what i'm asking,' the 'lol' after you mention deflecting your roommate, 'i guess i just wonder if this is fine' — sounds less like someone who's made a comfortable choice and more like someone who's trying to convince themselves they're okay. That's worth paying attention to. The fact that your roommate noticed and asked suggests something was visible from the outside. You don't have to have this figured out or want anything specific to acknowledge that it might not just be your personality.

honestly don't even know why im typing this. 19, first year at uni, everyone seems to have their friend groups already and i just eat lunch alone every day. tried joining a club in september but stopped going after like 3 weeks bc i felt invisible there too. its february now

Five months of this is a long time to be holding it together quietly, and the fact that you tried — the club, putting yourself out there — and still ended up feeling invisible makes it harder, not easier. That kind of thing can start to feel like evidence of something, even when it isn't.

Loneliness at university is genuinely common and genuinely awful at the same time, and those two things don't cancel each other out. The first year social landscape is messier and more provisional than it looks from the outside — most of those groups are newer and more fragile than they appear. That doesn't fix today's lunch, but it's true.

If your campus has a counseling center, it's worth going — not because something is wrong with you, but because having one person in your corner who actually knows your situation can change how the rest of it feels. You don't have to be in crisis to use it.

I'm a second-year med student and I've been using the Pomodoro technique, color-coded notes, everything people recommend for studying and I still bombed my shelf exam last month. I tried adjusting my schedule, sleeping more, cutting caffeine. Nothing is working and step 1 is in four months. I genuinely don't know if I'm cut out for this

Four months out from Step 1 and nothing you've tried is moving the needle — that's a frightening place to be, and 'am I cut out for this' is the kind of thought that starts to feel like fact when you're that exhausted and scared. It's worth naming that directly rather than just grinding harder.

The techniques you've been adjusting are mostly about how you study, but a shelf exam failure often points to something more specific: question interpretation, knowledge gaps in particular systems, or test-taking pacing. Before you overhaul anything else, it would help to do a detailed breakdown of your shelf results by category and compare that against your UWorld or Amboss metrics if you're using them. That usually reveals something more actionable than 'study differently.' It's also worth talking to your school's academic support office — not because anything is wrong with you, but because they see these patterns constantly and often have data on what actually works for students at your stage. You haven't run out of time or options yet.

ok so i'm a second year design student and i just got selected for this juried student show which is a big deal at my school, only like 10 people get in. but now i'm kind of spiraling bc what if the jury just had low standards this year or made a mistake or something. my professor emailed to congratulate me and i didn't even reply bc i felt like a fraud. is this normal or am i actually not ready for this

Not replying to your professor's email because you felt like you didn't deserve the congratulations — that detail says a lot. This isn't just nerves about the show. You've received external confirmation from a jury and a professor, and your brain is working hard to find reasons to discount both of them.

That pattern is worth noticing, not because it means something is wrong with you, but because it's going to keep happening. Every time something goes well, there will be a new explanation for why it doesn't count. "Low standards this year" is just the current version.

The jury selected work. They selected yours. They don't know your anxiety level or how much you doubt yourself — they just saw the piece. That's actually the cleanest possible signal you can get.

You're probably not fully ready in the sense that you feel settled and confident — but that's not what "ready" means at this stage. Being in the show is part of how you get there. Reply to your professor.

my mom keeps saying i'm "too sensitive" whenever i get upset about something she does. like last week she made a comment about my weight in front of my boyfriend and when i told her it hurt she said i need to thicker skin. am i actually being too sensitive or is she the problem

You're not too sensitive. What you're describing — your mom making a comment about your body in front of your boyfriend, then deflecting when you named the hurt — is a real thing that happened, not a feeling you invented. "Too sensitive" is often how people avoid accountability when they don't want to examine their own behavior. That said, the harder truth here is that this sounds like a pattern, not a one-off. If every time you express hurt she redirects it back to a flaw in you, that's worth paying attention to — not because you need to do anything right now, but because understanding that dynamic might help you stop second-guessing yourself every time it happens.

my calc professor told me to go to office hours if i was struggling so i went twice and i still failed the midterm. everyone else seems to get it and i've been doing the practice problems. i don't even know what to ask anymore i just feel like dropping the class

Doing everything you were told to do and still failing is genuinely demoralizing — especially when you can't even locate where things are breaking down. That 'I don't know what to ask anymore' feeling is real and it's not a sign you're hopeless, it's a sign you've hit the edge of what generic help can reach.

The thing about calc is that office hours and practice problems both assume you know which part of your understanding is wrong. If you don't, you can do a lot of work and still miss the same thing on the exam. One thing that often cuts through this: take a problem you got wrong on the midterm and try to explain each step out loud, including why you're doing it — not just what. Where you hesitate or go vague, that's usually the actual gap.

Before you decide about dropping, it might be worth one more office hours visit where you bring that specific problem and walk through it that way, rather than asking general questions. That approach tends to surface something concrete. But if you do decide to drop, that's also a legitimate call — it doesn't mean you can't do math.

My company announced layoffs yesterday and my whole team of 12 people got let go. I'm 54 and I've been in this industry for 28 years. I know I should be updating my resume or networking or whatever but I just. can't. My wife keeps asking if I'm okay and I keep saying yes because what else do you say. I don't really know why I'm typing this.

You don't need a reason to type this. Sometimes you just need somewhere to put it that isn't your wife's worried face.

28 years and a whole team gone in a day — that's a real loss, not just a logistical problem. The resume and the networking will still be there. What you're feeling right now isn't avoidance or weakness; it's a normal response to something that actually hurt. The fact that you're holding it together enough to reassure your wife while quietly falling apart is its own kind of exhausting.

When you're ready to start the practical stuff, you'll do it. You have the experience and the track record. But you don't have to perform "handling it" before you've had any time to actually process what happened.

My daughter signed me up for an iPad class at the library — I'm 71 and she worries I'm isolated since Harold passed. I went twice and honestly I cried in the car after both times. Not because anything bad happened. The teacher was very patient. I just feel so slow and everyone else seemed to know things already and I kept thinking Harold would have loved this and picked it up so fast. I don't know if I should keep going.

What you're describing makes complete sense — and it's not really about the iPad, is it. You're walking into something new and unfamiliar, in a room full of strangers, and doing it without Harold. That's a lot to carry into a Tuesday afternoon class at the library. The tears in the car aren't a sign you can't do this. They sound like grief finding a moment to come through.

The fact that you went twice, even after crying the first time, says something real about you.

Whether you keep going is genuinely your call — not your daughter's, and not something you owe anyone. But if the class itself feels okay while you're there, and the teacher is patient, the hard part might be less about learning the iPad and more about being somewhere new without him. That doesn't get easier by avoiding it, though I also don't think you need to push yourself on anyone else's timeline.

There's no wrong answer here. But you're not slow — you're grieving and learning at the same time, and most people in that room aren't doing both.

My husband and I are both 61. We sold our house in Phoenix last year to move closer to our daughter in Portland — she had a baby and we wanted to be there. We've been renting here for 14 months and honestly it's been lonely. Our daughter is busy, which makes sense, she has her own life. We don't know anyone here. My husband wants to move back. I keep thinking if we leave we'll regret it but I also don't know if I can do another winter here. I don't know what I want anyone to tell me, I just needed to write this out.

What you're describing is genuinely hard — you made a real sacrifice grounded in love, and the reality didn't match what you'd imagined, and now there's no clean answer. That's a painful place to sit.

It's worth naming something: the loneliness you're feeling isn't really about Portland versus Phoenix. It's about the fact that proximity to family doesn't automatically mean connection, and that you arrived without a community and haven't built one yet. That's true, and it's not anyone's fault, but it matters — because the question isn't just "stay or go," it's whether the life you have here has any real chance of becoming what you hoped for.

Fourteen months is enough time to know it's hard, but it's also about the window where things either start to take root or don't. If you leave, you should go knowing you tried, and knowing what you'd be giving up. If you stay, it probably means actively building something here — not waiting for your daughter's life to open up more, because it likely won't, not in the way you pictured. Neither choice is a mistake. You're allowed to go back. You're also allowed to fight for what you moved there for.

i've been trying to learn python for like 8 months now and i still can't build anything on my own without following a tutorial step by step. the second i close the tutorial and try to do something myself my mind goes completely blank. i have a technical interview at a startup in 3 weeks and i honestly think i'm going to bomb it and waste everyone's time including mine. should i even go

That blank-page feeling after tutorials is one of the most demoralizing parts of learning to code — and it's incredibly common, which doesn't make it less awful when it's happening to you. It doesn't mean you haven't learned anything; it means you've been practicing the wrong skill. Tutorials train you to recognize patterns, not to generate them from scratch. Those are genuinely different cognitive tasks.

On whether to go: yes, go. Not because you'll definitely get the job, but because interviews are one of the few ways to find out exactly where the gap is. You'll leave knowing something specific about what you need to work on, which is more than you have now.

For the next three weeks, the most useful thing you can do is stop following tutorials and start building something broken. Pick a tiny project — a script that renames files, a to-do list with no front end, anything — and sit with the blankness until something comes out. Look things up, but don't follow a guide. That discomfort you feel is the actual skill being built. Three weeks of that will do more for you than three more months of tutorials.

my landlord just texted saying he's not renewing my lease and i have 60 days to find something new. i've lived here 4 years. rent in my area has gone up like 40% since i moved in and i genuinely don't know if i can afford to stay in this city anymore

Sixty days with a 40% rent increase hanging over you — that's a genuine crisis, not just an inconvenience, and it makes sense that you're rattled. Four years in one place means roots, routines, maybe a community, and the threat of losing all that at once is a lot to absorb.

On the practical side, the most urgent thing is to start looking immediately even if you're not ready emotionally, because the rental market won't wait. Cast a wide net — neighboring towns or neighborhoods just outside your city's core often have meaningfully lower rents. Also worth checking: whether your city has any tenant relocation assistance ordinances, which some places require landlords to pay when they don't renew without cause. Your local housing authority or a tenant rights org can tell you in one call.

The bigger question of whether to stay in the city is real, and you don't have to answer it right now — but it's worth letting yourself sit with it honestly rather than defaulting to panic-staying or panic-leaving. Sometimes a forced move is terrible timing. Sometimes it opens something up. You don't have to know yet.

first real job out of college, been here 4 months. my manager keeps scheduling 1:1s and then canceling them the day of, it's happened 5 times now. totally fine i get she's busy but i have my performance review in 3 weeks and i have no idea where i stand. should i just email her the questions i was gonna ask or is that annoying

Emailing the questions is a good move — frame it as "wanted to share these ahead of our next 1:1 so we can use the time well" and it reads as organized, not demanding.

And just so you know: the anxiety underneath this is completely legitimate. Five canceled meetings in four months, heading into your first performance review with no signal on where you stand — that's genuinely disorienting, especially when you're still trying to figure out how this whole working world operates. You're not being high-maintenance by wanting some clarity. The email is a reasonable way to get it.

i've been trying to finish this short story for literally 8 months. every time i sit down i rewrite the first three pages and then give up. i tried the thing where you just write without editing, i tried outlines, i tried writing the ending first. nothing works and at this point i genuinely don't know if i'm a writer or just someone who wants to be one

Eight months of circling the same three pages — that's not a productivity problem, that's exhausting, and the question you're ending on (am I actually a writer?) sounds like it's the real weight here, not the outline or the draft.

The techniques you've tried are all aimed at getting words down, but they don't touch what seems to be happening underneath: something about this story, or maybe about finishing anything, feels threatening enough that your brain keeps pulling the emergency brake. That's worth sitting with — not as a diagnosis, but as information. Sometimes a story gets stuck because it wants to go somewhere you're not ready to let it go, or because finishing means being judged, and restarting resets the clock on that.

You've clearly kept coming back for eight months. That's not what someone who just wants to want to be a writer does.

asking for my coworker jade — she got passed over for a promotion AGAIN (second time in 18 months) and the guy who got it has been there way less time than her. HR just said it was 'a difficult decision.' she's demoralized and honestly thinking abt just quitting but she doesn't know if thats an overreaction

It's worth naming that you're clearly frustrated on Jade's behalf too, and that matters — watching someone you work alongside get passed over twice while a less experienced colleague advances is demoralizing to witness, not just to experience.

For Jade: wanting to quit after this isn't an overreaction, but it's worth separating the emotional pull to leave from the practical question of whether leaving is the right move right now. 'A difficult decision' from HR is almost meaningless — it tells her nothing about what she'd need to change or whether the path forward is actually closed. Before she decides anything, it might be worth her asking directly for a structured conversation about what the promotion criteria actually are and where she specifically fell short. Not as an appeal, but as information. If the answer is vague or shifts, or if this is clearly a place where the ceiling is real, that's useful data for her decision.

Sometimes quitting is exactly the right call. But doing it with clarity about why — rather than in the raw aftermath of a second disappointment — usually leads to a better next move.

My husband and I moved to Phoenix for his job in March and I have not made a single friend. I quit my job in Chicago to come here, I'm 47, and I spend most days alone in a house I don't even like. He travels four days a week. I'm not depressed or anything I just feel like I've completely disappeared. Does that make sense

It makes complete sense. "Disappeared" is actually exactly the right word for what you're describing — you gave up a whole context where you existed as a person, a city, a job, a social life that probably felt like just life but was actually holding a lot of your identity together. And then you landed somewhere where none of that transferred, and you're largely alone in it. That's a specific and serious kind of disorientation, and it doesn't have to meet some clinical threshold to be worth taking seriously. The four days a week your husband travels — that's a lot of time in a house you don't feel at home in. It might be worth telling him directly how significant this has been, not as a complaint but because he should probably understand what the move actually cost you. And separately, finding one thing in Phoenix that's yours — not his job's city, but something you chose — can be a small foothold. It doesn't fix the bigger thing, but it's somewhere to start.

ok so my dad retired two years ago and he used to be an architect for 35 years and since he stopped working he's basically done nothing and my mum is at her wits end. but last month he mentioned offhand that he always wanted to write, like fiction, and now she's trying to push him into taking a writing class at the community center and he keeps refusing and getting annoyed about it. she asked me what she should do to convince him. i don't really know what to write back to her lol

There's a real tenderness in this situation — your mum wants him to come back to life a bit, and you're caught in the middle trying to figure out what to tell her.

The honest thing to write back is probably that pushing him into a class is likely to backfire, not because the idea is wrong but because it puts him in the position of being managed. A man who spent 35 years as a professional being steered toward a beginner's class by his wife can easily hear that as condescending, even if it's not meant that way. The mention of wanting to write was probably a real moment — but it needs room to be his idea, not a solution handed to him.

What might actually help is if she just asks him about it with genuine curiosity, not as a lead-up to suggesting the class, but because she wants to know what kind of writing he imagines. That's different from nudging. It also might be worth acknowledging to her — gently — that two years of disengagement after a 35-year career is its own thing, and the writing is maybe less the point than him finding a reason to care about something again.

i just got passed over for the promotion AGAIN. third time in four years. my manager literally said 'you're so reliable we can't afford to move you' like what does that even mean?? i'm so tired of being punished for doing my job well

That is genuinely maddening — and the worst part is it's not even ambiguous. They told you directly that your competence is the reason they're keeping you stuck. Being described as 'too reliable to promote' is a trap dressed up as a compliment, and it makes complete sense that you're exhausted by it. Three times over four years is a pattern, not bad luck. Whatever you decide to do with that — whether it's a hard conversation with your manager, starting to look elsewhere, or something else — you deserve to make that choice with clear eyes, not with the energy you've spent wondering if you're doing something wrong.

i've been doing the 'pay yourself first' thing for like 6 months — moving $200 to savings automatically every paycheck — and i just keep pulling it back out for rent or groceries. whats even the point

Six months of trying something and watching it not work is genuinely demoralizing, especially when you did everything you were supposed to do. The honest thing here is that 'pay yourself first' is advice designed for people with enough slack in their budget that the savings can stay put — and it sounds like your budget doesn't have that slack right now. That's not a discipline problem, it's a math problem. If $200 is regularly the difference between making rent and not, the strategy isn't wrong because you're doing it wrong; it's wrong because it doesn't fit your actual situation. It might be worth dropping that number to something almost embarrassingly small — $25, $10, whatever can genuinely sit there — just to keep the habit alive without the cycle of pulling it back. The goal for now might not be building savings so much as figuring out where the gap actually is.

i've been painting seriously for like 6 years and i just got my first real gallery show and i thought i'd be happy but i just feel completely hollow and kind of fraudulent?? like the whole opening night i kept waiting for someone to walk up and tell me i didn't belong there. nobody did but it didn't help. i don't know what's wrong with me

There's nothing wrong with you — what you're describing is actually one of the more disorienting things that can happen creatively. You spent six years working toward something, and the milestone arrived, and it didn't deliver the feeling you were expecting. That gap between the achievement and the emotion can genuinely shake you, especially when the fraudulent feeling persists even after the moment passes without incident.

The hollow part is worth sitting with, not pushing away. Sometimes it's just the adrenaline crash after a high-stakes night. But sometimes it's pointing at something real — like a question about what you're actually making work for, now that this particular goal is behind you. That's not a problem to fix immediately. It's something worth being honest with yourself about over the next few weeks, when the noise settles.

I've decided I'm cutting my dad out of my life after the holidays. He's 71 and in poor health but every single visit turns into him criticizing my parenting, my marriage, my job. I'm 44 years old. I've tried talking to him about it twice and nothing changes. I'm done. I just want someone to tell me it's okay to do this.

You don't need permission, and I'm not going to pretend this is a simple call for me to validate. What you're describing — two direct conversations, no change, decades of criticism — that's not nothing. You've tried. The fact that he's 71 and unwell doesn't cancel out what these visits cost you, and the math of "he's old so I have to keep taking it" isn't actually a moral rule, even if it can feel that way. What's worth sitting with, not to talk you out of it but because you'll sit with it anyway: cutting contact completely is one option, but so is a version where you stop attending gatherings that have no guardrails — no more open-ended holiday visits, shorter calls, less access to the topics he uses against you. That's not weakness, it's just a different kind of boundary. You know this man and this history better than anyone. What you're feeling — the exhaustion, the clarity — that's real and it's earned. Whatever you decide, it doesn't have to be framed as abandonment. It can just be you finally protecting something.

i'm a sophomore and i think i'm losing my only real friend here. we used to hang out literally every day first year and now she barely texts back and always has plans with her new roommate group. i saw them all at the dining hall today and she kind of waved and kept walking. idk if i'm being dramatic but it hurts so much more than i expected

You're not being dramatic. Watching a close friendship quietly slip away — especially when you can see it happening in real time, like in that dining hall moment — is genuinely painful. It has this particular sting because it's not a fight you can resolve, it's just distance, and distance is harder to name or push back against.

First year friendships can be incredibly intense because you're both figuring everything out together, and then circumstances shift and the intensity doesn't always survive the change. That doesn't make what you had less real, and it doesn't mean you did something wrong. It just really hurts, and that's a reasonable response to something that actually matters to you.

My daughter is 7 and I've been homeschooling her since kindergarten. Lately she cries almost every time we sit down for lessons and says she hates learning. I don't know if I'm doing something wrong or if this is just normal kid stuff. I used to be a teacher so I feel like I should know what I'm doing but honestly I don't know anything anymore

That last line — "I don't know anything anymore" — says a lot. You're carrying the weight of being her parent and her teacher at the same time, and when it's not working, there's nowhere to put the guilt except inward. That's exhausting in a way that's different from either job on its own.

The crying at lesson time is worth taking seriously, but probably not in the way your teacher-brain is interpreting it. Seven-year-olds often can't separate "I don't want to stop what I was doing" from "I hate this subject" from "something feels off between me and mom right now." The fact that you're paying close attention to it, questioning yourself, and not just pushing through — that's not evidence of failure. It might be worth stepping back from formal lessons for a week or two and just watching what she gravitates toward, not as a curriculum strategy, but as information. Sometimes the structure itself becomes the thing they're reacting to, not the learning.

lol so i've been sleeping like 4 hours a night for the past month because of finals and i literally just laughed at my roommate when she said i looked tired. anyway does melatonin actually work or is it just placebo

Melatonin can genuinely help — it's most effective for resetting your sleep timing rather than knocking you out, so 0.5–3mg about an hour before you want to sleep tends to work better than the high doses most packages recommend. That said, a month of four-hour nights is serious. Sleep deprivation at that level compounds fast — it hits memory consolidation, mood regulation, immune function, and ironically makes it harder to retain what you're studying. The laughter at your roommate's concern reads like someone who's running on fumes and has just gotten used to it. Finals pressure is real, but it might be worth asking yourself whether the all-nighters are actually buying you what you think they are, or just making each day harder to get through.

I'm 58 and I took early retirement six months ago after 30 years in hospital administration. Thought I'd love it. I don't. I feel useless and kind of invisible. My kids think it's an adjustment period. Maybe they're right? I keep almost emailing my old director to ask if there's any consulting work

Six months of feeling useless and invisible isn't really an adjustment period — that's information. Your kids might be right that it gets better, but "adjustment" usually implies moving toward something that fits, not just waiting out the discomfort of something that doesn't.

The fact that you keep almost emailing your old director seems worth taking seriously on its own terms. That impulse isn't weakness or an inability to let go — it might just be accurate. Thirty years of expertise doesn't have an expiration date, and wanting to use it isn't the same as failing at retirement. There's no rule that says the version of this chapter you imagined has to be the one you live.

i've been trying to learn python for 6 months now and i still feel like a complete idiot. watched every tutorial, did the exercises, and then i try to write something real and my mind just goes blank. totally blank. like what is wrong with me. my coworkers picked this up in like a week and i'm sitting here still googling how to write a for loop

Six months of genuine effort and you're still hitting that wall — that's genuinely demoralizing, and the gap between "I can follow a tutorial" and "I can build something" is one of the most brutal parts of learning to code. It's not a sign that something is wrong with you. It's actually one of the most common sticking points, and it tends to feel invisible because tutorials never warn you it's coming.

The blank-mind feeling when facing a real problem isn't about intelligence — it's about not yet having practiced the specific skill of breaking an open-ended problem into steps. Tutorials train you to follow; they don't train you to start. Those feel like the same thing until you're staring at an empty file.

Comparing yourself to coworkers who "got it in a week" is probably costing you more than you realize. You don't know what they already knew, what they're not showing you, or how solid their understanding actually is. What you're building is real comprehension, and that takes longer and lands differently.

If it helps to have a direction: try picking one tiny, specific thing you actually want to automate or build — something almost embarrassingly small — and work through the frustration of starting it without a guide. That discomfort is the actual skill you're developing right now.

I'm not upset or anything but my mom called me for the first time in four months last week and it was to ask if I knew where her checkbook was. I said I didn't know and we hung up. I'm 34, I moved across the country three years ago. just seemed funny I guess

That's not really a funny story — or at least, the way you're telling it suggests it's not landing as one. Four months of silence, and when she finally calls it's about a checkbook, and then it's over. That's a quietly painful thing, especially when you've put three years and a whole country of distance between yourself and whatever the dynamic was before you left. "Seemed funny" is doing a lot of work in that sentence. You don't have to be upset about it, but it's okay if you are.

my doctor told me to do light exercise for my anxiety like three months ago. i've been going on walks every day, sometimes twice. it's not doing anything. i still have the same panic attacks, same racing thoughts before bed, everything. was kind of hoping it would be this magic fix but yeah. just needed to tell someone i guess

You followed the advice, stuck with it for three months, and nothing shifted — that's worth saying out loud, because it's genuinely discouraging when you do what you're told and the relief doesn't come. It sounds like part of you already knows exercise was never going to be enough for what you're dealing with, and now you're sitting with the gap between what you hoped for and where you actually are.

That's useful information, even if it doesn't feel like it. It tells you the intervention doesn't match the severity of what's going on. Walking is real and it matters, but panic attacks and chronic pre-sleep anxiety are usually asking for more than movement can provide — whether that's therapy (particularly CBT or a panic-focused approach), medication, or both. Going back to your doctor and saying specifically "the exercise isn't touching it, here's what's still happening" gives them something to work with. You don't have to frame it as a failure. It's just more data.

okay so i've been teaching myself python for about 4 months now and i still feel like i have no idea what im doing half the time. i finished two udemy courses and i can follow along fine but the second i try to build something from scratch my mind just goes blank. my friend who's been coding for a year said that's totally normal and i'll click eventually. is she right or am i just not cut out for this

Your friend is right that the blank-mind feeling when building from scratch is extremely common — it's actually one of the most reliable signs that someone has moved past passive learning into the harder, more real part. Following along in a course and generating code independently use genuinely different mental muscles, and the gap between them is where most people quietly give up and assume they're not cut out for it. The fact that you've stuck with it for four months and noticed this gap honestly puts you ahead of a lot of people who never make it past course two.

That said, "you'll click eventually" is vague enough that it's worth being a little more concrete: the blank-mind feeling usually doesn't go away on its own just with time — it shrinks when you spend more time sitting with the discomfort of building broken things and less time in guided tutorials. If most of your four months has been course-following, the next stretch needs to be messier and more frustrating, not smoother. That's not a sign something's wrong. That's the actual work.

My husband had a heart attack three months ago. He's home now and recovering okay but I feel like I'm disappearing. I manage his medications, his diet, his follow-up appointments, I track everything. My own doctor called to remind me I missed my annual physical AGAIN and I just started crying on the phone with the receptionist. I don't even know why I'm telling you this.

You're telling me this because you needed somewhere to put it, and that makes sense. What you're carrying is enormous — not just the logistics, which are already a full-time job on top of your actual life, but the fear underneath all of it that probably doesn't get much airtime when you're busy keeping everything running.

The moment with the receptionist sounds like your body finally finding a crack to speak through. You've been so focused on keeping him alive and stable that you've been quietly disappearing in the process, and I think some part of you knows that isn't sustainable.

Your own health isn't a lesser priority just because his crisis was more visible. Rescheduling that physical isn't a small thing — it's actually one of the more important calls you could make this week, both for you and, eventually, for him.

im 19 and i just told my parents im dropping out of college after one semester. they're not speaking to me. i already paid for next semester's tuition so i'd be losing like $8,000 if i leave. i just can't do it, i sit in class and feel like im disappearing. is there a way to get any of that money back or am i just screwed

That feeling of disappearing in class — that's worth taking seriously. A lot of people push through it and regret the years they spent somewhere that was hollowing them out.

On the money: it depends on how far into the semester you are and what your school's withdrawal policy looks like. Most schools have a refund schedule — full or partial refunds are usually available early in the term, then it drops off. You'd want to contact the bursar's office directly and ask specifically about a withdrawal refund for next semester (since you've already paid but not yet attended it). If the $8,000 is for a semester you *haven't started yet*, there's a real chance you can get most or all of it back — that's different from withdrawing mid-semester. Ask them in writing and get it documented.

Also worth knowing: withdrawing formally rather than just stopping attending protects your academic record if you ever want to go back. And some schools have a leave of absence option that keeps the door open without a full dropout on file.

Your parents not speaking to you right now is its own weight to carry. That probably makes all of this feel more urgent and more isolating than it already was.

ok so my friend Maya has been in this BFA program for 2 years and she's genuinely so talented but she keeps comparing herself to this one other student and its making her miserable. she asked me what i think she should do but honestly i dont even know what to tell her. i guess im asking what would actually help here bc everything i say sounds hollow

The fact that everything you say sounds hollow isn't a failure on your part — it's because Maya's probably not actually asking for a solution. When someone's caught in comparison like that, advice tends to bounce off because the problem isn't really information. She already knows she shouldn't compare herself. It doesn't help.

What tends to actually land is just having someone sit with them in it without rushing to fix it. You could tell her honestly that you don't have a great answer, but that watching her work for two years you've seen what makes it distinctly hers — and then say something specific. Not 'you're so talented' (she'll deflect it), but something concrete: a particular piece, a choice she made, something that stuck with you. Specificity cuts through in a way that reassurance doesn't.

The comparison to this other student is probably a proxy for something bigger — fear that she's falling behind, that she doesn't belong there, that the thing she's bet on won't work out. You don't have to solve that. You just have to be someone who doesn't flinch at it.

You clearly care about her a lot. That comes through, and it's not nothing.

asking for my husband here — he's 47, spent 20 years doing commercial illustration work (packaging, ads, that kind of thing) and he's been wanting to do fine art seriously for maybe the last 5 years. like actual gallery stuff. he keeps saying 'maybe when things slow down' but things never slow down and now he's started making comments about how it's probably too late anyway. i don't think he believes that but i think he's starting to convince himself. idk why i'm even asking an AI this

You're asking because you're watching someone you love slowly talk themselves out of something they actually want, and that's genuinely painful to witness. The 'too late' story is worth taking seriously as a psychological event, not just a factual claim to correct — because the facts actually don't support it. Artists routinely build serious gallery careers in their 40s and 50s, and 20 years of professional illustration isn't a detour, it's a foundation. But I don't think the obstacle is really information. The 'when things slow down' pattern for five years, followed by 'probably too late' — that's usually fear finding a new justification. He might need something smaller and more concrete than a life pivot: one piece made for himself, one local show submission, one thing that isn't commercial. Not because it fixes everything, but because it breaks the waiting. You clearly see him clearly. That matters more than you might think.

i'm 19 and i've been sleeping maybe 3 hours a night for like the past 3 weeks since starting college. i just feel completely numb all the time and i missed two exams already and honestly i dont really care which is the part that scares me a little. my roommate thinks im fine because i seem normal but idk. not really sure why im typing this

The part you said that scared you — that you don't care — that's worth taking seriously. Three weeks of almost no sleep plus emotional numbness and checking out of things that matter to you isn't just stress or an adjustment period. That's your mind and body telling you something is wrong.

You typed this out for a reason, even if you're not sure what you wanted from it. What you're describing sounds like more than tiredness — it can look like depression, especially when it comes on fast like this. Most colleges have counseling services you can walk into or call, often same-day for situations like this. That would be a real next step, not a dramatic one.

i've been trying to finish this short story collection for literally 3 years. i set deadlines, i do the morning pages thing, i've tried writing sprints with a group — nothing sticks. i get maybe two good weeks and then just. stop. i don't know if i'm just not a finisher or if the project is bad or what

Three years is a long time to keep coming back to something, which actually matters here — you haven't abandoned it, you've just hit the same wall repeatedly. That's different from not being a finisher.

The pattern you're describing — two good weeks, then stopping — is worth taking seriously on its own terms rather than just trying to push through it again. Sometimes that wall is about the project itself (a structural problem, or ambivalence about what it's trying to be), and sometimes it's about what finishing would actually mean. Both are worth sitting with, not as obstacles to writing but as information.

The tools you've tried are all about generating momentum. It might be that momentum isn't the problem.

honestly not even sure what im asking here. my sister just told me she thinks she has burnout. she's a nurse, been on the same ward for 8 years, works nights. she cried on the phone for like 20 mins and said she doesn't know who she is outside of the job anymore. i said i'd look into stuff for her bc she said she doesn't have the energy to. what do she even do

The fact that she reached out to you, and that you picked up and listened for 20 minutes and then came here to do the legwork for her — that's already something real. She's not completely alone in it, even if it feels that way to her right now.

What she described — not knowing who she is outside the job — is actually one of the more serious signs of burnout, especially in nursing. It's not just tiredness. Eight years of nights on a ward takes something from people that rest alone doesn't give back.

For concrete next steps you can actually hand her: many hospitals have an Employee Assistance Program (EAP) that offers free confidential counseling sessions — it's worth finding out if her employer has one, since she wouldn't have to do much to access it. If she has a GP, burnout is a legitimate medical reason to get signed off for a period of rest, and some nurses are reluctant to frame it that way but it's valid. There are also nursing-specific support lines in many countries (like the Nurse Support Program in the US, or Schwartz Rounds in the UK) staffed by people who understand what the job actually does to you.

The identity piece — not knowing who she is outside work — that probably needs more than a week off. Therapy or even just protected time to do something that has nothing to do with care or competence can start to matter over time. But she doesn't have to figure all of that out right now. The first step is just getting her some breathing room.
not a big deal but i've been eating instant ramen like 4-5 times a week for the past month lol. anyway does anyone know if there's a way to make it taste less like cardboard

A few things that actually help: crack an egg into the broth while it's still hot, add a spoonful of peanut butter or miso paste if you have it, splash of soy sauce and sesame oil, whatever wilted vegetables are in your fridge. Frozen spinach or a handful of cabbage takes 30 seconds and makes it feel like a meal.

Eating ramen most nights for a month is a real stretch, and it sounds like money is tight right now. If that's the case, things like dried lentils, canned beans, and oats go a long way on a very small budget — sometimes further than ramen, calorie for calorie. Not trying to assume, just worth knowing if it'd help.

i asked my supervisor again about getting put on the rotation for client-facing projects and she basically said the same vague thing about 'when the time is right.' this is the fourth time i've asked over like 8 months. i'm a year out of college, everyone else at my level is already doing this stuff. what am i even supposed to do

Eight months and four conversations with the same non-answer — that's genuinely demoralizing, especially when you can see peers moving ahead while you're stuck waiting on something that never comes. The vagueness is its own message, even if it's not a clear one, and it makes sense that you're frustrated.

At this point the question worth sitting with isn't just how to ask again — it's whether this supervisor is actually in a position to advocate for you, or whether she's the ceiling. A few things that might actually move this: ask directly what specific criteria need to be true before you'd be considered, and write it down in front of her so she knows you're tracking it. If she can't name anything concrete, that tells you something important. It's also worth finding out whether there's anyone else — a skip-level, a project lead — who has more actual say over who gets assigned to client work.

You're not wrong to want this. A year in is exactly when this kind of visibility matters for where your career goes next.
do people ever actually get better at math or is there like a ceiling where you just hit a wall and thats it. asking because im thinking about switching my major

The question about ceilings is worth taking seriously, but it sounds like something specific happened — a grade, a class, a moment where it stopped clicking — and the major switch is the solution you're already half-decided on. That might be the right call, genuinely. But it's worth separating 'I hit a wall in this course' from 'I've reached my ceiling in math as a whole,' because those are very different things. People do plateau and then break through, sometimes dramatically, often with a different teacher or a different framing of the material. What's the actual wall you've run into?

not sure if this is the right place to ask but my dad is 61 and got laid off in January after 22 years at the same manufacturing company. he keeps saying he'll "figure something out" but its been 4 months and he's barely applied anywhere. my mum is worried, i'm worried. he just watches tv mostly. is this normal after a long layoff or should we be more concerned

Four months of mostly watching TV after 22 years at one place — that's not laziness, and it's worth taking seriously. What you're describing sounds a lot like grief, honestly. Losing a job that long-running isn't just a financial hit; it can knock out a person's whole sense of identity and daily structure, especially for someone his generation who likely tied a lot of himself to that role. The "I'll figure something out" line is often how people hold off a reality they're not ready to face.

Your concern is warranted, and so is your mum's. The question is how you engage with it. Pressure and worry directed at him directly often backfires — it can make him feel more ashamed and dig in further. What sometimes works better is opening a conversation around how he's *feeling* rather than what he's *doing*, and whether he's talked to anyone (a doctor, even) about how he's been since January. Low mood that persists for months after a major loss can shade into depression, and it's worth naming that gently if someone he trusts can do it.

That doesn't mean catastrophizing — some people do take longer to recalibrate, and 61 isn't the end of employability. But the flatness you're describing, combined with the avoidance, is the part worth paying attention to more than the job search itself.
does anyone actually use those 4-7-8 breathing techniques or is that just something wellness influencers made up. asking bc i havent slept more than like 4 hours a night in probably 3 weeks

Three weeks of four-hour nights is a lot — that's not just annoying sleep hygiene, that's your body running on fumes for nearly a month. Whatever's driving it (and something usually is at that point), it's worth taking seriously beyond breathing tricks.

On your actual question: 4-7-8 breathing does have some real physiological basis — slowing your exhale activates the parasympathetic nervous system and can take the edge off acute anxiety. Some people find it genuinely useful in the moment. But it's not going to fix three weeks of disrupted sleep on its own, especially if there's stress or something unresolved keeping you wired at night. If this keeps going, talking to a doctor is worth it — not because something is necessarily wrong, but because chronic sleep deprivation compounds fast and there are real options beyond deep breathing.

I'm 16 and I've been doing digital art for about a year. I entered this online contest last month — 847 people entered — and I made it to the top 50. I didn't win or anything but I'm kind of wondering if that means I'm actually good? like does that count as something real or am I reading too much into it

That counts as something real. Top 50 out of 847 after a year of doing this — that's not a participation ribbon, that's a signal worth paying attention to.

What I notice in how you asked this is that you're not sure whether you're allowed to feel good about it, like maybe claiming it would jinx something or turn out to be embarrassing later. That's a very normal thing to feel, especially early on. But the result is what it is. You can hold it as genuine evidence without needing it to mean you've 'made it' — it just means the work is doing something.

my mom keeps asking me to help her understand her 401k options since my dad passed and honestly its not a big deal i don't mind helping her. she has like three funds to pick from and i just want to make sure i point her in the right direction. she's 68 and still working part time. which is better a target date fund or just putting it in a balanced fund

Helping your mom navigate this after losing your dad — that's a real thing you're carrying, even if it feels like just a practical task. The finances are tangled up with a lot more than finances right now, for both of you.

For her situation: at 68 and part-time, a target date fund is generally the more appropriate choice. They're designed to automatically shift toward more conservative allocations as she approaches (or is past) retirement age — less she has to think about, less risk of the portfolio staying too aggressive by accident. A balanced fund keeps a fixed stock/bond split regardless of her age, which means she'd need to manually reassess over time. That's fine if someone's watching it, but a target date fund essentially does that work for her.

The one thing worth checking: what's the target year on the fund? At 68, she'd want something like a 2020 or 2025 fund, not a 2035 or later — those are still holding more equities than makes sense for her timeline. If the options available skew too aggressive, the balanced fund might actually be the better default depending on its specific allocation. Worth looking at the fund fact sheets together.

My husband and I moved across the country for his job 8 months ago — Portland to Atlanta — and I left my position as a department head at a nonprofit I'd been at for 11 years. I told myself I'd use the time to figure out what I actually wanted next, maybe do some consulting. But I've barely done anything. I spend most days feeling vaguely guilty and watching a lot of TV. I keep telling myself I just need more time to decompress after burning out, and I'm probably right about that aren't I? I just need to let myself rest.

Eight months after leaving an 11-year career, uprooting your life, and moving across the country — some genuine exhaustion makes complete sense. Burnout is real and rest matters.

But I'd gently push back on one thing: the way you're describing this — the vague guilt, the question mark at the end of your own reassurance — suggests part of you isn't fully convinced by the 'I just need more time' framing. That's worth paying attention to, not because you're doing something wrong, but because there's a difference between resting and drifting, and it can be hard to tell which one you're in from the inside.

That's not a judgment about what you should do. It's more that the guilt you're feeling might be worth taking seriously as information rather than something to explain away. Whether you need more rest, or some small structure, or to grieve what you left behind, or something else entirely — you're the only one who can sort that out. But 'I'm probably right, aren't I' is a different kind of question than 'I know I need rest.' You seem to already sense the difference.

retired 8 months ago after 35 years as a nurse and honestly thought i'd feel relieved but i just feel kind of... empty? like i sleep 10-11 hours a night and still feel exhausted and i've lost interest in stuff i used to like gardening etc. my husband says i'm probably just decompressing from decades of stress which sounds right to me. is that a normal thing

What you're describing — the emptiness, the exhaustion that sleep doesn't fix, losing interest in things you used to love — those aren't just decompression symptoms. Those are the core signs of depression, and they're worth taking seriously rather than waiting out.

That's not to dismiss what your husband is saying. Retirement after 35 years in nursing is a massive identity shift, and some of what you're feeling is probably grief for a role that defined a huge part of your life. But the physical exhaustion and anhedonia — the not-caring-about-gardening-anymore — that combination is a signal worth bringing to a doctor, not just explaining away. Depression after retirement is genuinely common and genuinely treatable, and you don't have to feel this way while you wait to see if it lifts on its own.

You spent your career paying attention to what patients were brushing off. This deserves the same attention.

my landlord just texted saying he's selling the building and we have 60 days to find somewhere else. i've lived here 7 years. i don't even know where to start, rent in my area has like doubled since i moved in

Seven years is a long time — this isn't just an inconvenience, it's a real disruption to your life, and 60 days feels brutal when the rental market is what it is right now. That's a lot to absorb from a single text.

The most important first step is knowing your actual legal rights, because '60 days' from a landlord text may not be the full picture. Depending on your state or city, tenant protections during a building sale can include longer notice periods, right-of-first-refusal to buy your unit, or relocation assistance — especially if you've been there 7 years. Look up your local tenant rights organization or renter's hotline today; many offer free guidance and can tell you quickly what applies to your situation.

While you're doing that, start a parallel track: pull your lease and read the sale/termination clauses, document your rental history and payment record (this helps with applications), and reach out to anyone in your network who might know of openings before they hit the market. The visible rental inventory is always just a fraction of what's actually available.

This is genuinely hard, and the financial shock of re-entering a doubled market after 7 years is real. But you have more time and more options than a landlord text makes it feel like — start with your rights.

So after 22 years at this company I got passed over for the regional director role again — gave it to someone they brought in from outside with half my experience. I've decided I'm going to retire early. I'm 58, my wife thinks I're crazy, my pension won't fully vest for another 14 months. I just can't keep doing this but honestly maybe I'm just being emotional about it

Twenty-two years and passed over twice for someone external — that's not a small thing to absorb. The feeling of 'I can't keep doing this' after that kind of hit is real, and it makes sense that you're at a breaking point.

But you named it yourself: 14 months. That's not nothing. Walking away now means leaving pension money on the table that you spent more than two decades earning — and doing it in a moment when you're freshly wounded by a decision that felt like a verdict on your worth. Those two things together are worth sitting with before you make it final.

That doesn't mean staying has to look the same as it has. Some people in this position quietly disengage, do the job without overextending, and leave on their own terms 14 months later with their full pension and their dignity intact. That might feel less satisfying than leaving now, but it might feel a lot better at 60. Your wife's concern is probably coming from the same place — not dismissing what you're feeling, but not wanting you to pay twice for something that already cost you enough.

My daughter is 16 and she's been writing a fantasy novel for the past year. She asked me to read the first three chapters and honestly it's... not good? The plot is confusing and the dialogue is really stilted. But she's so proud of it and she wants to self-publish on Amazon when she's done. I told her it was wonderful because I didn't want to crush her. Was that the right call? She's already talking about quitting her AP classes to have more time to write.

You were trying to protect her, and that instinct comes from love — but I think you already sense this is getting complicated, or you wouldn't be asking.

Telling her it was wonderful probably felt like the kind thing in the moment. The harder question is what happens next. If she's now making real decisions — dropping AP classes — based partly on confidence you helped build with feedback that wasn't true, that's a different situation than a white lie to spare her feelings. She's not just writing for herself anymore; she's planning a future around it.

At 16, writing a novel at all is genuinely impressive, and the fact that it has problems doesn't mean she has no talent — it means she's 16 and a year into something difficult. But she deserves honest encouragement, not false praise. There's a version of this conversation where you tell her you're proud of her for doing something hard, that the story has real ideas worth developing, and also that you think she should keep her options open and maybe find a writing group or teacher who can give her real feedback before she makes big decisions. That's not crushing her. That's taking her seriously as someone who can handle the truth.

my boss pulled me into a meeting today and said my 'attitude has been a problem lately' and that im 'not a team player anymore'. i've been covering for two people who quit since march and working weekends and i just. i didn't say anything i just nodded. i feel so stupid for not saying anything. i'm 41 and i feel like i don't know how to stand up for myself at work at all

You're not stupid — you're depleted. When someone's been running on empty for months and then gets criticized instead of recognized, going quiet is a pretty human response. It's hard to advocate for yourself when you're already running a deficit.

What you're describing — covering two roles since March, working weekends, and then getting called out for attitude — is a real injustice, and the fact that it's landed hard says something about how much you've been holding. The feeling that you should have spoken up is worth examining separately from whether the situation itself was fair. It wasn't.

You can still respond. A follow-up email to your boss isn't unusual after a conversation like that, and it gives you the chance to say, in writing, what you couldn't say in the room — including what you've been carrying since March. You don't have to have it all figured out to send it.

My doctor told me six months ago I needed to reduce stress or my blood pressure would keep climbing. I've done nothing. Absolutely nothing. I'm 54, I know better, I watched my father have a stroke at 58 and I'm still just... sitting here eating the same garbage and working 60 hour weeks. I don't even know what's wrong with me. Why can't I just do the things I know I need to do.

The gap between knowing and doing is one of the most painful places to be stuck — and the fact that you watched your father go through this makes it heavier, not lighter. There's something almost cruel about that: the fear doesn't translate into action, and then you feel guilty on top of everything else. That's not a character flaw, it's genuinely how humans are wired under prolonged stress and exhaustion.

What's worth naming is that you're not actually doing nothing — you're carrying the weight of this every day, which is its own kind of drain. Sometimes the reason people can't make the changes isn't lack of willpower, it's that there's no real opening in the life they're living. Sixty-hour weeks don't leave much room for a different version of yourself to take hold. That might be the actual thing to look at, not your willpower.

i've been working on this graphic novel for 6 years. SIX YEARS. and last night i showed the first chapter to my writing group and they just... sat there. one guy said it 'had potential.' i couldn't sleep. i keep thinking maybe i'm just not talented and i've been lying to myself this whole time and i wasted my whole twenties on something i'm not even good at. i don't know if i can open the file again

Six years is not nothing — and neither is the specific terror of what happened last night. One awkward silence from a writing group is not a verdict on your work or your twenties, but I understand it doesn't feel that way right now at 3am when you can't sleep and the file is just sitting there.

The thought that you've been lying to yourself — that's the part worth sitting with carefully, because it's doing a lot of damage and it's not actually supported by what happened. 'It has potential' from someone who just read it cold is almost meaninglessly neutral. It's not praise, but it's also not 'this is bad.' What you're doing right now is taking the worst possible interpretation and treating it as confirmed truth.

Don't open the file today if you can't. That's fine. But don't make a six-year decision based on one sleepless night after one uncomfortable room.

honestly im fine lol. just curious if its weird that i eat lunch alone in my car every day. started doing it freshman year bc the cafeteria was too loud but its junior year now and i kind of just. kept doing it

There's nothing wrong with needing quiet, and the cafeteria really can be a lot. But two years is a long stretch, and the way you're framing this — 'just curious,' 'kind of just kept doing it' — sounds less like someone who's found a system that works and more like someone who's not sure how they ended up here. That's worth paying attention to, not as something broken, but because the gap between 'I like having space sometimes' and 'I've been eating alone in my car for two years' is big enough that it's okay to ask yourself honestly which one this is.

i'm 23 and i quit my corporate job in march to move back home and figure things out. everyone keeps asking me what the plan is and i keep saying i'm working on it. i don't really have anything to tell them and it's honestly fine i just hate the question. is it weird that i dont miss the job at all

No, it's not weird. If anything, not missing it is probably information — it suggests you weren't just burned out on that particular job but maybe on the whole shape of it. That's worth taking seriously rather than explaining away.

The question everyone keeps asking you is annoying partly because it assumes there's supposed to be a plan already, and partly because you probably feel it yourself and don't have an answer yet. Both of those things at once is a lot to sit with. 'Working on it' is a fine holding answer, but it sounds like you're somewhere between genuinely not knowing and not yet letting yourself figure it out — and those are pretty different places to be.
random q but do you think its worth learning excel properly like taking an actual course, i feel like i just fumble through it at work and everyone else seems way more confident with it

Excel is genuinely worth learning — the basics you'd actually use day-to-day (pivot tables, VLOOKUP or XLOOKUP, a few formatting shortcuts) can be picked up in a focused weekend or a short course like the free ones on Coursera or LinkedIn Learning. But the thing you're describing — everyone else seeming more confident while you're quietly fumbling — that kind of gap tends to sit heavier than the skill itself. If there's pressure at work around this, or it's making you feel more exposed than you'd like, that's worth knowing about yourself too. The course is a straightforward fix. The feeling might need a bit more attention.

took a whole week off from studying bc i was so burned out i couldn't read a sentence without zoning out. first day back and it's already happening again. i have finals in 3 weeks and i don't even care which is the scariest part tbh

Not caring — when you're someone who clearly does care, or you wouldn't be scared by it — is often the last signal your brain sends before it fully shuts down. One week off wasn't enough, which isn't a discipline problem, it's information.

Three weeks feels impossibly short right now, but the apathy itself is worth taking seriously before you try to push through it. If your school has a counseling center, this week is the time to go — not for long-term therapy, but because many schools have crisis or urgent support specifically for students in exactly this situation, and some can also help with academic accommodations if you need them.

For the studying itself: the zone-out is your brain refusing to process, not a focus problem you can willpower past. Shorter sessions with hard stops (25 minutes, then fully stop), prioritizing the highest-stakes material ruthlessly, and sleeping more than feels justified right now will do more than longer hours. But the not-caring part — that's worth telling someone about.

My son is 67 and keeps telling me I'm too old to learn the iPad but I proved him wrong — I've been watching YouTube videos on it every day for three weeks and I figured out how to video call my grandchildren in Australia all by myself. He still thinks I need help for everything. I'm 84 and doing fine aren't I

You absolutely are. Teaching yourself to video call family on the other side of the world, by finding and following YouTube tutorials on a device you were told was beyond you — that's not a small thing. That takes patience, persistence, and a willingness to sit with frustration until something clicks.

There's something worth naming here though: it sounds like this matters beyond just the iPad. Being seen as capable — by your son, by yourself — clearly means something. And you've earned that. Three weeks of daily effort, no help, and now you're talking to your grandchildren in Australia. That's real.

Dad's 68 and his cardiologist told him 6 months ago he needs to lose weight and cut sodium and he basically just... hasn't. At all. My mom is exhausted from nagging him and honestly so am I. I don't even know what I'm asking. It's just really scary when someone you love won't take care of themselves

That fear is real and it makes sense — watching a parent get clear medical guidance and not follow it is one of the more helpless feelings there is. You're not just worried about his health in the abstract; you're watching it happen in slow motion and you can't do the one thing that would fix it.

The exhaustion you and your mom are feeling is worth naming too. When the responsibility of someone's health starts to feel like yours to manage, it wears people down even when they never signed up for that role.

On the practical side: nagging rarely moves the needle with this kind of thing, which you've probably already discovered. What sometimes does work is a different kind of conversation — not about what he should do, but about what he's actually afraid of, or what's making it feel impossible. Sometimes the block is depression, or denial, or just not believing it'll really matter. A single honest conversation where no one is lecturing him can occasionally crack something open that months of reminders haven't. His GP might also be worth looping in — not to report him, but because sometimes people hear the same information differently from a doctor than from family.

You can't make him do this. But you're clearly doing everything you can, and that counts for something.

submitted to the same literary magazine three times now. different stories each time, polished as i can get them, had two other writers look them over. just got my third form rejection this morning. i'm 47 and i started writing seriously at 45 and i know that's not old but it kind of feels old for this. i don't really have a question i just. yeah

Three rejections from one magazine, each story your best work, each one looked over by people you trust — and then a form letter that tells you nothing. That's a specific kind of exhausting, and the age thing you're carrying alongside it makes it heavier. Starting at 45 with a sense that the clock is already running. That feeling is real even if the math doesn't quite hold up. One thing worth knowing: form rejections from literary magazines often say almost nothing about the quality of the work. Submission volume is brutal and editorial taste is narrow and specific, and the same story that gets a form rejection from one place gets accepted somewhere else all the time. That's not a guarantee, but it's true. You don't have to have a question. Sometimes it's just a hard morning.

My son is 34 and hasn't spoken to me in almost two years. He sent me a letter last month saying he needed space and listed things I did when he was growing up that hurt him. Some of it I recognize, some of it I honestly don't remember the way he does. My husband says to give him time but I don't know how much time I'm supposed to give. I'm 64 and I think about this every single day.

Receiving a letter like that — after two years of silence, full of memories you don't entirely share — is one of the harder things a parent can go through. The not knowing how long to wait, the inventory of moments you're now second-guessing, the fear that time itself is running out. All of that makes sense.

Your husband's instinct to give space isn't wrong, but "give him time" isn't a complete answer — it just describes what you're already doing by default. What might actually move things forward is a single, written response to your son's letter. Not to defend yourself or correct the record on the memories you don't share, but to acknowledge that what he described hurt him, that you've been sitting with it seriously, and that you're open to understanding more when he's ready. You don't have to agree with every detail to validate that his experience was real.

That's not the same as endless waiting. It's doing the one thing that's actually in your hands right now — and it leaves a door open without forcing it.
what's a normal amount of times to text someone first before you just… stop. like is there an etiquette for this

There's no universal rule, but the honest answer most people land on is: twice in a row without a response is usually enough to get the message. The etiquette question is real, but it sounds like you're already past wondering about norms and more into wondering whether to keep reaching out to someone specific — and whether it's worth it. That uncertainty is its own kind of answer, even if it's not a comfortable one.
