okay so i skipped my 8am lecture again today, that's like the 4th time this month. but honestly the prof just reads off the slides and i can watch the recording later so it's fine right? everyone does it

The recording logic is genuinely reasonable for a class like that — but four times in one month is worth paying attention to, not because of some attendance rule, but because that pattern usually means something. Whether it's the course feeling pointless, sleep being off, or just a low-grade drag you haven't named yet, it tends to compound. The 'everyone does it' framing is doing some work here too — it sounds less like a justification and more like you're trying to talk yourself out of noticing something. That's worth a second look.

does anyone else just completely blank on stuff they studied like the night before?? had my ochem midterm today and i knew the mechanisms i swear i did but i sat down and it was like my brain just. nothing. anyway i think it did okay probably fine

That kind of blanking mid-exam — when you *know* you knew the material — is one of the more demoralizing experiences in school, and "probably fine" doesn't quite cover how that actually feels. It sounds like the test itself went okay enough, but the scarier part is wondering whether your brain is going to betray you again. That's worth paying attention to, not because something is wrong with you, but because blanking under pressure is often a stress response, not a memory failure — your recall was fine the night before because there was no threat. Some people find that practicing retrieval under mild pressure (timed quizzes, explaining mechanisms out loud to no one) trains the brain to access that knowledge even when cortisol spikes. If this keeps happening it might be worth talking to someone at your school's academic support center — not as a last resort, just as a tool.
my landlord just told me i have 3 days to get out and i have nowhere to go. i have a 6 year old. i dont even know why im typing this i just panicked

That's a terrifying thing to be hit with, especially with your kid depending on you. The panic makes complete sense.

Three days sounds final but it often isn't — a landlord can't legally remove you without going through an eviction process, which takes weeks even after a notice. So you likely have more time than it feels like right now.

The most important call to make today is to a local legal aid office (search "legal aid" + your city). They handle exactly this, they're free, and they can tell you your actual rights under your state's eviction law. If you're in the US, 211.org can also connect you to emergency housing resources and family shelters that prioritize parents with young children.

You don't have to figure out the whole thing tonight. Start with that one call.
my roommate ate my leftovers AGAIN (third time this month) and i'm about to leave a really nasty note on her door. like i already wrote it. should i just slide it under?

The frustration makes complete sense — having someone repeatedly take your food without asking is genuinely disrespectful, and three times in a month means it's a pattern, not an accident. But a nasty note tends to create a different problem than the one you're trying to solve. It gives her something to be defensive about instead of something to actually reckon with, and you still have to live together after she reads it. You'd probably get further — and feel better — confronting it directly, even just a quick "hey, the leftovers thing keeps happening and it needs to stop." That's harder in the moment but it's the version that actually has a chance of working.

my husband and i moved to Portland for his job two years ago and I gave up my whole career to come here and now he just told me he wants a divorce. I'm 47, I don't know anyone in this city, I have a 9-year-old, and I genuinely do not know what I'm supposed to do next. not asking for advice just. I don't know why I'm even typing this

You don't need a reason to type this. What you're describing is a lot of loss hitting at once — your marriage, the career you set aside, the life you built around a choice that's now been taken from under you, and all of it in a city where you don't have anyone to call. That's not just hard, it's disorienting in a way that makes "what do I do next" feel like an impossible question.

You don't have to know what comes next right now. The practical stuff will need to happen eventually, but you're in the middle of a shock, and it makes complete sense that you're just trying to get your bearings.

okay so I'm 19 and in my second year of art school and everyone around me seems to just GET it and make work that feels so confident and I keep making things and hating them and starting over. I've talked to my advisor twice about this and she keeps saying 'trust the process' which. okay. but I've been trusting the process for like a year and a half and I still feel like a fraud. is there something actually wrong with me or

There's nothing wrong with you. And I don't mean that as reassurance — I mean it as a counterpoint to the specific story you're telling yourself, which is that everyone around you 'gets it' while you don't. Art school is a place where people perform confidence as part of the work, and what you're seeing in your peers almost certainly isn't the full picture.

But I also want to acknowledge that 'trust the process' is genuinely unhelpful advice when you're the one doing the trusting and still feel like you're drowning. Your frustration with it makes sense. The fact that you keep starting over isn't evidence that you're a fraud — it's evidence that you have enough taste and self-awareness to know when something isn't working. That's not a liability. It's actually the thing.

The hard part is that taste tends to develop faster than skill, especially early on. The gap between what you can see and what you can make is real, and it's uncomfortable, and it doesn't mean you don't belong there.

retired 2 years ago, 68, thought we had planned well but inflation has just destroyed our budget. we're spending about $400 more a month than we expected and i've started lying awake at night running numbers. looked into going back to work part time but my wife has health issues and needs me around. i don't even have a question i guess. just feels like the ground shifted

That image of lying awake running numbers — that's a particular kind of dread, and it makes complete sense. You did plan. The ground did shift. Those two things are both true.

You don't need a question to deserve a response. But since you're carrying this: $400 a month is real, and it's also a specific number, which means it's a problem with edges. A few things that have genuinely helped people in your situation — reviewing whether your Social Security timing or any pension options still have flexibility, checking whether you qualify for any Medicare Savings Programs if healthcare is part of the squeeze, and going line by line on fixed expenses (insurance premiums especially tend to drift). A one-time session with a fee-only financial planner — not someone selling products — can sometimes find $200-400 a month in places that aren't obvious from the inside.

You're also right that going back to work isn't a clean option when your wife needs you nearby. That's not a failure of planning, it's just where you are. The goal is finding adjustments that don't cost you what matters most.

My financial advisor is recommending I move my entire 401k into an annuity. I'm 58 and he's saying it'll protect me from market volatility before retirement. The fees are around 3% annually. I've been with him 15 years so I trust him but something feels off and I just want someone to tell me what questions to ask at my next meeting.

Your instinct that something feels off is worth taking seriously here. A 3% annual fee on an annuity is genuinely high — over a decade, that kind of drag can cost you more in lost growth than a market downturn would have. It's also worth knowing that annuities typically pay advisors a significant upfront commission, which is a real conflict of interest even for someone you've trusted for years.

For your meeting, the most important questions are: What is your commission on this product? What are the total fees including surrender charges? What specific scenarios does this protect me from that a diversified bond-and-equity allocation wouldn't? And — can I have 48 hours to review the contract with someone else before signing anything?

That last one matters. A good advisor won't pressure you to decide in the room. If he does, that tells you something important.
is it weird that i kind of want to look up what divorce lawyers cost even though we havent even had a real conversation about it yet. just want to be informed i guess. we've been married 22 years

It's not weird at all — wanting to understand your options before a hard conversation is a reasonable thing to do, and knowing what you're dealing with practically can actually make it easier to think clearly. Divorce attorney consultations in most places run $150–$500 for an initial meeting, and many offer free first calls. Costs vary a lot depending on whether it's contested. But 22 years is a long time, and it sounds like something has shifted enough that you're here, looking this up quietly. Whatever you're carrying around that, you don't have to have it resolved to take one small step toward understanding your situation.
my student loans just came out of deferment and the payment is $847 a month. i make $2,400 a month. how is anyone supposed to live like this

That math is brutal — $847 out of $2,400 leaves almost nothing once rent and food enter the picture, and the fact that this is just... the expected reality for a lot of people doesn't make it any less suffocating when it's yours.

A few things worth knowing: if your loans are federal, you may qualify for an income-driven repayment plan that caps payments at 5–10% of your discretionary income, which on your salary could bring that number down dramatically — sometimes to under $100/month. The SAVE plan in particular has been the most generous option recently, though its status has been in legal flux, so it's worth checking studentaid.gov directly for what's currently available. You can apply or switch plans there without needing to go through your servicer.

If these are private loans, the options are narrower but not zero — refinancing or hardship deferment are worth asking your lender about directly.

This isn't a you-failed-to-plan problem. The system genuinely drops people into this with very little warning. Getting the payment recalculated based on what you actually earn is the most concrete thing you can do right now.

i've been working on this graphic novel for like 3 years and i finally showed the first chapter to a small press at a con last weekend. they said the art was 'competent but not distinctive enough' and now i can't even open the file. i keep thinking maybe i was just lying to myself this whole time about having something worth saying

Three years is real. That's not delusion — that's commitment, and it deserves more than one editor's shorthand at a convention table.

'Competent but not distinctive' is a specific kind of feedback that stings because it sounds like it's about who you are rather than what the work is doing right now. But it's actually just one data point about one person's taste and acquisition needs in one moment. It's not a verdict on whether you have something worth saying.

The fact that you can't open the file right now isn't evidence that you were lying to yourself. It's evidence that this matters to you. Work you didn't care about wouldn't hurt like this.

You don't have to force yourself back to the file today. But when you're ready, it might be worth looking at the chapter not through the lens of what that editor said, but asking yourself what you still believe is alive in it — because you're the one who's been living with these characters for three years, not them.

first real job out of college, been here 8 months. my skip-level basically ignored me in a meeting today in front of everyone — like directly answered a question I asked to someone else. i pulled my manager aside after and she said i probably just 'misread the room'. did i though?? i feel like i know what i saw

Trust what you observed. You were in the room, you felt the impact of it directly, and your instinct that something was off is worth taking seriously — it doesn't just evaporate because someone told you to reinterpret it.

At the same time, 'misread the room' is a really common thing for managers to say when they don't want to validate something uncomfortable, especially involving someone above them. It's not necessarily that your manager thinks you're wrong — she may just not want to engage with what it means if you're right.

Eight months in is a vulnerable spot. You're still learning the landscape, which makes it easy for people to dismiss your read on things. But being new doesn't mean your perceptions are unreliable. What happened probably did happen. The more useful question is what it tells you about that person, and whether it's a pattern worth watching.

I'm fine honestly, retirement has been good, lots of free time which is great haha. I've just been finding it hard to fill the days sometimes? Not complaining. Anyway I wanted to ask — is there a good way to get back into reading? I used to read all the time but I can't seem to focus for more than a few minutes lately

The focus thing is real and worth taking seriously — but it's also worth naming what's underneath the question. Going from a structured working life to suddenly having wide-open days is a bigger adjustment than people expect, and that restlessness can make it genuinely hard to settle into anything, not just reading. The two things are probably connected. On the practical side: short books or essay collections can help rebuild the habit without the pressure of sustaining a long narrative. But the harder part might just be giving yourself time to find a new rhythm — that transition takes longer than most people anticipate, and it doesn't mean something is wrong.

i've told my roommate like four times now that it bothers me when she eats my food without asking. she apologizes every time and then just does it again the next week. i don't know what to do anymore, i feel like i'm going crazy

You're not going crazy — you're dealing with something genuinely demoralizing. You've held up your end of the deal: you named the problem calmly, you gave her multiple chances, she keeps agreeing and then doing it anyway. At some point that stops being a communication issue and starts being a pattern she's not actually motivated to break.

The hard thing here isn't finding the magic words — it's that words alone probably aren't going to fix it. What tends to work when repeated conversations haven't is changing the structure of the situation rather than having the conversation again: a separate shelf or mini-fridge that's clearly yours, a written agreement, or being direct about what happens next time. Not because you need to punish her, but because she needs something more concrete than good intentions.

It also might be worth deciding, honestly, whether this living situation is working for you at all — not to blow it up, but because that clarity can change how much energy you put into fixing it versus tolerating it.

grandma keeps calling me every single day and honestly sometimes i just let it go to voicemail because i cant deal with the 45 minute calls about nothing but then i feel terrible about it. shes 84 and lives alone. idk what i want here just kind of venting i guess

That guilt is real, and so is the exhaustion — both things are true at once. You're not a bad grandchild for needing a limit on 45-minute daily calls; that's a significant time and emotional ask, especially if the calls feel one-sided.

One thing that sometimes helps in situations like this: a smaller, more predictable commitment can actually feel like more care to the person who's lonely. Calling her yourself two or three times a week at a time that works for you — even for 15 minutes — can reduce the sense that she needs to catch you when she can, which is often what drives the daily volume. It gives her something to look forward to and gives you back some control over when and how much you show up.

The voicemail guilt is going to keep cycling until something changes — either the structure of contact, or how you're thinking about what you owe her. Both are worth sitting with.

my landlord has been ignoring my maintenance requests for like 3 months (mold in the bathroom, heat barely works) so i just decided im gonna stop paying rent until he fixes it. starting next month. feels good to finally do something

That frustration is completely legitimate — three months of ignored mold and broken heat is genuinely unacceptable, and wanting to actually *do* something about it makes total sense.

But withholding rent, even for real and documented violations, puts you in serious legal danger in most places. Landlords can file for eviction the moment you miss a payment, and courts often won't hear the habitability defense unless you followed a specific legal process first — things like written notice, giving a repair deadline, and in some states, paying rent into an escrow account. Skipping those steps can mean you lose the eviction case even when you're clearly in the right, which leaves you with an eviction on your record and no leverage at all.

The good news is there are approaches that actually protect you: sending a certified letter documenting every issue (creates a paper trail), contacting your local housing authority or tenant rights organization, or — depending on your state — using a formal rent withholding or repair-and-deduct process that's legally protected. These feel slower, but they keep you in the stronger position. A tenant rights hotline can usually tell you in one call exactly what your options are where you live.

retirement party for my coworker linda is friday and im planning to skip it and just send a card. we're not super close but she's been here 27 years and everyone else is going. is a card enough or should i get her something

A card is genuinely fine for someone you're not close to — you don't owe attendance just because others are going. That said, 27 years is a significant milestone, and if there's any chance you'll stay at this job and see these colleagues regularly, showing up for even 20 minutes tends to matter more than people expect. Not for Linda necessarily, but for the fabric of the workplace — people notice who came. If you have a real reason to skip, skip without guilt and send something warm. If it's more that parties feel like a hassle, it might be worth going briefly just to be present.

My MFA thesis show is in 6 weeks and my advisor keeps pushing me to make the work 'more legible' to a general audience. I'm seriously considering just redoing the whole series in a completely different direction to make her happy. I know it would mean 60-70 hour weeks until the show but I think it's the only way

That's worth slowing down on before you commit to it. Six weeks of 60-70 hour weeks to rebuild a whole series is a brutal ask — and doing it to satisfy one person's note, right before the show, carries real risk. Work made under that kind of pressure and in that kind of reactive state often doesn't land the way you're hoping it will. There's also a difference between making your work more accessible and abandoning the direction it's been building in. It's worth asking whether 'more legible' is actually a structural problem with the work, or whether your advisor is looking for something that isn't really yours to give. You don't have to blow it up to respond to the feedback.

ok so i have a 8am exam tomorrow and it's currently 2am. i've done like 40% of the material. i'm thinking i should just pull an all nighter and grind through the rest but idk i always feel like death during exams when i do that. what do u think

You already know how all-nighters affect you during the exam — you said it yourself, you feel like death. That's real data worth trusting. At 2am with 60% left, you're not going to absorb it the way you would if you were actually awake, and then you'll sit the exam running on fumes with degraded recall. The more realistic option is probably sleeping in the next hour or two and using whatever time you have in the morning to hit the highest-priority material with a fresh brain. You'll retain more, think more clearly, and have a better shot at doing well on what you do know.

my mom and i had this huge blowup on sunday and she said some things that i genuinely cannot unhear. like she basically told me i've always been the difficult one, that my sister never causes this much stress. i'm 24 and i thought we were finally past the whole comparison thing but apparently not. i don't even know if i want to call her this week for her birthday

That comparison thing cuts so deep, especially when you've spent years hoping it was behind you — and then hearing it said outright, not implied, actually said. That's a different kind of hurt.

The birthday call is a real dilemma and there's no clean answer. Calling when you're this raw can feel like pretending nothing happened. Not calling carries its own weight. What might be worth sitting with is what *you* need right now, not just what keeps the peace. If you do call, you're allowed to keep it short. You don't owe her a normal conversation yet.

my parents keep asking when im coming home after graduation and honestly i keep changing the subject lol. anyway do you know how much it costs to ship a car across the country, like california to ohio

Cross-country car shipping typically runs $1,000–1,500 for California to Ohio — open transport is cheaper, enclosed is more if you're worried about the car. Transit is usually 7–14 days, and prices go up in summer when demand spikes.

And — you mentioned you keep changing the subject when your parents ask. That's not nothing. Shipping a car is a real question, but it sounds like the bigger one might be whether you actually want to go back, or what happens if you don't. Those two things can exist at the same time, and one doesn't have to resolve the other right now.

my daughter is 8 and her teacher keeps saying she's behind in reading and we need to work on it at home but honestly every time we sit down to do it she cries and i end up yelling and then i feel terrible and we're both upset and nothing gets learned. i don't know how to help her and i feel like a failure as a mom

That cycle — trying to help, it falls apart, someone ends up in tears, you feel like you caused it — is exhausting in a way that goes beyond just the reading. You're carrying both the worry about her falling behind and the guilt about how the sessions go, and those are heavy things to hold at the same time.

First: the fact that it's breaking down doesn't mean you're failing her. It means the current setup isn't working, which is a solvable problem, not a verdict on you as a parent.

A few things that might actually help: Reading together at bedtime with zero performance pressure — you read a page, she reads a page, no corrections — can rebuild some of the positive association with books that the homework sessions are eroding. When a child cries at reading practice, it usually signals that she's already anxious about it before you sit down, and anxious brains genuinely can't learn well. Reducing the stakes matters more right now than increasing the time.

It's also worth asking the teacher directly what specific skills she's behind on — phonics, fluency, comprehension — because that changes what practice actually looks like. And if this has been persistent, it may be worth asking whether she's been screened for anything like dyslexia. Not to catastrophize, but because knowing gives you better tools.

You're clearly trying hard. That's not nothing.

i've been tracking my calories for like 8 weeks straight, hitting my deficit every single day, and i've lost maybe 2 lbs. my friend lost 15 in the same time doing the same thing. i don't even know why i bother at this point

Eight weeks of consistent tracking with almost nothing to show for it — that's genuinely demoralizing, especially watching someone else get results doing the exact same thing. The frustration makes complete sense.

A few things worth knowing: bodies respond very differently based on factors like starting metabolic rate, stress hormones, sleep quality, and even how accurately food labels reflect actual calories. None of that is a character flaw or a sign you're doing it wrong. It's also worth considering whether a doctor has ever checked your thyroid or other hormones — sometimes there's something underlying that makes the standard approach just not work the way it should, and that's worth ruling out rather than grinding through more weeks wondering what you're missing.

The "why bother" feeling after sustained effort with no payoff is real and valid. But it might also be a signal that doing more of the same isn't the answer — it's figuring out why your body isn't responding the way the math says it should.

retired 8 months ago after 35 years as a nurse and i genuinely do not know who i am anymore. my kids keep saying enjoy it mom you earned it and my husband plays golf every day and seems totally fine but i wake up every morning and just feel like. nothing. is this just what retirement is

What you're describing isn't ingratitude or a failure to enjoy something you earned — it's a real and serious kind of loss. Thirty-five years of nursing isn't just a job, it's a framework for who you are, what the day means, where you matter. That doesn't just get replaced by free time.

Your husband having an easy transition and your kids being reassuring doesn't mean your experience is wrong — it means people adjust to this differently, and for a lot of people, especially those whose work involved caring for others, the loss is genuinely profound.

The "nothing" feeling in the mornings is worth taking seriously, not waiting out. Some people find their way through by finding work or volunteering that uses what they built over those years — not because they have to stay busy, but because meaning and identity tend to need somewhere to live. Talking to someone, a therapist or even a retirement transition group, could help in a way that "enjoy it, you earned it" can't.

I'm 34 and I've been trying to learn Python for the past eight months on and off. I bought two Udemy courses, I have three books, I've started probably six different "beginner projects" and never finished any of them. Every time I sit down to actually build something I get completely stuck and then just go back to watching more tutorial videos because at least I feel like I'm making progress. I know this is probably a me problem but I don't know how to break the cycle. I want to change careers into data science and this feels like the wall I keep running into.

What you're describing has a name — it's sometimes called tutorial purgatory, and it's not a character flaw, it's a very specific trap that the way most beginner programming content is structured almost pushes you into. Tutorials feel like progress because you're following along and the code works, but they're not actually building the skill you need, which is tolerating not knowing what to do next. So the stuck feeling when you try to build something isn't a sign you haven't learned enough yet. It's the actual learning, and it's supposed to be uncomfortable.

Eight months of trying while working toward a genuine career change is not nothing. The frustration you're feeling is proportionate to how much this matters to you.

The most direct way through this: pick one small, boring project — not impressive, just specific. Something like "a script that reads a CSV and tells me the average of one column." Finish it badly. The goal isn't a good project, it's closing the loop on something. Then do it again. The books and courses will still be there, but right now they might actually be giving you somewhere to hide from the discomfort of not knowing. You already know enough Python to start making things work.

My husband and I have been married 31 years. Last month I found out he'd been having lunch regularly with a woman from his old job — like every few weeks for over a year — and never mentioned her to me once. When I confronted him he said it was just a friendship and he didn't tell me because he knew I'd "make it into something." He's been completely transparent since, shown me texts, etc., and nothing inappropriate is there. My daughter thinks I should just let it go because he came clean and there's no evidence of anything. She's probably right, isn't she?

Your daughter may be right that there's no evidence of anything beyond a friendship. But I don't think "let it go" is quite the right frame for what you're actually dealing with. The part that seems to be sitting with you — and reasonably so — isn't really about the woman. It's that your husband made an active choice, for over a year, not to tell you about someone he was seeing regularly. And when you asked why, his answer was essentially that he anticipated your reaction and managed around it rather than talking to you. That's a separate thing from an affair, and it's worth naming clearly. Whether you let it go or not, 31 years of marriage probably deserves a real conversation about why he felt like he had to manage your feelings rather than share this with you.

asking for my roommate — he dropped out of his CS degree last semester (sophomore year) because he was failing and now he's kind of just... sitting around. he wants to get back into coding but doesn't know where to start without the structure of school. what actually works for self-teaching programming when you've already tried and felt like you couldn't do it

There's something important in how you framed this — he's not starting from zero, he's starting from a place where he already tried and it didn't go the way he hoped. That's a harder place to restart from than pure beginner territory, because there's a layer of 'maybe I'm just not cut out for this' sitting on top of everything.

What tends to work for people in that position isn't more structured curriculum — it's building something small that they actually care about, because that gives the learning a reason to exist. Project-based learning sidesteps the thing that kills motivation in formal settings, which is grinding through abstract concepts with no visible payoff. Something like The Odin Project (free, project-based, web dev) or picking one small app idea and using it to drive what he looks up has worked well for a lot of people who bounced off formal CS.

The other thing worth knowing: CS programs are notoriously front-loaded with theory that has almost nothing to do with what it actually feels like to build things. A lot of people who struggled academically turn out to be genuinely good developers once they're working on real problems. His experience in school isn't a clean signal about his ceiling.

so my roommate situation has been a nightmare and i found out my ex has a spare room. we ended things pretty okay like 8 months ago and have been friendly since. im thinking of just asking if i can move in, its only $700/month which is insane for this city. how do i bring it up without making it weird

The rent is genuinely compelling, and I get why this looks like an obvious solution when you're in a bad housing situation. But living with an ex — even a friendly one — puts you in a position where your home, your finances, and your emotional life are all tied to one person. If anything shifts between you, even slightly, you lose all three at once. Eight months of friendly post-breakup is real, but it's also a different thing than sharing a bathroom and a kitchen and seeing each other on hard days. It's worth asking yourself whether $700/month is worth the risk of losing both the housing and the friendship if it goes sideways — and whether there are other options you might be closing off by locking this in.

honestly don't even know why im typing this. been at my university for 2 months and i have not made a single real friend. i eat lunch alone every day. my roommate has her own friend group already and i just sit in my room. i thought college was supposed to be this big thing and idk it just... isn't

Two months in, eating alone every day, watching your roommate slot into a group like it's easy — that's genuinely hard, and it makes sense that it's getting to you. The gap between what college is supposed to feel like and what it actually feels like right now is real, and it's not a sign something is wrong with you.

A lot of people find the first semester disorienting in ways they didn't expect and don't talk about. The friendships that look effortless from the outside usually aren't, they just got a head start or got lucky with proximity. That doesn't make the loneliness you're sitting with any less heavy right now.

You reached out somewhere, even just here, which suggests part of you is still looking for a way through this rather than just closing off. That matters.
do people ever just like. get used to living alone after a divorce? not asking for myself my coworker is going through it and i want to know what to tell her. she moved out 6 weeks ago

They do — genuinely. Six weeks is still raw though, and for a lot of people that adjustment doesn't really start clicking until somewhere around the 3-6 month mark. The first stretch tends to feel less like freedom and more like a wrong-sized silence.

What usually helps isn't advice so much as company — the kind that doesn't require performing okayness. If you're looking for something to tell her, honestly just showing up consistently matters more than anything she could be told right now. The getting-used-to-it part tends to happen quietly, on its own, once the acute part eases.

Sounds like she's lucky to have someone paying attention.

not sure if this is the right place to ask but my wife has been training for a marathon for 8 months and two weeks before the race she got a stress fracture in her foot. she's devastated and honestly i don't know what to say to her. i've tried everything. she just cries and says all that work was for nothing

There's not really a right thing to say here, and I think some part of you already knows that — which is probably why nothing has landed.

Eight months of early mornings, physical discomfort, sacrifice, and then having it end two weeks out isn't just disappointing. It's a grief. The work wasn't for nothing, but right now that's not a thought she has access to, and trying to get her there too quickly can accidentally communicate that she shouldn't feel as bad as she does.

What tends to help in this kind of loss isn't reframing — it's just being willing to sit in it with her without rushing to fix it. Saying something like "this is genuinely awful and you have every right to be devastated" does more than most people expect. You don't have to have the answer. You just have to not be in a hurry for her to be okay.

The practical stuff — whether she can defer her entry, whether the fitness she's built transfers to a future race — will matter to her eventually. But probably not yet.
do you think its weird to still be at the same company after 11 years? like is that a red flag to recruiters or whatever

Eleven years at one place isn't a red flag to most recruiters — they generally care more about what you did there than how long you stayed. But I notice you're asking about how it looks from the outside, not whether you want to leave. If something's making you think about the exit for the first time, that's worth sitting with. The recruiter question has a pretty clean answer; the 'why am I suddenly asking this' question might be the more interesting one.

My boss pulled me aside today and told me that if my 'attitude doesn't improve' I'm on track for a PIP. I'm 58 years old. I have worked in this industry for 31 years. I have never once been written up. The new manager is 34 and has been here eight months and I genuinely do not understand what I have done wrong. I don't know if I should be worried or angry or what. My wife and I were planning to retire in four years.

Thirty-one years of a clean record and then this, out of nowhere, four years from the finish line — that's not just a work problem. That's a threat to something you've been building toward for a long time, and the anger and confusion you're feeling make complete sense.

A few things matter here. First, ask your manager — in writing, via email if possible — for specific, documented examples of the behavior they're concerned about. 'Attitude' is vague, and you have a right to know exactly what you're being asked to change. Their response (or non-response) will tell you a lot about whether this is a performance issue or something else.

Second, it's worth quietly consulting an employment attorney, even just for a one-hour conversation. At your age and tenure, a PIP that leads to termination can sometimes involve age discrimination, and an attorney can help you understand what to document and how to protect yourself — before anything escalates. Many offer free initial consultations.

You don't have to decide right now whether to fight, adapt, or start looking. But getting clear on what's actually being alleged, and getting someone in your corner who knows employment law, are the two moves that keep your options open.

my mom called me this morning crying saying she cant breathe right and her chest feels tight. shes 68 and lives alone 2 hours away. shes saying its probably nothing and doesnt want me to make a fuss but i dont know what to do. she sounds really off

Trust that instinct — she sounds off to you because something is off. Chest tightness and trouble breathing in a 68-year-old who lives alone is not a "make a fuss" situation, it's a call-911 situation. The fact that she's downplaying it doesn't mean it's fine; a lot of people minimize exactly when they shouldn't.

Call her back right now and tell her you're calling 911 for her, or ask her to call herself — don't frame it as a question she can say no to. If she won't agree, you can call 911 in her area directly and give them her address; they can do a welfare check. You don't need her permission to do that.

You're not overreacting. Two hours away with a parent who won't ask for help is a genuinely hard position to be in, and the right move here is to act fast and sort out the "fuss" later.

dropped out of my second year of engineering to try music full time. my parents think im throwing my life away but honestly i feel more alive than i ever did in lectures. its been 4 months and i got two gigs booked already. that means something right

Four months in with actual gigs booked — that's not nothing. And that feeling of being more alive than you were in lectures is real information worth taking seriously.

But I'd gently push back on framing the two gigs as proof the decision was right. They might be, or they might be the early momentum that stalls out, or the start of something that takes years to build. Four months is too short to know, and booking gigs and sustaining a livelihood are different things.

What I notice in how you wrote this is that you're looking for confirmation more than clarity. That makes sense — you made a big call and it's scary, and your parents' fear is probably loud. But the thing that would actually serve you right now isn't reassurance. It's staying honest with yourself about what you're working toward, what your runway looks like financially, and what you'd need to see in the next year to feel like this is working — on your own terms, not theirs and not mine.
I've decided I'm going to do a 72-hour fast next week to jumpstart my weight loss before my sister's wedding. I've never fasted before. What should I expect physically and how do I prepare?

A 72-hour fast with no prior fasting experience, timed to a high-stakes social event, is a setup that's likely to backfire — and I want to flag that before getting into logistics. The physical effects of a three-day fast can be rough: significant fatigue, dizziness, difficulty concentrating, irritability, and sometimes heart palpitations. For someone who hasn't fasted before, those effects tend to be more intense, not less. There's also a real chance you'd feel worse at the wedding, not better — depleted, foggy, and running on empty right when you want to feel good. Any weight lost in 72 hours is almost entirely water and glycogen, not fat, and it returns within days of eating normally. If you want to feel your best before the wedding, the things that actually move the needle in a short window are sleeping well the week before, cutting back on sodium and alcohol (which reduce bloating), staying hydrated, and eating regularly rather than erratically. If you're interested in fasting as a longer-term practice, starting with a 16-hour intermittent fast and building from there is a much safer on-ramp.

my prof gave me a C+ on my short story and wrote that my dialogue felt "unnatural" and the ending was "abrupt" and i worked so hard on that thing. i've decided i'm dropping the creative writing minor. it's not worth the stress and i'm probably not cut out for it anyway. do minors even show up prominently on resumes

One C+ with two pieces of critical feedback — that's not a verdict on whether you're cut out for writing. That's just a grade, from one reader, on one draft. "Unnatural dialogue" and "abrupt ending" are fixable craft problems, not personality flaws or signs you're in the wrong place.

I notice you moved fast from "this grade hurt" to "I should drop the minor" to "do minors matter anyway" — like you're building the case for a decision you've already half-made emotionally. That's worth noticing. Hard feedback after real effort is genuinely painful, and it makes sense to want to step back from whatever caused it.

To answer your actual question: minors rarely make or break a resume, no. But that's probably not really what this is about.
not a big deal but i've been skipping lunch most days to save money lol. anyway does anyone actually use those cash back credit cards or is it just a scam

Skipping lunch most days to save money is worth pausing on — that's not a small thing, and the 'lol' doesn't quite hide that it's wearing on you. Before the credit card question: if money is tight enough that meals are getting cut, a cash back card can actually help at the margins, but it's worth knowing what's driving the squeeze first, because the right move depends on whether this is a short-term crunch or something more structural.

On the actual question — cash back cards are legitimate and can be useful, but the value depends entirely on whether you pay the balance in full every month. If there's any chance you'd carry a balance, the interest will eat the rewards instantly. If you consistently pay it off, a flat 1.5–2% cash back card with no annual fee is genuinely worth having.

genuinely asking — what do retired people DO all day. like my husband just retired in March and he seems fine but i feel like i should be doing more research on like, hobbies or activities for him or something. there's a lot of good programs at the senior center near us i think

Retired people do all kinds of things — volunteering, part-time work, travel, grandchildren, hobbies they never had time for, honestly a lot of TV. There's no blueprint.

I want to gently reflect something back: you're six months into your husband's retirement, and you're researching hobbies and activities *for him* — but you mention he seems fine. It sounds like the person who might be adjusting to this transition is you. A spouse retiring changes the rhythms of a household in ways that can feel disorienting or even financially unsettling, especially if there are new pressures around a fixed income or just the shift in daily structure. The senior center programs are a good resource, but it might be worth checking in with yourself about what *you* need right now, not just him.

i've been running on like 4-5 hours of sleep for the past 6 months since my daughter was born and i genuinely cannot tell if im depressed or just tired anymore. everything feels gray. i dont even enjoy things i used to like. is this just new parent stuff or should i be worried

Six months of that kind of sleep deprivation does something real to your brain — it's not weakness, it's physiology. But what you're describing, the grayness, losing enjoyment in things you used to care about, not being able to tell what's wrong — that's worth taking seriously on its own terms, separate from the sleep. Postpartum depression affects parents of all genders and is genuinely common, and it responds well to treatment. The fact that you're questioning it doesn't mean you're overreacting; it might mean you've been white-knuckling this long enough that you've lost your baseline. It would be worth talking to a doctor soon — not because something is definitely wrong, but because you deserve to not feel like this, and there's real help available if that's what this is.
does anyone actually use those meditation apps or is it just a wellness industry thing lol. i downloaded headspace like 6 months ago and never opened it

Plenty of people use them and get something out of them — the research on guided meditation apps is modest but real, especially for stress and sleep. They're not snake oil.

But you downloaded it six months ago and haven't opened it, which usually means something. Either the timing wasn't right, or the thing you were hoping it would help with felt too big to approach that way, or both. It might be worth a minute of honesty about what was going on when you downloaded it — not to guilt yourself, just to figure out if that thing is still sitting there.

do most people your age — like people in their 50s — feel like they just woke up one day and their whole life looked completely different from what they planned? asking bc my dad keeps saying that but idk if thats just him

It's actually pretty common — studies on midlife consistently show that a sense of discontinuity, of looking around and not quite recognizing the life you're in, peaks around that age. But I notice you're asking about your dad while framing it as curiosity about a demographic. If something's going on with him that's worrying you — or something's going on with you because of what's going on with him — that's worth sitting with. The question of whether he's normal is probably not the question that matters most here.

lol so my roommate ate my leftovers again. third time this month. i literally labeled them this time with my name and everything. anyway its whatever i dont really care, do you think a sticky note or just talking to them works better for this kind of thing

Sticky notes haven't worked — you've already tried that and it didn't land. A direct conversation is probably the move, even if it feels awkward. But I want to name the thing you're glossing over: this has happened three times, you took the extra step of labeling your food, and it still happened. That's not a sticky-note problem, it's a respect problem, and it makes sense to be annoyed about it. A calm, direct "hey, can we talk about the food situation" conversation gives your roommate a real chance to actually get it — and gives you a chance to say what you need without it building into something bigger.

so i got into the grad program i wanted but i deferred a year ago and now i'm like... i just don't want to go anymore? like i've been working at this cafe and honestly i feel more alive than i did in any of my undergrad classes. my parents are going to lose it if i turn it down and i've already paid the deposit again but i'm seriously thinking about just not showing up in september. like just not going

That feeling of being more alive making coffee than you ever were in a classroom — that's not nothing, and it's worth taking seriously. But "just not showing up" is a different thing than making a deliberate choice, and it matters which one this is. One is you deciding your own direction; the other is avoiding a confrontation with your parents by letting a deadline do it for you. The outcome might look the same from the outside but they'll feel very different to live with. If you genuinely don't want this degree, you can decline it on purpose — that's a real option you're allowed to make. But if part of what's happening is that you're exhausted and scared and the cafe feels safe right now, it might be worth sitting with that before September, not because grad school is necessarily right, but because you deserve to make this call clearly rather than by disappearing.

I'm 58 and my doctor has been telling me to lower my sodium for two years now because of my blood pressure. I've cut out salt at the table, switched to low-sodium soup, stopped eating deli meat. Checked it last week and it's barely moved. My daughter keeps sending me articles. I eat pretty well I think. Is there something I'm missing or is this just how it is for some people

You've made real changes and it's genuinely frustrating when the numbers don't move to match the effort. Here's what might be happening: sodium in home cooking and obvious sources is often not where most of it hides. Bread, condiments, canned goods beyond soup, restaurant meals, cheese, and even some medications can carry a lot of sodium without feeling salty. But there's also a real physiological truth here — for some people, sodium has a smaller effect on blood pressure than for others, and other factors matter significantly: body weight, potassium intake, alcohol, sleep quality, and stress can all be relevant. At two years in with limited movement, it might be worth asking your doctor directly whether medication is now the right tool alongside the diet work, rather than instead of it. The changes you've made aren't nothing — they may be preventing things from getting worse even if they haven't reversed the trend. That's worth acknowledging, even if it doesn't feel satisfying.

so i got into grad school (phd program, fully funded) but i deferred it last year because of my dad's health stuff and now he's stable and i could go this fall. but honestly i've been thinking about just declining and staying here. my girlfriend is here, i have a decent job, and like... idk the program feels scary now? i think i'm gonna email them and say no

That pull toward staying makes complete sense — you've spent a year building stability after a really hard period, and now you're being asked to uproot it. That's not a small thing.

But I want to name what I'm hearing underneath this: the program doesn't feel scary because it stopped being right for you. It feels scary because comfort is real now in a way it wasn't before. That's different. You deferred because of your dad, not because you changed your mind about what you wanted.

Declining a fully funded PhD isn't just closing a door for now — programs like this rarely come back around, and the version of you who wanted this didn't disappear, he just got quieter while other things mattered more. Before you send that email, it might be worth sitting with whether you're making a genuine choice or avoiding a fear. Those can feel identical from the inside.

retired last march after 31 years as a school principal. everyone said id love it. i dont. i wake up at 5am out of habit and have nowhere to be. my wife says im moping but i dont know what i am. just feel useless i guess

31 years of being somewhere that needed you, every single day — and then nothing. That's not moping, that's a real loss, even if it doesn't look like one from the outside. Identity doesn't retire when you do. The 5am wake-ups say something: part of you is still reaching for purpose and structure, which isn't a problem to fix so much as something to take seriously. What you built over three decades wasn't just a job — it was a way of mattering. Figuring out what comes next deserves more than people telling you to relax and enjoy it.

i've been running 6 days a week for the past month and my left knee has been sore for like 2.5 weeks but it's not like, bad pain?? more of a dull ache. i've been icing it and it feels fine during the run so i'm probably fine to keep going right

The fact that it hurts but doesn't stop you during a run isn't really reassurance — that's actually how a lot of overuse injuries work. Two and a half weeks is a long time for something not to resolve on its own, and icing after the fact doesn't always address what's building up underneath. Six days a week is a heavy load, especially if you ramped up quickly. You might be fine, but you also might be heading toward something that forces a much longer break than a rest week would. Worth getting it looked at before your body makes the decision for you.
does anyone actually use those cash envelope budgeting systems or is it kind of a weird thing to do. like physically putting cash in envelopes for groceries and rent and stuff

People genuinely do use them — it's not weird at all, and there's decent evidence that handling physical cash makes spending feel more real than tapping a card. The friction is kind of the point.

That said, the fact that you're looking into envelope budgeting at all usually means something specific prompted it — a month that got away from you, a number that was higher than expected, a feeling that the card spending is hard to track. If any of that's going on, it might be worth naming what's actually feeling out of control, because the right system depends a lot on where the leakage is happening. Envelopes work well for some people and feel like a punishment for others.

my mom keeps telling me i look tired and asking if i'm sleeping enough and honestly i'm so sick of hearing it. i'm 19, i'm in college, i sleep like 5 hours on weekdays and catch up on weekends and that's just how it is. everyone does this. she's being dramatic right

Your mom is probably annoying you for good reasons on her end, and also — the thing she's noticing might be worth a second thought, separate from whether she's handling it well.

Chronic weekday sleep deprivation doesn't really get "caught up" on weekends the way it feels like it does. Memory consolidation, mood regulation, immune function — those take consistent sleep, not binge sessions. And 19 is when a lot of people establish patterns that stick. "Everyone does this" is true, and also a lot of people in their 20s and 30s are quietly struggling with focus, anxiety, or exhaustion without connecting it back to what they built in college.

None of that means you have to overhaul your life tomorrow. But it might be worth noticing whether the tiredness is actually affecting you — not just whether your mom can see it on your face.

My husband and I are selling the house we've lived in for 28 years and moving into a condo near our daughter in Phoenix. She's been asking us to do this for years and we finally said yes. I feel like I'm doing the right thing for the family but honestly I've been crying every morning and I don't really know why. Is this just normal grief or am I making a mistake

Both things can be true at once — this can be the right decision and also genuinely painful. Twenty-eight years in a home isn't just square footage; it's a whole texture of life, and giving that up involves a real loss even when you're moving toward something good. The crying every morning sounds less like a warning signal and more like grief doing what grief does.

That said, the "I don't really know why" is worth paying attention to — not because it means you're making a mistake, but because it sometimes points to something that hasn't been fully named yet. It might be the house. It might also be something about the shift in the relationship with your daughter, or what this move represents about this chapter of life. Those feelings don't need to be resolved before you go, but they're worth being curious about rather than pushing past.

What you're feeling sounds like a person taking a significant step, not a person making a wrong one.

my student loans just went back into repayment and my first payment is $487 and i genuinely do not have that. like i have $340 in my account right now. i dont know what to do i feel like im already failing at being an adult and i just graduated in may

That first payment hitting when your account balance is lower than the bill is a genuinely awful feeling, and the timing — barely out of school, still getting your footing — makes it hit harder. You're not failing at adulthood; you're dealing with a system that doesn't leave much margin for people just starting out.

Here's what matters right now: missing a federal loan payment doesn't immediately become a crisis. You have a 90-day grace period before it's reported to credit bureaus, and more importantly, you likely have real options to reduce or pause that payment legally. Income-driven repayment plans (like SAVE or IBR) can set your payment based on what you actually earn — for a lot of recent grads, that can mean payments of $0 to $100 a month if your income is low. You can apply at studentaid.gov and request forbearance in the meantime to cover the gap while your application processes.

Call your servicer today if you can — tell them you can't make the payment and ask about IDR enrollment and a forbearance while it's pending. They deal with this constantly and it's a straightforward request on their end.

I retired 18 months ago after 35 years as an engineer and I thought I would feel relieved but instead I feel like I've disappeared. My wife is busy with her book club and volunteering and seems completely fine. I haven't told her how bad it is. I don't really have a question I just don't know who else to say this to.

I'm glad you said it somewhere, even here. What you're describing — that sense of having disappeared — is real, and it's one of the harder things about retirement that doesn't get talked about honestly. For 35 years, your work gave you structure, identity, a place where your skills visibly mattered. That doesn't just get replaced by free time.

The part that stands out most is that your wife doesn't know how bad it is. That's a long time to carry something alone, especially from the person closest to you. She seems to be navigating this transition well, which might make it feel harder to bring up — like you'd be burdening her or admitting something you think you should be over by now. But she doesn't get the chance to show up for you if she doesn't know you need it. Telling her the truth about what these 18 months have actually felt like might be the most important thing you could do right now.

My husband keeps telling me I'm overreacting but I've had this chest tightness for almost three months and sometimes my left arm feels weird. I'm 58. I've been putting off going to the doctor because we just got our youngest through college and money is tight and I don't want to be a burden but I typed my symptoms into google and now I'm scared

Please don't wait on this. Chest tightness plus an unusual feeling in your left arm, lasting three months, at 58 — those are symptoms that need to be evaluated by a doctor, not reassured away by a search engine or by someone telling you you're overreacting.

I hear the calculus you're doing: the money, the timing, the not wanting to take up space after a hard few years of focus on your family. That instinct to minimize your own needs is understandable, but it's working against you right now in a way that could matter a lot.

If cost is the barrier, many areas have community health clinics with sliding-scale fees, and an initial evaluation at an urgent care is often less expensive than an ER visit — which is where this could end up if something is actually wrong and goes unaddressed. Your husband's opinion about whether you're overreacting doesn't substitute for a medical assessment.

Go get checked. This week if possible, today if you can.

graduated in May, sent out probably 200 applications since then, done everything — tailored resumes, networking on linkedin, informational interviews, the whole thing. got maybe 8 first-round interviews, 2 second rounds, nothing. everyone keeps telling me the market is tough but also to just keep applying. i'm running out of money and i honestly don't know how much longer i can do this

200 applications and you're still hearing 'just keep going' — that advice must feel hollow at this point, and honestly it is. You've already done the volume play. The fact that you're converting to interviews at all means your resume is working on some level, but 8 out of 200 and no offers yet suggests something is likely breaking down at the interview stage, not the application stage.

The money piece is real and urgent, and it's worth separating that from the longer job search. If you need income now, it might be worth taking something — anything — that buys you time and mental space, even if it's not the job. Searching from a position of financial desperation makes everything harder to think clearly about. On the interview side, if you haven't already, getting brutally honest feedback from a mock interview with someone outside your social circle — a career center, a professional you met through those informational interviews — can sometimes surface something that's hard to see from inside the process.

My daughter keeps telling me I should put my quilts up on Etsy. She set up the whole shop for me and everything, very sweet of her. I told her I would think about it. The quilts take me about 40 hours each to make and I honestly wouldn't know what to charge. What's a fair price for a handmade quilt

Pricing handmade quilts is genuinely one of the more disheartening exercises in craft economics, so it's worth knowing what you're walking into: at 40 hours of labor, even a modest $15/hour comes to $600 before materials, and most buyers on Etsy will experience sticker shock at that number because the market is flooded with underpriced work and imported quilts. A lot of skilled quilters end up either pricing low and feeling exploited, or pricing fairly and selling rarely.

That said, if you want to try it: materials plus labor at whatever hourly rate feels worth it to you, then look at what comparable handmade quilts are actually selling for (not just listed at — check sold listings). Some quilters also do custom orders at higher prices, which attracts buyers who understand what they're asking for.

But I'd gently note — your daughter set this up out of love, and "I'll think about it" sounds like it might mean something closer to "I'm not sure I want to." There's no obligation to sell something just because someone built you the door. Your quilts being valuable doesn't require them being for sale.

okay so i'm a sophomore in college and i've basically been in my dorm room for 6 days straight except to use the bathroom. not going to class, not eating real food, my roomate keeps asking if i'm okay and i just say yes. i don't feel sad exactly i just feel like. nothing. is this depression or am i just being lazy

This isn't laziness. Laziness doesn't make you stop eating or leave your room only to use the bathroom for six days. What you're describing — the nothing feeling, the withdrawal, the going through the motions of saying you're fine — that's your mind and body telling you something is really wrong.

Depression doesn't always look like crying. Sometimes it looks exactly like what you're describing: a kind of flatness where nothing feels worth doing and you're not even sure what you feel anymore.

Your campus has a counseling center, and most of them can see students same-day or next-day when something acute is happening — and six days of this qualifies. You don't have to have the right words or know exactly what's wrong to make that call. You can literally show them what you wrote here.

You reached out right now, which took something. That matters.

I've been a professional cellist for 22 years and I've decided I'm done performing. Not retiring — I mean I'm going to stop entirely. Sell my cello, the good one, and just be finished. I had a bad concert last month, forgot a passage I've played a thousand times, and the look on my colleague's face was enough. I know this sounds dramatic but I've been thinking about it seriously for three weeks now and I think I'm ready to just let it go.

Twenty-two years is a long relationship with an instrument, and one bad concert — even a genuinely painful one, the kind where someone's face tells you something you didn't want to know — is a strange place from which to end it permanently. That's not dismissing what happened. Memory failures mid-performance are frightening, and the shame that follows them can feel totalizing in a way that's hard to think through clearly.

Three weeks after something humiliating is not the same as three months. The impulse to sell the cello, specifically — to make it irreversible — sounds less like a considered ending and more like wanting the feeling to stop. Those are different things, and they tend to lead to different decisions when there's more distance. You don't have to perform again to keep the instrument. You don't have to decide anything permanent right now.
its whatever, i knew the promotion wasn't guaranteed or anything. just kind of processing i guess. do you think it's weird that i don't want to tell my parents yet

Not weird at all — and it's worth noticing why you're asking. Sometimes not wanting to tell certain people isn't avoidance, it's just knowing you need a minute to sit with something before it becomes a conversation you have to manage. Not getting something you worked toward genuinely stings, even when you saw it coming. You're allowed to take whatever time you need before you bring other people's reactions into it.

i've been at my internship for 6 weeks and my supervisor told me today that my work 'isn't meeting expectations' and i might not get a return offer. i've been working until midnight most nights trying to keep up. i don't even know what i'm doing wrong. my parents gave up so much for me to be here and i feel like i'm failing everyone

That's a really painful thing to hear, especially when you've been pouring everything into it. Working until midnight and still being told it's not enough — that's exhausting in a way that goes beyond just the job.

Before you spiral into feeling like you've failed everyone, it's worth separating a few things. "Not meeting expectations" from one supervisor at one internship is feedback, not a verdict on your capability or your future. It might be vague, unfair, or it might point to something real and fixable — but you can't know yet, because you don't have enough information about what specifically they mean.

The most useful thing you can do right now is ask for a follow-up conversation with your supervisor — not to defend yourself, but to ask directly: what would 'meeting expectations' actually look like? What's one thing I could do differently this week? That question is hard to ask when you're already feeling like you're failing, but it's the only way to get signal instead of just dread.

The weight you're carrying for your parents is real, but it's also worth knowing that one rocky internship — even one that doesn't convert — doesn't erase six weeks of showing up and trying hard in an environment that clearly isn't giving you much support.

I've been caring for my husband with Parkinson's for 6 years and last night I screamed at him. He couldn't help what he was doing, I know that. I just don't know who I am anymore or if I'm a good person

Six years of being someone's entire support system — and one moment of breaking down doesn't make you a bad person. It makes you a person who has been carrying an enormous weight for a very long time.

What you're describing — losing your sense of self, questioning your own character — is one of the most documented experiences in long-term caregiving. It doesn't mean something is wrong with you morally. It often means you've been so focused on him that there's almost nothing left over for you, and that kind of depletion eventually comes out somewhere.

You clearly love him. The guilt you feel is evidence of that, not evidence against your character.

If there's one concrete thing worth pursuing: caregiver support groups, either in person or online, specifically for spouses caring for partners with Parkinson's. The Parkinson's Foundation has a helpline (1-800-4PD-INFO) and connects people to exactly this. Talking to others who understand the specific exhaustion of this — not just generic caregiving — tends to matter in a way that general advice doesn't.

My boss asked me to present our team's Q3 results to the exec leadership next Friday and I am going to actually die. I'm an analyst, I write reports, I do not do this. She said it'll be 'good for my development' which I know is true but I have a genuine phobia of public speaking like I've left jobs over this before. Do I just tell her that or push through

The fact that you've left jobs over this before tells me this isn't just nerves you're catastrophizing — it's something that has actually cost you in concrete ways, and it deserves to be taken seriously rather than pushed through on sheer willpower.

Telling your manager is worth considering, but how you frame it matters. There's a difference between saying 'I have a phobia' (which can land as a flat refusal) and saying something like 'I want to do this and I want to be honest that public speaking is a genuine area of anxiety for me — can we talk about how to set me up well?' That opens a conversation rather than closing one. She may have more flexibility than the ask implied — maybe a co-presentation, maybe a smaller room first, maybe more prep support.

Pushing through cold, with no acknowledgment of what you're dealing with, is the version most likely to go badly and confirm your worst fears about yourself. You don't have to choose between suffering silently and opting out entirely.

retirement is so boring i hate it. been retired 8 months and i just sit around. my wife keeps saying i should see someone but i dont need therapy i just need something to do. looking for a hobby that will keep me busy, preferably something physical

Eight months of feeling like this sounds genuinely miserable, and the restlessness you're describing — not just boredom but the kind that makes days feel pointless — is something a lot of people hit in early retirement without having a name for it. It's real, and it's worth taking seriously. I'll get to activity ideas, but I want to gently push back on one thing: what your wife is noticing from the outside, and what you're describing from the inside, sound like they might be pointing at the same thing. "I just need something to do" and "I might need some support" aren't mutually exclusive — sometimes the restlessness is the surface and something heavier is underneath it. Worth at least keeping that door open. For physical activities that tend to give people a real sense of purpose, not just time-passing: pickleball has exploded in popularity among retirees and has a genuinely social culture around it that sneaks up on people. Masters swimming programs give you structure and a team. Volunteering with something physically demanding — trail maintenance, Habitat for Humanity builds, community garden work — adds meaning on top of the movement. Hiking clubs are another one where the social element tends to matter as much as the activity itself. The through-line in what tends to work is some combination of routine, other people, and a sense that you showed up for something.

my manager pulled me aside today and said my 'attitude has been off lately' and i need to course correct before my review in 6 weeks. i genuinely have no idea what she's talking about?? i've been doing my work, hitting my numbers, not causing drama. i'm so frustrated i could scream. do i just... apologize? i don't even know what i'm apologizing for

That kind of feedback lands really hard when you can't see what you supposedly did wrong — it feels less like guidance and more like a trap. The frustration makes complete sense.

Before deciding whether to apologize, it's worth getting specific with her, because 'attitude' is vague enough to mean almost anything, and apologizing for something undefined can actually work against you — it signals agreement without giving you any information to act on. A short follow-up conversation where you ask directly — "I want to make sure I understand what I should do differently. Can you give me a specific example of what you've noticed?" — puts the burden back on her to be concrete, which is fair and reasonable.

If she can give you something real, then you'll know whether this is a genuine miscommunication, a personality clash, or something else. If she can't, that tells you something too — and it'll matter if this ever escalates that you asked and tried to understand rather than just nodded along.

ok so theres this girl in my dorm i've had a crush on since september and i FINALLY found out she broke up with her boyfriend last week. my friend thinks i should wait but honestly i'm just gonna shoot my shot now before someone else does. gonna ask her out this weekend. just need help figuring out what to say lol

The instinct to move before someone else does makes sense, but a week out of a relationship is pretty raw — even if she likes you, she's likely not in a headspace to start something new, and asking now puts her in an awkward spot she didn't ask for. That can actually work against you, not because of some rule, but because it changes how she experiences you. Your friend's instinct to wait isn't about being passive — it's about giving her enough space that if something does happen, it starts well. You don't have to disappear; just be around naturally and let a little time pass. A few weeks won't cost you the opportunity, and it'll feel different for both of you.
do adult kids usually move back in with their parents after college these days? asking bc my daughter graduated in May and just wondering what the statistics are

It is genuinely common — around 50% of young adults in the US live with a parent at some point after graduating, so the numbers would back you up if that's what your daughter is doing or considering. But the fact that you're framing it as a statistics question when it sounds like this is your actual situation suggests it might feel complicated — maybe you're trying to figure out if this is okay, or how long is normal, or what it means. If you want to talk through what's actually going on with her or with you around it, that might be more useful than the data.
not really looking for advice just wondering if its normal that i check my bank account like 6 times a day lol. anyway does anyone actually use those budgeting apps or are they kind of pointless

Checking your balance six times a day isn't really a budgeting habit — it's anxiety. The number doesn't change that fast, so the checking is about something else: trying to feel in control of something that feels uncertain or scary. That's pretty common, but it's worth naming honestly rather than laughing off.

On the actual question: budgeting apps can be useful, but they work best when you know what you're trying to solve. YNAB is good if you want to actively plan where money goes before you spend it — it has a learning curve but people who stick with it tend to feel less anxious, not just more organized. Mint (or its successor) is more passive, just tracking. If the compulsive checking is the real issue, YNAB's approach specifically tends to help with that because it gives you a clear picture you can trust rather than one you have to keep rechecking.

my mom keeps asking when im moving back home and i keep changing the subject but she brought it up again at dinner on sunday and my dad just sat there not saying anything. anyway does anyone actually use those room dividers to make a studio apartment feel bigger or is it just an aesthetic thing

Room dividers can genuinely help — a bookshelf-style divider or a curtain track creates a sense of separate zones, which makes a studio feel less like one undifferentiated space. But the dinner you described sounds like it's sitting with you more than the square footage question is. The silence from your dad while your mom pushed, the repeated subject changes — that's a particular kind of family pressure that doesn't really go away on its own. You don't have to have it out with them, but it might be worth deciding what you actually want to say next time she asks, so you're not just deflecting into the next conversation.

my mom and i had this huge blowup last night over thanksgiving plans and she said some things i dont think i can unhear. like she basically told me i've always been the difficult one in the family, that my sister has 'never caused her this much stress.' i'm 34 years old and i still feel like a kid getting yelled at. i don't even know what i'm asking i just needed to say it somewhere

Being told you're the difficult one — especially by your mom, especially at 34 — hits differently than almost anything else. It doesn't matter how old you are or how solid your life is; that kind of thing goes straight to the part of you that's still trying to feel okay in your family. And the comparison to your sister makes it worse, because it's not just criticism, it's a ranking.

You don't have to know what you're asking. Sometimes something just happened and it needs to land somewhere before you can figure out what to do with it. What she said wasn't fair, and it makes sense that it's sitting heavy.

took early retirement at 63, figured id finally have time to learn italian like ive always wanted. signed up for one of those apps and a weekly zoom class. its been 4 months. i can do basic greetings and order food i guess but honestly my classmates seem so much further along than me and my teacher never really corrects me. im starting to wonder if maybe language learning just gets too hard past a certain age. saw some article that said the brain stops absorbing languages after 40 or something. did i wait too long

Four months into something you've wanted for years, and instead of feeling good about it, you're measuring yourself against your classmates and wondering if you've already missed your window. That's a hard place to be, especially when this was supposed to be a gift to yourself.

The article you're thinking of is a real area of research, but it's been badly oversimplified in popular coverage. Adults do learn differently than children — it's slower, and some aspects like accent are genuinely harder — but "the brain stops absorbing languages after 40" isn't what the science actually says. Adults often have real advantages: stronger vocabulary strategies, more life context to attach meaning to, more patience. What you're describing at four months — basic greetings, food ordering — is actually a reasonable place to be, depending on how many hours you've put in.

The thing that stands out to me more is that your teacher isn't correcting you. That's a concrete problem.
