Feedback is how you actually improve, and if you're practicing errors without knowing it, you're not going to progress the way you could. That's worth addressing directly — either by asking your teacher for more correction, or finding a class or tutor where you get more of it. You haven't waited too long. But the setup you're in might not be giving you what you need.

retired 2 years ago at 68, thought we had enough saved, now with everything so expensive i'm genuinely scared we're going to run out of money before we die. wife has some health stuff going on which adds costs. i worked 40 years for this and it feels like the rug got pulled out. is this just how it is now

Forty years of work, and now you're doing the math at night wondering if it holds. That fear is one of the most disorienting things a person can face — not because you did anything wrong, but because the ground shifted after you'd already made your plans. It's a real loss, and it makes sense that it feels that way.

To your question: you're not imagining it. Inflation since 2021 hit retirees on fixed incomes harder than almost any other group, and healthcare costs add a compounding pressure that's genuinely difficult. So no — this isn't just you.

What that means practically is worth looking at carefully. A fee-only financial planner (one who charges a flat fee rather than commissions) can do a realistic assessment of your actual runway given current spending and your wife's health costs — sometimes the picture is more stable than the anxiety suggests, and sometimes there are adjustments that create real breathing room. Social Security optimization, Medicare supplement coverage, and sequence-of-withdrawals strategy are all areas where small changes can matter a lot at your stage. If cost is a concern, AARP and many nonprofits offer free financial counseling for retirees.
do you think its weird to still be living at home at 26? like my parents are fine with it, my moms actually happy i'm here. just wondering what the average age people move out is in the US these days

The average age has been creeping up — somewhere around 24-25 now, and plenty of people are well into their late 20s or beyond, especially in high cost-of-living areas. But I notice you're framing this as a statistics question when it sounds like there might be something underneath it — whether to stay, whether you're falling behind, what it means about where your life is headed. Those are real questions, and the demographic average doesn't actually answer any of them. If the arrangement is genuinely working for you and your family, that matters a lot more than what other 26-year-olds are doing. If something about it is feeling off to you, that's worth sitting with too.

my daughter is 8 and her teacher says she's 'struggling with reading comprehension' but like... she reads fine at home?? she reads to her little brother every night. i dont understand why school is so different and she's starting to say she hates reading now which is breaking my heart a little

That shift — from a kid who reads to her brother every night to one who says she hates reading — is genuinely worth taking seriously, and it makes sense that it's getting to you. The gap between home and school is actually a real and well-documented thing: reading aloud to a sibling she loves, in her own space, with no performance pressure, is a completely different experience from being evaluated on comprehension in a classroom. She's probably not struggling with reading itself — she may be struggling with the specific way comprehension is being tested or taught, which often involves inferencing questions, vocabulary out of context, or timed exercises that feel nothing like a story. What helps most at this stage is figuring out exactly what the teacher means by 'comprehension' — is it answering questions about the text? Summarizing? Making inferences? Once you know the specific skill, you can work on it in low-stakes ways at home, like just chatting about the books she already loves. The most important thing right now is that she doesn't internalize 'I'm bad at reading' — because from what you're describing, she really isn't.

so i've decided i'm dropping out next semester. i'm a junior, one year left, and i just can't do it anymore. my parents are gonna lose it but honestly i feel like i could be doing so much more with my time than writing papers about stuff i don't care about. thinking about moving to portland with my friend and figuring it out from there. just need help writing a message to my advisor so i can start the process

One year out is a brutal place to hit a wall — you're close enough to see the finish line and exhausted enough that it looks meaningless. That's real, and it makes sense you're done.

Before I help with the advisor message: withdrawing as a junior has some specific consequences worth knowing about. Depending on your school and your loans, leaving now can trigger repayment timelines faster than leaving earlier would have, and some programs let you take a leave of absence instead — which keeps the door open without forcing you to decide permanently right now. It's worth a five-minute check on both of those before you send anything official.

If you've thought through all that and this is still the call, here's a straightforward message you can adapt:

---
Hi [Advisor's name],

I'm reaching out because I've made the decision to withdraw from the program at the end of this semester. I'd like to understand the formal process for doing so and any deadlines I should be aware of. Could we find a time to meet, or can you point me to the right office to get started?

Thank you,
[Your name]
---

Keep it short — you don't owe them an explanation at this stage.

okay so i've been working on this graphic novel for like 4 years and i finally have 80 pages done. my cousin saw it last week and said it was 'too niche' and that i should pivot to doing corporate illustration work instead bc thats where the money is. honestly maybe shes right. im thinking about shelving the whole project and reaching out to some agencies tomorrow

Four years and 80 pages is not a small thing — that's a real body of work, not a hobby sketch. What your cousin said might have landed hard enough to feel like a verdict, but one person's 'too niche' isn't a market analysis, and it's worth noticing that she's not your audience.

Corporate illustration is a legitimate path and there's nothing wrong with pursuing it, but shelving the novel tomorrow — the day after one piece of critical feedback — is a very different decision than shelving it after you've genuinely thought it through. The urgency here sounds like it's coming from pain, not from a clear-eyed assessment of what you want.

You don't have to choose between the two paths this week. The agencies will still exist in a month. The 80 pages will too.

i just got passed over for promotion AGAIN. this is the third time in two years and they gave it to someone who's been here 8 months. i've trained half this department. i don't even know why i bother anymore

Three times in two years, and you trained the people around you — that's not a small thing to absorb. The 'why do I bother' feeling makes complete sense when effort and loyalty keep getting met with this. It's worth sitting with whether this place is actually capable of valuing what you bring, or whether you've been patient with a system that's just not going to change. That's not a defeat — it's information.

dropped out of my sophomore year at ohio state last semester and told my parents i was still enrolled lol. they think im going to class every day. i've just been working at a bar and honestly? i dont hate it. but i feel like such a fraud and idk when this blows up its going to be really bad. do i just tell them or keep going

That's an exhausting thing to carry — showing up every day pretending to be somewhere you're not, waiting for something to detonate. That part sounds genuinely awful, separate from whatever the right move is.

The honest answer is that the longer this goes, the harder it gets. Not because of some moral principle, but practically: your parents will eventually find out, and finding out after six months of deception lands much worse than finding out now. The bar job and the dropped classes aren't the catastrophe — the sustained lying is what tends to damage trust in ways that take years to repair.

Before you think about the conversation with them, it might be worth getting clear on what you actually want. Do you want to go back to OSU eventually? Transfer somewhere? Keep working and figure it out? Because "I left school and I'm figuring out what's next" is a different and much more defensible conversation than "I have no idea what I'm doing." You don't need a perfect plan, but having thought it through even a little will help you feel less like you're confessing and more like you're telling them something true about your life.
do you think it's weird to still be at the same company after 11 years? like is that uncommon nowadays

It's not uncommon, but I notice you're asking whether it's *weird* — which is a different question. Eleven years somewhere can mean a lot of things: stability you've built deliberately, comfort that's become harder to leave, or a place that's genuinely been worth staying. The fact that you're framing it around whether other people would find it strange makes me think you might be less settled about it than the question lets on. Whether to stay or go is worth thinking through on its own terms — not by measuring yourself against some norm of how often people are supposed to move on.

my doctor wants me to come in because my blood pressure has been high two appointments in a row but honestly im fine i just get anxious at the doctors office, white coat thing you know. its not like i have symptoms or anything. is 148/92 actually that bad or are they overreacting

148/92 is in the Stage 2 hypertension range — that's not an overreaction on your doctor's part. The tricky thing about blood pressure is exactly what you're describing: it often has no symptoms until something serious happens, which is part of why it gets called a silent condition. White coat hypertension is real, and your doctor likely knows that too, which is probably why they want to see you — to figure out whether that's what's happening or whether it's elevated outside the office as well. Some doctors will suggest home monitoring for a few weeks to sort it out. It's worth going in. Two readings in a row is the kind of pattern that deserves a real look, not reassurance.

honestly im fine, 22 and just started my first real job out of college two months ago. i just wanted to ask — is it normal to cry in your car before going in? like genuinely asking if thats a thing people do or if im being dramatic. i dont hate it or anything the people are nice

You're not being dramatic. Crying in the car before work is something a lot of people do, and the fact that it's happening at two months in — when everything is still new and exhausting — matters more than whether the job is technically fine or the people are nice. Those things can both be true: decent workplace, kind colleagues, and also something about going in there every day that's costing you more than you expected.

Starting a first job is a real adjustment, and it hits some people harder than others. The question worth sitting with isn't whether you're being dramatic — you're not — but whether this is the "still adjusting" kind of hard or something that's pointing at a bigger mismatch. Two months is still early. But you're also allowed to take what you're feeling seriously.

been at my company 11 years. asked for a promotion to senior director last spring, got told 'not yet, maybe next cycle.' asked again in january, same thing, they said i needed to show more 'executive presence' which nobody will define for me. i have two direct reports who got promoted faster than me and i trained both of them. 54 years old and honestly starting to wonder if this is just what it is now

'Executive presence' that no one will define is often not feedback — it's a way of declining without committing to a reason. After 11 years, two cycles, and watching people you trained move ahead of you, that pattern is telling you something real, even if it's uncomfortable to name.

The 'is this just what it is now' thought deserves to be taken seriously rather than brushed off. Sometimes it is. Not because of your age, but because some organizations have decided, consciously or not, who they're building toward — and if you're not in that picture after this long, more patience with the same people may not change it.

That doesn't mean giving up, but it might mean shifting where you're putting your energy. At your level and with your experience, you likely have more external options than you're giving yourself credit for — and knowing what those look like, even just exploratorily, tends to change how you feel about the situation you're in. It gives you back some agency in a place where you've been waiting for other people to decide your value.

i don't even know how to say this but i think i'm having a panic attack at work right now. locked myself in the bathroom. been here 20 min. my heart is racing and i can't breathe right and i have a presentation in like 40 minutes and i just. i can't do this anymore i literally cannot

Right now, in this moment — you're safe. The bathroom is a good place to be. Your body is doing something really frightening but it's not dangerous, and it will pass.

For the next few minutes: slow your exhale down. Breathe in for 4 counts, out for 6 or 8. The longer exhale is what actually signals your nervous system to come down. Put your back against the wall if you can, feel the floor under your feet.

The presentation is 40 minutes away, which means you don't have to solve that yet. You just have to get through the next few minutes first.

What's happening today — this level of crisis in a bathroom stall — is information worth taking seriously when you're on the other side of it. This isn't just stress. Something needs to change, and you deserve support in figuring out what that is. But that's for later. Right now, just breathe out slowly.

okay so i know this is dumb but i took out $3000 in student loans 'for school' and used it to cover my car payment and groceries bc i had no other way. now im scared i did something illegal?? im a sophomore and nobody told me you weren't supposed to do that i just needed to eat

You're not dumb, and you're not a criminal. What you did is actually really common — student loan funds are meant to cover 'cost of attendance,' which schools define to include living expenses like food, housing, and transportation. Using loan money for groceries and a car payment almost certainly falls within that. The fear you're feeling right now is understandable, but you can let go of the legal panic.

The part worth paying attention to is longer-term: that $3,000 will accrue interest, and if this is a pattern you need to repeat each semester to get by, it's worth knowing that your school's financial aid office can sometimes adjust your aid package if you demonstrate unmet need — they don't always advertise this. There are also emergency funds at most universities specifically for students in situations like yours. You were trying to survive, and there are actually systems designed to help with exactly that.

my mom called me again tonight, third time this week, crying about how lonely she is since dad died. i love her but i have two kids and a job and i dont know how much more i can give. i feel like such a horrible person for even thinking that

You're not a horrible person. You're a person who is already stretched thin, trying to hold together your own family while also absorbing your mother's grief — and grief like hers doesn't have a bottom, which means there's no amount of giving that will feel like enough. That guilt you're feeling isn't evidence that you're selfish. It's evidence that you care about her and you care about your limits at the same time, which is actually a hard and honest thing to hold.

What you're describing — the drain, the dread of the phone ringing — is a signal worth taking seriously, not as a character flaw but as information. Sustainable support for your mother probably looks different from what's happening right now, and it's okay to think about what that could look like. That might mean involving other family members, looking into grief support groups for her, or setting some boundaries around call times. None of that makes you a bad daughter or son. It makes you someone trying to stay in this for the long haul.

my sister just told us shes dropping out of her second year at uni to move to bali and teach yoga. my parents are losing their mind and honestly so am i a little. shes 20. is this just a phase or do people actually do this and not regret it

People really do make this choice and not regret it — and some do regret it. There's no clean answer on the statistics, because it depends almost entirely on who the person is and why they're leaving, not just the fact of leaving.

What I'm noticing in how you wrote this is that you're not just worried about your sister — you're a little unsettled yourself, maybe by how certain she seems, or how fast it happened. That's worth sitting with separately from your parents' reaction, because their panic and your unease might be about different things.

The most honest thing you can do for your sister right now is probably to talk to her without the noise of your parents' crisis in the background. Not to talk her out of it or into it, but to actually understand what's driving it — whether she's running toward something or away from something, whether she's thought about what a return path looks like if she wants one. That conversation will tell you a lot more than any pattern about 20-year-olds dropping out.

i've been trying to get my 4 year old to sleep in his own bed for like 3 months now. we do the whole routine, bath, books, song, back rub, then i leave and he just screams until i come back. tried letting him cry it out twice and i gave up both times because it felt awful. last night i was in there until 11:30pm. i don't even know what i'm asking i'm just so tired

Three months of this, and two attempts at something that felt genuinely awful to you — that's not a parenting failure, that's exhaustion on top of exhaustion. The 11:30pm part especially: you're not just losing sleep, you're losing the only quiet hours you probably get.

Since cry-it-out clearly doesn't sit right with you (and that's a legitimate position, not a weakness), it might be worth looking into the "chair method" — you stay in the room but gradually move toward the door over several nights, so he's not abandoned but also not getting the full comfort response. It's slower but a lot of parents find it more sustainable precisely because it doesn't require you to override every instinct you have. The key is that whichever approach you pick, consistency matters more than the specific method — and that's genuinely hard to pull off when you're already running on empty.

You're not doing anything wrong. You're doing something hard.
do people usually feel better after quitting a job or does it take a while. not planning anything just genuinely curious

It varies a lot — some people feel immediate relief, others hit a weird flatness a few weeks in once the adrenaline wears off, especially if the job was stressful enough that their whole nervous system was calibrated around it. There's often a grieving period even when leaving was the right call.

The "not planning anything" disclaimer suggests this might be more than academic curiosity. If you're somewhere where the question of quitting is actually alive for you, that's a real thing to be sitting with — the uncertainty of it is its own kind of exhausting.

my roommate sarah keeps forgetting to pay her half of the electric bill — we're talking like 3 months in a row now. she's not broke she just... forgets?? i don't want to make it weird but i also can't keep covering her. what would you even say to someone like that

Three months of covering someone who isn't actually struggling financially is a lot to carry quietly, especially when you're also managing the anxiety of not wanting to damage the living situation. That tension — not wanting conflict but also not being able to keep absorbing the cost — is real.

The most effective approach is usually to make it structural rather than personal, so it doesn't feel like an accusation. Something like: "Hey, I want to figure out a better system for the bills so neither of us has to think about it — can we set up a standing transfer on the same day each month?" Framing it as a logistics fix rather than a complaint about Sarah gives her an easy way to correct course without embarrassment, which usually gets better results anyway. If she's genuinely just forgetful, a reminder system is the actual solution. If she's not, then you'll learn that too.

I'm a 58 year old man and I haven't slept more than 3 or 4 hours a night in almost two months. I take melatonin, I've tried the sleep hygiene stuff, nothing works. I'm starting to make mistakes at work and I snapped at my wife last week in a way I'm not proud of. I don't even know what I'm asking. I just needed to write it down somewhere.

Two months of sleeping 3-4 hours a night is genuinely hard on a person — on your body, your judgment, your relationships. The fact that it's showing up at work and at home tells you it's already past the point where self-help tools are going to cut it. Writing it down somewhere matters, and so does what comes next: this is worth a real conversation with a doctor, not because something is necessarily wrong in a frightening way, but because chronic insomnia at this level has effective treatments — CBT-I in particular has strong evidence behind it, often better than medication — and you don't have to just endure this. You've already tried the standard advice. That's useful information. It means the next step is a professional who can actually assess what's driving it.

been trying to keep up with everything since the divorce and i just bounced a check for my kids school lunch account lmao. like its $47 and i literally cannot cover it right now until thursday. is this going to affect my credit

A bounced check on a school lunch account won't go to the credit bureaus — schools don't report to credit agencies, and this is too small and too informal a transaction to end up on your credit report. You'll likely owe a returned check fee to your bank (usually $25–35), and the school may charge a small fee too, but that's the extent of it financially.

And honestly — keeping the lights on, the kids fed, and the whole thing moving after a divorce while watching $47 become a crisis moment is exhausting in a way that's hard to explain to people who haven't been there. You're not failing. You're in a genuinely hard stretch. Thursday will come.

my dad retired 8 months ago after 35 years as an engineer and he is just... lost. sits around the house, stopped seeing his friends, my mum says he barely talks. he wont discuss it. i live 4 hours away and feel completely useless. i dont even have a question i just dont know

Not having a question makes sense — this is one of those situations where there's no clean fix to ask for. What you're describing with your dad is actually pretty common after long careers end: the structure, the identity, the daily sense of purpose, all gone at once. That doesn't make it less painful to watch, especially from four hours away. The helplessness you're feeling is real, and it's not because you're failing him — it's because you can't hand someone back a sense of meaning from a distance. What sometimes matters more than solutions is just sustained contact: a call that isn't about checking in on the problem, a visit where you're not visibly worried, keeping the thread going. It's slow and it doesn't feel like enough. But it's not nothing.

dropped out of my second year of engineering last week. told my parents yesterday and my mom just cried and didn't say anything and my dad hasn't texted me back. i know it was the right call i was failing everything and having panic attacks before every exam but now i just feel like i destroyed something and i don't know what to do with that

What you're carrying right now is real — the relief of making a hard call and the grief of what it cost you at the same time. Those two things don't cancel each other out. Your parents' silence hurts, and it makes sense that it does, even if you stand behind the decision.

Leaving when you were failing and falling apart wasn't giving up — it was recognizing something wasn't working before it broke you further. That matters. But knowing that doesn't make the aftermath feel clean, and it doesn't mean you have to rush into figuring out what comes next right now. Give yourself a little room before you try to rebuild a plan.

got laid off in March, 58 years old, been sending out resumes for 4 months and nothing. savings are starting to actually scare me. i worked at that company for 19 years. idk what i'm even asking i just. it doesn't feel real still

Nineteen years, and then it just ends. Of course it doesn't feel real — that's not denial, that's a reasonable response to something that genuinely shouldn't have happened the way it did. That job was probably part of how you understood yourself, not just a paycheck.

Four months of sending resumes into silence at 58 is demoralizing in a very specific way, and I don't want to paper over that with optimism. The job market for experienced workers is genuinely harder and that's real, not a reflection of your worth.

A few things that sometimes make a difference at this stage: the hidden job market matters more than it does for younger applicants — a significant portion of roles at senior levels get filled through networks before they're posted, so direct outreach to former colleagues and managers often moves faster than applications. If your resume hasn't been looked at by someone who hires in your field recently, that's worth doing — formatting and keyword optimization has changed a lot and it can quietly tank applications. On the financial side, if you haven't already mapped out exactly how long your savings can carry you at your current spending rate, doing that math — even when it's scary — usually helps more than not knowing. It gives you a real timeline instead of a looming feeling.

I'm 19 and I got into this really competitive summer arts program in Chicago — painting, which is what I've wanted to do since I was like 8. But now that I'm actually here I can't paint anything. Like I sit in front of the canvas and I just freeze. Everyone else seems so confident and their work is so good and I've been here 2 weeks and I have basically nothing to show.
