What you're describing — the freezing, the sudden doubt, the fear that you've been wrong about yourself your whole life — that's not a sign that you don't belong there. It's actually a pretty classic response to finally being in the room you've wanted to be in. The stakes feel enormous because this matters to you enormously.

But I want to take the real fear seriously, not just reassure you past it: the question of whether you have something real to say is one every honest artist asks. The difference is that most people around you are probably asking it too and not showing it. Confidence in that room is often a performance, especially at 19, especially in week two.

You were painting since you were 8 not because someone told you to — that's something. The program saw something real when they accepted you. The blank canvas right now isn't proof that it's gone; it's proof that you care what ends up on it. That's actually where real work comes from, even when it doesn't feel that way.

asking for my husband here — he's spent the last 8 years writing a novel, genuinely sacrificed a lot for it, and he just got his 12th rejection from agents. he's not really talking about it but I can tell he's devastated. I don't know if I should bring it up or just leave him alone. honestly not sure what I want from you, maybe just... idk

Eight years and twelve rejections — that's not just a creative setback, that's a grief. And the silence you're noticing probably isn't him being closed off; it's more likely him not yet knowing what to say about something this large.

The fact that you're here, uncertain what you even want, says something real — you're carrying this too, and you don't want to get it wrong with him.

You don't have to choose between bringing it up and leaving him alone. There's a third option: being present without making him perform okayness or talk before he's ready. Something simple and specific — "I know you got that news. I'm not going anywhere" — opens a door without pushing him through it. It also signals that you see what happened as significant, which matters when someone's quietly wondering if anyone really understands what they've lost.

And at some point, when the dust settles a little, it might be worth knowing that twelve agent rejections isn't the end of the road for a manuscript — but that's a conversation for when he's ready to think about next steps, not right now.

okay so i've been letting my 16 year old stay out until midnight on weekends and my sister keeps saying im too lenient and it's going to 'backfire.' he's a good kid, straight A's, never been in trouble. i think i know my own son right??

You clearly do know your son — and the picture you're painting, a kid with good grades and a clean track record, is genuinely reassuring. That context matters. At the same time, 'I know my kid' and 'this particular boundary is the right call' are two separate questions, and your sister's concern isn't obviously wrong just because your son has been responsible so far. Midnight at 16 isn't outrageous, but it's also not a universal standard, and whether it's right probably depends on specifics — where he's going, who he's with, how easy it is to reach him. The more useful question isn't whether you're too lenient in general, but whether this specific arrangement still feels right to you when you think it through carefully, not just when you're defending it.

I don't even know why im writing this. retired 8 months ago after 35 years at the same company and everyone said it would be wonderful and i just sit in the kitchen most mornings and don't really know what to do with myself. my wife says i seem fine. maybe i am fine. is this normal

Yes, it's normal — but "normal" doesn't mean it isn't hard, and I don't want that word to make you feel like you should be over it by now. Thirty-five years of structure, identity, purpose, colleagues — and then one day it just stops. What you're describing in the kitchen in the mornings sounds less like fine and more like grief, even if nobody calls it that. The people who said it would be wonderful weren't wrong exactly, but they skipped the part where it takes real time to figure out who you are when the job isn't answering that question for you anymore.

i'm 54 and just found out my company is doing layoffs. my brother says i should take the severance package without even trying to negotiate because at least it's something guaranteed. i think he's right. gonna sign tomorrow

It's completely understandable to want certainty right now — layoffs are disorienting and the urge to just close it out is real. But signing tomorrow without any negotiation means you've already accepted their opening offer, and severance is almost always negotiable. At 54 with years of experience, you have standing to ask. Even a short email requesting more weeks of pay, extended health coverage, or a later end date costs you nothing before you sign — and you can still take the package if they say no. The guarantee doesn't go away just because you asked.

my dad is 61 and he just told me he's been quietly paying his younger brother's rent for like 18 months, around $900/month. he's got maybe 4 years until he wants to retire and i don't think he's accounted for this at all in his savings. he doesn't want to talk about it and says it's family. i don't know if i should push or just leave it alone

The thing that stands out here isn't really the math — it's that you're carrying the weight of something your dad has decided not to look at directly, and you're trying to figure out how much of that is yours to carry too.

You're right that $16,000+ over 18 months, ongoing, with retirement four years out is worth taking seriously. But you probably already know that pushing harder when he's said "it's family" is likely to make him less open, not more. That instinct you have — to not force it — is probably correct.

What might actually land better than a direct financial conversation is coming at it from a different angle: asking him if he has a clear picture of where he stands for retirement, not framing it around his brother at all. Some people can hear concern when it's not structured as criticism. A fee-only financial planner (one who charges a flat fee rather than commission) could also be a neutral third party — sometimes it's easier to hear hard numbers from someone outside the family dynamic.

You can care about his future without being able to control his choices. That's a genuinely uncomfortable place to sit, and it makes sense that you're unsettled by it.

is it actually possible to get good at math as an adult or is that just something people say to make you feel better. like i'm 34 and i never understood algebra in school and my kid is starting to hit the stuff i couldn't do and it's kind of embarrassing

Yes, it's genuinely possible — adult learners often do better with algebra than kids because you can understand *why* the rules work, not just memorize them. The research on this is pretty consistent: math difficulty in school is almost always about gaps in earlier concepts, not some fixed ceiling on ability.

But I want to name what's actually going on here, because it matters. Watching your kid approach the same wall you hit — that's not just an academic question, that's a specific kind of sting. The good news is that closing those gaps is very doable, and doing it alongside your kid rather than hiding from it tends to go better than you'd expect. Khan Academy covers algebra from the ground up, free, at your own pace, with no one watching. A lot of adults have gone back through it and found it clicked in a way school never allowed.

My husband lost his job in February and we burned through our savings faster than I thought possible. I'm working full time as a nurse but my salary alone doesn't cover everything. We're behind two months on the mortgage now and I got a letter this week saying they're starting the foreclosure process. I'm 54 years old. We were supposed to have this house paid off in 8 years. I keep thinking about how we did everything right and I don't understand how we ended up here.

That last line — "we did everything right" — that's the part that must make this so disorienting. This isn't the outcome of carelessness. You built something carefully over decades and now you're watching it be threatened by circumstances that came out of nowhere. That's not just stressful, it's a particular kind of grief.

I want to be direct with you: a foreclosure letter is serious, but it is not the end of the road, even now. The foreclosure process typically takes months, and there are intervention points that many people don't know exist. The most important thing you can do in the next few days is contact your mortgage servicer and ask specifically about forbearance or a loan modification — servicers are often required to review you for alternatives before foreclosure can proceed. You can also call the HUD-approved housing counseling hotline (1-800-569-4287), which is free, and those counselors deal with exactly this situation and know how to negotiate with lenders.

You're a nurse — you know what it means to catch something early. This is still catchable.

Been at my company 22 years. They just announced a restructuring and my entire department is being 'reorganized.' HR said they'd be in touch about 'next steps' which everyone knows means layoffs. I'm 54. My wife stopped working when we had kids and never went back. I just keep staring at my computer screen and can't think straight.

Twenty-two years, a family depending on you, and an HR phrase that everyone knows how to decode — that's a lot to be carrying right now. The fact that you can't think straight makes complete sense. This isn't just a job transition; it's a threat to something you've spent most of your adult life building.

Before anything else: don't wait for 'next steps' to come to you. Request a direct conversation with HR or your manager as soon as you can, and ask them plainly what the timeline is and whether your role is being eliminated. Uncertainty is its own kind of torture, and getting real information — even hard information — will help you think more clearly than staring at a screen waiting.

If a layoff is coming, a few things are on your side: 22 years likely means a meaningful severance negotiation is possible, especially if there's a package being offered broadly. That number is often not fixed. And while the job market at 54 is not without its frustrations, your depth of experience in one industry is genuinely valuable — it just requires being positioned correctly, which is different from starting out.

You don't have to have a plan today. But getting clarity on what's actually happening is the first step toward being able to make one.

i keep reading about people who retired early and traveled and im just like... is that actually sustainable or do they all just have inheritance money or whatever. genuinely curious how it works financially

Some do have a financial head start, but a lot of the well-documented cases are people who spent years aggressively saving — the FIRE movement stuff. The math usually involves getting investment assets to about 25x your annual expenses, then drawing down 4% a year. It's real, but it requires either a high income, very low expenses, or both for a sustained stretch. What's interesting is that question tends to come up most sharply when someone's already feeling the weight of the path they're on — not just abstract curiosity. If something about your current situation is feeling unsustainable or wrong, that's a real thing to sit with, separate from whether the FIRE numbers add up.

I don't really know how to say this but I've been thinking about cutting off my best friend of 8 years. She said something really cruel to me at my birthday dinner in front of everyone — made a joke about my weight and when I texted her after she said I was being too sensitive. I keep going back and forth and I feel like I'm losing my mind. We've been through so much together and I don't want to throw that away but I also can't stop thinking about how humiliated I felt

What she did was unkind, and the way she responded when you tried to address it — turning it back on you — made it worse. You're not losing your mind. The back-and-forth you're feeling is what happens when someone you love hurts you and then won't acknowledge it. Both things are true at once: the friendship matters, and what happened wasn't okay.

Cutting someone off entirely isn't the only option here, but neither is just absorbing it and moving on. There's space between those two things — a real conversation where you're clear that the 'joke' hurt you and that 'too sensitive' isn't an acceptable response to that. How she handles that conversation will tell you a lot. Eight years is significant, but it doesn't make you obligated to let things go unchallenged. What happened at your birthday dinner deserves to be taken seriously, by her.

Retired two years ago after 35 years as an engineer. Thought I'd love it. I don't. Wife says I seem depressed but I keep telling her I'm fine, just adjusting. But I've gained 22 pounds, I stopped going to the gym in October, and I had a full physical last month and everything came back fine so technically there's nothing wrong. I don't really have a question I guess.

You came here without a question, which sometimes means the real question is hard to say out loud. So let me reflect back what you wrote: you gave 35 years to a career, you're now two years into a life that was supposed to feel like a reward, and it doesn't. Your wife sees something. Your body is showing signs. And everything 'technically' checks out, so there's no official permission to feel like something is wrong.

That gap — between 'fine on paper' and 'not fine' — is where a lot of men your age quietly get stuck. Identity built over decades doesn't just smoothly transfer. The structure, the competence, the sense of mattering at something — those don't retire with you, and rebuilding them takes longer and more deliberate effort than most people expect.

The 22 pounds and the gym aren't the problem. They're usually symptoms of the same thing: forward momentum stalling out. Getting the movement back — even small, even imperfect — tends to be one of the faster levers, not because of the calories but because it's a daily proof that you're still doing things on purpose.

If 'adjusting' has looked roughly the same for two years, it might be worth letting your wife be right, not as a defeat, but as information.

My son keeps telling me I should learn to use the iPad he got me for Christmas but every time I sit down with it I feel stupid. I'm 71 and I never had to use computers for my job. He gets frustrated when I ask the same questions and I end up feeling worse than before I started. I just don't think my brain works that way anymore

What you're describing — feeling stupid, asking the same questions, your son getting frustrated — that's a really discouraging loop to be stuck in, and it has nothing to do with your brain not working. It has to do with the fact that learning something genuinely new at any age is hard, and it's much harder when the person teaching you has forgotten what it's like not to know it.

You're not behind where you should be. You're learning something that didn't exist for most of your life, without the decades of background context your son grew up with. That's a real difference, not a deficiency.

One thing that can help: many public libraries run free iPad and tablet classes specifically for older adults, taught by people who are patient by design and used to exactly these questions. It takes the pressure off both you and your son, and lets you ask the same thing five times without anyone's frustration getting in the way.

my roommate keeps eating my food even after i asked her to stop and im literally about to put a lock on the fridge and send a message to our whole group chat calling her out. like everyone in the house should know what shes doing right

That's genuinely infuriating — you asked directly and she ignored you, so it makes sense you're done being patient. The group chat move is tempting because it feels like it matches how disrespected you feel, but it'll almost certainly make the living situation worse for everyone, including you. You still have to share that space. The fridge lock is actually the smarter play — it solves the problem without blowing up the house dynamic. If you want her to feel the social pressure, a direct follow-up conversation where you tell her you're now locking your food because she didn't respect your first ask tends to land harder than people expect, and it keeps you in the position of someone who handled it well.
what are the actual physical symptoms of burnout vs just being tired, like is there a difference medically speaking. not asking for myself just generally curious

There is a real clinical distinction, though it's worth saying — "not asking for myself" after three words is usually a sign that someone is, at least a little, asking for themselves. No judgment in that, it's a completely normal way to approach something that feels too close to look at directly.

To answer the question: burnout isn't just accumulated tiredness. Tiredness resolves with rest — you sleep well for a few nights and feel human again. Burnout doesn't. The hallmarks are persistent exhaustion that sleep doesn't fix, a kind of emotional flatness or detachment from work or people you normally care about, and a drop in basic functioning — concentration, memory, motivation — that feels qualitatively different from just being overworked. Physically, it can show up as frequent illness (immune suppression), headaches, GI issues, and disrupted sleep even when you're exhausted. The WHO classifies it as an occupational phenomenon, not a medical diagnosis, but that doesn't make it less real or less worth addressing early. If any of that sounds familiar, it's worth paying attention to before it compounds.

my coworker keeps taking credit for stuff in front of our boss and i dont know if im being paranoid or if its actually happening. like last week i sent an email with an idea and then in the meeting she presented it as hers and our boss said 'great thinking sarah' and i just sat there. do i say something??? i hate confrontation so much i would rather quit honestly

You're not being paranoid — you have a specific, recent example where you sent an idea in writing and then watched someone present it as their own while your boss praised them for it. That's not a vibe, that's a pattern you can point to.

The 'I'd rather quit' feeling makes sense as an impulse, but it's worth separating the discomfort of confrontation from the actual cost of letting this continue. If it keeps happening, your contributions stay invisible, and that has real consequences for how you're perceived and what opportunities come your way.

You don't have to confront Sarah directly if that feels impossible right now. One lower-stakes move: start making your contributions more visible in the moment. In that meeting, you could have said something like 'yeah, building on what I sent over Monday—' — not accusatory, just quietly anchoring the idea to yourself. It also helps to follow up meetings with short emails summarizing what was discussed and what you contributed, so there's a paper trail. If it escalates, you'll have something concrete to bring to your manager.

i've had the same fight with my mom like 6 times this year. every time i try to calmly explain how her comments about my weight make me feel, she cries and somehow i end up apologizing to HER. i don't even know why i keep trying

That pattern — where you go in with a genuine grievance and come out apologizing for having it — is exhausting in a specific way. It's not just that the conversation failed, it's that it got flipped on you, which makes you question whether you're the problem. You're not.

The thing worth sitting with is that you've now run this experiment six times with consistent results. That's not a you problem, it's information about what this particular dynamic is capable of. Some people, especially parents, have a defensive structure that converts their child's hurt into an attack they need to survive — and no amount of calm, careful framing gets through that because the issue isn't your delivery.

That doesn't mean giving up on the relationship. It might mean letting go of the specific goal of being understood by her about this, and deciding separately what you want the relationship to look like given that limitation. Those are hard things to sit with, but they're probably more useful than trying to find the right words for a conversation that keeps ending the same way.

retired two years ago and thought the burnout from my old job would just go away on its own once i stopped working. it hasn't really. i still feel flat most days, no motivation to do much of anything, which is embarrassing to admit because everyone acts like retirement is this big reward. my wife thinks i just need to find hobbies but i tried a woodworking class in the spring and it didn't stick. what am i missing

What you're describing — the flatness, the missing motivation, the fact that it hasn't lifted after two years — that's worth taking seriously, and it doesn't have anything to do with being ungrateful for retirement. The "embarrassing to admit" part stands out; you've probably been carrying this quietly for a while.

Burnout that persists this long after the source is removed sometimes isn't just burnout anymore. It can shade into depression, and retirement itself — loss of structure, identity, purpose, daily social contact — is actually a known trigger for it in people who were high-functioning in their careers. The woodworking class not sticking isn't a clue about hobbies; it's a clue that something deeper might need attention first.

It might be worth talking to your GP and being specific: not just "I've been low since retiring" but that it's been two years, that motivation is genuinely absent, that you're not feeling better. That's a clinical picture worth evaluating, not just a life adjustment problem to solve with the right activity.

I'm 54 and I just found out my husband has been hiding a second credit card with $23,000 on it. We've been married 28 years. I don't even know if I'm more upset about the money or the lying. I'm not asking for marriage advice I just need to know what this actually does to us financially if we split up

What you're carrying right now — the money and the betrayal tangled together — that's an enormous thing to find out, and it makes sense that you can't even separate the two yet. You said you just found out, so please give yourself a moment before you feel pressure to have it all figured out.

On the financial question specifically: in most U.S. states, debt accumulated during a marriage is considered marital debt regardless of whose name is on the account, which means it typically gets divided in a divorce. However, there are exceptions — if a spouse can show the debt was hidden, wasteful, or used for something that didn't benefit the marriage (gambling, an affair, etc.), a judge may assign more of it to the spouse who incurred it. This is called "dissipation of marital assets" and it's a real legal argument. The $23,000 doesn't automatically become half yours.

The most important near-term step is getting a free consultation with a family law attorney in your state — many offer 30-minute consultations at no cost. Before that conversation, pull your credit report at annualcreditreport.com to make sure there are no other accounts you don't know about. Knowing the full picture before any decisions get made is the most protective thing you can do for yourself right now.

My husband and I have been fighting constantly about money for almost two years now. He thinks I spend too much, I think he's controlling, and honestly I'm starting to wonder if we even want the same life. Last week he showed me a spreadsheet he made tracking every purchase I made for the past 3 months without telling me. I don't even know if this is a money problem anymore

You're right to notice that — because what you're describing isn't really a budgeting disagreement. A secret three-month spending log isn't a financial planning tool. It's surveillance. And the fact that he presented it to you as though it were reasonable is worth sitting with, separate from any question of whether your spending habits are a problem.

Two years of constant fighting, feeling monitored, and now questioning whether you want the same life — that's a heavy weight to carry. It sounds like you're somewhere between exhausted and scared, and trying to figure out what's actually true about your relationship versus what's just the noise of ongoing conflict.

If there's a practical thread to pull here, couples counseling with someone who has experience in financial conflict and relationship dynamics can sometimes help name what's actually happening — whether that's a values mismatch, a control issue, or something else. But you don't have to frame this as "fixing the budget" to get that help. What you described is bigger than that, and it's okay to treat it that way.

my landlord is being a total ass about renewing my lease and i'm so done. found a place i like better anyway but it's $400 more a month. i make like $3200/month after taxes and my current rent is $1150. gonna sign the new lease tomorrow, just need to know what utilities usually run in a 2br apartment

Utilities for a 2BR typically run $150–250/month depending on your climate and whether gas is separate — so figure $200 as a working estimate.

Before tomorrow though: at $3200 take-home, your current rent is 36% of your income, which is already a stretch by most standards. Adding $400 brings the new place to $1550 — that's nearly half your monthly income before utilities, groceries, or anything else. That's a real constraint, not just a number on paper.

The landlord situation sounds genuinely frustrating, and wanting out of it makes sense. But it's worth separating "I want to leave" from "I want this specific place at this price" — because signing a 12-month lease at that ratio when you're already stretched could create a different kind of stress that follows you around for a year. If there are other options you haven't fully looked at yet, it might be worth 48 hours before committing.

my roommate situation is fine honestly, i've just been eating in my room every night for like 6 weeks because the common area feels weird after we argued. anyway do you think i should get one of those mini fridges for my room or just deal with it

Six weeks of eating alone in your room to avoid a common area you're paying for — that's a long time to be managing around one unresolved argument. A mini fridge might make the isolation more comfortable, but it won't make the apartment feel like somewhere you actually want to be. Whatever happened with your roommate, it sounds like it's still sitting there unresolved, and that kind of low-grade tension has a way of quietly grinding you down. A mini fridge is an easy fix to get, but it might be worth asking whether what you actually need is a harder conversation.

i'm 19 and i just told my parents i'm dropping out of college after one semester and they completely cut me off. like effective immediately, no more tuition, no more phone plan, nothing. i have $340 in my account and i don't know a single person in this city. i thought i was making the right choice but now i'm just sitting in my dorm room that i have until the end of the month and i genuinely don't know what to do

That's a terrifying position to be in — making a decision you believed in and then having the floor drop out from under you all at once. The financial pressure is real and immediate, and the isolation makes it so much harder to think straight.

The most urgent thing right now is the end-of-month deadline on your housing. Before anything else — before figuring out the bigger life questions — you need a plan for where you're sleeping on the 1st. If your school has a Dean of Students office, they often have emergency housing resources even for students who are leaving. It's worth a call tomorrow morning, and worth being honest about your situation. Local shelters and transitional housing programs for young adults (search your city + "youth housing") are also real options, not last resorts.

For income fast: gig work like DoorDash or Instacart can pay out within days and doesn't require a car in most cities. Temp agencies can place people quickly for warehouse or admin work.

The question of whether dropping out was right — that's a real question, and it deserves real thought. But you can't think clearly about your future when you're worried about where you'll sleep. Stabilize first. The bigger decisions will still be there once you're not in crisis mode.

i've been trying to learn python for 6 months now and i still can't build anything without copying from stack overflow. everyone else in my bootcamp seems to get it and i just sit there pretending. i feel so stupid i'm thinking about dropping out

Six months in and you're still going — that's not nothing, even when it feels like nothing. The thing you're describing, copying from Stack Overflow, not feeling like you actually *get* it — that's genuinely one of the hardest parts of learning to code, and it doesn't mean your brain doesn't work. It means you're at the stage where things haven't clicked into a coherent whole yet, which is uncomfortable and demoralizing and also pretty normal.

What worries me a little is the 'pretending' part — carrying that alone in a group setting is exhausting and it tends to make the learning harder, not easier, because shame closes things off. Dropping out might feel like relief right now, but it might also be worth asking whether you'd regret it in six more months.

If you're open to it: building something embarrassingly small and broken, just yours, no tutorial — even a script that does one dumb thing — can start to shift that feeling of copying without understanding. Not because it's easy, but because it forces a different kind of thinking.

my roommate of 2 years just told me she's moving out at the end of the month to live with her boyfriend and I found out literally because she posted it on instagram before telling me. I have 3 weeks to find someone new or figure out rent on my own and I don't even know how to do that, I've never posted a roommate listing or anything. but also I just feel really stupid for not seeing this coming I guess

Finding out through Instagram before she told you directly — that stings, and it makes sense you feel blindsided. The practical pressure is real, but so is the feeling of being an afterthought to someone you've lived with for two years.

On the practical side: three weeks is tight but workable. Your best options for finding a roommate quickly are Facebook Groups (search "[your city] roommates" — usually faster than apps), Craigslist (still effective despite its reputation), and SpareRoom. Post in all three at once. Your listing needs a few basics: rent amount, move-in date, a photo of the room and common areas, and a sentence or two about what you're like to live with. Be honest about the timeline — some people are actively looking to move fast.

While you're searching, it's worth checking your lease to understand your options if you can't fill the spot — whether you can cover solo for a month, whether your landlord needs notice, or whether there's any flexibility.

You're not stupid for not seeing this coming. People don't always give you the signals they should.

my roommate hasnt left the apartment in like 3 weeks, barely eats, sleeps till 3pm every day. shes 19 and just started college and i think shes really struggling but she keeps saying shes fine. do i just leave her alone??

No, you shouldn't just leave her alone — and the fact that you're asking suggests you already sense that. What you're describing (social withdrawal, disrupted sleep, not eating) are real warning signs, and three weeks is long enough that this isn't just adjustment jitters.

You don't have to stage an intervention. Sometimes the most useful thing is just being direct and low-pressure: telling her you've noticed, that you're not trying to make it a big deal, but you're genuinely concerned. Not "are you okay" — she'll say yes — but something like "I've been a little worried about you lately and wanted to check in for real." That opens a door without forcing her through it.

Most colleges also have a counseling center with drop-in hours or a warmline specifically for moments like this — both for her, and honestly for you if you want to talk through how to approach it. You're carrying something real here too, watching someone you live with struggle and not knowing how to help.

my roommate hasnt slept properly in like 6 weeks, she keeps saying shes fine but shes falling asleep in class and snapping at everyone. she wont see a doctor bc she thinks itll just fix itself. what do i even do

Six weeks is a long time to watch someone you live with deteriorate and feel like you can't get through to them — that's exhausting and genuinely worrying, not just for her but for you too.

The 'it'll fix itself' logic is hard to argue against directly because it's not entirely wrong — sleep issues sometimes do resolve — but six weeks of classroom blackouts and mood changes is past the self-resolving window. The thing that sometimes moves people who resist doctors is reframing it: not 'something is wrong with you' but 'you're running on empty and there might be a simple fix.' Sleep issues often have straightforward causes — iron deficiency, stress hormones, a sleep cycle that's shifted — and a GP visit is low-stakes compared to what she's dealing with now.

If she's still resistant, you can't force her. But you can be honest with her once, clearly, without a lecture: tell her what you're actually seeing from the outside, because sometimes people don't realize how visible it's become. That's different from nagging, and it gives her real information to make her own call.
does anyone actually use a budget app or is it just one of those things people download and forget about lol. asking because im trying to get better at like. managing stuff

Budget apps work for some people and collect dust for others — it really depends on whether the format matches how your brain actually works. But I notice you framed this as 'getting better at managing stuff,' which is doing a lot of work. If there's something specific that's feeling out of control right now, the app question might be a few steps downstream of the real one. What's actually going on with money lately?

i've watched like 15 youtube videos on calculus derivatives and done every practice problem in the textbook and i still don't get it. my exam is in 4 days and i'm starting to think i'm just not a math person

Four days out, after 15 videos and a full textbook — that's not someone who isn't a math person. That's someone who's been working really hard and hitting a wall, which is genuinely exhausting and scary when an exam is close.

Here's what I'd actually look at: watching videos and doing practice problems are both somewhat passive ways to learn derivatives. The thing that usually breaks through is being forced to explain *why* each step works, not just execute it. If you can, try solving a problem and narrating out loud — even to yourself — what rule you're applying and why. Where you get stuck or go quiet is usually exactly where the understanding is missing, and that's actually useful information at this point.

Also worth knowing: the feeling that you'll never get it is almost always loudest right before something clicks. That doesn't make the next four days less hard, but you're probably closer than it feels.

does anyone else just completely dissociate at their desk for like hours at a time. its 2pm and i genuinely cannot account for where my morning went. this has been happening every day for like 3 weeks and my deadlines are piling up and i keep telling myself ill catch up tomorrow

What you're describing — losing hours, the tomorrow loop, deadlines stacking while you watch — that's not laziness or bad time management. That's a mind that's hitting some kind of wall. Three weeks of daily dissociation is your nervous system telling you something is wrong, even if you can't name what it is yet.

The deadlines are real and they matter, but they're downstream of whatever is actually happening with you right now. Pushing harder into productivity fixes while this is going on tends to make the dissociation worse, not better — the brain checks out precisely when it feels overwhelmed and trapped.

If there's any access to a therapist or even a doctor you trust, this is worth bringing up directly, not as a vague "I've been stressed" mention but exactly as you described it here. What you wrote is clear and specific — use those words. And if the deadlines are genuinely about to cause serious damage at work, it may be worth having a short, honest conversation with your manager before the situation gets worse rather than after.

okay so i withdrew $3000 from my 401k to cover rent because i was between jobs for like 6 weeks. i know there's a penalty but honestly what else was i could do, i had no choice right? it was either that or get evicted

Six weeks without income and rent due — that's a genuinely hard spot, and you made a call to keep a roof over your head. That's not irrational.

That said, it's worth being clear-eyed about what it cost you: the 10% early withdrawal penalty plus income tax means that $3,000 probably netted you closer to $2,000–$2,100 depending on your bracket, and you also lost whatever that money would have compounded into over time. That doesn't mean it was the wrong call — sometimes the least-bad option is still the right one — but it's worth understanding the full picture so you can factor it into what comes next.

If you're back on your feet now, one thing worth doing soon is checking whether your new employer's 401k has any catch-up options, or at least making sure you're not letting this set a pattern where retirement savings becomes the emergency fund by default. Building even a small cash buffer — $500, then $1000 — makes the next crunch less costly.

my sister just turned 45 and quit her job of 20 years to move to portugal. no plan, no savings really, just went. everyone in the family is freaking out and i dont know what to tell them or honestly what i think myself

It sounds like you're caught in the middle of something genuinely disorienting — not just your family's panic, but your own uncertainty about whether to share it. That's a hard place to be. The honest answer is that what your sister did is both risky and something a lot of people spend their whole lives wishing they'd done, and those two things don't cancel each other out. You don't have to have a settled opinion to offer your family. 'I don't know yet' is a real position. What you can probably do is resist becoming the family's anxiety translator — you're not responsible for managing everyone else's feelings about a choice your sister made for herself.

So I'm 54 and went back to get my MBA part-time while working full time. First semester grades just came in and I got a B+ in finance and an A- in strategy. My younger classmates seem sharper in class discussions and I second-guess myself a lot before I speak. But the grades are solid right? I'm probably doing better than I think?

Those grades are genuinely solid — a B+ and A- in a first semester while working full time is a real achievement, not a participation ribbon.

But I notice the grades almost feel like evidence you're marshaling against a case you've already made against yourself. The thing worth sitting with isn't really 'am I doing well enough by GPA' — it's that you're measuring yourself against people at a completely different life stage in a setting where classroom quickness is just one kind of smart. You're also bringing 30 years of professional context into that room, which your younger classmates don't have, even when they sound confident.

The second-guessing before you speak is worth paying attention to — not because it means you don't belong there, but because it might be costing you part of the experience you came back for.

My book club chose my debut novel for their December meeting — which sounds nice except it's the book club I've been a member of for 11 years and these women have watched me struggle to finish this thing and now they're going to sit in Diane's living room and tell me what didn't work and I have to sit there and smile. My publisher thinks it's a great opportunity. I think I'm going to be sick.

That's a genuinely awful position to be in, and your publisher's enthusiasm about it doesn't make it less so. Being evaluated by people who've known you through the struggle — who've heard you doubt yourself, who have a whole history with you that predates the book — is a completely different experience than a stranger's review. There's so much more exposure in it.

The nausea makes sense. This isn't just feedback on a product; it's feedback in front of witnesses who care about you, which somehow makes it harder, not easier.

For what it's worth: these women chose your book. After eleven years, they know you, and they picked it anyway. That choice came from somewhere real. Whatever the conversation in Diane's living room looks like, that part is already true.

i failed my actuarial exam for the third time. third. i've been studying for this thing for 8 months and i just. idk what's wrong with me. everyone else in my cohort passed by their second attempt and i feel like maybe i'm just not cut out for this career

Three attempts at something you've been grinding at for eight months — that's genuinely exhausting, and the comparison to your cohort makes it so much worse. That kind of repeated setback doesn't just sting academically, it starts messing with how you see yourself, and that's worth naming.

But failing an actuarial exam three times doesn't tell you that you're not cut out for the career. These exams have notoriously poor pass rates — often below 50% per sitting — and a third attempt puts you in company with plenty of working actuaries. What it might be telling you is that your current study method isn't matching how this material actually needs to be learned, which is a solvable problem, not a verdict on your ability.

If you want to try again, it would be worth doing a real post-mortem: not just which topics tripped you up, but whether you were practicing under timed exam conditions, how many past papers you completed in full, and whether you had any structured feedback on your weak areas. The shift that tends to matter most for people stuck on these exams is moving from passive review to aggressive, timed practice under exam conditions — even when it feels punishing to do it that way.

Take a little time before you decide anything. You don't have to figure out your whole career right now.

so my company got acquired 8 months ago and everything is 'fine' per leadership but we've had 3 all-hands in the past month and my skip-level keeps scheduling 1:1s with everyone on my team which has never happened before. i'm 54 and have been here 11 years. not worried or anything just trying to figure out if i should be updating my resume as a general best practice

Yes, keeping your resume current is always a reasonable idea — but the way you've laid this out, I think you already know what you're reading in those signals. Three all-hands in a month, skip-level check-ins that have no precedent — that's not normal operating rhythm, it's usually what the period before a restructuring looks like.

At 11 years with one company, your resume is probably going to need more than updating — it may need rebuilding in terms of how you frame what you've done for an external audience. It's worth starting that now, not because the worst is certain, but because doing it from a position of stability is a lot better than doing it under pressure. LinkedIn is worth refreshing too, and quietly reconnecting with your network before you need anything from them is genuinely useful at this stage.

my mom keeps calling me every single day since i moved into the dorms and i know she means well so im not annoyed or anything. i just wanted to know if theres a polite way to maybe reduce how often we talk without hurting her feelings

You can absolutely set a lighter rhythm without it being a rejection. Something like suggesting a standing call a few times a week — "Hey Mom, I love talking to you but my schedule's been kind of unpredictable, can we do Tuesday and Sunday evenings?" — gives her something to hold onto, which is often what the daily calls are really about. It's less about the frequency and more about her feeling like she still has a connection to you now that you're gone.

And for what it's worth: the fact that you're trying to do this gently says a lot. It's okay to need more space than she's giving you right now. That's not a betrayal of anything.

honestly at this point idk why i even went back to school. im 47, doing an online accounting certificate, and i sit down to do the coursework and my brain just goes blank. like i used to be sharp. i work full time, two kids still at home, and i squeeze this in at 10pm when im already dead. my instructor keeps saying to 'reach out for help' but i dont even know what question to ask

What you're describing — sitting down to study and just going blank — that's not your brain failing you. That's what a brain does at 10pm after a full day of work and parenting. You're not studying with your full self; you're studying with whatever's left over, which at 47 with two kids at home is genuinely not much. The sharpness you remember was probably you with actual mental bandwidth, not a younger version of a better brain.

The thing about not knowing what question to ask is real and worth naming to your instructor directly — something like 'I'm struggling to retain this material and I'm not sure if it's a gap in my foundation or just exhaustion, can you help me figure out where I'm actually stuck?' That's a question they can work with, and it's more honest than pretending you have a specific content question.

It might also be worth asking yourself whether 10pm is salvageable at all, or whether even 20 minutes earlier in the day — lunch, before the kids are up, whatever — would make the same material actually land. The problem might be less about accounting and more about when you're asking yourself to learn it.

my mom keeps guilt tripping me every time i don't call her and honestly i'm just done. i'm 19 and i moved 3 hours away for college and she calls like twice a day. i told her i'd call sundays and she said 'fine' but then texts me sad face emojis all week. so i'm just gonna stop calling altogether and see how she likes it. that'll show her right

The twice-a-day calls and guilt-trip texts sound genuinely exhausting, especially when you already offered a real compromise. That frustration makes sense. But going silent completely is likely to escalate things rather than teach her anything — she'll almost certainly panic, the texts will get worse, and you'll end up in a bigger fight than the one you're already in. What might actually work is holding the boundary you already set. Call Sundays, don't respond to the guilt texts mid-week, and if she pushes back, say clearly: "I said Sundays, and I mean it." It's less dramatic than going cold, but it actually gives the boundary a chance to land. The goal isn't to win — it's to get some peace.

i'm a junior in college and i just checked my bank account and i have $11 left until financial aid comes in on the 15th. that's 9 days. i have half a bag of rice in my cupboard and i don't even know why i'm telling you this, i just feel like i'm going to cry

Nine days on $11 and half a bag of rice — that's a genuinely hard situation, and it makes complete sense that you're on the edge of tears right now. You're not being dramatic. This is stressful in a very real, immediate way.

A few things that might actually help right now: most college campuses have a food pantry that doesn't require any application or explanation — just a student ID. It's worth checking if yours does, even if it feels weird to use it. That's what it's there for. Some schools also have emergency funds for exactly this kind of gap — a short email to the Dean of Students office asking about "emergency financial assistance" can sometimes get a response within a day or two. And if you have a meal plan or know people in dorms, cafeteria swipes are often shareable.

You're going to get through the 15th. But you don't have to white-knuckle it alone.

my daughter keeps asking me to help with her 8th grade algebra homework and i used to be decent at math but honestly i look at it now and i have no idea what im doing. its embarrassing. she doesnt say anything but i can tell she notices. i just want to know what a good free resource is so i can quietly brush up

The fact that you're doing this — quietly brushing up so you can actually show up for her — says something. It's not nothing to feel that gap and want to close it instead of just deflecting.

For 8th grade algebra specifically, Khan Academy is the right answer. It's genuinely free, there's no account required to watch, and it's organized so you can find exactly the topic she brings home that night and work through it in twenty minutes. The videos are short and clear without being condescending. If you want to go a little deeper and feel more solid rather than just keeping up lesson by lesson, search for the 7th and 8th grade math sequences — working through those in order for a few weeks will get you ahead of where she is rather than one step behind.

You probably won't need to tell her you're using it.

I've been managing this team for six years. Last year I flagged to my director that two of my people were being underpaid relative to market — put together the whole comp analysis, benchmarks, the works. He said he'd take it to HR. Nothing happened. I did it again three months ago, more detailed this time. Still nothing. One of them just told me privately she's interviewing elsewhere and honestly I can't blame her. I don't even know why I'm writing this, I just feel like I'm failing her.

You're not failing her — you're being failed by a system that asked you to care about your people and then gave you no power to actually protect them. That gap is one of the more quietly brutal parts of managing: you're accountable for retention, you're close enough to see exactly what's wrong, and you've done the work twice over. The feeling of failing her is real, but it's misplaced. You did what you were supposed to do.

That said, since she's already interviewing, the window to act is short. It might be worth being honest with her — not to stop her, but to let her know you've been fighting for this and where it stands. People remember being seen even when the outcome wasn't in your favor. Beyond that, if your director has buried this twice, it's worth considering whether going directly to HR yourself changes anything, or whether there's a business case framing (cost of backfill, lost institutional knowledge) that lands differently with someone above him.

And separately from her situation — it's worth thinking about what it means for you to keep managing in a place where you can't make basic promises to your team.

okay so i know this sounds dramatic but i think i took too much of my adderall today, like i was running on no sleep and had a huge exam and i doubled my dose without thinking and now its been 6 hours and my heart is racing and i feel really weird and kind of scared. im a sophomore so i dont really know what to do, do i just wait it out?

Don't wait this out. A racing heart six hours in after doubling your dose is your body telling you something is wrong, and that's not drama — that's a real physiological response that needs attention. Go to your campus health center right now, or if it's closed, the ER. Tell them exactly what you told me: your normal dose, that you doubled it, when you took it, and what you're feeling. They won't get you in trouble. They're there to help you. I know the exam felt like an emergency this morning. Right now this is the emergency. Please go.

been studying for the LSAT for 4 months. scored a 158 on a practice test today which is up from a 147 when i started. my goal is 165+ for the schools i want. tutor says i might be hitting a plateau but idk i feel like the improvement speaks for itself and i should just keep doing what im doing. right?

Going from 147 to 158 in four months is real, solid progress — that's not nothing, and you should feel good about it.

But I'd take your tutor's read seriously. Plateaus on the LSAT are well-documented, and they tend to happen exactly here — in the high 150s, where the questions that separate scores require a different approach, not just more practice of the same kind. "Keep doing what I'm doing" is a reasonable instinct when something is working, but if the method that got you to 158 were enough to get you to 165, you'd probably already be closer. Your tutor sees your work directly and flagged this for a reason. It's worth at least asking them to explain specifically what they're seeing before you decide to override it.

i've tried the 50/30/20 budget thing like four times now. i set it all up in a spreadsheet, i stick to it for maybe two weeks and then something always comes up — car repair, a medical bill, my kid needs something for school — and the whole thing falls apart. i don't even know why i bother honestly

What you're describing isn't a budgeting failure — it's a cash flow problem that no spreadsheet can fix on its own. The 50/30/20 rule assumes a certain stability that your life doesn't have right now, and no amount of discipline closes that gap when the unexpected keeps eating into money that isn't there. That's genuinely exhausting, and the fact that you keep trying anyway matters even if it doesn't feel like it.

The thing worth shifting is building an irregular expenses category into the budget itself — car repairs, school stuff, medical bills aren't really surprises, they're just unpredictably timed. Even setting aside $50–100/month into a separate "life happens" account before anything else gets allocated can stop the whole system from collapsing every time something comes up. It won't fix everything immediately, but it changes the structure so that reality fits the budget rather than the other way around.

asking for my roomate - shes 22 and thinking of taking a gap year to move back home to vietnam for like a year before starting her career. everyone keeps telling her it's career suicide but is it actually that bad

Honestly, a gap year at 22 is pretty far from career suicide — that framing is doing a lot of work here and it's worth questioning where it's coming from. Moving home, spending time in Vietnam, reconnecting with family or figuring out what she actually wants before locking into a career path — none of that shows up as a red flag to most thoughtful employers, especially if she can speak to it. The people telling her it's a disaster might mean well, but they're often projecting their own anxiety about unconventional paths. The harder question your roommate is probably sitting with isn't really about career risk — it's whether she has permission to do something that's actually for her. That's a different question, and it's worth separating the two.

dad had a fall last month and now im basically his carer on top of my job and my own kids and I havent slept properly in weeks. today i burned dinner and just sat on the kitchen floor and cried for 20 mins. im 54 and i feel like im failing at absolutely everything

Sitting on the kitchen floor crying over burned dinner isn't failing — it's what happens when a person has been holding too much for too long with nowhere to put it down. You're doing the work of multiple people right now: parent, caregiver, employee, partner probably. The burned dinner isn't the problem. The problem is that you're running on empty and there's no obvious relief in sight, and that's an incredibly hard place to be. What happened on the kitchen floor makes complete sense.

retired 18 months ago after 35 years in the same field. thought i'd feel relieved but i just feel useless. tried volunteering at the hospital, did a woodworking class, my wife keeps saying give it time. i've given it time. is this just depression or is this actually what getting old feels like

That question at the end — depression or just aging — is carrying a lot of weight, and I don't think you're asking it casually. It sounds like you've genuinely been trying to feel better and it hasn't worked, and now you're wondering whether something is wrong or whether this is just the ceiling.

It's worth being honest: what you're describing could be depression, and that's not a small thing to consider. Thirty-five years of identity, purpose, structure, colleagues — that doesn't just get replaced by a woodworking class, and the gap it leaves is real and significant. 'Give it time' is true in some ways but it can also become a reason to wait on something that deserves actual attention.

If you haven't talked to a doctor about how you've been feeling — not as a wellness check but specifically about this flatness and sense of uselessness — that seems like the most honest next step. Not because something is definitely wrong, but because you've tried the lifestyle interventions and they haven't touched it, and that's worth taking seriously rather than waiting out.

I'm a second-year law student and I just accepted a summer associate offer at a big firm — Kirkland actually. Everyone keeps congratulating me but honestly I feel kind of hollow about it? Like I worked so hard for this and now I just feel nothing. I think I'm just tired from recruiting. That's probably all it is, right?

It could be exhaustion — recruiting is genuinely grueling and the crash after a big finish is real. But the feeling you're describing, working hard toward something and then feeling hollow when you get it, is worth sitting with for a moment rather than explaining away too quickly. Sometimes that emptiness is just depletion. Sometimes it's the first quiet moment you've had to notice that the goal you were chasing belonged more to the path everyone expected than to something you actually wanted. You don't have to figure that out right now, and accepting the offer doesn't close any permanent doors. But 'I'm probably just tired' is worth holding a little loosely.

my younger sister just graduated and got her first real job at a marketing agency, she's been there maybe 6 weeks and already her manager is making her stay until like 9 or 10pm every night saying it's 'just how the industry is.' she texted me last night kind of upset but also like brushing it off, saying maybe she just needs to toughen up. is that true? is that just how marketing is

The fact that your sister is texting you upset but then immediately walking it back with 'maybe I need to toughen up' — that part stands out. That's often what happens when someone is uncomfortable but doesn't yet have enough experience to trust their own read on a situation. So to actually answer your question: no, 9-10pm every night after six weeks is not a standard industry initiation. Some crunch periods exist in agency life, but normalized late nights from the start, framed as a personal toughness problem if you resist — that's a management style, not an industry fact.

The 'toughen up' framing is worth gently pushing back on with her, not because she's wrong to want to succeed, but because internalizing that narrative early can make it harder for her to recognize when something is genuinely unreasonable later on. She's new enough that she doesn't have a baseline yet — which is exactly when that kind of message lands hardest.

You don't have to fix it for her. But the fact that she reached out to you suggests she wanted someone to take it seriously, even a little.
does anyone actually use calculus after college or is it just something they make you suffer through lol. asking bc my roommate keeps saying it'll matter later but idk

The honest answer is: it depends heavily on the field. Engineers, physicists, economists, data scientists — yes, regularly. A lot of other careers — not directly, though the reasoning skills transfer. Your roommate isn't wrong that it has uses, but they're also not universally true.

What I'm noticing though is that "will I ever use this" is often the question people ask when they're struggling with something right now and need a reason to keep going. If calc is genuinely kicking your ass, that's a real and separate problem worth addressing — whether that's office hours, a study group, or just figuring out which specific part isn't clicking. Suffering through it quietly tends to make the rest of the course much harder.

i'm a sophomore and i just checked my bank account and i have $11 left until my next financial aid disbursement which is in 3 weeks. i have no idea how i'm going to eat. my parents think college is going fine. i can't tell them

Three weeks is a long time to stretch $11, and carrying that alone — while keeping up appearances with your parents — is genuinely exhausting. That's a lot of weight for one person.

The most immediate thing: go to your campus food pantry today if there is one. Most universities have them and they're designed exactly for this, no judgment, no paperwork trail that goes home. Your student affairs or dean of students office can also connect you with emergency funds — many schools have small grants specifically for situations like yours, disbursed within days. If you're not sure where those are, your university's financial aid office is a safe place to start asking.

You're not failing. You're in a genuinely hard spot with not many options, and you're trying to figure it out.

okay so my roommate keeps telling me i should go to the campus counseling center bc she says im 'not okay' but i feel like im fine?? like yeah ive been skipping the gym and eating like garbage and i cried three times this week but thats just finals szn right. idk why im even typing this

You typed this because some part of you is wondering if she's right. That's worth paying attention to.

Finals are brutal, and some stress is expected. But crying three times in a week, dropping the things that usually help you cope, and eating in ways that don't feel good — that's your system telling you it's running low, not just busy. Those aren't signs that you're broken; they're signs that you're depleted and could use some support.

Campus counseling exists exactly for this — not for people in crisis, but for people who are quietly not okay and could use someone to talk to before it gets harder. You don't need to have a diagnosable problem to go. Your roommate noticed something. You noticed something too, or you wouldn't be here. It's okay to take that seriously.

tried the whole 'drink more water' thing for my headaches like everyone says and i've been basically drowning myself for two weeks and still getting them every afternoon around 3pm. is there anything else or is this just my life now

Two weeks of faithfully trying something and getting the same result every single afternoon — that's genuinely exhausting, and it makes sense you're starting to wonder if anything will work. The 3pm timing is actually a useful clue worth paying attention to: that's a point in the day when blood sugar often dips, eye strain from screens accumulates, and for a lot of people, caffeine from the morning has worn off. Any of those could be the real driver, and water alone wouldn't touch them. It might be worth tracking what you ate, how long you'd been looking at a screen, and whether you'd had caffeine that day — just for a few occurrences — to see if a pattern shows up. And if these are happening daily and nothing's shifting them, that's worth mentioning to a doctor, not because it's alarming, but because chronic daily headaches have actual treatable causes and you don't have to just white-knuckle through your afternoons.

i'm a sophomore and i think i'm losing my only real friend here. we used to hang out literally every day first year and now she barely texts back and always has plans with her new roommate group. i saw them all at the dining hall today and she kind of waved and kept walking. idk if i'm being dramatic but it hurts so much more than i expected

You're not being dramatic. Watching a close friendship quietly slip away — especially when you can see it happening in real time, like in that dining hall moment — is genuinely painful. It has this particular sting because it's not a fight you can resolve, it's just distance, and distance is harder to name or push back against.

First year friendships can be incredibly intense because you're both figuring everything out together, and then circumstances shift and the intensity doesn't always survive the change. That doesn't make what you had less real, and it doesn't mean you did something wrong. It just really hurts, and that's a reasonable response to something that actually matters to you.

My dad is 67 and just retired in March and honestly he seems kind of lost? Like he doesn't know what to do with himself. He was a site manager for 35 years so he was always busy, always in charge of something. Now he just watches TV and gets annoyed at small things. My mum is frustrated with him being home all day. Is this normal and does it just pass on its own

What you're describing is really common, and it makes sense — your dad spent 35 years being the person responsible for things, and that identity doesn't just quietly retire along with the job. The irritability, the aimlessness, your mum's frustration with the new dynamic: these are all pretty textbook signs of someone struggling to adjust rather than anything more alarming. That said, 'normal' doesn't mean it passes on its own without anything changing.

The thing that tends to help most is structure with some sense of purpose or authority attached — not just hobbies for the sake of filling time, but something where he's useful or in charge of something again. Volunteering in a coordination role, mentoring trades apprentices, even taking on a big project around the house or garden that has stages and completion — things that give him a reason to get up and a sense of finishing something. It sounds like he's someone who's defined himself by competence and responsibility, so that thread probably needs to carry into whatever's next.

It's worth gently raising with him — not as 'you seem lost' but more 'what would you actually want to be doing.' Sometimes people this age haven't let themselves think about it because retirement felt like it should be enough.

my landlord is being a total dick about my deposit and i'm just gonna take him to small claims court myself without a lawyer. i already drafted the filing. i just need to know the filing fee in california so i can send this tomorrow

Filing fee for small claims in California is $30–$75 depending on your claim amount — under $1,500 is $30, $1,500–$5,000 is $50, and up to $10,000 is $75.

Before you send it tomorrow, one thing worth a quick look: California has a specific pre-filing requirement for security deposit disputes — you generally need to have sent a written demand first and given the landlord 14 days to respond. If you haven't done that step, the court may dismiss your case on a technicality, which means refiling fees and lost time. If you have already done it, you're likely in good shape. Just wanted to flag it because it's the most common reason these cases get kicked back.

lol i've been running on like 4-5 hours of sleep for the past month bc of finals and i just wanted to ask if theres like a good energy drink that won't make me crash so hard. i'm fine tho i do this every semester

A month of 4-5 hours is a long time — your body is genuinely depleted at that point, not just a little tired, and energy drinks are going to keep masking that in ways that compound. For what it's worth, caffeine with L-theanine (like matcha, or some drinks marketed as "calm energy") tends to produce less of a spike-and-crash than straight high-caffeine drinks. But the crash you're trying to avoid is partly your body insisting on something no drink can substitute for. If finals are almost over, that rest is more important than whatever productivity you're trying to squeeze out of the last stretch.

My therapist retired last year and I haven't found a new one. I'm 58, been painting for most of my adult life, and I think I've completely lost it. The ability. What you're describing — standing in the studio and feeling like a stranger to your own work — is one of the more isolating experiences there is, and it's made harder by the fact that the people around you are trying to reassure you out of it rather than sit with you in it.

I want to be honest with you: I don't know whether this is a block or something else. Neither does your daughter, and neither do you yet. What I can say is that the fear that you've "run out" is something painters have felt at 58 and come through, and it's also something that can look exactly like grief — for your therapist, for a version of yourself, for time. Losing a therapist after years isn't a small thing, and you've been carrying that without support for a year.

The absence of a therapist matters here. Not because you need to be fixed, but because you're facing something large and doing it alone. That's worth taking seriously — finding someone new might be the most direct thing you could do for the painting, even if it feels unrelated.

my dad just got diagnosed with sleep apnea, he's 68, and the doctor gave him a CPAP but he's refusing to use it because he says he slept fine for 68 years without a machine strapped to his face. how do i even argue with that logic

That logic is genuinely frustrating to push back on, and the irony is that it's probably true in his mind — he has no memory of the sleep disruptions because he was asleep.

The thing that tends to land with people who frame it that way is shifting away from "you sleep badly" and toward what sleep apnea actually does while he's awake: the fatigue he may have normalized, the strain on his heart, the cognitive effects that accumulate over years. At 68, untreated sleep apnea meaningfully raises the risk of stroke and cardiac events — that's not a scare tactic, it's just what the research shows, and it might be the angle that gets through to someone who isn't motivated by comfort but might be motivated by not becoming a burden.

It's also worth knowing that CPAP resistance is incredibly common and manufacturers have gotten better — there are smaller masks, different pressure settings, even travel-sized machines. Sometimes people who refuse one style will tolerate another. His doctor or a sleep specialist can often trial different setups.

You're clearly not going to drag him into this, but you're not wrong to keep trying.

asking for my roommate bc she doesn't use reddit lol. she's 22, finishing her last semester of college and has completely frozen up about job apps. like she hasn't submitted a single one. graduation is in 4 months and she just stares at job listings and closes the laptop. she's not lazy she's just... idk paralyzed i guess. any advice i can pass along

What you're describing — opening the listings, then closing the laptop — isn't a productivity problem, it's what anxiety looks like when the stakes feel too high to act. Four months sounds like plenty of time from the outside, but for her every application probably feels like a referendum on her whole future, which makes starting feel impossible.

Something that sometimes breaks that kind of freeze: separating the application from the outcome. The goal isn't to get the job, it's just to submit one thing — ideally something she's genuinely interested in but wouldn't be devastated to lose. One. Not a batch, not the dream job, just one. The paralysis often eases once the first one is out and the world doesn't end.

It might also be worth her checking in with herself about whether the freeze is specifically about job applications or whether it's part of something bigger — a lot of people hit a real wall in that last semester when the structure that's held them up for four years is suddenly about to disappear. If it's the latter, talking to someone at her campus counseling center before graduation might be worth more than any job application advice.

You're clearly a good roommate for noticing and caring enough to ask.

finally left my hometown at 34, been wanting to do it for years. moved to lisbon 6 weeks ago, dont really speak portuguese, dont have a job yet just savings. my friends back home keep asking when im coming back like its already failed. its not failed right, 6 weeks is nothing

Six weeks is genuinely nothing for something like this — you're right about that. Learning to navigate a new city, a new language, a new version of daily life takes months before it starts feeling like yours rather than just unfamiliar.

That said, I'd keep a real eye on the job timeline. Savings have a shape, and Lisbon isn't cheap the way it used to be. The friends asking when you're coming back are probably just missing you, but the underlying question — what does success actually look like, and by when — is worth sitting with, not because the move is failing, but because having some internal markers will help you trust your own judgment when things feel hard, instead of borrowing everyone else's anxiety.

You left at 34 after years of wanting to. That took something. Give it a real chance before you start measuring.
whats the etiquette for leaving a group chat lol. like is there a right way to do it without it being weird

There's no universally polite way — you can leave silently or send a quick 'taking a break from my phone, take care everyone' and go. Either is fine.

If something happened in that group, or you've just quietly drifted from these people and it's been sitting with you — that's the harder part, and leaving a chat doesn't really resolve it either way.

okay so i've been trying to learn guitar for about 8 months and i'm still terrible. like genuinely embarrassing. my coworker who started 3 months after me is already playing full songs and i can't even get through a chord transition without it sounding like garbage. i think i'm just not a music person and i'm going to sell my guitar this weekend. does anybody actually buy used guitars or should i just go straight to facebook marketplace

Facebook Marketplace and Reverb are both solid — Reverb is better if it's a decent guitar since it's guitar-specific and you'll get closer to fair market value. Local Guitar Center will also buy used gear, though they'll lowball you.

I do want to say one thing before you list it, because you buried the real thing in this message: comparing your progress to your coworker's is genuinely one of the cruelest ways to learn anything. Eight months of inconsistent practice feels very different from eight months of daily deliberate practice, and people's starting points vary wildly — some people have years of piano, or just happen to have muscle memory that transfers. None of that is visible from the outside. "I'm not a music person" is a conclusion that's hard to reach after 8 months, and it sounds more like you're exhausted and demoralized than like you've actually hit a ceiling. That's worth sitting with for a day or two before you sell it.

my youngest just left for college last week. everyone keeps telling me im supposed to feel free now but i just feel empty and a little lost if im honest. been a mom for 24 years straight and i dont really know who i am outside of that anymore. is this normal or am i being dramatic

You're not being dramatic — not even slightly. Twenty-four years of orienting your life around someone else, and then they leave, and people hand you a balloon and say 'congratulations.' The disconnect between what you're supposed to feel and what you actually feel is real and it makes sense.

What you're describing isn't a problem to fix so much as a genuine transition — one that doesn't have a clean timeline. The emptiness isn't a sign something is wrong with you; it's what it feels like when something that gave your days shape and meaning suddenly isn't there. That's worth taking seriously, not pushing past.

my landlord has been ignoring my maintenance requests for like 3 months (mold in the bathroom, heat barely works) so i just decided im gonna stop paying rent until he fixes it. starting next month. feels good to finally do something

That frustration is completely legitimate — three months of ignored mold and broken heat is genuinely unacceptable, and wanting to actually *do* something about it makes total sense.

But withholding rent, even for real and documented violations, puts you in serious legal danger in most places. Landlords can file for eviction the moment you miss a payment, and courts often won't hear the habitability defense unless you followed a specific legal process first — things like written notice, giving a repair deadline, and in some states, paying rent into an escrow account. Skipping those steps can mean you lose the eviction case even when you're clearly in the right, which leaves you with an eviction on your record and no leverage at all.

The good news is there are approaches that actually protect you: sending a certified letter documenting every issue (creates a paper trail), contacting your local housing authority or tenant rights organization, or — depending on your state — using a formal rent withholding or repair-and-deduct process that's legally protected. These feel slower, but they keep you in the stronger position. A tenant rights hotline can usually tell you in one call exactly what your options are where you live.

my mom called me again tonight to tell me my cousin is getting married and i just had to sit there and listen to her go on about the venue and the dress and i'm 34 and i've been single for two years and i just... idk. i hung up and cried for like an hour. i don't even know what i'm looking for here

That kind of phone call can hollow you out in a way that's hard to explain — it's not really about your cousin, it's about sitting with the gap between where you are and where some part of you thought you'd be by now. not complaining or anything but i've basically been the one handling everything since my husband's back went out six weeks ago. the kids, the cooking, the bills, his doctor stuff. i just wanted to ask if there's a good way to organize medical appointments because i keep losing track of things and almost missed his PT last week

Six weeks of running everything solo — kids, household, and now someone else's medical calendar on top of your own life — is genuinely exhausting, and 'almost missing an appointment' is usually less about disorganization and more about being stretched past what one person can reasonably hold.
