Keeping a single running notes doc (even just in your phone) with appointment dates, provider names, and any follow-up instructions cuts down on the mental load of trying to hold it all in your head. But you're doing a lot right now, and it's okay if that's hard.

my mom called me again last night crying saying im abandoning her because i moved 2 hours away for college. this is the 4th time this month. i feel so guilty but also like... i cant keep doing this?? i have an exam tomorrow and i spent 45 min on the phone just listening to her cry. idk what to do

That's a genuinely hard position to be in — you're not being selfish for feeling stretched thin, and the guilt you're carrying doesn't mean you've done something wrong. Moving two hours away for college is a normal, healthy thing to do, and it sounds like part of you already knows that.

What's actually happening here is that your mom is struggling with the separation, and she's pulling on you to manage her distress — four times in one month, the night before an exam. That's a pattern, not a crisis, and it's worth naming to yourself clearly: her emotional pain is real, but it's not yours to solve at the cost of your own stability.

In the short term, it's okay to set a boundary on when and how long you talk. Something like "I can't do calls on weeknights before exams, but I'll call you Sunday" isn't abandonment — it's you being honest about what you can give. If this pattern keeps up, it might be worth gently suggesting she talk to someone; not as a deflection, but because what she's going through sounds like it needs more support than you're able to provide from two hours away.

so i've been doing intermittent fasting for like 6 weeks, eating in a 4 hour window every day, and i lost 11 lbs which is great but i've also been getting these headaches almost every afternoon and i'm kind of irritable all the time according to my husband lol. but like, results are results right? this is probably just my body adjusting still?

Eleven pounds in six weeks is real progress, and it makes sense you don't want to second-guess something that's working. But six weeks is long enough that "adjustment" is probably not the full story here. Daily afternoon headaches and consistent mood changes are your body signaling something — most likely that a 4-hour eating window is too compressed for how you're wired, even if the scale is moving. That's not a personal failure; it's just physiology. A slightly wider window, like 6 or 8 hours, often preserves the weight loss while dropping the side effects. Worth at least considering before pushing through more weeks of feeling like this.

okay so i tried the thing where you put your credit card in the freezer so you cant impulse buy and i just. ordered a new one lmao. i have $4800 in cc debt and i graduate in 8 months and i genuinely dont know how this happened. like i know how it happened but i dont know HOW it happened if that makes sense

Yeah, that makes complete sense — you can trace every transaction and still feel like a stranger made them. That gap between knowing and understanding is real, and it's not the same as being irresponsible or stupid.

The frozen card thing works for some people but it assumes the problem is access, when usually it's something else — boredom, anxiety, a bad week, social stuff. Ordering a replacement tells you something useful: friction alone isn't enough for you, which is actually good information.

Eight months is a real runway. $4,800 isn't a small number but it's also not an unworkable one, especially if you're about to have income. The more useful thing to look at right now is probably the interest rate — if it's high, even a small aggressive payment plan before you graduate changes how much you're actually dealing with by the time you get there. And if the spending is still happening, it might be worth getting honest with yourself about what it's usually covering emotionally, because that's the part no budgeting hack touches.

My husband and I are separating after 24 years. The kids are grown so everyone keeps acting like this is fine and simple and I should just be practical about dividing things up. I'm 51 and I don't even know who I am outside of being his wife and their mother. Is that pathetic?

No, it's not pathetic. It's what happens when you build a life around relationships that then change — your sense of self got woven into those roles over decades, and that's not a personal failure, it's just what long-term commitment does to identity. The fact that your kids are grown doesn't make this smaller. If anything, it removes the structure that would have kept you busy enough not to feel the full weight of it.

The people telling you to be practical aren't wrong that there are practical things to handle. But they're skipping over something real: you're grieving, and you're also facing a genuinely open question about who you are now. That question isn't pathetic — it's actually the most important thing in front of you, and it deserves more than being rushed past.

Fifty-one is not the end of figuring yourself out. It's just later than you expected to have to.

my mom called me three times today just to tell me the same story about my cousin's wedding and i love her but i genuinely wanted to scream into a pillow by the end of it. is this a terrible person thing to feel

No, it's not a terrible person thing to feel. Loving someone and finding them exhausting in a specific moment are not contradictory — they coexist all the time, especially with parents. The fact that you're even asking suggests you care about being a good daughter or son, which is actually the opposite of the concern. Repeated calls with the same story can wear anyone down, and feeling that doesn't cancel out the love.

my doctor wants me to go on metformin for prediabetes and i keep saying ill think about it but its been like 4 months. i know i need to lose weight and eat better but i just. cant seem to actually do it. every monday i restart and by wednesday im back to eating like garbage. idk why im telling you this i dont even have a real question

Four months of 'I'll think about it' while the Mondays keep coming and going — that's not laziness, that's someone who's genuinely stuck, and that's worth taking seriously.

The pattern you're describing — restart, collapse, restart — usually means the plan isn't matched to your actual life, not that your willpower is broken. And the metformin question is sitting underneath all of it: you're probably hoping that if you can just get the habits right, you won't need the medication, which is a reasonable hope. But four months is also long enough that it's worth being honest with your doctor about where you actually are, not where you planned to be. Metformin and lifestyle change aren't an either/or — a lot of people find the medication takes enough pressure off that the habits become easier to build, not harder.

You don't have a question, but you do have a situation that's slowly getting away from you. Calling the doctor back and telling them the truth — that you haven't made the changes — is probably the most useful next move.

i've sent my resume to like 47 places since graduating in May and i've gotten maybe 3 responses, all rejections. i rewrote my resume twice already using all the advice i could find online and it's still not working. at this point idk if i'm just unemployable or what

47 applications with almost no responses is genuinely demoralizing — especially when you've already done the work of revising and trying to do things right. That kind of silence doesn't mean you're unemployable. It usually means something structural is off, and it's hard to diagnose from the inside.

A few things worth actually investigating rather than just trying again the same way: Are you getting through applicant tracking systems at all? Pasting your resume text into a plain text document and checking whether key terms from job postings show up can reveal a lot. Also, the volume-and-apply approach tends to have diminishing returns — a smaller number of applications where you've made direct contact with someone at the company (even a LinkedIn message to a recruiter or recent hire) often outperforms blanket submissions. It's slower and more uncomfortable, but the math usually works out better.

You've been at this for months right out of school. That's a hard stretch. The frustration you're feeling is a reasonable response to a genuinely hard situation, not a sign that something is wrong with you.

my mom keeps saying i'm too sensitive whenever i try to tell her something bothers me and then i end up apologizing to HER somehow. happened again last night, i brought up how she never came to any of my college graduation stuff and she cried and now i feel like the worst person alive. was i wrong to bring it up??

You're not wrong for bringing it up. Missing your graduation is a real thing that happened, and wanting to talk about it with your mother is completely reasonable. What you're describing — where you raise something that hurt you and somehow end up comforting her for it — is a pattern worth noticing, not just a one-time misunderstanding. The guilt you're feeling right now is real, but it's worth separating 'I made her cry' from 'I did something wrong.' Those aren't the same thing, even though they can feel identical in the moment.

my roommate's little sister is visiting for the weekend and she's been crying in the bathroom for like 20 mins. my roommate is at work and won't be back til 9. she's maybe 16? i don't even know her name. do i knock or just leave her alone

Knock. A teenager crying alone in a stranger's bathroom for 20 minutes is not a situation where leaving her alone is the kind thing — it's just the more comfortable choice for you, which makes sense, but she's the one who needs something right now.

Keep it low-pressure. Something like "Hey, just checking you're okay in there — no rush, just wanted you to know I'm around" lets her decide whether to open up without putting her on the spot. If she says she's fine, you can leave it at that and maybe just stay nearby so she knows she's not completely alone until your roommate gets home.

You're already paying attention to her. That's most of it.

asking for my dad who is 67 and just retired — he got a letter saying his pension is being reduced by like 23% starting next year because the fund is underfunded. he's kind of in shock and doesn't really know where to start. is there anything he can actually do or is he just stuck

That's a gut punch, especially when he's just made the leap into retirement with certain numbers in mind. A 23% cut at 67, when the plan was already set — that's not just a financial adjustment, it's disorienting in a deeper way. Please make sure he knows that his reaction makes complete sense.

On the practical side: he's not necessarily stuck, though options depend on the type of pension. If it's a private sector pension, the Pension Benefit Guaranty Corporation (PBGC) provides federal insurance up to certain limits — he should check whether the fund is PBGC-insured and what the maximum guarantee would be for his benefit level. If it's a multiemployer plan, the rules are different and the PBGC limits are lower, but he still has the right to a formal notice explaining the cut and the fund's status, and he can request the fund's annual report to understand how underfunded it actually is.

A one-time consultation with a fee-only financial planner (not someone selling products) could help him look at the full picture — Social Security timing, any other assets — and figure out what the realistic adjustment looks like. It's a hard situation, but there's more information available to him than that letter probably conveyed.

honestly what is even the point of finishing my MBA at this point. im halfway through, $60k in debt, and every recruiter ghosted me after the campus job fair last week. my undergrad friends who went straight to work are making more than i will when i graduate. did i just throw away 2 years

Getting ghosted by every recruiter at the fair after two years and $60k is a brutal gut-check, and the comparison to friends who skipped grad school entirely makes it feel even worse. That's a real thing to sit with, not just anxiety to push through.

I don't think the answer is as clean as "yes you wasted it" or "no you didn't" — it depends on what you do with the next year and a half. The honest problem right now isn't the degree itself; it's that job fair networking rarely converts well without follow-up, and recruiters at those events are mostly collecting resumes. The people who get offers usually have a warm connection before they walk in the room. That part is fixable.

If you want to think through what's actually salvageable here — the specific industry you're targeting, what your outreach has looked like, whether there's a program office or alumni network you haven't tapped — that's worth working through concretely. The debt is real and the frustration is real, but the decision about whether to finish is better made from a clearer view of what's blocking you right now than from how last week felt.

so i just graduated in may and i got this offer from a decent company, 58k, but my old college roomate keeps telling me i should hold out for something better and honestly idk maybe shes right?? i already said yes to the offer tho lol. thinking about backing out

It sounds like you were feeling okay about this job until your roommate said something, and now you're second-guessing yourself — which is worth separating out from actually having new information.

Backing out of a signed offer is a real thing people do, and it's not catastrophic, but it does have consequences: that company and anyone connected to them is likely off the table for a while, and if it's an industry where people talk, word can get around. That's not a reason to stay in a bad situation, but it's a reason to be sure you're backing out for your reasons, not because someone else's confidence rattled yours.

$58k for a first job out of college is in a reasonable range depending on your field and location. "Something better" is always theoretically out there — the question is whether you have actual evidence it's likely for you right now, in this market, on this timeline. If you do, that's worth weighing. If it's more of a vague "you could probably do better," that's harder to act on.

Take a day before you do anything. Think about what you actually wanted from this job when you said yes — and whether any of that has changed.

After 22 years at this company I've decided I'm not going to train my replacement. They're outsourcing my whole department and gave me a 60 day notice, and I just feel like why should I? Let them figure it out. My manager already knows I'm not happy about it but hasn't said anything about the knowledge transfer yet. Is there not training my replacement something people actually do

Twenty-two years and a 60-day notice. That's a real betrayal, and the anger behind this makes complete sense.

To answer your direct question: yes, people do refuse knowledge transfer, or do the bare minimum, especially in situations like this. It happens. But I want to be honest with you about what it tends to cost the person doing it, not the company.

The company will absorb the chaos eventually. What tends to linger is the reference situation — 22 years means your manager and colleagues are likely your most credible professional references for the rest of your career. Ending on a note of visible refusal can complicate that, and depending on your field, it can also affect reputation in ways that follow you. There's also sometimes a practical angle: severance agreements or final bonuses occasionally have cooperation clauses.

None of that means you owe them enthusiasm or extra hours. But there's a version of this where you do the knowledge transfer in a minimal, professional way — not for them, but to walk out with your reputation clean and your leverage intact. That's a different thing than letting them win.

What you're owed is acknowledgment that this is genuinely awful. What you do with that is still your call.

been at my company 14 years. they just announced layoffs and my whole team is probably getting cut next month. i have a decent severance package coming and my wife thinks i should just take it and finally start the consulting business ive been talking about for years. part of me wants to but honestly im 52 and the idea of no steady paycheck is terrifying. i dont even know why im typing this out

Fourteen years and a layoff landing in the same moment — that's a lot to be sitting with, even if the severance softens it. The fear you're describing isn't irrational. At 52, with a mortgage or dependents or just the weight of knowing what financial instability actually looks like, a regular paycheck means something real. The consulting idea being something you've talked about for years doesn't mean now is automatically the right time — it means it's a real thing you actually want, which is different from it being the obvious move. What might be worth separating out is whether the fear is about the idea itself or about the timing and runway. Those have different answers. You don't have to decide what this means today.

my husband got a job offer in Singapore. really good one, life changing money. we have 3 kids, my mom is 71 and not in great health, and I just got promoted at my job for the first time in 8 years. everyone keeps telling me this is a no brainer but it doesn't feel that way to me at all and I don't know if I'm being selfish or just scared or what

The people calling this a no-brainer are doing the math on one part of it — the salary — and skipping over everything else you just listed. A promotion you worked eight years for. A mother whose health is declining. Three kids who would be uprooted. Those aren't small footnotes.

And the fact that it doesn't feel simple to you isn't selfishness or fear — it's you actually seeing the full picture, which the people saying "no-brainer" apparently aren't. Your career matters. Your ability to be near your mom during whatever comes next matters. Those things don't disappear because the offer is lucrative.

This is a genuinely hard decision with real costs on both sides, and you're allowed to name that. What might actually help is getting specific with your husband about what happens to each of those things — your job, your mom, the kids — not as obstacles to overcome but as real factors that deserve real answers before you decide anything.

i've been trying to get into oil painting for like two years now and every single canvas i finish looks like garbage. i watch the tutorials, i buy the supplies they recommend, i do the exercises. my stuff still looks like a kid made it. at what point do i just accept i'm not a visual person

Two years of consistent effort and still feeling like nothing's clicking — that's genuinely demoralizing, especially when you're doing everything you're supposed to do. The gap between what you can see and what your hands can make is one of the most brutal parts of learning to paint, and it doesn't close on the same schedule for everyone. That doesn't mean you're not a visual person; it might mean the tutorial-and-exercises path isn't how your particular brain is going to get there. Some people break through by working much smaller, or by copying a specific painting they love obsessively instead of doing general exercises, or by finding a teacher who can actually watch them work and name what's going wrong. The question isn't really whether you have some innate visual gift — it's whether you want to keep going badly enough to try a different angle, or whether two years is a reasonable place to decide painting specifically isn't worth it to you. Both of those are legitimate answers.

i've been a nurse for 22 years and i swear the last six months i don't recognize myself at work anymore. keep making small mistakes, forgetting things. nothing serious has happened thank god but i just wanted to vent i guess, idk what im even asking. i told my supervisor i was fine when she checked in last week

Twenty-two years of competence and now you're watching yourself make mistakes you didn't used to make — that's frightening in a way that's hard to name, especially in a job where the stakes are real. The instinct to tell your supervisor you're fine makes sense, but what you're describing — the forgetting, not recognizing yourself, the erosion over six months — that's your system telling you something is wrong, not a rough patch to push through.

You don't have to have a specific ask to take this seriously. The fact that you're noticing it, and that it worries you, is enough of a reason to actually get support — whether that's through your hospital's EAP, your own doctor, or someone you trust outside of work. You've given a lot to this profession. That doesn't mean you have to run on empty to keep proving it.
this is probably a dumb question but how much notice are you legally required to give when you quit a job? i know two weeks is like 'the thing' but is it actually required

Not a dumb question at all — and the short answer is no, two weeks isn't legally required in most of the US. The majority of states are at-will employment, which means you can technically quit the same day with no legal consequence. Some contracts or union agreements specify notice requirements, so it's worth checking if you signed anything.

The two-week norm is a professional courtesy, not a law — it protects your references and relationships, which matters in some industries more than others. If you're in a situation where staying two weeks feels genuinely difficult or unsafe, that's a real consideration, not just you being flaky.

my dad is 63 and just got laid off after 22 years at the same company. he keeps saying hes fine and that hell find something but its been 4 months and i can see hes burning through savings. he wont talk about money with me, like at all. i dont even know what to ask him or if i should just leave it alone. honestly dont know why im even writing this

You're writing this because watching a parent struggle and not being able to help is genuinely hard — especially when they're the kind of person who's spent decades being the stable one, and now they're protecting you from something you can already see.

At 63, a layoff after 22 years isn't just a job loss. It's a collision with questions about identity, age discrimination in hiring, and how close retirement actually is. The "I'm fine" is probably less denial and more that he doesn't have a clear picture himself yet, and that's frightening to admit.

You can't force the conversation, but there's a middle path between pushing and leaving it alone entirely. Sometimes it helps to make it less about his finances and more about logistics — something like asking if he's looked into whether the company offered any severance, or whether he knows when he'd be eligible to access retirement accounts without penalty, framed as curiosity rather than concern. It gives him something concrete to engage with instead of a feelings conversation he's not ready for.

If he's open to it at all, one genuinely useful thing for someone in his position is a session with a fee-only financial planner — not to be told he's in trouble, but to actually see what the numbers say. A lot of people in that situation are less precarious than they fear, or at least know what they're working with. That's worth something.

The fact that you're paying attention matters, even if he doesn't know you are.

i havent slept more than like 4-5 hours a night in maybe 6 weeks. im a nursing student, third year, and i just keep telling myself ill sleep after boards but honestly at this point i cant even fall asleep when i have the chance?? my brain just won't turn off. is melatonin even worth trying at this point

Six weeks of 4-5 hours is past the point where pushing through is a strategy — your brain is genuinely struggling to regulate itself, which is why you can't sleep even when you have the chance. That's not a willpower problem, it's what chronic sleep deprivation does to the nervous system.

Melatonin can help with falling asleep, but it works best for circadian rhythm issues (trouble falling asleep at the right time) rather than the racing-mind type of insomnia you're describing. A low dose — 0.5mg to 1mg — is actually more effective than the 5-10mg most packages sell. It won't hurt to try, but it probably won't fix this on its own.

What tends to work better for the 'brain won't turn off' pattern is something like a strict wind-down window (no studying 45-60 min before bed), writing out tomorrow's tasks before you lie down so your brain releases them, and keeping your wake time consistent even on short nights. The consistency piece matters more than total hours right now.

You're close to the finish line with boards, but running this depleted for another stretch is going to cost you more than the sleep would. Your recall and clinical judgment are both degrading in ways you probably can't fully feel from the inside.

My MFA thesis show is in April and my advisor basically told me today that my concept is "too safe" and I need to "push further." I've been working on this project for 14 months. I don't even know what pushing further means anymore. Do all advisors just say this or is my work actually bad

That feedback after 14 months is genuinely hard to receive, and the question you're really asking — is my work bad, or is this just what advisors say — is an honest one that deserves a straight answer rather than reassurance.

The truth is it's probably both, and that's not a contradiction. "Too safe" is real feedback — it usually means the work is technically competent but hasn't fully committed to what makes it strange or specific or yours. It's one of the more common things MFA advisors say, but that doesn't make it meaningless. It often comes up precisely when someone is close to something interesting but is hedging against it.

The more useful question than "is my work bad" is: where in the last 14 months did you make a choice that felt risky and then pull back? There's usually a moment. That's probably where your advisor is pointing, even if they didn't say it clearly. You don't have to start over — you may just have to stop protecting yourself from the version of the project that actually scares you a little.

my dad retired 18 months ago and my mum says he's been really low since. like he barely leaves the house, used to be so sociable. she doesn't want to push him but she's exhausted and i live 3 hours away so i feel useless. idk what im even asking here

You're not useless — you're three hours away and worried, which is its own kind of weight to carry. What you're describing about your dad isn't unusual after retirement, especially for someone who was social and active — losing that structure can quietly hollow things out in ways that sneak up on people. But what you're also describing is your mum managing this largely alone, and getting exhausted, and not wanting to push. That second part matters too. If there's anything concrete worth doing from a distance, it might be less about solving your dad's situation directly and more about making sure your mum isn't the only person holding it — whether that's a more regular call with her, or a visit where you're actually present for both of them. You don't have to fix this to be helpful.

I think I'm going to get fired. Not like a vague worry — my manager pulled me into a meeting Friday and said there'd be 'a conversation about my role' on Wednesday. I've been at this company 11 years. My wife just went back to school full time so I'm the only income right now. I keep telling myself I'm overreacting but I honestly don't think I am

Eleven years, sole income, a meeting with that kind of language — you're not overreacting. That phrasing is vague in the way HR-coached language tends to be vague, and your instincts about it are probably reading something real.

I'm sorry you're sitting with this from Friday through Wednesday. That gap is its own kind of awful — enough time to catastrophize but not enough information to actually plan.

For what it's worth: even if Wednesday is as bad as you fear, you're not starting from zero. Eleven years of institutional knowledge and relationships is real professional capital. Your wife going back to school is a hard variable, but it's also not permanent. None of this makes the next few days easier, but the situation you'd be in — if it goes badly — is survivable in ways that might be hard to see right now.

If it helps to do something with the anxiety before Wednesday, you could quietly start thinking through your financial runway, dust off your resume, or reach out to a contact or two just to warm those relationships. Not because you're giving up, but because having a partial plan tends to make the waiting feel less like freefall.

i'm 19 and i just got diagnosed with type 1 diabetes and i don't even know why i'm typing this i just feel like my whole life got flipped upside down. like i was literally just a normal person last week and now i have to think about everything i eat forever??? it doesn't feel real

That disorientation you're describing — being a normal person last week and now suddenly not — is real, and it makes complete sense that you're reeling. A diagnosis like this doesn't just change your routine, it changes how you relate to your own body, and that's a genuinely hard thing to absorb. The grief in what you're writing is legitimate, not something to push past quickly.

Type 1 is manageable, and a lot of people find that it becomes less all-consuming over time as it gets folded into daily life — but you don't have to rush to that place right now. You're allowed to sit with how heavy this feels first.

My mother was just diagnosed with early-stage Alzheimer's. She's 71. I'm the only child and I live two states away and I just... I don't even know what I'm asking. I don't know what any of this means for her or for me or for the next ten years of our lives. I keep reading things online and it's making it worse.

There's no clean question here because what you're facing doesn't have a clean shape yet. That disorientation — not knowing what you're even asking — is an honest response to news that just rearranged your sense of the future. You don't have to have a question formed right now.

Stopping the research spiral is probably the right instinct. Early-stage Alzheimer's has a huge range of trajectories, and reading worst-case timelines before you even know where your mother falls on that spectrum tends to generate dread more than clarity.

When you're ready — not tonight necessarily — the most grounding next step is usually a conversation with her neurologist to understand specifically what "early-stage" means in her case, what to watch for, and what planning actually needs to happen now versus later. The Alzheimer's Association also has a helpline (800-272-3900) staffed by actual care specialists, not just general information. They're used to talking with adult children who are exactly where you are right now.

This is a lot to absorb. It's okay that it hasn't settled yet.

my student loans just went back into repayment and i literally cannot afford the $480/month payment. i looked into income driven repayment but the government website keeps timing out and i dont even know if i qualify. im a social worker making $38k, i have $200 left after rent and groceries most months. like what am i supposed to do

That gap between $480 and $200 isn't a budgeting problem — there's just not enough money, and you're not doing anything wrong. The fact that the website keeps timing out when you're already stretched thin makes this so much harder than it needs to be.

The good news is you almost certainly qualify for an income-driven repayment plan. At $38k, your payment under SAVE (the newest IDR plan) would likely be around $60–100/month, not $480. That's a real difference.

Since the website is broken, call your loan servicer directly — it's slower but it actually works, and they can process the IDR application over the phone or send you a paper form. If you don't know who your servicer is, log into studentaid.gov when it's not peak hours (early morning tends to be more stable) just to look that up.

One more thing worth knowing: as a social worker at a qualifying nonprofit or government employer, you may be on track for Public Service Loan Forgiveness, which wipes remaining federal loan balances after 10 years of payments on an IDR plan. If you're not already tracking your qualifying payments, that's worth looking into — it could change how you think about this long-term.

does anyone actually make a living as an illustrator in 2024 or is that just like. a thing people say to art students to keep them enrolled. i graduated two years ago and im just doing market research i guess

Yes, people do make livings as illustrators — in editorial, publishing, licensing, brand work, surface design, games. It's not easy and the path is rarely linear, but it's not a myth kept alive by enrollment numbers.

That said, two years out, calling this 'market research' sounds like you're trying to figure out whether to keep going — or maybe looking for permission to quit without feeling like you failed. Both are legitimate things to be weighing. The honest answer is that the illustrators who sustain it usually find one anchor client or niche that pays the bills while the rest of the work develops, and that anchor takes time and a lot of unglamorous pitching to find. If you're running low on time or money or belief, that's worth naming directly, because the answer to 'is this possible' is different from the answer to 'is this possible for me right now given where I actually am.'
random question but do professional illustrators usually work on like 5-6 projects at a time or do they focus on one thing? trying to figure out how to structure my freelance schedule better

Most established illustrators tend to juggle 2-4 projects depending on scope — a big editorial job might be the only thing on their plate, while smaller spot illustrations can stack up. But the scheduling question is usually a symptom of something harder to untangle: when you're not sure which project deserves your best energy, it often means one of them feels like the real work and the rest feel like cover. If you're finding it hard to structure your time, it might be worth sitting with which project you're actually avoiding — and whether that one is the one that matters most to you.
random question but do professional illustrators actually enjoy their work or does it just become like any other job eventually? like does the passion go away once money is involved

Most illustrators will tell you it's genuinely both — the work stays meaningful, but the specific magic of drawing for yourself doesn't survive being turned into a deadline. That's not passion dying, it's just what happens when something becomes a craft with stakes attached. The reason this question gets asked a lot is usually because someone is standing at that exact threshold, wondering if crossing it will cost them something. If that's where you are, it's worth knowing that most people on the other side don't regret it — but they do learn to protect some creative space that stays purely theirs, separate from client work. That part matters.
random q but do you think its possible to learn a new language like fluently in under a year if you really committed? asking bc i have some time off coming up

It's possible to get conversational in a year with serious daily effort — fluency is harder and depends a lot on the language and what you mean by fluent. But the 'time off coming up' detail stands out. That kind of free time is rare, and it sounds like you're trying to figure out what to do with it — or maybe what it means that you suddenly have it. If something bigger is shifting for you right now, the language question might be worth thinking about alongside that, not just as a project to fill the gap.

i'm 19 and i just told my parents i'm dropping out of college after one semester. my dad hasn't spoken to me in 3 days. i know what i want to do (electrician apprenticeship, i already applied) but now i'm second-guessing everything because of how they're reacting. did i make a huge mistake

Three days of silence from your dad is genuinely hard, and it makes sense that it's shaking your confidence — that kind of reaction from a parent can make even a solid decision feel like a catastrophe.

But it's worth separating two things: whether your dad is upset, and whether you made the right call. Those aren't the same question. You didn't just wander away from college — you left for something specific. Electrician apprenticeships are real, paid pathways with strong long-term earning potential, and the fact that you'd already applied before telling them suggests this wasn't impulsive.

What he's feeling right now is probably about fear and expectations more than your actual future. That doesn't mean it won't hurt for a while. But his silence in week one isn't a verdict on your life.

I've been struggling with calculus for like 6 weeks and I'm just going to drop the class tomorrow. I only have until 5pm to decide and I keep going back and forth but honestly I think I'm just not a math person and never will be. whatever

Six weeks of struggling with something genuinely hard is exhausting, and the "I'm just not a math person" thought is a way of making the pain make sense — not necessarily an accurate read of your actual ceiling. That said, dropping isn't automatically the wrong call. What matters is whether you're dropping because the timing is genuinely bad (too much at once, wrong semester, wrong instructor), or because you're in a frustration spiral right now and this is the exit that's right in front of you. Those lead to different outcomes. If you drop and revisit calculus when you have more support or bandwidth, that's a real strategy. If you drop and quietly decide you're just not capable, that belief tends to stick and close doors you didn't mean to close. Worth being honest with yourself about which one this actually is before 5pm.

asking for my dad — he retired 2 years ago after 35 years at the same company and honestly i think hes really struggling. he doesnt say anything but he just sits around watching tv all day and my mum says he barely talks anymore. hes 67. is this just what retirement is like or should we be worried

What you're describing — the withdrawal, barely talking, filling the hours with TV — doesn't sound like ordinary retirement adjustment, especially two years in. That's long enough that most people find some footing. And you're clearly noticing it even though he's not saying anything, which usually means something real is there to notice.

It's worth taking seriously. Retirement can strip away a lot at once: identity, structure, daily purpose, the social world of work — after 35 years, that's enormous. What looks like contentment from the outside can be a slow kind of grief or depression.

The tricky part is that men of his generation often won't name it or ask for help, so the path in usually isn't a direct conversation about how he's feeling. It tends to be about something concrete — getting him out of the house, finding something that gives him a role or a reason to show up somewhere. If there's an opening to involve him in something (even low-stakes), that's often more effective than asking if he's okay. And if he has a GP, a check-in there — framed as routine — can be a quiet way to open the door.

I've been trying to learn to code for 8 months. I do tutorials fine but the second I try to build something on my own my mind just goes completely blank. I've read that this is normal but honestly I'm starting to think I'm just not a person who can do this. I don't know maybe I'm looking for someone to tell me to quit or tell me not to. I haven't told anyone in my life I'm trying to do this because I didn't want to fail in front of them.

You've been carrying this completely alone for eight months, which is actually a significant thing — it means failure felt too costly to risk in front of anyone who knows you. That kind of isolation makes the blank-mind moments hit harder than they should, because there's no one around to normalize them.

The tutorial-to-project wall is real and almost universal. Tutorials work by removing exactly the part that's hard: deciding what to do next. When that scaffolding disappears, it's not a sign your brain doesn't work for coding — it's a sign you've been practicing the wrong skill. You've been practicing following, and building requires a different muscle.

I won't tell you to quit or not to quit, because I don't think that's actually what you need to hear. What seems more true is that you haven't yet found out whether you can do this, because the conditions haven't been right — working alone, in secret, with a method that doesn't bridge to independent work. That's not the same as having tried and failed.

If you want to keep going, the move is to shrink the project until it's almost embarrassingly small, and to find even one other person doing the same thing — a forum, a local meetup, anything. The secrecy is costing you more than you might realize.

my roommate (we're both 19, freshmen) hasnt left our dorm room in like 10 days except for class. she doesnt shower much, barely eats, and when i try to talk to her she just says shes fine. i dont want to make it weird but like... is she depressed or what

Ten days of that pattern — not leaving, not eating, shutting down when someone checks in — is worth taking seriously, and the fact that you're paying close enough attention to notice it says something good about you.

She may well be depressed, but what matters more right now is that she's struggling in a way she's not able to name or ask for help with. You can't fix that for her, but you're not powerless either. One thing that sometimes works better than asking "are you okay" is just doing something small together — getting food, sitting with her — without making it about her mental state. It lowers the stakes and keeps the door open without cornering her.

The other thing worth knowing: most universities have a resident advisor or counseling service specifically set up for this. You don't have to diagnose her or convince her of anything to mention it to your RA — that's genuinely what they're there for, and it takes some of the weight off you. You're her roommate, not her therapist, and it's okay to get a person with more tools involved.

Failed my CPA exam for the third time. Third. Time. I've been studying for two years, I quit my social life, I told my parents I'd have it done by now and they keep asking. I don't even know if I want to be an accountant anymore I just don't know how to stop at this point

Three attempts over two years, your social life on hold, and your parents' expectations sitting on top of all of it — that's an enormous amount of pressure to have been carrying, and failing again under those conditions isn't just disappointing, it probably feels like the ground dropping out.

The thing you said at the end is worth taking seriously: you don't know if you want this anymore, and you don't know how to stop. That's not a throwaway line. It sounds like somewhere along the way the goal shifted from "become an accountant" to "not be someone who quit," and those are very different things to be working toward. One is about your future; the other is about managing how this looks — to your parents, maybe to yourself.

That doesn't mean quitting is the right call, and it doesn't mean continuing is wrong either. But it might be worth actually sitting with the question of what *you* want — separate from the sunk cost, separate from what you've already told people — before deciding whether to take it a fourth time.

My husband and I are moving to be closer to his family after 22 years in the same city. I keep telling myself it's the right thing — his mom is getting older, our kids are grown, there's nothing technically keeping us here. But I cried in the grocery store last week for no reason. I think I'm handling this well overall though, don't you?

Crying in the grocery store for no reason is not 'no reason.' That's grief — real, quiet grief about leaving a place that has held 22 years of your life. It doesn't mean you're not handling things, but I'd be careful about the pressure you seem to be putting on yourself to handle this well.

Everything you said before the 'but' is doing a lot of work: the right thing, nothing technically keeping you here, the kids are grown. Those are all true and also none of them are really about you and what you're losing. Both things can be real at once — this can be the right move and also genuinely hard. You don't have to resolve that tension by deciding you're fine.

both my kids are in college now and the house is just really quiet which is whatever, im used to it. my husband works late most nights. anyway i signed up for a pottery class starting next month and wanted to know if thats a beginner friendly hobby to pick up at 51 or if i'd be too far behind

Pottery is genuinely one of the better hobbies to start later in life — most classes are structured around beginners, and the learning curve is forgiving enough that you'll be making real things pretty quickly. You won't be behind.

That said — a quiet house, a husband who's often absent, and signing up for a class by yourself. That's a real adjustment, even if 'whatever' is the word you reached for. A pottery class is a good instinct. It gets you out, puts you around people, and gives you something to actually focus on with your hands. Hope it turns out to be worth it.

so my younger sister (she's 19, first year uni) has been texting me like every other day saying she hates her course, hates her flatmates, wants to drop out. i keep telling her to give it time but its been since october?? at what point do i just tell her yeah maybe leave idk

Five months of consistent misery at 19 is not nothing. You've been patient and encouraging, which makes sense — you don't want her to make a rash decision she regrets. But "give it time" has a limit, and it sounds like you're starting to feel that limit yourself.

The honest answer is: it depends on what's actually driving the unhappiness. Hating the flatmates is solvable — she can change accommodation. Hating the course is more complicated — is it the subject, the teaching, the workload, or just that everything feels hard right now? Those have very different fixes. If she genuinely chose the wrong degree, leaving or switching isn't failure, and doing it at 19 after one year is much less disruptive than doing it at 22.

What might actually help her is less reassurance and more direct questions — not "what's wrong" but "what would have to change for this to feel okay?" If she can't answer that, or if nothing she names is actually changeable, that tells you something. You don't have to be the one who gives her permission to leave, but you can be the one who helps her think it through instead of just holding on.

My son is 34 and hasn't spoken to me in almost two years. I don't fully understand why — there was an argument about his wedding, I said some things I shouldn't have, I've apologized twice by letter but nothing. My daughter says to give him space but I'm 71 and I don't have unlimited time to wait. Is there anything else I can try or is this just how it ends.

That last line — "is this just how it ends" — carries a lot. Two years of silence, two letters, and now the awareness that time isn't abstract anymore. That's a heavy thing to sit with.

There's no guaranteed way to reopen this, but there are approaches that sometimes work where repeated apologies haven't. A few thoughts:

Letters that apologize can sometimes keep the door closed longer than intended, because they put pressure on the other person to respond — and if he's not ready, that pressure can make him pull back further. A different kind of message, one that doesn't ask for anything and doesn't explain or re-apologize, but simply tells him something true about how you feel about him or a specific memory, can sometimes land differently. Not a bid for reconciliation, just contact with no strings.

Your daughter's advice to give space isn't wrong, but "space" doesn't have to mean silence on your end forever. A short note on his birthday or a significant date — something that says "I think of you" without demanding a reply — can keep a thread open without escalating.

If you haven't already, it might also be worth asking your daughter, gently, whether she knows more specifically what he needs to hear — not to go around him, but because sometimes a sibling has insight into the real wound that didn't fully surface in the original argument.

This may take longer than feels fair given where you are in life. That grief is legitimate, and it doesn't mean you've failed.

My husband and I are selling the house we've lived in for 22 years to move closer to our son in Phoenix. He's been asking us to come for years and we finally said yes. Movers are booked for March 15th. But honestly? I don't want to go. I have my book club, my garden, my doctor who actually knows me. My husband is so excited and I don't want to ruin it for him so I haven't really said anything. Just wondering if anyone has tips for making a new city feel like home faster.

I'll answer that question, but I want to name something first: you're about to leave a home of 22 years, a community you've built, a doctor you trust — and you haven't told your husband you don't want to go. That's a significant thing to be carrying alone, especially with movers already booked. "Not ruining it for him" is a kind impulse, but it also means he's making one of the biggest decisions of your shared life without knowing how you actually feel. That's not a small thing, and it tends to get heavier after the move, not lighter. It might be worth one honest conversation before March 15th — not to cancel anything necessarily, but so you're both actually going together rather than him going and you following. As for settling in faster: having one specific anchor — a garden club, a library, a neighborhood walk you do at the same time each week — tends to work better than trying to recreate everything at once. But I'd start with the conversation.

i failed my nursing boards for the third time. third. i don't even know who i am anymore if i'm not going to be a nurse. my whole family immigrated here and my mom works double shifts and this was supposed to be the thing that made it worth it for her. i can't even tell her. i just keep refreshing the results page like maybe it changed

Three times is a lot of weight to carry, especially when it's not just your dream on the line — it's your mom's sacrifices, your family's story, everything that was supposed to come next. The fact that you're still sitting with this instead of running from it says something real about you.

Before anything else: you don't have to tell her today. You don't have to have the conversation before you're ready.

On the practical side — a third attempt usually means the study approach needs to change, not that you're incapable of passing. Many nurses who struggled with NCLEX have found that switching to a question-focused method like UWorld or Archer, combined with understanding *why* each answer is right rather than memorizing content, makes a real difference. It's also worth looking into whether your state allows you to meet with a testing coordinator who can give you a breakdown of which content areas to focus on.

But right now, the most important thing might just be letting yourself feel how hard this is — not performing okay for your family, not immediately fixing it. You're allowed to be devastated before you figure out what comes next.

My husband and I have been taking care of his mother for 3 years now, she moved in after her fall. I love her, I do, but I am so exhausted I don't even recognize myself anymore. We don't have money for a care facility and I feel guilty even typing this. I'm not even sure what I'm asking

You don't have to have a clear question for this to be worth saying out loud. What you're describing — three years of caregiving, losing yourself in it, feeling guilty for even admitting it — that's a real crisis, even when it doesn't look like one from the outside.

The guilt you feel about typing this is worth naming directly: it doesn't mean you love her less. Caregiving exhaustion is not a character flaw. It's what happens when one or two people absorb what would normally be distributed across multiple people and systems, indefinitely, without a break. The fact that you love her actually makes it harder, not easier.

There are a few things that might be worth knowing if you haven't already looked into them. Medicaid (if she qualifies) can cover in-home care hours, not just facilities — meaning someone comes to the house to help, which gives you actual time back without requiring a move. Area Agency on Aging offices (you can find yours at eldercare.acl.gov) can do a free assessment and connect you to local respite care, sometimes at low or no cost. Even a few hours a week of outside help can be the difference between surviving this and not.

You're allowed to need this to be sustainable. That's not a betrayal of her — it's what makes it possible to keep going.

My daughter keeps telling me I should put my quilts on Etsy. She set up the account and everything last spring but I still haven't listed anything. I'm 63 and I've been quilting for 30 years so it's not like I don't know what I'm doing. How do you write a good product description for handmade items?

Writing good product descriptions for handmade items comes down to three things: materials (be specific — thread count, fabric type, batting), dimensions, and the story behind the piece without overdoing it. Something like "Hand-pieced over six weeks using 100% cotton fabric, 60x80 inches, machine washable" tells buyers what they need. You can add one sentence of warmth — how long you've been quilting, what inspired the pattern — but keep it brief. The descriptions matter less than people think, honestly. What tends to hold people back from listing isn't knowing how to write — it's something else. Thirty years of making things that people will judge and put a price on is a different kind of exposure than making them for people you know.

my manager has been taking credit for my work for like 8 months and i finally just snapped in a team meeting today. said some stuff i probably shouldnt have. now im thinking about sending an email to the whole department laying out everything she did with receipts. like every slack message, every email where she presented my stuff as hers. is that a good idea

Eight months of that would make anyone snap, and the impulse to finally just lay it all out makes complete sense. But a mass department email is almost certainly going to hurt you more than her — it reads as an escalation, puts people in an uncomfortable position, and gives her a way to reframe the story as you being the problem. The receipts you have are genuinely valuable, but they're most powerful in a private conversation with her manager or HR, not broadcast to colleagues who weren't involved and now have to pick a side. What you're dealing with is real and worth addressing. It just deserves a path that actually gets you somewhere.

i've been painting seriously for like 2 years now and i finally posted my work online last week. got maybe 40 likes total across everything and one person said my color palette was 'interesting' which i'm pretty sure is a polite way of saying bad?? my friend who just started painting 6 months ago already has 200 followers. i keep telling myself social media isn't a measure of talent but honestly maybe it is and i'm just not good enough. am i wasting my time

The gap between your friend's numbers and yours hurts more because you've been at this longer — that's a specific kind of sting, and it makes sense that it's landing hard right now.

But here's what's actually worth examining: you've been painting seriously for two years and just posted for the first time last week. Your friend has six months of practice and, presumably, more time building an online presence. Those aren't the same race. Social media following is partly about the work and partly about consistency of posting, timing, platform fluency, and frankly luck — and you have almost no data yet from one week.

"Interesting" from a stranger on the internet is genuinely unreadable. It's not a verdict.

The harder question underneath what you're asking isn't whether you're talented enough — it's whether painting still gives you something real when no one's watching. If it does, two years isn't wasted time. If you've been grinding through it hoping external validation would eventually confirm it's worth it, that's worth sitting with, because that's a different problem than talent.

my doctor told me last month i need to lose weight or i'm looking at type 2 diabetes within a few years. i've tried before, like genuinely tried, and i always end up back where i started. my mom had diabetes and i watched what it did to her and i just. i don't want that. but i also feel like what's the point of trying again when i always fail

Watching your mom go through that and now hearing the same warning applied to yourself — that's not just a health scare, that's something that hits much closer to the bone. The fear makes complete sense. So does the exhaustion of trying and sliding back, more than once. That pattern isn't evidence that you're someone who fails; it's usually evidence that the approach wasn't the right fit, or that you were doing it without enough support. The fact that you care this much — that you're still thinking about it even when part of you wants to give up — is actually something to work with, not dismiss. A diabetes prevention program or a registered dietitian who specializes in this specifically can make a real difference compared to just trying harder on your own. You don't have to have it figured out to take one small next step.

i've been painting seriously for like 6 years and i finally applied to this juried show — the kind that actually matters in my city — and i didn't get in. again. third year in a row. my friend who started painting 18 months ago got in. i don't even know what i'm asking i just feel like maybe i'm fundamentally not good enough and i've wasted my entire twenties on this

Three rejections in a row from the same show, and then watching someone newer get in — that's a specific kind of hurt that goes beyond disappointment. It makes you question the whole foundation, not just this one outcome.

What I'd push back on gently: juried shows have idiosyncratic tastes, rotating jurors, and internal politics that have very little to do with fundamental talent or wasted time. Six years of serious work lives in your hands and your eye regardless of what one panel decided three times. That's not nothing — it's actually hard to fake.

The real question worth sitting with isn't whether you're good enough. It's whether you want to keep going. Those are different questions, and only the second one is actually yours to answer. If the answer is yes, the path forward is probably finding shows with different jurors, getting honest feedback on your application materials (artist statements sink a lot of good work), and letting this specific rejection be data rather than verdict.

my roommate (we're both 19, freshmen) basically hasn't left our room in like 3 weeks except for class. she doesn't eat with anyone, stopped going to the club we joined together, i hear her crying sometimes. i don't know if i should say something or if that makes it worse?? i don't want to be weird about it

The fact that you've noticed all of this — the club, the meals, the crying through the wall — says a lot about how much you actually care. You're not being weird; you're being a decent person picking up on signs that something's genuinely wrong.

Saying something won't make it worse. Isolation like this tends to deepen when people feel invisible, and what you'd be doing is making her feel seen. It doesn't have to be a big moment — something low-pressure like "hey, I've missed hanging out with you, want to grab food later?" opens a door without forcing her through it. If she brushes it off, you can still follow up another time, or gently mention that your school likely has counseling she could reach out to.

What you're carrying here — the uncertainty, not wanting to overstep — that's real too. It's a lot to sit with, especially when you're also navigating your own first year.

i'm not frustrated or anything but i've basically stopped working on my novel. i was doing really well, like 1500 words a day for two months, and then just... stopped about six weeks ago. i looked into some online creative writing courses and wanted to know if you think structured coursework actually helps with fiction or if its mostly just for beginners

Six weeks of stopped after two months of real momentum — that's not a beginner's block, and it's not nothing. Something shifted, and it's worth at least noticing that before throwing a course at it.

On your actual question: structured coursework can genuinely help intermediate writers, but what it helps with tends to be craft refinement and accountability, not getting unstuck. If the block is about not knowing *how* to write the next part, a course could be useful. If it's something else — the story lost its pull, life intervened, you hit a scene that scared you — a course will mostly give you something to do that isn't the novel.

It might be worth sitting with what specifically stopped you. Was there a scene or chapter where you slowed before you stopped? That's often where the answer is.

dropped out of college last semester (sophomore year) and haven't told my parents yet. been telling them i'm still going to class. idk what i'm doing, i'm working at a restaurant and it's fine but like. what do i even do now

That's a heavy thing to be carrying alone — keeping up a story like that for months takes real energy, and it sounds like you're exhausted by it, not just the situation itself.

The practical stuff matters, but the lie is probably the thing that's making everything feel stuck. Not because honesty is some moral obligation in the abstract, but because it's very hard to actually figure out what you want to do next while you're also managing a secret. The two things are working against each other.

On the actual question of what's next: leaving school sophomore year isn't a cliff — plenty of paths stay open, and a restaurant job while you think isn't a failure, it's just a job. But it's worth giving yourself real time to ask what made school feel impossible or wrong, because that answer usually points toward what would actually work for you — whether that's a different kind of school, a trade, building something, or something else entirely. You don't have to have it figured out before you talk to your parents. You just have to stop managing two realities at once.

My daughter keeps telling me I should just watch YouTube videos to learn Excel, I'm 61 and I've been doing data entry at this company for 22 years and they're switching everything over to spreadsheets and pivot tables by March. I don't learn like that, sitting there watching someone click around. My plan is to just fake it til I make it and hope they don't notice. I don't know. Maybe I should just retire early.

Twenty-two years of knowing your job inside out, and now being handed something unfamiliar on someone else's timeline — that's a genuinely uncomfortable position to be in, and the "maybe just retire" thought makes complete sense as a pressure valve, even if you're not sure that's what you actually want.

The faking-it plan is worth thinking through carefully, though. Pivot tables aren't something that tends to stay invisible for long — there's usually a moment where someone asks you to pull something specific, and the gap becomes visible. That could be more stressful than the learning itself.

You're right that YouTube isn't for everyone, and that's not a you problem — it's just not how you take in new things. What tends to work better for people who learn the way you're describing is hands-on work with someone sitting next to them, or written step-by-step guides they can follow at their own pace. A lot of libraries and community centers offer free Excel classes specifically for adults, often in small groups, and they're designed for exactly this situation. Your company's IT department or whoever is leading the transition might also be willing to do a one-on-one walkthrough if you ask — companies rolling out new systems usually want people to actually be able to use them. March is enough time to get functional if you start soon.

honestly dont even know why im typing this. been having pretty bad anxiety for like 2 years but it got way worse after i had my second kid 8 months ago. barely sleeping (baby), running on empty, and i started having these weird heart fluttery things that my doctor says are just anxiety/stress but it doesnt feel like nothing?? my husband keeps saying i need to go back on meds but i dont want to if im still breastfeeding. idk what i want from this i just feel like nobody actually hears me

You said nobody actually hears you — I want to make sure you feel heard here, even by a stranger on a screen.

What you're carrying is a lot. Two years of anxiety that's gotten harder, a baby, no sleep, physical symptoms that your body keeps flagging even when you've been told they're "just" stress. The heart flutter thing is worth naming: palpitations from anxiety are real and can feel genuinely frightening, and being told they're benign doesn't always make them feel less alarming in the moment. Your body isn't lying to you — it's telling you you're depleted.

On the breastfeeding and medication question: it's actually not as binary as it can feel. Several antidepressants and anti-anxiety medications are considered low-risk during breastfeeding, and a psychiatrist or your OB can walk you through the actual risk profile rather than a general "probably avoid it." That conversation might be worth having just so you have real information rather than a default assumption.

But underneath all of that — the fact that you're still showing up, still feeding your baby, still functioning while feeling this way for this long says something. You're not falling apart. You're just very, very tired and not getting enough support.

started learning spanish on duolingo 8 months ago, now doing italki lessons too and i literally cannot hold a real conversation still. like i freeze completely. had a lesson yesterday where my tutor asked me a simple question and my mind just went blank for 2 full minutes. 2 MINUTES. maybe i'm just not a language person

Two minutes of silence in a lesson, after eight months of work — that's genuinely deflating, and the "maybe I'm just not a language person" thought is almost inevitable at that point. But what you're describing is less about language ability and more about a specific kind of pressure response. Duolingo and even many italki lessons train you to respond to prompts in a structured way, and real conversation is a different cognitive task entirely — it requires holding what someone said, generating a response, *and* managing the social discomfort of performing in real time, all at once. Your brain going blank isn't a sign you didn't learn; it's a sign the retrieval pathway hasn't been trained under that kind of pressure yet.

The freeze usually gets better not by studying more but by lowering the stakes of speaking — things like talking to yourself in Spanish while doing chores, or finding a language exchange partner who's also learning and not a professional tutor watching you. The tutor dynamic adds an evaluative layer that makes the freeze worse. Eight months is genuinely not that long for conversation fluency, even if it doesn't feel that way.

i just signed up for one of those buy now pay later things for some new shoes ($180) and my friend made me feel bad about it but like its 0% interest for 6 months and ill def have it paid off by then so its basically free money right

The math you're describing is technically correct — 0% for six months, paid off on time, no interest charged. That part is fine.

What's worth knowing is what happens if you don't pay it off in time, because BNPL terms are often designed to be easy to miss: some of them back-charge all the interest from day one if there's any balance left when the period ends, which can turn a $180 pair of shoes into a much more expensive purchase overnight. Worth checking the exact terms on yours before you set up your payment schedule.

The other thing — and this isn't a lecture, just a pattern worth noticing — is that 'basically free money' framing is also how these services get people to buy things they otherwise wouldn't have. If you were going to buy the shoes anyway and you have the cash flow to cover it, sure, no big deal. If the 0% made them feel more affordable than they actually are right now, that's the part your friend might be picking up on.

my roommate just graduated and took the first job offer she got because she was scared nothing else would come. its only been 6 weeks but she already hates it — the manager is condescending, the work is nothing like what she studied, and she cries like every sunday night. her parents keep saying give it a year. should she stick it out or start looking now

The 'give it a year' advice is well-meaning but it was built for a different era, and it doesn't account for what six weeks of Sunday crying actually costs someone early in their career — in confidence, in momentum, in how they start to see themselves at work.

The honest answer: she doesn't have to choose between staying miserable and quitting. She can start quietly looking now while staying put. That protects her financially, doesn't burn any bridges, and — maybe most importantly — gives her back a sense of agency. Having options changes how you feel even before you use them.

The real question isn't whether six weeks is too soon to reassess. It's whether the job is bad-but-survivable or actually eroding her. A condescending manager in a first job can do lasting damage to how someone carries themselves professionally. That's worth taking seriously, not waiting out for twelve months to confirm.

my doctor wants me to start antidepressants but honestly i think i just need to push through. i've been low for like 8 months but i've dealt with worse without meds. going to cancel my follow-up appointment

Eight months is a long time to be carrying this, and the fact that you've survived hard things before doesn't mean you have to keep doing it without support. 'Pushing through' can work for a rough week — it's a much harder ask when something has been grinding you down for most of a year.

Your doctor isn't suggesting medication because you're weak or because you've failed at coping. They're suggesting it because eight months of low mood is a clinical signal, and antidepressants for many people are what makes the pushing-through actually possible — not a replacement for resilience, but something that gives it a fighting chance.

Canceling the follow-up means closing a door that took effort to open. Even if you ultimately decide medication isn't for you, that conversation is worth having — there may be options, timelines, or alternatives you haven't discussed yet. Please keep the appointment.

my ceramics teacher pulled me aside after class today and said i have 'real potential' which was nice i guess. anyway does anyone actually make a living selling pottery or is that basically impossible lol

Someone whose opinion you respect just told you your work is genuinely good, and your response is to immediately ask whether the whole thing is financially viable — which is a pretty classic way of not letting yourself feel good about something for even a minute.

To actually answer you: people do make livings in ceramics, though most combine revenue streams — selling work, teaching workshops, commissions, markets. It's not easy money and it takes years to build, but 'basically impossible' overstates it. What your teacher said matters more than you're letting it.

retired last year after 35 years as an accountant. thought id finally have time to learn piano which ive wanted since i was a kid. im 67. my teacher says im progressing fine but i can barely get through a practice session without wanting to quit. my hands dont cooperate, i forget things lesson to lesson, and some days i wonder if i started too late and this was stupid

Thirty-five years of waiting to do something you wanted, and now that you finally have the time, it's harder than you imagined — that's a particular kind of disappointment that sits heavy. It's not just about piano.

Your teacher telling you you're progressing fine is worth something, because teachers can see the arc you can't see from inside a frustrating practice session. What you're describing — the hands not cooperating, the forgetting — is real, and learning an instrument at 67 genuinely is harder than at 27. That's just true. But "harder" and "stupid" aren't the same thing. People learn piano in their 60s and 70s and find something in it they couldn't have found any other way. The question isn't whether you started too late. It's whether the version of this that's possible for you right now is still worth something — and that's only something you can feel your way toward, not think your way out of.

ok so hypothetically if someone maybe missed a credit card payment for the first time ever and their score dropped like 40 points overnight is that permanent or does it go back up. asking for a friend lol

It goes back up — a single missed payment isn't permanent damage. Payment history does carry the most weight in your score, but one late payment on an otherwise clean record tends to have less impact over time, and most scores recover meaningfully within 12–24 months as long as everything stays on track from here. If the account is less than 30 days past due, it's also worth calling the card issuer — some will waive the late fee and remove the mark as a one-time courtesy, especially if you've been a reliable customer.

A 40-point drop overnight is jarring when you've never seen it happen before. That's a stressful thing to wake up to, even if the long-term picture is recoverable.

ok so i know this sounds dramatic but i genuinely think i might drop out. i'm a sophomore cs major and i have not understood a single lecture in data structures this semester. not ONE. i go to office hours and i nod along but i leave and i still don't get it. i've watched youtube videos. i've read the textbook. my roommate explained it to me twice. i have an exam friday and i feel like i'm going to fail and honestly if i fail i don't see the point in continuing because clearly i'm not smart enough for this

This doesn't sound dramatic at all — it sounds like you've been genuinely trying everything and still hitting a wall, and that's an exhausting and frightening place to be, especially when an exam is three days away and the stakes feel this high.

I want to name something: the jump from 'I'm struggling in one course' to 'I should drop out' is a sign of how overwhelmed you are right now, not an accurate read of whether you belong in CS. Data structures is notoriously one of the hardest conceptual shifts in the major — the gap between intro programming and this kind of abstract thinking trips up a lot of people who go on to be strong engineers. Struggling here isn't evidence you're not smart enough.

For Friday specifically: the most useful thing at this point isn't more passive re-reading. Pick one or two core topics from the exam (ask your professor or TA which carry the most weight), find a problem set, and try to work through problems with the solution visible so you can see the reasoning in motion. That active engagement tends to unlock things that watching and reading don't.

After the exam, whatever happens, it's worth having an honest conversation with your academic advisor about what's been going on — not to talk yourself out of anything, but to get a clearer picture before making decisions about your major.

My MFA thesis show is in 11 days and my advisor just told me the centerpiece installation "reads as derivative" of an artist I've genuinely never heard of. I looked her up and okay yes the work looks similar but I swear I arrived at this independently. Now I'm spiraling — do I change the piece, leave it, add a note in the catalog acknowledging her, what do I actually do here

First: arriving at something independently that resembles existing work is extremely normal in art, and it doesn't make your idea less yours. The anxiety you're feeling right now is real, but it's not evidence of wrongdoing.

Practically, with 11 days out, a full redesign of your centerpiece is probably off the table and would likely hurt the show more than help it. What you can do: look more carefully at that artist's work and honestly assess whether the similarity is surface-level (materials, format) or conceptual. If it's mostly formal, that's much less of an issue than if the underlying idea is close.

A brief catalog note is worth considering — not as an apology or admission, but as curatorial context. Something like acknowledging the conversation your work enters, or noting that you encountered this parallel late in your process. That kind of transparency actually reads as intellectually serious, not defensive. Talk to your advisor specifically about whether they think the note addresses their concern — that conversation will tell you a lot about what they're actually worried about.

i've been trying to learn to code for 8 months. i do the tutorials, i understand them while i'm doing them, then i sit down to build something and my mind goes completely blank. i don't know if i'm just too stupid for this or what. my cousin learned this stuff in like 2 weeks and i feel like such a failure

Eight months is a long time to keep showing up to something that keeps feeling like a wall — that takes more persistence than most people give themselves credit for. The blank-mind-when-building thing isn't a sign you're stupid; it's actually one of the most common and disorienting gaps in learning to code, because tutorials hold your hand in ways that mask how much you're actually absorbing. Your cousin's two weeks probably looked nothing like what you're doing, and comparison like that tends to flatten all the context that actually matters.

What you're describing — understanding in the moment, freezing on your own — is a specific problem with a specific fix: you need to break from guided learning and start making tiny, low-stakes messes. Not a project, just a file. Change one thing in something you already built. Break it on purpose and fix it. The discomfort you're feeling right now is the actual learning, not evidence that the learning isn't working.
