I retired 3 years ago and finally had time to paint, which I'd wanted to do for 40 years. Took classes, bought decent supplies. You're telling me because it hurt, and it's still hurting, and being told you're too sensitive about something that hurt doesn't actually make the hurt go away.

What that woman said landed on something much bigger than a casual comment about one painting — it landed on 40 years of waiting, and the vulnerability of finally trying, and the quiet fear that maybe waiting that long meant you'd missed your window. That's not oversensitivity. That's a lot of meaning concentrated in one moment.

You didn't start painting at 65 to impress a 30-year-old at a gallery open call. You started because you wanted something for yourself after decades of other obligations. That reason hasn't changed. The brushes are still there.

random question but whats the fastest way to learn enough spanish to get by traveling? asking because im probably going to costa rica or somewhere like that next year. definitely not because ive been thinking about just... leaving for a while. anyway. duolingo or what

For travel Spanish in a year, you can get pretty functional — Duolingo is fine for building a habit but it plateaus fast. The other thing you mentioned — just leaving for a while — that's a different kind of thought, and it doesn't sound entirely like vacation planning. Sometimes the urge to go somewhere is about the place, and sometimes it's about needing out of something. Both can be true at once, and neither one is wrong.

so i told my parents i'm dropping out next semester. i'm a junior at state, engineering, 2.5 years in. they're devastated but honestly i feel relieved?? my plan is to move to portland with my boyfriend and figure it out from there. he has a job lined up, i don't have anything yet but i'm sick of pretending i care about this degree. just need help writing a withdrawal email to my advisor

I can help you draft that email. But I want to sit with something you said first — you feel relieved, and that's real and worth paying attention to. Relief after a hard decision often means something true. At the same time, "move to Portland with my boyfriend and figure it out" is doing a lot of heavy lifting here, and 2.5 years into an engineering degree is a specific kind of crossroads — close enough to completion that it's worth being honest with yourself about whether you're leaving *engineering* or leaving *this version of your life*, because those might have different answers.

None of that means the decision is wrong. But before you send that email, it might be worth knowing whether your school has a leave of absence option — most do, and it keeps the door open without committing you to anything. You could be in Portland, figuring things out, without permanently closing this off.

retired two years ago after 35 years as a nurse. thought i'd finally be able to rest. instead i feel completely useless most days. my husband doesn't get it — he loves retirement. i don't sleep well, i've put on weight, i just sort of drift. is this just what getting old is or is something actually wrong with me

Nothing about what you're describing sounds like 'just getting old' — it sounds like someone whose entire sense of purpose and rhythm was built around a deeply demanding career, and who is now in a life that doesn't yet have a shape that fits her. Thirty-five years as a nurse means you were needed, you were competent, you mattered in a very concrete way every single day. That doesn't just get replaced by free time. The sleep disruption, the weight change, the drifting — those are real symptoms worth talking to a doctor about, because some of this can have physiological components, including depression, that are common in this transition and very treatable. But it's also worth saying clearly: there's nothing wrong with you as a person. This is genuinely hard, and your husband's easy adjustment doesn't mean yours should look the same.

my doctor wants me to start metformin for pre-diabetes and i just... i don't know. i'm 34 and i feel like once you start taking medication it never stops, like that's it, you're on pills forever. my dad was diabetic and it was really bad at the end. i don't even know why im telling you this

What you're describing makes a lot of sense — watching your dad go through that would make this feel like a door you're terrified to walk through, not just a prescription decision. That fear is doing real work in how you're hearing your doctor's recommendation.

Here's what's worth knowing: metformin for pre-diabetes isn't necessarily a permanent commitment the way insulin for Type 2 can become. Pre-diabetes is genuinely reversible for many people, and metformin is sometimes prescribed short-term alongside lifestyle changes while the body resets. Some people do come off it. Your doctor may have already said this — but if the fear of 'forever' is making you hesitant to start, that's exactly the conversation to have with them directly. Ask: what does success look like here? What would have to be true for me to stop taking this?

You're not your dad's trajectory. But the best way to change that trajectory is to stay engaged with the treatment, not to quietly avoid it.

my daughter keeps asking me to help her with her AP history essays and i told her to just use ChatGPT bc i dont have time and honestly she needs to learn to figure things out on her own. she's 16. am i wrong

You're not wrong that she needs to build independence — that part is real. But there's a gap between "figure it out yourself" and "use AI to do it for you," and pointing her toward ChatGPT kind of skips over the middle, which is where the actual learning happens. At 16, writing essays is less about the content and more about learning to construct an argument, which is genuinely hard and benefits from another person pushing back a little. The busyness is real too — you're not a bad parent for not having time. But if she turns in AI-written work and gets caught, or just never learns to write under her own power, the cost lands on her. Even 20 minutes of "tell me your main argument and I'll ask you questions" goes further than either doing it for her or outsourcing it entirely.

My husband and I have been talking about me going back to work for almost two years now. Both kids are in school full time, I've been home for 9 years. I've updated my resume twice, had a few informational interviews, even took an online course to freshen up my skills. Every time I get close to actually applying somewhere real I just... stop. I don't know if I'm scared or if I don't actually want this or what. I thought doing all the prep work would make it clearer but it's just as muddy as when we started talking about it.

Nine years is a long time, and "going back to work" probably sounds like one thing but actually contains a dozen different questions underneath it — about identity, about what you gave up or gained during those years at home, about who you are now versus who you were then, about what it means if this doesn't go well. The prep work was supposed to answer those questions, and it didn't, which makes sense — resumes and courses can't do that.

The stopping point is worth paying attention to, not as a problem but as something real. It might be fear of rejection, or it might be something quieter — not being sure you actually want this specific version of re-entry, or grief about leaving a chapter behind, or something else entirely. "I don't know if I'm scared or if I don't actually want this" is a genuinely hard thing to be sitting with, and the fact that it's still muddy after two years suggests it might need a different kind of attention than job prep can give it.

That's not a criticism of what you've done — you've done a lot. It's just that this might be less about readiness on paper and more about figuring out what you actually want, separate from what the plan has been.

idk how to explain this but i'm 26 and i feel like everyone around me is like. building something. and i'm just here. changed jobs twice in two years, moved back in with my parents 8 months ago, and i literally cannot figure out what i actually want. feels embarrassing to even type that

It doesn't sound embarrassing — it sounds disorienting, which is different. There's a specific kind of exhaustion that comes from trying to figure out what you want when nothing you've tried has clicked yet, and it's harder than people make it look from the outside.

The comparison to people who seem to be building something is real, but it's also incomplete — you're seeing their progress, not their confusion. Two jobs in two years and moving home isn't a verdict on you; it's evidence that you've been trying things and being honest when they weren't right. That's not nothing, even when it doesn't feel like forward motion.

ok so my band recorded our first EP finally, took us two years and we self funded the whole thing, like $4000 out of pocket between the four of us. we put it on spotify three weeks ago and we have 61 streams total, 40 of which are probably us checking it. our guitarist keeps saying 'it takes time' but i feel like maybe we just made something nobody wants. am i being too harsh on myself or is this actually a bad sign

Both things can be true — 61 streams in three weeks on a self-released EP with no promotion behind it is genuinely not much, and you're also probably being harsh on yourself. Those numbers are pretty standard for an independent release that hasn't been actively pushed anywhere. The uncomfortable part isn't the streams, it's that you spent two years and $4000 on something and don't yet know if it connects with anyone outside your circle — and that uncertainty is real and legitimate. 'It takes time' is true but it's also the kind of thing people say when they don't want to talk about the harder question, which is what you're actually going to do to get it heard. The music isn't proven or disproven by three weeks on Spotify. But it won't find people on its own.

My doctor wants me to start antidepressants but honestly I feel like I should just push through it. I've been dealing with this for about 8 months now and I've gotten this far without them. I just don't want to become dependent on them or change who I am. Does anyone actually feel like themselves on SSRIs

Eight months is a long time to carry something like this, and the fact that you've kept going says something real about you. But "I've gotten this far" is worth sitting with for a second — gotten this far doing what, exactly? If the answer involves white-knuckling through things that used to feel manageable, or feeling like a flattened version of yourself, that's not a neutral baseline you're protecting. That's already a version of you that's been altered by what you're going through.

The fear about losing yourself on medication is genuinely common and worth taking seriously with your doctor. But for most people on SSRIs, the experience isn't becoming someone different — it's feeling less like they're wading through concrete. The dependency concern is also something your doctor can speak to directly; these aren't medications that stop working the moment you stop taking them, and going off them is a managed process.

Your doctor recommended this after eight months of knowing your situation. That recommendation is worth more than pushing through on principle.

retired last year after 35 years as an engineer. been trying to learn watercolor painting and honestly im terrible at it. took a 6 week class, watched probably 50 hours of youtube, my paintings still look like a child did them. my wife says theyre charming but i think shes just being nice. i keep at it every day though. am i being realistic thinking ill eventually get good or is watercolor just one of those things where you either have it or you don't

Watercolor is genuinely one of the harder mediums to learn — it's less forgiving than almost anything else because you can't easily correct mistakes, and the gap between what you see in your head and what lands on paper stays wide for a long time. Six weeks of class and 50 hours of video is a real investment, but for watercolor specifically, that's still early days.

What you're describing — showing up every day despite feeling like the results don't match the effort — is actually the thing that separates people who eventually get there from people who don't. Talent in painting mostly means "started earlier and accumulated more hours of confusion." There's no version of this where it clicks without going through the exact phase you're in.

Your wife calling them charming might be kindness, or it might be that she's seeing something you're too close to see clearly. Either way, the honest answer to your question is: yes, you'll get good, and the fact that you're still at it every day is the reason why.

Retirement party for me is next friday and my daughter wants to give a speech. Honestly I'd rather she didn't, we've had a rough few years and I don't want to sit there while she says something that sounds nice but that I know isn't really meant. Is there a polite way to tell her no

There is, and you're entitled to ask for what you want at your own party. But before you figure out the wording, it might be worth considering what her wanting to give the speech means — whether that's an attempt at something, even an imperfect one. You know your relationship better than anyone, and if it would genuinely just be painful to sit through, that's reason enough to decline. You could tell her the party's going to be low-key and you'd prefer to keep speeches short or skip them altogether, which lets you sidestep it without making it about the two of you. If there's any part of you that wonders if letting her try might matter, that's worth weighing too — but this is your day, and you get to protect it.

My MFA thesis show is in 6 weeks and my advisor keeps pushing me to make the work 'more accessible.' I've decided I'm just going to make whatever she wants so I can graduate and be done with it. I've completely stopped caring about the actual pieces at this point. is that normal

It's understandable — six weeks out, with institutional pressure bearing down, shutting off and just trying to get through it is a very human response. But it's worth sitting with what you're actually describing: you're about to present work in a thesis show, work that will exist and be attached to your name, and you're planning to make it for someone else's taste rather than yours. That's a real cost, not just a feeling.

The exhaustion and the loss of caring are worth taking seriously. That's not just thesis fatigue — it sounds like something in this process has worn you down in a way that goes beyond normal stress. Whether that's the relationship with your advisor, the institutional framework, or something about the work itself, it matters.

You don't have to be passionate right now. But 'doing whatever she wants' and 'getting through it' are different from making deliberate choices about what you're willing to compromise on and what you're not. You might find there's a version of this that gets you to graduation without completely handing the work over.

is it weird to feel relieved when you quit a job you had for 11 years? like i know i should be scared but i just feel... light? anyway what are the best sites for finding remote work these days, linkedin seems useless

Relief after leaving something that long isn't weird — it's actually information. Eleven years is enough time for a place to become part of your identity, and when the relief outweighs the fear, that usually means you'd been carrying more than you'd admitted to yourself. Let that feeling be what it is.

On the remote job search: LinkedIn isn't useless but it rewards active use — posting and engaging, not just applying through the portal, which is a black hole. The sites that tend to work better for dedicated remote roles right now are We Work Remotely, Remote.co, and Flexjobs (Flexjobs has a small fee but filters out a lot of noise). For tech and design specifically, Arc.dev and Contra are worth looking at. Your strongest leads will probably come from reaching out directly to people at companies you want to work for, or from your existing network — which after 11 years in one industry is likely more substantial than it feels right now.

i've been working on this graphic novel for like 3 years and i finally showed the first chapter to a small press at a con last weekend. they said the art was 'competent but not distinctive enough' and now i can't even open the file. i keep thinking maybe i was just lying to myself this whole time about having something worth saying

Three years is real. That's not delusion — that's commitment, and it deserves more than one editor's shorthand at a convention table.

'Competent but not distinctive' is a specific kind of feedback that stings because it sounds like it's about who you are rather than what the work is doing right now. But it's actually just one data point about one person's taste and acquisition needs in one moment. It's not a verdict on whether you have something worth saying.

The fact that you can't open the file right now isn't evidence that you were lying to yourself. It's evidence that this matters to you. Work you didn't care about wouldn't hurt like this.

You don't have to force yourself back to the file today. But when you're ready, it might be worth looking at the chapter not through the lens of what that editor said, but asking yourself what you still believe is alive in it — because you're the one who's been living with these characters for three years, not them.

my therapist retired last year and i never found a new one and honestly i think the art was kind of doing the job for a while. i write songs, have for 20 years, it's the thing that keeps me level. but i had a really bad depressive episode in the spring and since then i can't write at all. not a single song. and i'm 47 and i keep thinking, ok if it's gone it's gone, maybe that chapter is just done. but without it i genuinely don't know who i am. my kids are grown. my marriage ended 4 years ago. the songs were the one thing that were still just mine. and now i can't access them and i'm not sure what to do and i'm not sure i'm ok

I'm glad you said that last part — 'I'm not sure I'm ok' — because I think that's the most important thing in what you wrote, and it deserves to be taken seriously.

What you're describing sounds like more than a creative block. A depressive episode in the spring, losing access to the thing that kept you stable, your therapist gone, the scaffolding of your life having changed so much over the last few years — that's a lot of weight to be carrying without much support. The songwriting being gone might be a symptom of how depleted you are, not a verdict on who you are.

The thought that 'maybe that chapter is just done' — I'd be careful with that one. Depression has a way of making permanent conclusions feel obvious and earned when they're actually just the depression talking. Twenty years of something that's woven into how you understand yourself doesn't disappear; it goes quiet when you're struggling.

Finding a new therapist matters right now, not as a replacement for the songs but because you said yourself you're not sure you're ok, and that's worth attending to. That's a real thing to act on.

my husband of 22 years told me last week he hasnt been happy for a long time. we have 3 kids, youngest is 16. i keep walking around the house just picking things up and putting them down again. i dont know what im supposed to do with myself. i made a dentist appointment yesterday just to have somewhere to be

Making a dentist appointment just to have somewhere to be — that's not a small thing. That's you, in the middle of something enormous, still finding ways to hold yourself upright. Whatever comes next, the ground has shifted in a way that's real and serious, and the disorientation you're describing — picking things up, putting them down, not knowing where to put yourself — makes complete sense. retired last year after 30 years in nursing, thought i'd feel relieved but i just feel useless?? my whole identity was being a nurse. my daughter keeps saying enjoy it!! but i don't know how. i volunteered at the hospital last month and left crying in my car after because it reminded me of everything i don't have anymore. sorry this isn't really a work question

Please don't apologize — this is exactly a work question, because work was your life for thirty years, and now a version of you that you built over decades is just... gone. What you're describing — feeling useless, untethered from yourself — is something a lot of people who had deeply purposeful careers go through, and it's serious enough to deserve real support, not just time. Talking to a therapist who works with life transitions isn't about something being wrong with you; it's about having someone in your corner while you figure out who you are when you're not a nurse. That's a big question, and you don't have to answer it alone.

my mom called me selfish today because i didn't come home for my cousin's graduation party. i live 4 hours away and had to work a double shift. i feel terrible but like... i couldn't just not show up to work?? i think i made the right call right

You made a genuinely hard call — four hours each way plus a double shift isn't a small ask, and work obligations are real. At the same time, the guilt you're feeling might be worth sitting with for a second rather than just resolving it with a yes or no. Sometimes "I made the right call" and "this still hurt someone I care about" are both true at the same time, and it sounds like part of you is grappling with that. My colleague Priya is in her late 40s, been a professional painter her whole adult life, and she just told me she's been secretly taking commissions she hates — like corporate lobby art — just to pay rent. She seemed almost ashamed telling me. Idk she's worked so hard and it's just depressing to hear. What do you even say to someone in that position

The shame piece is the part worth paying attention to. Taking work you don't love to survive is just pragmatism — artists do it all the time — but it clearly doesn't feel that way to her, and that gap between what she expected her life to look like at this point and what it actually is can be a specific kind of painful.

She told you. That's not nothing. She wasn't venting into a void — she chose you, and the fact that you're sitting with it enough to bring it here suggests she probably chose well.

You don't have to say anything that resolves it. What tends to help in that moment isn't reassurance that everything will work out, or reframes about how the commercial work is actually fine, or success stories of artists who made it later. It's just being someone who doesn't flinch at the reality of it — who can hear that it's hard without immediately trying to make it less hard.

Something like "that sounds genuinely exhausting to carry" does more than almost anything else. It lets her stop performing okayness for a minute, which might be exactly what she needed when she told you.

my dad is 61 and just got laid off from a manufacturing job he had for 22 years. he keeps saying he's fine and he'll figure it out but he hasn't done anything in 6 weeks. my mom is worried. i don't know if i should say something or just leave him alone. he's not great at talking about stuff

Six weeks of stillness after losing a 22-year job isn't laziness — it's more likely shock, and possibly something heavier than that. For someone of your dad's generation, especially in manufacturing, that job probably wasn't just income. It was identity, routine, a place where he knew exactly who he was. Losing it at 61, when re-entering the job market feels genuinely uncertain, is a hard thing to sit with.

The fact that he's saying 'I'm fine' and not doing anything yet — those two things together are worth taking seriously. You're right to be paying attention.

You don't have to make it a conversation about feelings for it to matter. Sometimes the most useful thing is just showing up in a low-pressure way — going for a drive, watching a game, doing something ordinary together — and letting him know without a speech that you're around. If he does open up, listening without problem-solving is usually more valuable than any practical advice. And if a few more weeks pass and he's still completely stalled, gently naming what you're noticing — not as criticism, just as 'I see you' — can sometimes reach people who don't have language for what they're going through.

Your instinct to not just leave him alone is probably the right one.

If the issue is that you're depleted right now, it might be worth asking whether a short extension is possible — not because the poems aren't good enough, but because making this call from empty is a different thing than making it from a place where you can stand behind the decision. is it actually possible to learn a language at 54 or is that just something language apps say to sell subscriptions. not that im trying to learn one just curious

The research is pretty clear that adults can learn languages effectively — fluency takes longer than it does for children, and accent acquisition is harder, but functional proficiency is genuinely achievable. The 'just curious' framing is noted, and I'm not going to push, but there's something worth saying: the main thing that stops adults isn't biology, it's the feeling that starting something new at this point feels vaguely embarrassing or like it might not pay off. If there's a language that's been sitting in the back of your mind, that's usually there for a reason.
my mom keeps asking me to explain what a 401k match is so she can decide if she wants to take a new job. shes 61. i honestly have no idea how to explain it to her and i dont want to get it wrong

It's clear you're trying to look out for her here, and at 61, this decision carries real weight — a job change this close to retirement isn't just about the salary. A 401k match means the employer contributes money to her retirement account based on what she puts in, essentially free money up to a certain percentage of her salary. But the bigger question for her is whether this job makes sense at this stage: vesting schedules, how long she'd need to stay to actually keep the match, and how this fits her retirement timeline all matter. If she's seriously considering it, it might be worth a one-time conversation with a fee-only financial advisor — not because you got anything wrong, but because the stakes are high enough that she deserves a full picture.

retired last year after 35 years as a nurse and I thought I'd love it but I'm honestly miserable. My daughter keeps sending me articles about "staying active" lol. I've been thinking about going back to work part time but my husband thinks it's a bad idea, he says I earned the rest. I'm not asking for advice just kind of venting I guess

Thirty-five years of work doesn't just leave a schedule gap — it leaves an identity gap, and that's genuinely hard in a way that "staying active" articles don't really address. The people who struggle most with retirement are often the ones who were most committed to what they did, which tracks for someone who spent decades in nursing.

Your husband's framing — that you earned the rest — comes from a loving place, but rest isn't the same thing as what you need if what you actually need is purpose and usefulness. Those aren't the same thing, and wanting to go back part-time isn't a failure to relax correctly. It's you knowing something about yourself.

My doctor wants me to start metformin for pre-diabetes and I keep putting off filling the prescription. I'm 54, I've watched my diet for years, I exercise, I'm not overweight. I guess I just feel like if I start taking it that means I failed somehow. My appointment was 6 weeks ago.

Six weeks is a long time to carry that prescription around unfilled, and the fact that you're naming the real reason — feeling like it means failure — says you've already done some honest thinking about this.

But here's the thing: pre-diabetes developing in someone who eats carefully, exercises, and isn't overweight isn't a story about failure. It's often genetics, aging physiology, stress hormones, or factors that genuinely aren't in your control. The behaviors you've maintained have almost certainly slowed or delayed this — that's not nothing, that's real. Metformin in this context isn't a punishment for giving up. It's a tool that works well alongside everything you're already doing.

The six-week delay is the part worth paying attention to. Not because of urgency — though earlier is better — but because avoiding the pharmacy is a way of avoiding the diagnosis itself, and that tends to cost people more in the long run than the medication ever would.
random question but do professional artists actually enjoy making art or does it become like a job after a while? like does the passion go away

Plenty of professional artists describe exactly that shift — the thing that used to feel like play starts to feel like obligation, and that can be genuinely disorienting. But I'd guess you're not just asking about other people's experience. If making art has started to feel like a grind for you, that's worth sitting with — it doesn't necessarily mean the passion is gone, sometimes it means something about how you're working or what you're making needs to change. The question of whether it can stay alive is worth taking seriously as your own question, not just a theoretical one.

got a job offer in singapore. its a 2 year contract, way more money than im making now, and honestly the work sounds cool. been in chicago my whole life (28 now) and i've never really done anything like this. my girlfriend and i have been together 3 years and she cant come bc of her residency program. we'd do long distance. everyone i talk to says do it but something feels off and i cant figure out what it is

The fact that something feels off even when the checklist looks good is worth paying attention to — that's not cold feet, that's usually information.

It might help to try to locate where exactly the feeling lives. Is it about your girlfriend and what two years of that kind of distance actually does to a relationship you care about? Is it anxiety about going somewhere entirely new without a single person who knows you? Is it that the opportunity sounds good on paper but the actual work or company doesn't fully excite you? Or is it something harder to name — like the version of your life you'd be stepping away from?

Everyone saying "do it" is probably responding to the obvious upside: money, adventure, growth, a story to tell. Those are real. But they're not the only real things. The relationship piece especially — two years of long distance mid-residency is genuinely hard, and it's worth having a very honest conversation with your girlfriend about what you both think that looks like, not just whether you're "supportive" of each other in the abstract. That conversation might clarify a lot of the feeling.

I've been at my company for 11 years. I'm 47. Last week they announced a restructuring and my entire department is being 'evaluated for consolidation.' I have two kids in high school and my wife works part time. I'm not panicking yet but I think maybe I should be? I don't even know what my resume looks like anymore, I haven't touched it in a decade.

The fact that you're not panicking yet is probably your mind trying to hold things together while you figure out what's real — that's reasonable, and it doesn't mean you're in denial. The situation does warrant taking seriously, even if nothing is certain yet.

Eleven years at one company means your resume will need real work, but it also means you have a decade of accomplishments, relationships, and institutional knowledge that has genuine value. The gap won't be as bad as it feels right now — it mostly just needs to be translated into language that makes sense outside your company.

The most useful thing to do right now, before you know how the restructuring shakes out: quietly start updating your resume and reaching out to people in your network — not to ask for jobs, just to reconnect. If things stabilize, nothing is lost. If they don't, you'll have a weeks-long head start. Your industry contacts from 11 years are an asset most people your age underestimate.

failed my driving test again. third time. my examiner literally said i 'lack confidence' which like thanks i know. i'm 19 and everyone i know already has their license and i just feel so stupid about it

Failing three times when everyone around you seems to have breezed through it — that particular kind of embarrassment is hard to shake, and 'you just lack confidence' is about the least useful feedback an examiner can give you. It names the symptom without helping you fix anything.

Here's the thing about confidence in driving tests specifically: it usually isn't a personality trait you need to develop, it's a skill gap in disguise. Examiners tend to flag 'confidence' when they're seeing hesitation at junctions, late mirror checks, or inconsistent speed — things that feel like nerves but are actually just techniques that haven't been drilled enough to become automatic yet. If you can get more detail on the specific moments where you lost marks on this attempt, that's actually actionable.

A few things worth considering: some people genuinely do better with a different instructor whose style clicks better with how they learn — it's not disloyalty, it's just how it works. Mock tests with a third-party examiner can also help, because the formal setting stops feeling so high-stakes once you've been through it a few more times in low-stakes conditions.

You're not stupid. You're 19 and you haven't passed a driving test yet — those are genuinely different things.

My doctor told me last Thursday that the biopsy came back and it's cancer. Breast cancer, stage 2. I'm 41, two kids, my youngest is 7. I haven't told my husband yet because I don't know how. I keep just cooking dinner and helping with homework like everything is normal. I don't even know what I'm asking you.

You don't need to know what you're asking. You just found out something that changes everything, and you're still making dinner and checking homework — because that's what you do when you're holding something too big to put down yet.

You don't have to figure out how to tell your husband right now, or what any of this means for your family. You're allowed to still be in shock. Stage 2 breast cancer is serious, and it's also something a lot of people come through — but none of that makes this moment less terrifying.

When you're ready — not now, but soon — the conversation with your husband will probably be hard and also a relief. You shouldn't have to carry this alone for long. And your care team can connect you with someone whose whole job is helping people navigate exactly this, if you want that.

my mandarin tutor keeps telling me i need to practice speaking every day but honestly i hate it, i sound so stupid and i just freeze up. so i've decided im only gonna do reading and writing from now on. i've been studying for 8 months already and speaking is just not for me i think

The feeling of freezing up and sounding stupid is one of the most universal experiences in language learning, and it's genuinely uncomfortable — it makes sense you want to avoid it. But cutting speaking out entirely after 8 months is likely to calcify exactly the problem you're trying to escape. Reading and writing skill doesn't transfer to speaking the way people expect it to, and after another year you may find the gap feels even harder to close.

What might actually be worth trying is changing the conditions rather than dropping it altogether. A lot of people who freeze in lessons do fine with low-stakes recorded practice — just talking to yourself, or using an app like HelloTalk where there's no real-time pressure. The freeze response is usually about being watched and evaluated, not about speaking itself. Your tutor probably sees the potential that makes them keep pushing, but how you get there doesn't have to look the way it does right now.

moved to a new city for my husband's job 8 months ago. left my whole network behind, my therapist, my gym, everything. i've tried the meetup apps, joined a book club that fizzled out, said yes to every work happy hour. still feel completely alone here. i don't know if i'm doing something wrong or if this is just what it is now

Eight months of consistently trying — and I mean really trying, not just thinking about it — and still feeling alone is genuinely demoralizing. It's worth saying that out loud because there's a version of this conversation where someone just hands you more tactics, and I don't think that's what's missing.

What you're describing isn't a strategy problem. You've done the things. The harder truth about building connection in a new place as an adult is that it's slow in a way that feels almost broken, and the early stages — meetups, book clubs, happy hours — often produce pleasant acquaintances rather than anything that actually fills the gap. That lag between effort and belonging is real and it doesn't mean something is wrong with you or with how you're showing up.

The one thing worth considering: is there anything from your old life — not a replica of it, but something that mattered to you specifically — that you haven't tried to rebuild yet? Not because the meetup formula failed, but because sometimes the connection comes sideways, through doing something you'd be doing anyway rather than something designed for meeting people.

called my bank again today about lowering my credit card APR. 29.99% and i've been a customer for 11 years, never missed a payment. they said no again. second time this year. at this point idk if i should just cancel the card or what, carrying about $4,200 on it and its killing me every month

Eleven years, perfect payment history, and they still said no twice — that's genuinely frustrating, and it's worth naming that the system here isn't really set up to reward loyalty the way banks imply it does.

At 29.99% on $4,200, you're paying somewhere around $105 a month just in interest, which means a huge chunk of whatever you're paying isn't touching the principal. That's the real urgency.

Canceling the card probably isn't your best first move — it can ding your credit score by reducing available credit, which matters if you might need to borrow or refinance anything soon. What's more likely to actually help: a balance transfer card with a 0% intro APR (many run 15–21 months), or a personal loan at a lower rate to pay it off in a fixed timeline. Both let you stop the bleeding while you pay it down. The bank's answer being "no" twice doesn't mean your options are exhausted — it just means the option that required the least effort on your part is closed.

my daughter keeps asking me to learn how to video call her on the ipad she got me for christmas and i keep telling her i'll figure it out later. i figured out how to use a computer in 1987 so its not like i cant learn things. anyway do you know if there is a way to make the text bigger on the screen because its a little hard to read

To make text bigger on the iPad: go to Settings → Display & Brightness → Text Size, and drag the slider to the right. If that's not enough, Settings → Accessibility → Display & Text Size → Larger Text gives you an even bigger range.

And for what it's worth — you taught yourself computing in 1987, which was genuinely hard, and you're asking the right questions now. The video call thing probably won't take long once you sit down with it. Your daughter will likely enjoy walking you through it too, if you want the company while you learn.

I retired eight months ago after 35 years as an engineer and honestly I thought I'd love it but I just feel invisible. My wife has her book club, her garden, her whole life. I don't know what I do anymore. Not looking for advice just needed to say it somewhere.

Thirty-five years of knowing exactly what you contributed, what your days were for — and then that just stops. The invisibility you're describing makes a lot of sense. It's not ingratitude or weakness; it's a real loss, and it doesn't get named that way often enough.

You said you weren't looking for advice, and I'm not going to offer any. I just want you to know what you wrote landed.

my roommate just got laid off from her first job out of college, she's been there like 8 months. she keeps saying she's fine but she literally hasn't left the apartment in 4 days and i don't know what to do for her

Eight months in and laid off — that's a brutal way to start a career, and four days without leaving the apartment tells you she's not actually fine, whatever she's saying. The gap between 'I'm okay' and that kind of withdrawal is real and worth taking seriously.

The most useful thing you can probably do right now isn't to fix the job situation or push her toward action — it's just to make staying in feel less like hiding. Suggest something low-stakes and contained: a walk, grabbing food, anything that gets her out without framing it as 'getting back on track.' Let her talk about it if she wants, but don't make every conversation about next steps.

If the withdrawal goes on much longer or deepens, it's worth gently naming what you're seeing — not as a diagnosis, just as 'I've noticed you seem really down and I'm a little worried.' You clearly care about her, and that kind of honest, quiet attention matters more than any practical advice you could offer right now.

my mom called me again tonight. third time this week. she keeps saying she's fine but she sounds so tired and kind of... hollow? she's 71 and lives alone since my dad passed in march and i'm 4 hours away and i just don't know what i'm supposed to do with this feeling that something is really wrong

That hollow quality in her voice — you're right to take that seriously. Grief at 71, alone, four hours away from you: that's a lot of weight for one person to carry, and it doesn't always announce itself clearly. The fact that she keeps calling and saying she's fine might actually be the thing worth paying attention to. She may not have the words for what she needs, or she may not want to worry you.

The feeling you're sitting with isn't just anxiety — it's probably your read on a real situation. It might be worth finding a reason to visit soon, even briefly, not to investigate but just to be physically present and see for yourself. And if you have any family, neighbors, or anyone in her area who could check in on her more regularly, now is a reasonable time to ask that of them. You don't have to wait for a crisis to act on this.

We're moving my mom into assisted living next month. She's 81 and has moderate dementia. My siblings showed up for one afternoon. I don't even know why I'm writing this, I'm not really asking for anything I guess.

You don't need a question to have something worth saying. What you just described — carrying the full weight of a parent's transition into memory care, largely alone — is one of the more quietly devastating things a person can do. The logistics are exhausting enough. But there's also grief folded into all of it: grief for your mom, for the house, for the version of this where your siblings were actually present.

Feeling hollowed out after something like this isn't a sign something's wrong with you. It's what happens when you hold a lot for a long time and then the immediate crisis passes and there's nothing left to do but feel it.

You did something real and hard for someone who needed it. That matters, even if it cost you more than it should have.

i've watched like 15 youtube videos on how to read music and i still can't do it. like i sit down at the piano and my brain just goes blank. i'm 34 and i feel like i'm too stupid to learn this, which is embarrassing to even type

That blank-brain feeling when you sit at the piano isn't stupidity — it's what happens when you've been learning *about* something without enough practice doing the thing itself. Videos are great for concepts but they can't build the reflex of actually reading and playing at the same time, and that reflex takes weeks of slow, repetitive reps to wire in. The embarrassment makes sense, but it's pointing at the wrong cause.

What actually tends to break through this: pick one simple piece — genuinely simple, like a five-note beginner melody — and read through just two measures a day, very slowly, out loud naming the notes before you play them. Not fun, but it builds the connection between the symbol and your hand that videos can't.

Also worth knowing: 34 is not a late start. Adults often learn this faster than kids once something clicks because they can actually understand the underlying logic. You're not behind.

asking for my dad (67, retired engineer) — he's been trying to learn python for about 8 months now and keeps hitting this wall where he'll make progress for a few weeks then get stuck on something, spiral into thinking he's too old for this, and quit for a month. then restart from scratch. we've watched him do this cycle like 4 times. is there a better way to learn that might actually work for someone like him or is this just kind of how it goes

The restart-from-scratch pattern is the thing to fix more than the learning method itself. Each time he quits and comes back to the beginning, he's confirming the story that he didn't really learn anything — when actually getting stuck on something hard means he got far enough to reach something hard. That's progress, not failure.

For someone with an engineering background, Python tends to click better when it's attached to a real problem he actually wants to solve — something specific, even small, like automating a spreadsheet he uses or analyzing data from a hobby. Abstract tutorials can feel purposeless in a way that makes the stuck moments feel more defeating. A concrete project gives the frustration somewhere to go.

The other thing worth gently reframing with him: experienced engineers get stuck constantly, they've just built up tolerance for not knowing yet. The 'I'm too old for this' spiral is probably less about age and more about being used to competence in his field — learning Python puts him back at beginner, which is genuinely uncomfortable for someone who spent decades being the expert in the room. That's not a cognitive limitation, it's a psychological one, and it's very solvable.

If he can commit to not restarting — just picking up where he left off even if it takes a week to re-orient — the cycle breaks on its own.

I'm a second-year associate at a law firm and I basically rewrote a 40-page brief that a senior partner handed me in terrible shape. Like I reorganized the whole argument, rewrote most of the sections, found three cases he'd missed. He presented it to the client and took full credit, didn't mention me once. I didn't say anything because I don't want to make waves but honestly I handled that really professionally right? Staying quiet was the right move

You handled it gracefully in the moment — and I don't want to dismiss that, because reading a room and not blowing up a relationship with a senior partner early in your career is a real skill. You weren't wrong to think through the consequences before reacting.

But 'professionally' and 'right for you' might not be the same thing here. Staying quiet once is a judgment call. The harder question is what happens the next time this partner hands you a wreck and you fix it — because if he's learned there's no cost to this, it's likely to happen again. You're two years in, which means you're still building the reputation that's going to follow you. If no one senior knows what you actually contribute, that invisibility compounds over time. That doesn't mean you needed to say something in front of the client. But there's space between 'make waves' and 'say nothing' — a quiet word to the partner afterward, or making sure other people in the room understand your role, isn't unprofessional. It's just self-advocacy.

my mom keeps saying i should just pick any major and figure it out later but i've literally already done that. switched from business to psych sophomore year thinking it would click and it's junior year now and it still doesn't. i go to class and it's fine but i feel nothing. i don't think the problem is the major anymore but i don't know what the problem actually is and that's worse somehow

You've already tried the thing people told you to try, and it didn't fix it — so now you're stuck with a harder and more unsettling question than 'what should I study.' Feeling nothing where something is supposed to be, and not being able to name why, is genuinely disorienting. It makes sense that feels worse than a concrete problem would.

What you're describing — going through the motions, things being fine but flat — sometimes has less to do with the specific path and more to do with something underneath: burnout, depression, a mismatch between how you're living and what you actually need, or just the particular kind of lost that happens in your early twenties when you're supposed to be figuring everything out at once. It's worth taking seriously on its own terms, not just as a major-selection problem. If there's a counselor at your school you haven't talked to yet, that might be a more useful place to bring this than another conversation about switching tracks.

my roommate started a coding bootcamp in january and he's already talking about dropping out. he's like 3 months in and says he just doesn't get it and everyone else seems to catch on faster than him. i think he'd regret dropping out but also its his call. is there a point where someone is just not cut out for programming

The comparison trap he's in — watching others seem to 'get it' faster — is one of the most demoralizing parts of bootcamps specifically, and it's often an illusion. Some people in those cohorts have touched code before, some are just better at performing confidence, and three months in is exactly when imposter syndrome peaks for a lot of people.

To your actual question: no, three months is not enough time to know whether someone has a ceiling in programming. What it can reveal is whether the learning environment, the teaching style, or the pacing fits someone — and bootcamps are famously uneven in that regard. Dropping out at month three and trying a different path isn't the same as giving up on programming.

You're in a tricky spot because you can see the regret risk more clearly than he can right now, and you're right that it's ultimately his call. But if he's open to it, it might be worth him talking to someone who finished the program about what month three actually felt like for them.

took early retirement 8 months ago after 31 years at the same company. thought i was ready. now i wake up every morning and i don't know what to do with myself. my wife says i seem depressed but i keep telling her i'm fine. maybe i'm not fine

Thirty-one years is a long time to build a sense of who you are and what your days mean — and then one day that structure is just gone. That's a genuine loss, even when leaving was the right call, even when you earned it. The gap between 'I should feel relieved' and 'I feel untethered' is a confusing place to sit, and it sounds like you've been sitting in it alone for a while. The fact that you can say 'maybe I'm not fine' matters — that's not nothing. Your wife is seeing something real, and so are you.

my parents have been in the US for 30 years and somehow never really built any savings, they're both in their late 60s and my dad just lost his job. i keep reading articles about 'its never too late to start investing' is that actually true or is it just something financial influencers say to get clicks

The articles are technically true but they're usually written for people in their 40s or early 50s with decent income — at 68 or 69 with no savings cushion and a recent job loss, the math is genuinely harder and the timeline is compressed in ways those headlines don't acknowledge. I don't want to be glib about that. What's actually useful at your parents' age is less about growth investing and more about stabilizing: Social Security timing (if they haven't claimed yet, waiting even a year or two can meaningfully increase monthly payments), any benefits they might qualify for, and whether there are assets or housing situations that could be restructured. It sounds like you might be the one trying to figure this out for them, which is its own weight to carry. If that's the case, a one-time session with a fee-only financial planner who works with lower-income retirees could be more useful than anything you'll find in articles — many nonprofits offer this free.

not really looking for advice just kind of processing i guess. my doctor told me three weeks ago i need to start blood pressure medication and i keep not filling the prescription. i know i should, i'm 54 not 34, it's just — i don't know. it's fine. anyway do you know if there are specific foods that are genuinely proven to lower blood pressure or is most of that overblown

There are real dietary options that have solid evidence behind them — the DASH diet has the strongest research base, and within that: reducing sodium (the biggest lever for most people), increasing potassium through foods like leafy greens and bananas, limiting alcohol, and adding things like beets or hibiscus tea, which have modest but real effects. But I want to sit with what you actually said for a second. Three weeks is a while to hold onto an unfilled prescription, and "I don't know" after trailing off usually means something. Starting medication can feel like a line being crossed — like things have changed and you're now someone who takes medication for this. That's a real feeling, and it doesn't make you irrational. It just might be worth knowing what's actually in the way, because the food changes help but probably not enough to skip the prescription your doctor recommended.

my mom called me twice this week to tell me my cousin just got engaged and how 'wonderful' it is. im 34 and single and she knows exactly what shes doing. i didnt say anything mean, just kind of went quiet and got off the phone fast. i feel like that was the right call tbh

Going quiet instead of snapping back takes real restraint, especially when the dig is dressed up as innocent good news. You protected the relationship from a fight you didn't want to have, and that's not nothing.

That said — the reason this keeps landing hard is probably worth sitting with. Your mom may not fully clock how loaded these calls feel to you, and the pattern of going quiet might be keeping a real conversation from ever happening. That's your call to make, not an obligation. But if the calls keep stinging, silence might be protecting the peace without actually changing anything.

i've restarted my router like 4 times today and the wifi keeps dropping every 20 minutes. called the ISP and they said 'try restarting your router' and i wanted to scream. this has been going on for two weeks

Two weeks of this, plus an ISP that gave you the exact advice you've already exhausted — that's genuinely maddening, and your frustration makes complete sense. The restart cycle isn't going to fix what's actually wrong here. A few things worth trying: check if your router is overheating (if it's in a cabinet or against a wall, that can cause exactly this pattern), log into your router's admin page and look at the connection logs to see what's actually dropping, and when you call the ISP back, specifically ask them to check the line signal levels remotely — that forces them past the script. If the line signal is fine and the hardware isn't overheating, it may just be a dying router, especially if it's more than 4-5 years old. You've been patient with this long enough.

my younger sister just got her first real job out of college and shes already talking about putting 15% of her paycheck into savings every month but she also has like $28k in student loans at 6.5% interest. i told her to maybe pay off the loans first but she grew up watching our parents lose everything and she just wants to feel secure. is she making a mistake or not

She's not making a straightforward financial mistake — but she's also not making a purely financial decision, and it's worth understanding the difference before pushing her either way.

Mathematically, 6.5% is a meaningful interest rate. If she has no employer match on retirement savings, paying down the loans first (or aggressively splitting between the two) would likely come out ahead on paper. But your sister isn't optimizing a spreadsheet — she's trying to feel safe after watching financial security collapse up close. That's not irrational. A savings cushion can make someone stable enough to actually function, keep a job, not panic-spend. The psychological value is real.

The genuinely useful thing you could do for her is help her see that these goals don't have to be in total competition. A common approach: make minimum loan payments, build a small emergency fund (even $1,000–2,000 feels different than zero), then throw extra at the loans. That way she has something that feels like security without letting 6.5% compound unchecked.

You clearly care about her getting this right. The most helpful framing you can offer her probably isn't "you're doing it wrong" — it's helping her see a path where she gets both.

i haven't slept more than like 3 hrs a night in almost 2 weeks. started bc of finals but finals ended 5 days ago and i still cant sleep. i just lie there and my brain won't stop. took some melatonin last night, 10mg, didn't do anything. honestly starting to feel kinda unreal, like im watching myself from outside my body or something. is that normal

What you're describing — that detached, watching-yourself-from-outside feeling — is called depersonalization, and yes, it can happen with severe sleep deprivation. Your brain is genuinely struggling right now, not just tired. Two weeks of 3-hour nights is beyond normal stress exhaustion.

The fact that it's continuing after finals ended matters. Your nervous system got stuck in a high-alert state and hasn't been able to come down on its own. That's not a willpower problem or something melatonin is going to fix at this point.

This is worth talking to someone at your campus health center about today or tomorrow, not because something is catastrophically wrong, but because you're past the point where this resolves on its own and you deserve actual support — not just tips. The dissociation especially is a sign your body is telling you it needs more than you can give it right now.

my little sister is 19 and she's been doing graphic design for like 2 years and she's genuinely so talented but she keeps saying her work is 'mid' and won't show anyone. she entered one competition last year and didn't place and hasn't submitted anything since. how do I get her to just believe in herself a little

It's hard watching someone you love shrink away from something they're clearly good at — especially when the gap between their talent and their self-perception is so obvious to you.

The one competition not placing probably hit harder than it looked from the outside. At 19, with two years in, that kind of early rejection can quietly convince someone that the jury's already in on them — when really they're still in the middle of becoming.

The most useful thing you can do probably isn't pushing her to believe in herself, because that framing puts the problem inside her and she likely already knows she's being hard on herself. It tends to land better if the focus is external and specific — sharing her work with one person she trusts and getting a real reaction, or finding a low-stakes creative community where showing up matters more than placing. Small exposure, not a confidence lecture.

Also worth knowing: sometimes the person watching from the sidelines needs to hear that their concern is landing. Telling her directly — not "you're so talented" but something like "I actually think about your work sometimes, it sticks with me" — can cut through in a way that general encouragement doesn't.

got my performance review today and my manager said i'm 'meeting expectations' which like... i've been staying late every single week, covered for two people who quit, basically ran the whole Q3 launch by myself. meeting expectations?? i feel like i'm going crazy. that's not fair right

That gap — between what you actually did and how it got labeled — is real and it makes sense that it stings. 'Meeting expectations' after absorbing two people's workloads and carrying a major launch isn't just an oversight, it's a signal worth paying attention to. It might mean your manager doesn't fully see what you've been doing, or that the bar keeps shifting without being named, or that the contributions you're making aren't the ones being tracked and rewarded here. None of those possibilities are great, and none of them are your fault. What matters now is figuring out which one it is — because that determines whether this is a conversation worth having with your manager, or whether this place is going to keep taking what you give without reflecting it back.

honestly not even sure why im typing this. im 61 and i just found out my pension from the plant got cut by like 40%. worked there 28 years. was supposed to retire in 4 years. i don't know what retiring even looks like now

28 years of work, a plan you'd built your life around, and now the numbers don't add up the way they were supposed to. That's not just a financial problem — it's a loss, and it's okay to sit with how heavy that feels before doing anything else.

When you're ready to think practically: a 40% cut is serious but four years is also not nothing. A fee-only financial advisor (one who doesn't earn commissions) can look at your full picture — Social Security timing, any other assets, what part-time work might look like — and help you figure out what retirement actually can look like now, even if it's different from what you imagined. It may be later, or smaller, or structured differently, but it's worth knowing the real numbers rather than just carrying the fear of them.

You don't have to have this figured out today.

My husband thinks I should quit my ceramics studio after 22 years because it's never been profitable and we're retiring soon. He's not wrong that it loses money. But I had a show last spring at a real gallery — small, local, but still — and the curator told me my work has 'quiet authority.' I keep thinking about that phrase. I feel like I'm just starting to hit my stride and he wants me to close up shop. I don't know why I'm even telling you this, I just needed to say it somewhere.

Twenty-two years, and a curator's phrase is still rattling around in your head weeks later — that tells you something about what this means to you.

Your husband's concern isn't wrong on its own terms. But 'it loses money' and 'it matters' aren't mutually exclusive, and retiring doesn't automatically mean shrinking your life. The harder question underneath all of this is whether the financial reality actually requires closing the studio, or whether that's become the argument being used for a decision that's really about something else — convenience, worry, different visions of what this next chapter looks like.

You're not being irrational for not wanting to let go of something you've spent 22 years building, especially right when it's starting to feel like yours. That's worth a real conversation with him, not just an agreement.

my dad is 68 and retired and i think he's really lonely but he would never say that. my mum passed 2 years ago and he just watches tv all day when i call he says he's fine but you can just tell. i live 4 hours away and i have two kids so i cant exactly drop everything. i dont even know what im asking i just feel guilty all the time about it

The guilt makes sense — you love him, you can see something's wrong, and you can't close the distance in the way you wish you could. That's a genuinely hard place to sit.

Two years out from losing your mum, what you're describing in your dad is really common and really serious. Quiet withdrawal, 'I'm fine,' TV as a way to fill the hours — it can harden into something chronic if nothing changes, and he's unlikely to name it or ask for help.

You can't be there in the way you want to be, but that doesn't mean you're powerless. Some things that actually help with isolated older adults: a standing weekly call at a specific time (routine matters more than frequency), gently encouraging one concrete thing — a class, a local group, even a part-time volunteer role — without pushing too hard. If he has a GP he trusts, a check-in framed as routine health stuff can sometimes open a door he wouldn't open himself.

And the guilt — it's worth noticing that you're carrying it even though you're doing what you can within real constraints. That's not nothing. You're paying attention to him even from 4 hours away, and that matters to him even if he doesn't say so.

my mom keeps saying i look tired and asking if im eating enough. im fine, im in my second year of med school. is there like a quick high calorie snack i can keep in my bag that doesnt need refrigeration

Mixed nuts, nut butter packets, dried mango or dates, protein bars like RX Bars or Larabars — all solid, calorie-dense, and bag-stable. Second year of med school is genuinely brutal, and "I'm fine" can be true and also not the full picture at the same time. If you're eating enough but still running on empty, sleep and sustained stress tend to show up on your face even when nutrition is handled. Not saying your mom is right — just that if the tired is real and not just optics, it's worth noticing before third year.

I'm gonna CC my boss's boss on this email calling out Marcus for the third time missing our sprint deadlines. I've tried talking to Marcus directly twice and nothing changes, so I'm done being polite about it. Can you help me write it?

The frustration here is completely legitimate — you've done the right thing twice already, and nothing changed. That's genuinely exhausting.

Before I help you write it, it's worth being honest about what this email is likely to do. CC'ing your boss's boss on a callout email tends to land as an escalation move, and even when you're 100% in the right, it can shift how people see you — suddenly you're the one who went over heads, not Marcus who keeps missing deadlines. That's not fair, but it's real.

A more durable path is usually emailing your direct boss first, just the two of you, laying out the pattern with specifics: dates, which deadlines, what impact it had on your work. That creates a paper trail, puts the accountability on your manager to act, and keeps you clearly positioned as the professional who raised it properly. If your boss does nothing, then escalating higher is much easier to justify — and much harder for anyone to spin.

If you want, I can help you write that version. It can still be direct and specific — it doesn't have to be soft.

ok so theres this guy in my friend group who i hooked up with like twice sophomore year and it was kind of a whole thing but we're fine now. my roomate just told me he likes my best friend and i am absolutely going to tell her he's bad news so she doesn't pursue it. i know i sound crazy but i just feel like she deserves better

It's worth sitting with what's actually driving this for a second — because "she deserves better" and "I still have feelings about this" can coexist, and they'd lead to pretty different conversations. If you tell her he's bad news based on something that ended two years ago, she'll probably find out the context eventually, and that could put a dent in her trust in you more than in him. If there's something genuinely concerning about how he treated you, that's worth sharing honestly — as your experience, not as a verdict on him. That's a real thing she'd want to know.

do therapists actually help with like, not having anyone to talk to? asking because my sister keeps telling me to go but i dont really think im depressed or anything. im 34 and just moved to a new city 8 months ago and still havent really made any friends here which is fine i just wonder sometimes

Eight months in a new city with no real social footing yet — that's genuinely hard, and 'I wonder sometimes' is doing a lot of quiet work in that sentence.

To answer your actual question: yes, therapy can help with exactly this, and it doesn't require a depression diagnosis to be worthwhile. A good therapist isn't just someone to vent to — they can help you figure out what's actually getting in the way of connecting with people, whether that's the logistics of a new city, something about how you're showing up socially, or just the accumulated weight of months of isolation. The loneliness of a new place at 34 is real and specific — you don't have the built-in structures of school anymore, and building from scratch takes real effort. That's worth taking seriously, not just waiting out.
random question but whats the recommended amount of sleep for someone my age (19). asking for a friend lol. i've been pulling like 4-5 hrs a night since september and i feel totally fine tbh

The standard recommendation for your age is 7–9 hours. But I want to be straight with you — four to five hours since September isn't a quirk, that's months of meaningful sleep debt, and the tricky thing about chronic sleep deprivation is that it erodes your ability to notice how impaired you actually are. 'Feeling fine' starts to feel like your baseline when it isn't. The research on this is pretty consistent: cognition, mood regulation, immune function, long-term mental health — all take real hits at those levels, even when you stop feeling tired. Worth taking seriously, not just as trivia.

i'm fine honestly, just haven't been to the gym since before my mom passed in february and i can't really figure out how to get back into it. do i just restart my old program or should i start lighter

I'm sorry about your mom. February isn't that long ago, and the fact that something you used to do regularly now feels impossible to restart — that's not a scheduling problem, that's grief doing what grief does.

On the practical question: start lighter, without question. Your body has had a hard few months even if you haven't been tracking it that way, and trying to pick up exactly where you left off usually ends in injury or discouragement. A couple weeks of lower weight and shorter sessions to rebuild the habit matters more than the numbers right now. But honestly, just getting back through the door once is the real milestone — the program details are secondary.
lol so i pulled my second all-nighter this week for orgo and i just need to know if caffeine pills are actually bad for you or if thats just something people say. i feel totally fine btw

Two all-nighters in one week is a lot to put your body through, and the 'I feel totally fine' thing — that's often the sleep deprivation talking. Your brain gets worse at detecting how impaired it actually is the more tired it is, which is a cruel trick.

On the caffeine pills: they're not inherently dangerous for a healthy person in low doses, but the risk is that pills make it easy to overshoot — a standard pill is 200mg, which hits faster and harder than coffee and is easier to stack without realizing it. High doses can cause heart palpitations, anxiety spikes, and make it genuinely harder to retain what you're cramming, which defeats the point. If you're going to use them, one pill, not on an empty stomach, and not after 2pm if you want any sleep tonight.

But honestly — even a 90-minute nap before your next study block will do more for your recall than another hour of reading on fumes.

so i told my parents i'm dropping out next semester. i'm a junior at state, engineering, 2.5 years in. they're devastated but honestly i feel relieved?? my plan is to move to portland with my boyfriend and figure it out from there. he has a job lined up, i don't have anything yet but i'm sick of pretending i care about this degree. just need help writing a withdrawal email to my advisor

Relief after a hard decision often means something true. At the same time, "move to Portland with my boyfriend and figure it out" is doing a lot of heavy lifting here, and 2.5 years into an engineering degree is a specific kind of crossroads — close enough to completion that it's worth being honest with yourself about whether you're leaving *engineering* or leaving *this version of your life*, because those might have different answers.

None of that means the decision is wrong. But before you send that email, it might be worth knowing whether your school has a leave of absence option — most do, and it keeps the door open without committing you to anything. You could be in Portland, figuring things out, without permanently closing this off.

If you've thought all this through and you're sure, I'll help you write a clear, professional note to your advisor. Just let me know.

my roomate (we're both 22, just graduated) got offered a really well paying corporate job but she's been crying about it every night this week. she keeps saying she doesn't know if she should take it and i don't know what to say to her. the job is in finance, she studied english lit. i think she feels like she's selling out but also she has like 40k in student loans

The crying every night tells you this isn't really a practical question she's trying to solve — she's grieving something. Maybe the version of herself she thought she'd be after an English degree. Maybe a future she hasn't fully let go of yet. The loans are real, but they're not why she's crying; they're just the thing making it feel like she has no choice.

The most useful thing you can do probably isn't to help her think it through logically, because she's already done that — that's what's making her miserable. She can see both sides. What she might actually need is someone who will just sit with how hard it is without immediately moving to 'but here's why it'll be okay.'

For what it's worth: taking a job isn't the same as becoming it. Plenty of people spend a few years in finance, pay off debt, figure out what they actually want, and leave. It's a real option, not a life sentence. But that's only useful to say if she's ready to hear it — and right now it sounds like she might just need someone to acknowledge that it genuinely sucks to feel like your choices got narrowed before you even started.

so we're selling the house. 23 years in this house. kids are grown, husband retired, makes sense to downsize, totally logical decision. i found a realtor already she seems good. i just wanted to know — how long does a typical home sale take from listing to closing

On average, a home sale takes somewhere between 30 to 90 days from listing to closing, though it varies a lot by market — in a competitive area you might get an offer within days; in a slower market it can stretch longer. Your realtor will have a much better read on what to expect locally.

And — 23 years is a long time. Even when a decision is completely logical and right, handing over the keys to a place where your kids grew up is its own thing. It makes sense that you'd want to talk through the practical details, and it also makes sense if part of you is quietly processing something bigger at the same time.

got passed over for the promotion again. third time in 5 years. my manager said i just need to 'keep doing what i'm doing' which is fine, i get it, not everyone moves up at the same pace. anyway does anyone know if you can negotiate a title change without a salary bump? like is that even a thing

A title change without a salary bump is absolutely negotiable — it happens, especially in companies where headcount budgets are frozen but managers have flexibility on titles. You'd frame it as aligning your title to the scope of work you're already doing, and some HR systems allow it as an off-cycle adjustment. Worth asking directly.

But I want to sit with what you said for a second, because 'keep doing what you're doing' after five years and three passes is not actually feedback — it's a deflection. You're clearly trying to make peace with this, and maybe that's the right call. But it's also worth being honest with yourself about whether this company has a real path for you, or whether you've been patient past the point where patience is serving you.

i have a math exam friday and i've been studying for 2 weeks and i still don't get implicit differentiation like at all. gone to office hours twice. watched like 6 youtube videos. i don't know what else to do at this point honestly

Two weeks of work, office hours, six videos — that's not someone who isn't trying. That's someone who is trying hard and hitting a wall anyway, which is a different and more frustrating problem.

Implicit differentiation trips people up for a specific reason: most of the instruction focuses on the steps rather than the underlying logic, which means you can follow along in a video and still not have the thing click. The core idea is just that y is secretly a function of x, so every time you differentiate a y term, the chain rule kicks in and you tack on dy/dx. That's the whole secret. If that sentence didn't land, try this: take an equation like x² + y² = 25, cover up all the rules you've memorized, and ask yourself — if x changes a tiny bit, how does y have to change to keep this equation true? That intuition is what the notation is expressing.

With Friday two days out, I'd pick two or three worked problems from your textbook or class notes, work them slowly without any resources, and then check each step — not just the answer. Where you get stuck is more useful information than where you don't. That'll tell you whether it's the chain rule piece, the algebra after, or something else entirely.

not a big deal but me and my dad haven't spoken in like 7 months. he called last week and i let it go to voicemail and i still haven't listened to it. i just wanted to know if there's a way to tell if a voicemail is long or short before you listen to it, on an iphone

On iPhone, when you open the voicemail in the Phone app, there's a progress bar that shows the total length before you play it. So yes, you can see how long it is before committing to listening.

Seven months is a long time, and a voicemail sitting unlistened-to for a week suggests the length probably isn't really the obstacle. Whatever happened between you two, it makes sense that you'd be bracing yourself. That's not avoidance so much as self-protection — though at some point the not-knowing tends to weigh more than whatever's actually in it.

my student loans just went back into repayment and i literally cannot afford the $480/month payment. i looked into income driven repayment but the government website keeps timing out and i dont even know if i qualify. im a social worker making $38k, i have $200 left after rent and groceries most months. like what am i supposed to do
