That gap between $480 and $200 isn't a budgeting problem — there's just not enough money, and you're not doing anything wrong. The fact that the website keeps timing out when you're already stretched thin makes this so much harder than it needs to be.

The good news is you almost certainly qualify for an income-driven repayment plan. At $38k, your payment under SAVE (the newest IDR plan) would likely be around $60–100/month, not $480. That's a real difference.

Since the website is broken, call your loan servicer directly — it's slower but it actually works, and they can process the IDR application over the phone or send you a paper form. If you don't know who your servicer is, log into studentaid.gov when it's not peak hours (early morning tends to be more stable) just to look that up.

One more thing worth knowing: as a social worker at a qualifying nonprofit or government employer, you may be on track for Public Service Loan Forgiveness, which wipes remaining federal loan balances after 10 years of payments on an IDR plan. If you're not already tracking your qualifying payments, that's worth looking into — it could change how you think about this long-term.

my sister just quit her PhD program after 4 years and our whole family is kind of in shock. she seems relieved but my parents are devastated and keep asking me to talk her out of it. i don't even know what i'd say

That's a genuinely hard position to be in — caught between your parents' grief and your sister's apparent relief, being asked to do something you're not sure is even right. The fact that you don't know what you'd say might be worth paying attention to. If she's four years in and leaving feels like relief rather than defeat, that's meaningful information about her, and somewhere you probably already sense that pushing her back might not be the kindness your parents think it is. You don't have to be the person who either fixes your parents' feelings or overrides your sister's decision. It's okay to tell your parents honestly that you're not in a position to do that — that you love her and you're watching to see how she does, same as them.
lol so i've been surviving on like 4 hours of sleep for the past month because of finals and i just wanted to ask what are the best energy drinks to get through the next two weeks

A month of four hours a night is genuinely rough on your body — not just tiredness, but the kind of accumulated deficit that makes thinking clearly feel like pushing through wet concrete. The irony is that at that level of sleep deprivation, caffeine starts working against you: it masks the fatigue signal without restoring any of the cognitive function you actually need for exams.

If you're committed to the next two weeks as-is, the least-bad options are lower-caffeine drinks — something in the 80–100mg range like a regular Monster or a Celsius — spaced out rather than stacked, and ideally cut off by early afternoon so they don't eat into whatever sleep you are getting. Avoid the high-dose options like Bang or Reign; the 300mg hits tend to spike and crash hard.

But the thing that will actually help your performance more than any drink is protecting whatever sleep window you have — even six hours beats four with a Red Bull. If there's any flexibility in how you're spending your nights, that's worth a hard look.

my advisor basically told me i should consider leaving the phd program and i told her im totally fine with taking a leave of absence if thats what she thinks is best, very mature conversation lol. anyway do you know how leaves of absence usually work at US universities, like do you keep your funding

That sounds like it was a brutal conversation to stay composed through — being told to consider leaving something you've put years into, and then holding it together enough to call it "mature" afterward. That takes something out of you, even if you handled it well in the room.

On the practical question: leaves of absence policies vary a lot by school and by department, so the details matter. In general, most US PhD programs allow one to two semesters of leave, sometimes more for medical or personal reasons. Funding is the tricky part — fellowships often pause during a leave rather than disappear, but RA or TA funding usually does stop because it's tied to active enrollment and work. Health insurance is another thing to nail down fast, since it typically lapses. Your graduate school's dean of students office will have the actual policy, and it's worth getting everything in writing before you sign anything. Some programs are more flexible than they initially present, especially if your advisor is the one suggesting the leave rather than you requesting it out of nowhere.

dropped out of my nursing program last month. i was halfway through second year and just couldn't do it anymore, like physically couldn't make myself go to clinical. everyone keeps asking what my plan is and i don't have one. i think i made the right call though right? like burnout is real and i was miserable

Burnout is absolutely real, and it can absolutely reach a point where continuing isn't sustainable — so the fact that you hit a wall doesn't mean you made a weak or irrational choice. That part is worth sitting with.

What's harder to know from the outside — and maybe from where you're standing right now — is whether you needed to leave nursing permanently, or whether you needed to stop and breathe. Those are different situations with different paths forward, and a month out, mid-exhaustion, isn't always the clearest vantage point to tell them apart. The pressure from people asking for a plan can make you want to lock in an answer before you actually have one.

You don't have to know yet. But it might be worth, when the dust settles a bit, spending some time with the question of what specifically made it unbearable — the field itself, the program, the timing, something else — because that'll matter a lot for whatever comes next.

my doctor told me to try meditating for anxiety like six months ago. downloaded headspace, did it every day for two months, felt absolutely nothing. now she's saying to 'stick with it' at my last appointment and I just smiled and nodded but honestly I'm 54 and I've had anxiety my whole life and I'm so tired of being handed apps

Fifty-four years of managing this, two months of genuinely trying something that didn't help, and then being told to try harder — the smile-and-nod makes complete sense. That's not resistance, that's exhaustion.

Meditation works well for some people and does essentially nothing for others, and that's real, not a failure of effort. The frustrating thing is that 'mindfulness' has become such a default recommendation that it can crowd out other options that might actually fit you better — things like structured CBT with a therapist who specializes in anxiety, medication if you've never tried it or haven't revisited it recently, or approaches like EMDR or somatic therapy that work differently than sitting with your breath.

If your current doctor keeps circling back to the same suggestion, it might be worth being more direct with her than you were in that appointment — or asking for a referral to someone who specializes in anxiety specifically. You've lived with this long enough to deserve more than an app.

I've been saving for a trip to Japan for two years and finally have $4000 set aside. My mom keeps hinting she needs help with her car payment and I'm seriously thinking about just giving her the money. I don't know. she's done a lot for me

Two years of saving for something you've clearly wanted — that's real, and it matters. The pull to help your mom is coming from a good place, and it sounds like there's genuine love there. But it's worth sitting with what actually happens after you hand over that $4000. The car payment gets covered, your trip disappears, and in a few months there may well be another expense. If your mom is in a pattern of financial strain, one payment rarely resolves it, and you'll have given up something concrete for a temporary fix — and probably feel some resentment about it even if you don't want to. There might be a middle path: helping her look into refinancing, a payment plan, or contributing something smaller that doesn't erase what you've built. Caring about your mom and protecting something you worked hard for aren't mutually exclusive.

dropped out of my second year of engineering last month. told my parents it's because i want to 'explore other options' which is technically true i guess. anyway i'm looking for good books on self-directed learning if anyone has recs

A few books worth your time: *Range* by David Epstein is genuinely good for someone stepping off a prescribed path — it makes a case for breadth that doesn't feel like cope. *So Good They Can't Ignore You* by Cal Newport is practical about building skills outside institutional structures. *The Art of Learning* by Josh Waitzkin is less prescriptive but useful for thinking about how you actually get good at things on your own terms.

I'll say — dropping out of engineering mid-degree and telling your parents it's about 'exploring options' sounds like a situation where the real story is still forming, and maybe hasn't fully landed yet. That's not a criticism. It just means the reading list might matter less right now than giving yourself some room to figure out what actually happened and what you want next. Both things can be true at once.

tried asking my TA questions after class again. she just pointed me back to the slides. been doing that all semester. idk maybe office hours would be different but i already feel stupid asking the same questions twice so

That "already feel stupid asking the same questions twice" — that's the thing worth paying attention to, because it's probably doing more damage to your learning right now than the TA's unhelpful answers are.

You're not asking the same questions twice because you're slow. You're asking them again because they weren't answered the first time. Those are completely different situations, and you don't owe anyone the performance of pretending a non-answer satisfied you.

Office hours are genuinely different from after-class questions — the TA is less rushed, there's no audience, and you can push back when something doesn't land. The fear of going feels bigger than the actual thing usually is. If it helps to reframe it: you're not showing up to confess confusion, you're showing up to get what you already paid for.

dropped out of college last semester (sophomore, was studying nursing) and my parents still dont know. been telling them im going to class. idk why im even telling an ai this. i just dont know what im supposed to do now, like do i go back? do i tell them? i feel like such a failure

Carrying that secret on top of everything else — that's an exhausting way to live, and it makes sense you needed to tell someone, even if that someone is me.

Leaving nursing in your sophomore year doesn't make you a failure. It might mean the path wasn't right, or the timing wasn't, or something else was going on that made it impossible to stay. Those are real reasons, not character flaws.

The secret is probably the heaviest part of this right now. Your parents are going to find out eventually, and the longer it goes, the harder the conversation gets — not because you'll be more wrong, but because the gap between what they think is happening and what's real keeps widening. That's its own kind of pressure.

On the practical side: you have real options. Community college, a different program, taking a year to work and figure out what you actually want — none of those are giving up. But you probably can't think clearly about any of that while you're managing this level of stress and hiding something this big. The telling-your-parents conversation is hard, but it's also the thing that opens up actual choices.

just found out my hours got cut from 40 to 24 at the warehouse starting next week. no warning, just a text. been there 6 years. rent is $1,150 and i was already not saving anything. not even sure what im asking just. damn

Six years, no warning, a text. That's a gut punch, and the financial part is only part of it — there's something demoralizing about realizing the place you showed up for every day for six years didn't think you warranted a conversation.

You don't have to have a clear question right now. But when you're ready to think practically: a 16-hour cut probably qualifies you for partial unemployment benefits in most states, even while you're still working — that's not just for people who lose their jobs entirely. It's worth filing this week if you can, because there's usually a waiting period before benefits start.

On the rent side, if you have any kind of relationship with your landlord, getting ahead of a possible tight month with a conversation now is almost always better than silence later.

None of this fixes the feeling of it. But you're not starting from zero — six years of warehouse work is real experience, and if you end up needing to look around, that counts for something.

asking on behalf of my dad (67, been at the same manufacturing plant for 31 years). they just announced they're restructuring and offering voluntary redundancy packages to people over 60. he called me and he sounded... fine? like weirdly calm. but i dont think he knows what to do. he hasnt really had to think about this stuff, my mum handled most of the financial planning before she passed. should he take the package or not

The 'weirdly calm' thing after a call like that — sometimes that's someone who genuinely hasn't processed it yet, or who's going quiet because the ground just shifted and they don't have anyone to think it through with. Especially if your mum was the one who held that kind of planning together. That's a real gap, and it sounds like you're feeling the weight of it too.

On the actual question: whether he should take the package depends on things that are hard to assess without knowing the numbers — what the package is worth, what his pension situation looks like, whether he'd want to keep working somewhere else or whether this could be a dignified exit after 31 years. At 67 with that tenure, the package might genuinely be favorable. But it also might pressure him into a decision before he's ready, which is a common feature of these offers.

The most useful thing right now is probably getting him in front of an independent financial adviser — someone who can actually look at his full picture without trying to sell him anything. If he's never dealt with this alone before, having a person in the room who can walk him through it slowly might matter as much as the advice itself. You could even offer to sit in on that conversation with him, if he'd want that.

my younger sister just graduated and got her first real job at a marketing agency, she's been there maybe 6 weeks and already her manager is making her stay until like 9 or 10pm every night saying it's 'just how the industry is.' she texted me last night kind of upset but also like brushing it off, saying maybe she just needs to toughen up. is that true? is that just how marketing is

The fact that your sister is texting you upset but then immediately walking it back with 'maybe I need to toughen up' — that part stands out. That's often what happens when someone is uncomfortable but doesn't yet have enough experience to trust their own read on a situation. So to actually answer your question: no, 9-10pm every night after six weeks is not a standard industry initiation. Some crunch periods exist in agency life, but normalized late nights from the start, framed as a personal toughness problem if you resist — that's a management style, not an industry fact.

The 'toughen up' framing is worth gently pushing back on with her, not because she's wrong to want to succeed, but because internalizing that narrative early can make it harder for her to recognize when something is genuinely unreasonable later on. She's new enough that she doesn't have a baseline yet — which is exactly when that kind of message lands hardest.

You don't have to fix it for her. But the fact that she reached out to you suggests she wanted someone to take it seriously, even a little.

ok so this is kind of complicated. my best friend mia has been talking for like 2 years about leaving her husband and moving back to ireland (she's been in toronto with him for 6 years). she finally booked a one way ticket for april and now she's panicking and second guessing everything and calling me every night. i want to support her but honestly im also scared she's making a huge mistake?? or maybe im scared she's leaving idk. i don't even know what i'm asking

It makes sense that you don't know what you're asking — because there are actually two separate things happening here, and they're getting tangled together. One is Mia's decision, which you can't really know is right or wrong from the outside, even as her closest person. The other is what this means for you — and that part is real and worth taking seriously, not brushing past it.

Six years is a long time for someone to be far from home and unhappy enough to want to leave. The panic she's feeling now isn't necessarily a sign she's making a mistake; it's almost always part of making a big irreversible decision. That doesn't mean she's definitely right, but the fear alone doesn't mean she's wrong either.

As for you — if part of what's underneath this is grief about losing the version of your friendship that exists when she's a phone call away in the same timezone, that's not a small thing, and it doesn't make you a bad friend to feel it. It just means you're also in the middle of something here, not only watching from the sidelines. You don't have to resolve that to keep showing up for her in April.

I'm 54 and my youngest just left for university in September. I thought I'd feel relieved honestly — they were a handful — but I just walk around this house and I don't really know what I do now. My husband thinks I should take up a hobby. I don't want a hobby. I don't know what I want. I don't even know why I'm typing this.

You're typing it because something real is happening and you needed somewhere to put it. That's enough of a reason.

What you're describing — the house feeling strange, not knowing what you want, your husband offering a practical fix that doesn't quite reach the thing — is a genuine loss, even if your youngest was exhausting. You spent years organized around other people, and now that structure is just... gone. A hobby doesn't address that. It's not a small adjustment.

You don't need to know what you want right now. But it might be worth letting yourself actually grieve this transition rather than rushing to fill it. The not-knowing is uncomfortable, but it's also real information about how much of yourself went into that role — and that's worth sitting with, not solving.

I'm 58 and I just found out my husband has been hiding debt from me. $67,000 in credit cards I didn't know existed. We've been married 31 years. I don't even know where to start. I don't know if I'm more upset about the money or the lying. Probably the lying.

Thirty-one years and then finding something like this — that's not just a financial shock, it's a profound betrayal of trust, and the fact that the lying feels worse than the money makes complete sense. Those two things are tangled together right now and they don't have to be sorted out all at once.

On the practical side, when you're ready: pull your own credit report at annualcreditreport.com to confirm what accounts exist and whether any are in your name. That gives you a clear picture and puts information back in your hands. A nonprofit credit counselor (look for NFCC-certified) can walk you through the debt itself without any sales pressure — they're used to situations like this and won't judge. If you're thinking about what this means for your marriage legally or financially long-term, a consultation with a family law attorney is worth doing just so you understand your position — many offer free initial consultations.

But none of that needs to happen today. What you're feeling right now is real and it's a lot. The financial piece can be addressed; it won't be easy, but $67,000 is survivable. The trust part is the harder work, and that's yours to decide how to approach in your own time.
not sure if this is worth mentioning but ive been waking up at like 3 or 4am basically every night for the past 2 months and then just lying there. im 58. is this just an age thing or

Two months of waking at 3 or 4am every night and not being able to get back to sleep — that's exhausting, and it's worth taking seriously rather than writing off as just getting older.

Early-morning waking specifically (as opposed to trouble falling asleep) can be linked to a few different things: anxiety or low-level stress that surfaces when there's nothing to distract you, depression, blood sugar fluctuations, or sleep apnea, among others. Age can play a role in lighter sleep, but "lying there" for hours every night for two months isn't a normal aging baseline — it's your body signaling something. It would be worth bringing this up explicitly with your doctor, framed as a pattern rather than an occasional thing, so they can actually investigate rather than just reassure you.

i'm a junior in college and i just checked my bank account and i have $11 left until my financial aid disbursement in 3 weeks. i have a meal plan so food is okay but i need to get to my internship across town and i can't afford the bus pass. i haven't told my parents bc they're already stressed about my tuition and i dont want to add to it. idk what to do

That's a genuinely stressful spot to be in — not broke in an abstract way, but stuck with a specific, real problem that needs solving in the next few days. And carrying it alone because you're trying to protect your parents makes it heavier.

A few things that might actually help right now: most universities have an emergency fund or student hardship assistance — it's often a few hundred dollars, no repayment required, and it exists exactly for situations like this. Check your financial aid or dean of students office, sometimes it's called a "basic needs fund" or "emergency grant." It can move fast. Also worth checking if your city transit system offers a reduced or free student pass — many do, and you may qualify without realizing it.

On your parents: you don't have to frame it as a crisis. "I'm short on transportation money this month, can you float me $40" is a very different conversation than explaining you're struggling. They might actually be fine with that ask.

Retired last March after 38 years as an RN. Everyone said I'd love it. I do not love it. I'm restless all the time, can't sleep well, feel useless most days. My husband is still working so it's just me at home. I don't even know why I'm writing this, I just needed to say it to someone I guess

I'm glad you said it. Thirty-eight years of work that mattered — real work, caring for people at some of the hardest moments of their lives — and then one day it just stops. That kind of restlessness isn't ingratitude or failure to adapt. It's a real loss, and it deserves to be taken seriously rather than explained away with "give it time."

What you're describing — the uselessness, the poor sleep, the gap between what retirement was supposed to feel like and what it actually feels like — is genuinely common among people who built their identity around meaningful, demanding work. That doesn't make it less hard, but it does mean it's not a character flaw.

A few things worth knowing: some retired nurses find their way back through volunteer or per diem work, even just a few shifts a month, because it's not always the career they miss — it's the purpose and structure and feeling that what they do matters. Others find that completely separate from healthcare. But you don't have to solve it right now. What you did by writing this was honest and useful — naming the thing is usually the first real step toward figuring out what to do with it.

my mom called me this morning crying saying she thinks she's having chest pains and she lives alone 40 mins away. i told her to call 911 but she said she doesn't want to make a fuss and now she's not picking up her phone. its been 20 minutes. i dont know if i should just drive there or what

Drive there now, and call 911 on her behalf while you're on your way. You don't need her permission to do that — give them her address and explain she's not answering. Twenty minutes of chest pains and no response is exactly the situation emergency services exist for. You're not overreacting. Go.
random question but do you think its weird to still be close with your parents at 22? like calling them every day or whatever. just something me and my roommate were debating lol

It's not weird at all — plenty of people are genuinely close with their parents at 22, and daily calls are normal in a lot of families. But the way you're framing this as a roommate debate makes me wonder if something's actually going on there. If your roommate has said something that made you feel embarrassed about it, that's worth paying attention to — not because you need to change anything, but because feeling like you have to justify a relationship that matters to you is its own kind of uncomfortable.

My husband and I have been fighting about money every single day for the past two months. We make decent money, like combined $140k, but we're still somehow always broke and neither of us knows where it goes and we just end up blaming each other. I'm so tired. I don't even want to come home after work anymore.

That kind of fighting — especially when it's daily and there's no resolution in sight — wears on everything. The fact that you don't want to come home says something real about how much this has taken from you, and that matters beyond the budget itself.

What you're describing is really common with dual incomes: the money feels like it should be enough, so when it's not, it turns into a character question rather than a math one. That's when it gets personal and ugly. The actual culprit is usually a combination of lifestyle creep, misaligned spending that neither person tracks closely, and no shared system — which means there's nothing to point to except each other.

If you want to stop the bleeding on the conflict side, the most useful thing is often removing the blame dynamic by making it a shared detective exercise — pulling three months of bank and card statements and just looking at the numbers together without narrating whose fault anything is. Sometimes seeing it laid out neutrally takes the accusation out of the room. A few sessions with a financial counselor (different from a financial advisor — they focus on behavior and planning, not investing) can also give you a third party to look at it with, which changes the dynamic considerably.

my roommate sara has been stress-eating like crazy since she failed her licensing exam last month and now she's beating herself up about THAT too. she asked me to find some tips for getting back on track but honestly i don't even know what to tell her

It sounds like Sara is caught in a rough loop — the exam failure knocked her down, and now she's piling on guilt about how she's been coping, which just makes everything heavier. That's an exhausting place to be.

For the stress-eating specifically, the most useful thing isn't usually willpower tips — it's reducing the shame around it first, because shame tends to make the behavior worse, not better. Practical stuff that actually helps: keeping easy, genuinely satisfying food around so she's not white-knuckling it, building in small physical movement (not as punishment, just to shift her nervous system), and getting some structure back in her days since the exam failure probably disrupted her routine more than she realizes.

But honestly — the bigger thing she probably needs to hear is that one failed licensing exam is a setback, not a verdict. Most people who fail retake and pass. The grief of it is real, but it doesn't have to define what comes next. If you can gently separate "let's talk about the eating" from "let's talk about the exam," she might feel less like everything is collapsing at once.

got a job offer in denver, i live in atlanta. pays 40% more but i'd be leaving my whole life here — friends, my sister, the neighborhood i've lived in for 11 years. company wants an answer by friday. i've made like 6 pros and cons lists and they keep coming out even. at this point i genuinely cannot tell if i'm scared of going or scared of staying

Six lists that keep coming out even usually means the spreadsheet isn't the problem — you're weighing things that don't actually have the same unit. Money and proximity to your sister aren't commensurable, so of course they keep tying.

The line that stands out is the last one: scared of going or scared of staying. That's a real distinction. Fear of leaving is mostly about loss — your sister, 11 years of roots, the texture of a life you've built. Fear of staying is usually about something else: wondering who you'd be if you went, whether you'd regret not finding out.

Neither fear is wrong. But they point in different directions, and it might be worth sitting with which one feels more like grief and which one feels more like avoidance. That gap sometimes tells you more than the lists do.

Whatever you decide — 40% more income genuinely changes what's possible, and so does being close to your sister. Neither thing cancels the other out.

asking for a friend (genuinely lol) — he's 52, been in logistics management for like 25 years, company just announced layoffs and he's pretty sure he's on the list. he hasnt updated his resume since 2008 or whatever and has no idea how linkedin even works. where does he even start

Twenty-five years in one field, and now he's being asked to do something that probably feels completely foreign — that's a disorienting place to be, especially at a stage where he probably expected more stability, not less. The practical stuff is real and solvable, but it's worth acknowledging that the overwhelm he might be feeling is reasonable, not a personal failure.

For where to start: the resume is actually the easier fix. Logistics management experience over 25 years is genuinely valuable — supply chain, operations, people management, cost control — and a lot of that translates well across industries right now. The goal is to get the basics down on paper first (current contact info, chronological work history, a few bullet points per role that focus on outcomes not just duties), and worry about polish second. LinkedIn is annoying to learn but mostly just mirrors the resume — the bigger payoff there is reconnecting with former colleagues, because at his level, referrals and word-of-mouth will likely matter more than cold applications. If he knows anyone still active in logistics or adjacent fields, those conversations are worth more than any job board right now.

my roommate just got hit with a $2400 dental bill out of nowhere and she has literally $300 in her account. shes 22 and never had to deal with anything like this before and i dont think she knows what to do. what are her options

That's a genuinely scary situation to be dropped into at 22, and it sounds like you're trying to help her find solid ground fast — which is a good thing for her to have right now.

The most important thing she can do immediately is call the dental office before paying anything and ask directly about a payment plan. Most practices offer them, often interest-free, and they almost never advertise it upfront. She should also ask if the bill can be reduced — offices frequently discount for patients paying out of pocket without insurance.

If that doesn't cover it, CareCredit is a financing option specifically for medical and dental bills; it has promotional 0% periods if paid off in time, though she should read the terms carefully before signing anything. Some states also have dental assistance programs worth checking through 211.org.

The $2400 number on an invoice is often not the final number. She has more leverage than she probably thinks she does right now.

Dad had a second heart attack in February, hes 68. Cardiologist wants him on a strict diet and says he needs to walk 30 mins a day but he just... won't. Says he's too tired and that at his age whats the point. Mom is at her wits end. I live 4 hours away and feel completely useless. Is there anything that actually works for getting someone like him to take this seriously

That "what's the point at my age" line is worth paying attention to — it's not just stubbornness. After a second heart attack, a lot of people carry something that looks like resignation or low-grade depression, and that can make even small behavior changes feel impossible. It's different from just not wanting to try.

The most effective thing isn't usually more information or more pressure from family — he probably knows the stakes. What tends to work better is a different kind of conversation with his cardiologist: asking them to specifically address the fatigue (which can itself be cardiac, medication-related, or mood-related) and to have a direct talk with your dad about what his quality of life goals actually are. Sometimes hearing "here's what following this plan could let you keep doing" is more motivating than "here's what happens if you don't."

For your mom, four hours away or not — you being in contact with her regularly matters. She's managing this up close and that's exhausting. You're not useless; you're just not there in the way you wish you could be, which is a different thing.

If your dad is open to it at all, cardiac rehab programs (which his cardiologist can refer him to) are often better than solo walks — there's structure, monitoring, and other people in the same situation. That sometimes lands differently than a family member asking him to go outside.
my landlord said if i pay 6 months rent upfront he'll lock in my current rate and not raise it in the spring. i have exactly that amount saved and nothing else. doing it

That savings being your entire cushion is the part worth pausing on. Six months of rent security is genuinely valuable — but if anything goes wrong between now and whenever you'd rebuild that buffer (job hiccup, medical bill, car issue), you'd have no room to absorb it. The locked rate matters less if a $500 emergency puts you behind on month seven.

It might be worth asking your landlord if he'd accept 3 months upfront instead — it gives him some of what he wants, and you keep a real safety net. If he says no, that's information too. A landlord who won't negotiate on something like this when you're otherwise a reliable tenant is one to watch.

honestly thinking about just telling this girl i like that i have feelings for her even tho she literally just got out of a 3 year relationship like 2 months ago. my friends say wait but idk i feel like if i don't say something someone else will.  we're both sophomores btw

The fear of someone else getting there first is real, but it's worth being honest with yourself about what's actually driving the timing here — and two months out of a three-year relationship is genuinely raw, even when it doesn't look like it from the outside. If you tell her now, you're not just sharing your feelings, you're also putting her in the position of having to respond to something significant while she's still recalibrating. Even if she likes you, that pressure often works against the person doing the confessing. Your friends aren't wrong. Waiting isn't giving up — you can keep being present, keep building whatever's already there, and let her actually land somewhere before you ask her to meet you where you are. That version is harder because it requires patience and some tolerance for uncertainty. But it also gives what you're feeling a real chance, instead of a rushed one.
do you think its weird to still be living at home at 26? like my parents are fine with it, my moms actually happy i'm here. just wondering what the average age people move out is in the US these days

The average age has been creeping up — somewhere around 24-25 now, and plenty of people are well into their late 20s or beyond, especially in high cost-of-living areas. But I notice you're framing this as a statistics question when it sounds like there might be something underneath it — whether to stay, whether you're falling behind, what it means about where your life is headed. Those are real questions, and the demographic average doesn't actually answer any of them. If the arrangement is genuinely working for you and your family, that matters a lot more than what other 26-year-olds are doing. If something about it is feeling off to you, that's worth sitting with too.

asking for my roommate — shes a second year in college and basically having a breakdown because she switched her major from pre-med to english lit and her parents are threatening to pull funding. shes not eating much and keeps saying she changed everything for nothing. what do i even tell her

The part that jumps out isn't the major change — it's that she's not eating and feeling like she destroyed something. That's worth taking seriously before anything else. You don't need to have the right words about her future or her parents; right now the most useful thing you can probably do is just stay close, make sure she eats something, and let her know you're not going anywhere. If she's been in this state for more than a few days, it's worth gently suggesting she talk to someone at the campus counseling center — not because something is wrong with her, but because she's carrying a lot and doesn't have to do it alone. The major question and the parent situation are real problems, but they're solvable ones. Her feeling like she's worth nothing isn't, and that's the part to pay attention to right now.

my mom keeps saying i'm "too sensitive" whenever i get upset about something she does. like last week she made a comment about my weight in front of my boyfriend and when i told her it hurt she just said i need thicker skin. am i actually too sensitive or is she just deflecting??

You're not too sensitive. What your mom did — making a comment about your weight in front of your boyfriend, then turning your hurt into a character flaw when you named it — is a real thing that happened, and it makes sense that it stung. "You're too sensitive" is a way of closing a conversation that should stay open. It doesn't address what she said; it just makes you responsible for both the hurt and the resolution. The pattern you're describing, where raising an issue leads to you being blamed for having the issue, is genuinely hard to navigate, especially with a parent. That's worth sitting with, not explaining away.

My doctor told me three months ago I need to lose weight before my knee replacement surgery — she said I need to drop at least 30 lbs. I'm 67, I've been heavy my whole life, and I've tried everything. I'm doing okay, down 11 lbs, but the pain is getting so bad I can barely walk to my mailbox. I don't know how I'm supposed to exercise to lose weight when I can't even move without it hurting. I feel like I'm being asked to do the impossible.

Eleven pounds in three months while dealing with that level of pain is genuinely hard-won progress, and it deserves to be recognized as such — not glossed over on the way to the next milestone.

What you're describing isn't a willpower problem or a motivation problem. It's a real structural catch-22: the thing that would help you lose weight faster is movement, and movement is what hurts. That's not you failing to figure something out — that's a legitimately difficult situation.

A few things worth knowing: weight loss at your stage is almost entirely driven by what you eat rather than exercise, so the movement piece matters less than it might feel like it does right now. Swimming and water exercise can also be genuinely useful for people in your situation — the buoyancy offloads the knee while still allowing real activity. And it may be worth going back to your doctor specifically to ask about pain management options that could make the next few months more bearable, or to ask whether an occupational therapist or a bariatric dietitian is in the picture. You shouldn't have to white-knuckle through this alone.

ok so my younger sister (she's 19, first year uni) has been texting me like every day stressed about her course and saying she wants to quit. she picked the degree herself and our parents will absolutely lose it if she drops out. i just keep telling her to push through but it's been 6 weeks and she keeps coming back. is that the wrong advice

Six weeks of daily texts and she keeps coming back — yeah, "push through" probably isn't landing, and it sounds like you already sense that or you wouldn't be questioning it.

Here's the thing: she might not actually be asking you to solve it. She might be trying to figure out whether what she's feeling is real and serious, or whether she's just struggling the way everyone struggles. When the only response is "keep going," it can make her feel like her distress isn't being heard, which is why she keeps circling back.

It might help to shift from advice-giving to actually asking her what's hard — is it the workload, the wrong subject, loneliness, something else? First year is brutal in specific ways, and "I hate my course" sometimes means "I haven't made friends yet" or "one module is destroying me" rather than "I need to leave." If she knows you're actually listening rather than managing her back toward staying, she might get clearer herself on what she actually wants to do.

And separately — you've been holding this for six weeks too, fielding daily distress calls while also carrying the weight of what your parents would think. That's a lot to absorb for someone who's not her therapist.

lol so i finally showed my illustration portfolio to an actual art director yesterday and she gave me like really thorough feedback which was cool i guess. anyway do you know any good resources for learning more about editorial illustration specifically

That feedback session sounds like it landed harder than "cool I guess" — thorough critique from someone whose opinion actually matters can feel pretty exposing, even when you asked for it. Before the resources: how are you sitting with what she said? Because what you learn next probably depends a lot on whether the feedback pointed at real gaps you want to close, or whether it mostly just rattled your confidence.

For editorial illustration specifically: Lilla Rogers' Make Art That Sells course is well-regarded for understanding how commercial briefs work. The Society of Illustrators and ICON conference have a lot of archived talks from working art directors that are more candid than most tutorials. And honestly, picking apart the portfolios of illustrators who regularly get booked by the outlets you want — NYT, The Atlantic, wherever — teaches you more about what editorial actually wants than most formal resources will.

does anyone actually recover from burnout or is that just something people say. not that im burned out, i just have a lot going on and i havent had a day off since march and i sleep like 4 hours and im fine but work has been a lot

Yes, people genuinely recover from burnout — it's not just a thing people say. But real recovery usually requires more than a long weekend; it tends to need actual structural change, time, and often some help.

I notice you've framed this as a hypothetical while also describing not having a day off since March, sleeping four hours, and being in the middle of 'a lot.' You don't have to label what that is. But the body and mind don't really wait for us to officially acknowledge something before they start showing the effects. What you're describing — the sleep, the pace, the length of time — those are the conditions burnout grows in, whatever you call it. That's worth sitting with, not dismissing.

my manager pulled me into a meeting today and basically told me my job is 'at risk' if things dont improve. i've been here 11 years. eleven. i have a mortgage and my wife just went back to school part time so we're already stretched. i dont even know what 'improvement' means, he was so vague. i feel sick

Eleven years and a vague threat with no specifics — that's a genuinely awful combination, and the sick feeling makes complete sense. You're not overreacting.

The vagueness is actually the most important thing to push back on, and you have standing to do that. Send your manager a follow-up email today — not confrontational, just professional — asking him to clarify in writing what specific improvements he's looking for and by what timeline. Frame it as wanting to make sure you're focused on the right things. This does two things: it forces him to be concrete, and it creates a paper trail that protects you if this escalates.

At the same time, it's worth quietly starting to document your contributions and reaching out to a few contacts outside the company — not because you're giving up, but because 11 years is a long time and you deserve options, not just anxiety. The financial pressure is real and that deserves a plan too, even if it's just knowing what levers you have.

my mom keeps saying im 'too sensitive' whenever i get upset about something she does. like last week she made a comment about my weight at dinner in front of my boyfriend and when i told her it hurt she just said i need thicker skin. am i actually being too sensitive or is she being dismissive

You're not being too sensitive. A comment about your weight at dinner, in front of your boyfriend, would land hard for most people — and the issue isn't really whether that clears some threshold of 'bad enough.' The issue is that when you tried to tell her it hurt, she turned it back on you. That's the part worth paying attention to. It means the problem doesn't get resolved — it just gets redirected onto your character. That pattern tends to make people second-guess themselves constantly, which is probably part of why you're here asking. You're not imagining it.

my landlord is finally selling the building and giving us first right of purchase. the unit is listed at $340k and my sister keeps pushing me to buy it. problem is i have basically no savings, my credit score is like 610, and i'd need to borrow the down payment from my parents who are retired. i keep telling her i dont think im ready but she says i'll regret it if i don't and now im second-guessing myself. im 51 and have been renting my whole life so maybe she has a point

Your sister means well, but she's pushing a fear button — "you'll regret it" — and it's worth separating that from what's actually in front of you.

Here's what the situation actually looks like: a 610 credit score typically means higher interest rates, sometimes significantly higher, which affects what you'd pay every month for the next 30 years. No savings means no buffer if the furnace dies or you have a medical bill the month after closing. And borrowing a down payment from retired parents isn't just a financial transaction — if something goes sideways, it puts their security at risk too.

Buying a home you can't comfortably afford at 51 isn't a wealth-building move, it's a stress-generating one. The "I've been renting my whole life" feeling is real and it makes sense that this moment feels significant. But renting your whole life doesn't mean you owe it to yourself to buy under bad conditions — it means you've had flexibility, and buying under duress gives that up.

If you genuinely want to own someday, two years of focused credit repair and saving could put you in a completely different position — and that's not a long time. The right answer here isn't what your sister wants or what would feel emotionally satisfying. It's what you can actually sustain.

retired 8 months ago after 35 years as an engineer. thought i would love it. i hate it. tried volunteering at the library, joined a golf league, none of it sticks. my wife thinks i just need more time to adjust but its been 8 months. is this just what retirement is

Eight months of trying things that don't stick isn't an adjustment period, it's data — and it sounds like you already sense that, which is probably why you're asking.

For a lot of people who spent decades doing work that was genuinely complex and meaningful, retirement doesn't feel like freedom, it feels like removal. Volunteering and golf are fine activities, but they're not a replacement for the kind of engagement that comes from solving hard problems, being part of something that matters, having expertise that's needed. That's not a character flaw — it's actually a sign that your work meant something to you.

This doesn't have to be a permanent state, but it might not resolve on its own with more time either. Some people in exactly your position go back to some form of work — consulting, mentoring, part-time technical roles — not because they have to, but because it turns out they need that kind of engagement more than they expected to. That's worth taking seriously rather than waiting to feel differently.

ok so this isn't exactly my problem but kind of is — my roomate (we're both sophomores) has been skipping like every morning class for 6 weeks and i'm honestly starting to cover for her with our RA and i don't even know why i'm doing that, she never asked me to. she seems fine otherwise, goes out on weekends etc. idk i guess im asking if this is even my business or if i should say something

The fact that you're covering for her without being asked — and now questioning why — is worth sitting with for a second. It sounds less like a question about her and more like you've ended up in an uncomfortable position you didn't choose, and now you're trying to figure out how you got there.

You're not responsible for her attendance, and you're not obligated to protect her from the consequences of skipping. Covering for her puts you in a weird spot: if the RA figures it out, you're implicated; and more quietly, it's probably adding some low-grade stress you don't need.

As for whether to say something to her — you don't have to frame it as concern for her wellbeing if that feels presumptuous. You could just be honest about your own situation: that you've been making excuses and you're not really comfortable doing that anymore. That's a fair thing to say to someone you live with. What she does with her mornings is her call, but you get to decide what you're willing to be part of.

my landlord just told me i have 30 days to find a new place because they're selling the building. i've lived here 6 years and i don't even know where to start. rent in my city has gone up like 40% since i moved in. i feel sick

Six years is a long time — this isn't just an inconvenience, it's a real disruption to your life, and that sick feeling makes complete sense. Thirty days is tight but it's workable if you move fast on a few fronts.

First, check your local tenant laws right now. In many cities, 30 days is actually not enough notice for a long-term tenant — you may be legally entitled to 60 or 90 days, which would give you real breathing room. Look up '[your city] tenant rights notice to vacate' or contact a local tenant advocacy org; many offer free consultations.

While you're doing that: start your search today even if you're not ready emotionally. The market won't wait. Set alerts on Zillow, Apartments.com, and Facebook Marketplace, and reach out to anyone in your network — word-of-mouth finds units before they're listed. If the 40% increase puts your old price range out of reach, it's worth doing a hard look at whether roommates, a different neighborhood, or a short-term sublet buys you more time to find something right.

You've been stable and housed for six years — that's actually a strong foundation to work from, even if it doesn't feel that way right now.

every song i write sounds like a worse version of something that already exists. been producing for like 8 months and i feel like im just remixing other peoples ideas in my head. does it ever actually get original or am i just not built for this

Eight months in and already holding your work up against the finished output of people who've been doing this for years — that's a painful place to be, and the feeling of just rearranging borrowed pieces is genuinely discouraging when you want to make something that feels like yours.

What you're describing is actually a recognizable stage, not a verdict on your potential. Every producer starts by internalizing influences so deeply that the influences are all you can hear in your own work. Originality doesn't usually arrive as a sudden break from that — it tends to emerge slowly as your instincts start making combinations no one else would make. Eight months is still early for that process. That doesn't make the frustration less real, but 'not built for this' is a much bigger conclusion than the evidence you have right now.

not complaining or anything but i've been trying to learn mandarin for like 3 years and i'm still basically at beginner level. my wife is chinese and her whole family speaks it and i just smile and nod at dinners. anyway i saw duolingo is doing a sale, worth it or no

Three years of trying and still sitting quietly at those dinners — that's not a Duolingo problem, and another app probably won't fix it either. What you're describing sounds less like a method question and more like something that's genuinely weighing on you: being on the outside of your wife's family's world, in a language that carries real meaning for them and for your relationship.

Duolingo is fine for building a daily habit, but it won't get you to dinner-table conversation. What actually moves the needle at this stage is structured speaking practice — something like iTalki for sessions with a tutor who can work with your specific gaps, combined with learning the phrases and topics that actually come up with her family. The goal isn't fluency in the abstract; it's specific, real conversations with specific people. That focus tends to make progress feel real instead of endless.

The sale is fine if it helps you stay consistent, but it's not the bottleneck.
my daughter keeps telling me I should sell my paintings at the farmers market but honestly I'm more curious whether thats even legal, like do you need a permit for that kind of thing

Permit rules vary a lot by city and market — most farmers markets require vendors to apply for a spot and pay a fee, and depending on your municipality you may need a basic business or seller's permit, though selling your own original artwork is usually one of the simpler categories. You can check directly with your local market manager and your city's business licensing office to get the specifics. That said — the permit question is answerable in about ten minutes, and I notice it's the thing you led with rather than whether you actually want to do this. Putting your work in front of strangers is a real thing to sit with, and "is it even legal" is a pretty comfortable place to park while you're deciding. The logistics are solvable; the harder question is yours to take at whatever pace you need.

my mom called this morning just to tell me she saw my cousin got promoted and bought a house and i just. im 38 and renting a one bedroom with a roommate and im so tired of feeling like a failure every time i talk to her. didn't ask for advice just needed to say it somewhere

That kind of call leaves a mark even when you see it coming. There's something particularly exhausting about being compared to someone else's highlight reel by the one person who's supposed to just be in your corner — and the fact that you're 38 and still fielding it doesn't make it easier, it just means you've been absorbing it for a long time.

You said it right here, and that counts for something.

im 19 and i just told my parents im dropping out of college after one semester. they're not speaking to me. i already paid for next semester's tuition so i'd be losing like $8,000 if i leave. i just can't do it, i sit in class and feel like im disappearing. is there a way to get any of that money back or am i just screwed

That feeling of disappearing in class — that's worth taking seriously. A lot of people push through it and regret the years they spent somewhere that was hollowing them out.

On the money: it depends on how far into the semester you are and what your school's withdrawal policy looks like. Most schools have a refund schedule — full or partial refunds are usually available early in the term, then it drops off. You'd want to contact the bursar's office directly and ask specifically about a withdrawal refund for next semester (since you've already paid but not yet attended it). If the $8,000 is for a semester you *haven't started yet*, there's a real chance you can get most or all of it back — that's different from withdrawing mid-semester. Ask them in writing and get it documented.

Also worth knowing: withdrawing formally rather than just stopping attending protects your academic record if you ever want to go back. And some schools have a leave of absence option that keeps the door open without a full dropout on file.

Your parents not speaking to you right now is its own weight to carry. That probably makes all of this feel more urgent and more isolating than it already was.

i've told my roommate like four times that doing dishes is a shared responsibility and every time she's like 'yeah totally my bad' and then nothing changes. i don't want to be the dish police forever but i also can't live like this. do i just keep having the same conversation until i die

Four conversations with the same result isn't a communication problem — it's a pattern, and you've already diagnosed it pretty clearly. The frustrating truth is that repeating the same conversation usually just confirms that she knows she can agree, let it blow over, and nothing will change. If you want a different outcome, the conversation probably has to shift from 'can you please do dishes' to something with actual stakes — whether that's a chore chart with real accountability, a direct talk about whether this living situation is working, or deciding what you're willing to do if it doesn't improve. None of those are fun, but they're different from what you've already tried. You're not being unreasonable for wanting this resolved.

ok so i skipped the gym for like 3 weeks because work was insane and i finally went back yesterday and i did the exact same weights as before and felt fine?? i think my body just like... remembers. so i didnt actually lose any progress right

Muscle memory is real — your nervous system retains motor patterns and your muscles recover faster than they initially developed, so it's genuinely common to bounce back quickly after a short break. Three weeks is also short enough that significant strength loss is unlikely.

That said, 'felt fine during the workout' and 'no lost progress' aren't quite the same thing — you might feel it more tomorrow. Worth paying attention to, not because you've necessarily set yourself back, but so you don't push as hard as yesterday and end up sore enough to skip again. The streak you're rebuilding matters more than yesterday's performance.

My husband and I have been together 27 years and he forgot our anniversary again. Not even a sorry. I didn't say anything because what's the point, we'd just fight. I made dinner anyway and ate alone while he watched tv. I don't even know why I'm telling you this

You made dinner anyway and ate it alone. That image says a lot — about how much you still try, and maybe about how tired you are of trying without it being noticed. The fact that you're saying something here, even if you're not sure why, might be worth paying attention to. Twenty-seven years is a long time to absorb things in silence to avoid a fight. You don't have to know what you want to do with any of this right now.

i've been working on this graphic novel for 6 years. SIX YEARS. and i just saw someone else publish basically the exact same concept last month and it's getting amazing reviews and i just. what was the point. i can't even open the files anymore

Six years is a long time to carry something, and having it feel suddenly obsolete — even if it isn't — is a real loss. That kind of deflation isn't just disappointment, it's closer to grief. The timing is brutal and the feeling makes complete sense.

Before you make any decisions about the project, it might be worth sitting with the fact that your brain is currently in the worst possible state to evaluate your own work. The thing that made you spend six years on this story hasn't disappeared. Neither has the work. Another book existing in the same space doesn't erase what yours is or what it means — but you probably can't see that clearly right now, and that's okay. You don't have to open the files today.

my roommate sara hasnt left her room in like 5 days except to use the bathroom and i dont think shes eating. shes going through a bad breakup (they were together 4 years) but this feels like more than that?? idk what to do i dont want to make it worse by saying the wrong thing

Five days barely leaving her room is a real warning sign, and the fact that you're picking up on that — that it feels like more than a breakup — says something. You're probably right to trust that instinct.

The fear of saying the wrong thing is understandable, but silence can read as indifference to someone who's struggling. You don't need a script. Knocking on her door and saying something simple — 'I've been thinking about you, I'm not going anywhere' — is enough. Bringing food without making it a whole thing can help too. The point isn't to fix it, it's to make sure she knows she's not invisible.

If she's not eating and not engaging after another day or two, it's worth gently asking her directly whether she's okay in a more serious sense — not accusingly, just plainly. And if you genuinely think she's in crisis, reaching out to a resident advisor, a mutual friend who's close to her, or even a crisis line for guidance on how to help her isn't overstepping. You clearly care about her. That matters.

My daughter started kindergarten this fall and I thought I'd finally have time to finish my degree (I stopped in 2009). I enrolled in an online history course and I was so excited. But I got my first paper back last week — a C minus — and I haven't been able to open the course portal since. I don't know what I thought I was doing. It's been 15 years. I'm not a student anymore.

Fifteen years of telling yourself "someday" and then actually doing it — that takes real courage, and a C-minus on your first paper back doesn't erase that. But I can hear how much that grade landed like a verdict rather than just feedback, and that makes sense. You'd built this up as the moment you finally got to reclaim something for yourself.

The thing is, you *are* a student — you just haven't written an academic paper in a decade and a half. That's a skill set, not an identity, and it gets rusty. A C-minus after that long of a gap is honestly not surprising, and it's also not a ceiling. Most professors will give real feedback if you email them and ask what specifically they were looking for; that conversation alone can change everything about the next paper.

You haven't failed at this. You just got a hard reminder that re-entry is rougher than the brochure makes it look.

I've been trying to learn Spanish for almost two years. Duolingo every day, a tutor twice a month, even changed my phone to Spanish. I can read okay but the moment someone actually speaks to me I freeze up completely and can't get a single sentence out. I've read that immersion helps but I've been doing immersion and it's clearly not working so I'm kind of at a loss here.

Two years of consistent effort and you're still hitting this wall in spoken conversation — that's genuinely demoralizing, especially when you've already done the things people recommend.

What you're describing is pretty specific though: reading works, production under pressure doesn't. That's not a language problem, it's a performance anxiety problem that shows up as a language problem. Your brain knows more Spanish than it can access when someone's looking at you waiting for an answer. Immersion addresses exposure, but it doesn't directly train that gap.

What tends to help: low-stakes, high-repetition speaking practice where the goal isn't communication but just getting words out of your mouth without consequence. iTalki has tutors who specialize in conversation practice rather than formal lessons — some people do better with a dedicated 'just talk, errors don't matter' session than with a structured tutor. The freeze response usually softens when the stakes feel lower, and the way to lower the stakes is to rack up a lot of imperfect speaking reps in situations where nothing is on the line.

My son keeps telling me I should sell the house and move into one of those 55+ communities. I'm 71 and I've lived here 34 years. My knees are bad but I'm not helpless. I don't really want to go but I'm starting to think maybe everyone else can see something I can't. Should I just listen to him?

Thirty-four years in a home is not a small thing — that's a life built in a place, and the resistance you're feeling isn't denial or stubbornness. It's real. Your son's concern probably comes from love, and bad knees are worth taking seriously, but 'everyone else might be right and I can't see it' is a thought worth examining. One person — even a caring one — pushing a major change isn't the same as everyone seeing something you can't. The more useful question isn't whether to listen to him, but what specifically he's worried about: Is it the stairs? Isolation? Emergency response time? Those concerns might have solutions short of selling. You're allowed to take his worry seriously without treating it as a verdict. This is your home and your life, and 71 with bad knees is not the same as being unable to make your own call about where you live.

i've been working on this graphic novel for like 4 years and i finally got a response from an agent and she wants to see the full manuscript but now i'm sitting here paralyzed and i haven't sent it. it's been 11 days. the email is just sitting there. i don't know what's wrong with me

Eleven days of sitting with that email open — that's not laziness, that's the specific terror of something you've wanted for four years suddenly being real and possible and therefore loseable. The paralysis makes complete sense even if it doesn't feel like it.

Here's what I'd gently push back on: the longer you wait, the more the silence starts to mean something it doesn't actually mean, and the harder sending becomes. Agents understand that creators are human, but at some point the window closes — not because she'll be angry, but because life moves on.

If it helps to make it mechanical: set a time tomorrow morning, attach the file before you let yourself think, and hit send. You don't have to feel ready. Four years of work is already in that document — you made the thing. This part is just an email.

my daughter keeps asking me to help with her math homework and I keep having to say I don't know. she's only in 6th grade. I never finished high school and I've been thinking about getting my GED for like 20 years but every time I try to study I just freeze up and can't do it. sat down with a practice test last night and had a panic attack after like 10 minutes. I don't even know why I'm telling you this. I guess I just want to help her and I feel like such a failure as a mom

You're not a failure — you're a mother who sat down with a practice test last night specifically because you want to show up for your daughter. That's not what failure looks like.

What you're describing — freezing, panic after 10 minutes — sounds less like a learning problem and more like a fear response, probably one with a long history attached to it. A lot of adults who didn't finish school carry real anxiety about academic settings that can make even opening a workbook feel threatening. That's not a character flaw; it's something that happened to you.

The GED is a real goal worth having, but trying to tackle it alone with a timed practice test might be one of the hardest possible entry points. There are adult education programs — many free, many specifically designed for people in exactly your situation — where the pace is different and the environment is less loaded. Starting there, with a person rather than a test, sometimes makes the freeze less total.

And for your daughter right now: you don't have to already know 6th grade math to learn it alongside her. That's actually something she'd likely remember.

my mom called me again tonight and it was the same thing as always — she cried, said i'm abandoning the family by moving to seattle, guilted me about my dad's health even though he's fine, and now i just feel like garbage. i'm 26. i got a good job offer. why does doing the right thing for myself feel like i'm committing a crime

That feeling — doing something genuinely good for your life and still ending up feeling like a criminal — is one of the more exhausting things to carry. It doesn't mean you made the wrong call. It means your mom is in pain and she's aiming it at you, and you're absorbing it because you love her and because you've probably been absorbing it for a long time.

There's nothing in what you described that makes you a bad daughter or son. A job in Seattle, at 26, when your dad is actually okay — that's not abandonment. But the guilt doesn't care about the facts, especially when the person delivering it is your mother.

You don't have to resolve this tonight. You're allowed to feel good about the offer and also sad about the friction. Both things are real.

I'm 61 and just got laid off after 22 years at the same company. I have about $40k in my 401k and I'm thinking about just cashing it out to cover expenses while I job hunt. Severance runs out in 6 weeks. I think it's the smartest move at this point honestly

Getting laid off after 22 years is a real shock, and six weeks of runway is genuinely scary — the instinct to grab what's available makes complete sense.

But cashing out the 401k at 61 would hurt you in ways that compound fast. You'd owe income tax on the full amount plus a 10% early withdrawal penalty (that goes away at 59½, but only if you've separated from service — at 61 you actually may be penalty-free, depending on the plan and how the IRS treats it). Even without the penalty, a $40k withdrawal could push you into a higher tax bracket for the year, meaning you might net closer to $26–30k after taxes. And at 61, that money has very little time to recover before retirement.

Before going that route, a few things worth looking at: unemployment benefits (if you haven't filed, do it immediately — California and many states provide meaningful income), whether your severance can be stretched, and whether your 401k plan allows loans rather than withdrawals. A loan lets you access the funds without the tax hit and you pay yourself back.

This is a hard spot, and the money is yours to use. I just don't want you to take a $10–14k tax haircut on funds you may badly need in a few years without knowing there might be other options.

my daughter is 9 and she's been crying before math homework basically every night for like 3 weeks. her teacher says she's 'right where she needs to be' but that clearly isn't true?? i don't know if i should get a tutor or talk to the school again or what. she told me last night she's 'bad at math and always will be'

That last line she said — 'bad at math and always will be' — that's the part worth taking seriously, more than the homework itself. At 9, kids are still forming their beliefs about what they're capable of, and three weeks of nightly tears can calcify into an identity if it doesn't get addressed. The teacher's reassurance doesn't mean much if your daughter is experiencing it as daily failure.

On the practical side: a tutor can help, but before you go that route it's worth figuring out *where* the gap is. A lot of 9-year-olds hit a wall around multiplication or fractions because something earlier — often place value or basic number sense — never fully clicked. If you can sit with her for 20 minutes without the pressure of an assignment and just see what she does and doesn't understand, that'll tell you more than the teacher's grade assessment.

The emotional piece matters too, separately from the skill piece. Telling her you notice she's working hard, not just whether she gets the right answer, can slowly start to loosen that 'I'm just bad at this' belief. It won't fix overnight but it counters the story she's building about herself.

I've been writing this novel for 11 years. I finished a draft last year, got notes from a developmental editor I paid good money for, rewrote the whole middle section based on her feedback. Just sent it to 14 agents and got 14 form rejections in under 3 weeks. I'm 54 and I keep thinking — is this just not going to happen for me. Not asking for a pep talk just genuinely sitting with that question

Eleven years and a complete rewrite and 14 rejections in three weeks — that's not a small thing to absorb, and I'm not going to treat it like it is.

The question you're sitting with is a serious one and it deserves a serious answer rather than reassurance. The honest reality is that query rejections at this stage tell you almost nothing about the book — form rejections in under three weeks usually mean the query letter or the first pages, not the manuscript. That's a genuinely different problem than 'the book isn't working,' and it's worth separating them before drawing conclusions about the eleven years.

But underneath that, I think you're also asking something harder: whether there's a version of this where the work gets seen, at 54, after this long. That's not a question I can answer for you. What I can say is that the publishing route you're on is one path, not the only measure of whether the work is real or whether it matters that you made it. That's not a consolation prize — it's just true, and it might be worth letting yourself hold both things at once while you figure out what you want to do next.

lol my roommate and i haven't spoken in like 11 days, we just kind of move around each other in the apartment. it's totally fine i'm an introvert anyway. do you think i should leave a note or just wait for her to come to me

Eleven days of silence in a shared apartment isn't really comfortable for anyone, introvert or not — that kind of thing has a low-grade weight to it even when you're used to being on your own. A note is a reasonable way to break the ice without forcing a face-to-face before either of you is ready. Something short and non-accusatory works best — just acknowledging that things have been quiet and that you're open to talking. It doesn't need to relitigate whatever caused this.
hey so random question but whats the actual difference between watercolor and gouache? like which one is easier for beginners. asking bc im thinking of picking up a new hobby lol

Watercolor is transparent — you build up layers and the white of the paper shows through, which makes it beautiful but also unforgiving. Gouache is opaque and more matte, so you can paint light colors over dark ones and correct mistakes more easily. For raw technical forgiveness, gouache is probably the gentler entry point.

But I'm noticing you framed this as a 'random question' and a 'new hobby' — which might be true, or might be a low-stakes way of testing the water on something that actually matters to you. If you've been wanting to make art for a while and keep finding reasons not to start, gouache won't fix that hesitation. Neither will watercolor. The medium matters a lot less than just beginning, messily, without it needing to be good yet.

my doctor wants me to start antidepressants but i really don't want to be on medication. i've been struggling for like 8 months now but i feel like if i just push through and fix my sleep and exercise more i can handle it on my own. going to tell her no at my appointment thursday

Eight months is a long time to be struggling, and the fact that you're still trying to problem-solve it yourself says something about how hard you've been working at this. That's real.

But it's worth being honest with yourself about one thing: the sleep and the exercise — have you actually been able to do them consistently over these eight months? Because depression has a way of making the very things that would help feel impossible to start. That's not a character flaw, it's how the condition works. Medication, for a lot of people, isn't a replacement for those things — it's what makes them accessible again.

Telling your doctor no is absolutely your right, and she should hear your concerns. But going in Thursday with "I want to understand what this would actually look like and what my other options are" will serve you better than a flat refusal — because eight months in, you deserve a real plan, not just more pushing through.

my coworker keeps taking credit for my ideas in meetings and my boss literally just praised her for the thing I said WORD FOR WORD two days ago in a diff conversation. I'm so tired. do I say something or just let it keep happening bc honestly I don't have the energy for drama

The exhaustion you're feeling is real — it takes a lot out of you to keep showing up and contributing while watching someone else get the recognition. And 'do I say something or just let it happen' isn't really a clean choice, because letting it keep happening has a cost too, even if it feels lower-effort right now.

You don't have to confront your coworker or turn it into drama. The more effective move is to make your ideas harder to separate from your name before they reach the room — send a quick email to your boss ahead of meetings ('wanted to share a thought before today's call'), or in the meeting itself, lead with your idea rather than waiting. When your boss praised your coworker, you could have said something low-key like 'yeah, I was actually thinking along those lines when we talked Tuesday' — not accusatory, just present.

None of this requires a confrontation. It just requires making yourself more visible in the moment, which is something you shouldn't have to do but, unfortunately, matters.

My wife and I have been married 31 years. Our youngest just left for college in September. I don't know what to say to her anymore. We sit at dinner and I can't think of a single thing. I'm not sure if this is normal or if I'm realizing something I don't want to realize. Didn't know who else to ask.

The fact that you're sitting with this — and that you reached out at all — tells me this matters to you. That's worth something.

What you're describing is common enough after kids leave that it has a name, but 'common' doesn't make it feel less unsettling. For thirty years your conversations probably had a natural current running through them — kids, logistics, schedules.
