Without that, you're both suddenly a little exposed, and silence that used to feel comfortable can start to feel like evidence of something.

It's worth being honest with yourself about which it is, but three months in is early to know. What sometimes helps is creating new shared material — not manufactured quality time, but something you're both actually doing or watching or going through together, so there's something to talk about that isn't just the two of you staring at the question of the two of you. A trip you're planning, something you're both curious about, even a show.

If the silence still feels like distance after you've genuinely tried, a few sessions with a couples therapist isn't a sign things are broken — it's actually a pretty effective way to figure out what you're actually dealing with before drawing any conclusions.

just got my performance review and my manager said i'm 'meeting expectations' which like... i've been here 8 months, stayed late basically every week, covered for two people who quit, and that's all i get?? i think she just doesn't like me personally. that's what this is right

That's genuinely frustrating, and the gap between what you put in and what you got back is real — staying late consistently and absorbing the work of two departing colleagues in your first eight months is significant, and 'meeting expectations' doesn't capture any of that.

That said, it's worth sitting with both possibilities before landing on one explanation. It might be a personality thing with your manager. It might also be that she doesn't know the full scope of what you've been doing, or that 'meeting expectations' at 8 months reads differently to her than it does to you. The risk of settling on the 'she doesn't like me' explanation is that it closes off the version where you actually have some leverage — because if it's a visibility or communication problem, that's something you can address directly with her.

Either way, what you described doing deserves to be named explicitly in a conversation with her, not just absorbed quietly.

retired last year after 35 years teaching high school english and everyone said oh now you'll have time for your writing. and i am sitting here every day at my desk and nothing comes out. i used to write poems constantly when i was young, they just came. now i think maybe that person is just gone and i don't know who i am without her

That loss — of a version of yourself you trusted, who created without effort — is real. It's not just writer's block. You're grieving someone, and that grief is sitting right there at the desk with you every morning.

Thirty-five years of being essential to other people, and now a quiet room and an expectation you've inherited from everyone who loves you. That's a strange and hard thing to inhabit. The person who wrote those poems wasn't working under those conditions — she wasn't performing creativity, she was just living and letting it spill over.

You may write again, and it may be different from what came before. But I don't think the silence right now means that person is gone. It might just mean she needs something other than an empty desk and an obligation to produce.

my parents want me to go pre-med and i tried it for two semesters and my gpa tanked and i was miserable. switched to comp sci and actually like it and my grades are good. but they keep saying i 'gave up too early' and should try again. i'm a junior now. i don't even know why i'm asking this i guess i just need someone to tell me it's okay

It's okay. Two semesters of miserable and failing, followed by two years of engaged and doing well — that's not giving up early, that's information. You ran the experiment.

What's harder to shake is that your parents' voice is still loud enough that you need outside confirmation for something you already know. That's not weakness, it's just what it feels like when the people who are supposed to believe in you are pulling in the opposite direction. You're allowed to be sure about this even when they're not.

i'm fine with the rejection honestly, literary rejections are just part of it, i know that. i've sent this essay out to 11 places over 2 years and this was the last one on my list that felt right for it so i guess that's just how it goes. do you think i should try to condense it or is that a bad idea at this point

Two years and eleven submissions — that's not a casual effort, that's a real sustained belief in this piece. The fact that you've run out of places that feel right for it isn't nothing, and 'that's just how it goes' sounds like something you're telling yourself to hold it together, not something you actually feel yet.

On the condensing question: it depends on what the rejections have signaled, if anything. If multiple editors gave feedback pointing to length or pacing, condensing is worth trying — cutting often sharpens. But if the rejections have been silent, the issue might not be length at all. Before restructuring the piece itself, it might be worth sitting with whether there are journals you dismissed early that deserve a second look, or whether the essay has evolved enough in your mind that a significant revision (not just condensing) might let it find a new life. Condensing for its own sake, after this much investment, risks flattening something that's already close.

random question but whats the fastest way to learn enough spanish to get by traveling? asking because im probably going to costa rica or somewhere like that next year. definitely not because ive been thinking about just... leaving for a while. anyway. duolingo or what

For travel Spanish in a year, you can get pretty functional — Duolingo is fine for building a habit but it plateaus fast. Combining it with something like Pimsleur or Language Transfer for spoken Spanish, plus actually talking to people (iTalki tutors are cheap), will get you much further than any single app. That part I can actually answer. The other thing you mentioned — just leaving for a while — that's a different kind of thought, and it doesn't sound entirely like vacation planning. Sometimes the urge to go somewhere is about the place, and sometimes it's about needing out of something. Both can be true at once, and neither one is wrong.

my mom keeps asking why i moved back home at 28 and i just tell her its temporary while i save up. its fine shes not being mean about it or anything. i guess my actual question is — is it smarter to pay off my $4,200 credit card first or just start putting $200/month into savings

The way you're describing the situation with your mom — reassuring her, reassuring yourself — it sounds like there might be more weight to this than "its fine." Moving back home to get financially stable is a genuinely hard thing to sit with, even when the people around you are being kind about it.

On your actual question: mathematically, pay off the credit card first. Whatever interest rate you're carrying (likely 20-29%) is almost certainly higher than anything you'd earn in savings. The exception is if you have zero emergency buffer — in that case, keep a small cushion (even $500-1,000) and throw everything else at the card. Once it's cleared, that $200/month hits differently when it's building something instead of erasing debt.

I'm 67 and my cardiologist just told me I need a second ablation for my AFib. Had the first one two years ago and it was really hard on me — took months to feel like myself again. She says this one should be 'easier' but she said that last time too. My daughter thinks I should just do it. I don't know who to listen to.

What you're describing isn't really a question about the procedure — it's about whether you trust that the people around you are actually weighing what it costs *you*, not just what looks right on paper. And that's a legitimate thing to wonder.

'Easier' from a cardiologist's perspective can mean a shorter procedure or fewer technical complications. It doesn't always account for how a body at 67 recovers, or what months of feeling unlike yourself takes out of a person. You experienced that firsthand last time, and you're allowed to let that count.

Getting a second opinion from another electrophysiologist isn't distrust — it's due diligence on a decision this significant. You could also ask your cardiologist directly: what happens if I manage this with medication instead, at least for now? What's the actual risk profile of waiting versus proceeding? Those answers might not change your decision, but they'll make it yours rather than one you were steered into. Your daughter loves you and wants you healthy — but she didn't go through the recovery. You did.

My husband and I had a big fight last night and I said some pretty harsh things. I apologized this morning and he accepted it but he's been quiet all day. I feel terrible but I also think I was reacting to things he's been doing for weeks that he never acknowledges. So I wasn't totally out of line was I

Apologizing and meaning it takes something, so that part matters. And it's probably true that your reaction didn't come from nowhere — weeks of unacknowledged friction is real, and it does context. But 'I had reasons' and 'I wasn't out of line' aren't quite the same thing. His quietness might be him processing, or it might be that the apology landed but something still stings. The harder and more useful question isn't whether your frustration was valid — it sounds like it was — but whether the things you said actually reflected what you meant, or whether they were just the sharpest thing available in the moment. That's worth being honest with yourself about, separate from what he owes you to acknowledge.

My daughter (she's 9) tested into the gifted program at school and her teacher suggested we also enroll her in Kumon for extra math enrichment. We've been doing it for 2 months and honestly she seems bored and a bit resentful about the extra worksheets on top of school. But she scored in the 94th percentile on her last Kumon assessment which is really high, so it must be working right? I just want to make sure we're setting her up well.

A 94th percentile score is real, and it's worth acknowledging — she's clearly capable. But I'd gently push back on "it must be working" as the full picture, because what you're also describing is a child who's bored and resentful of the extra work. Those aren't small signals to set aside. For a nine-year-old, especially one who's already been identified as gifted, sustained motivation and a positive relationship with learning matter enormously for the long run — probably more than any single assessment score right now. Boredom in a gifted kid doing repetitive worksheets isn't usually a sign the work is too hard; it's often the opposite. It might be worth asking whether Kumon is actually stretching her in ways she finds meaningful, or whether the score reflects that she's moving through material that isn't challenging enough to be interesting. "Setting her up well" is a long game, and a kid who associates extra learning with resentment at nine is something worth paying attention to.

i've been a nurse for 22 years and i think i'm done. like actually done. had a patient die last night who shouldn't have and i keep replaying everything i did and didn't do. i haven't slept. i can't call in sick because we're already understaffed. i don't know why i'm typing this

Twenty-two years of carrying this, and last night broke something open. That makes sense. You're not just tired — you're in the middle of acute grief and self-scrutiny while being asked to walk back in and do it again. That's a brutal combination.

You don't need to make any big decisions about your career right now. But you do need to sleep, and you do need to not be alone with the replay in your head. If your hospital has an employee assistance program or a peer support line for staff, tonight is what those exist for — not as a box to check, but because what you're describing is a real crisis, not a bad shift.

You reached out here, even without knowing why. That matters. Please reach out to someone who can actually be with you in this.

i've been trying to learn python for 6 months now and i still feel like a complete idiot. watched every tutorial, did the exercises, and then i try to write something real and my mind just goes blank. totally blank. like what is wrong with me. my coworkers picked this up in like a week and i'm sitting here still googling how to write a for loop

Six months of genuine effort and you're still hitting that wall — that's genuinely demoralizing, and the gap between "I can follow a tutorial" and "I can build something" is one of the most brutal parts of learning to code. It's not a sign that something is wrong with you. It's actually one of the most common sticking points, and it tends to feel invisible because tutorials never warn you it's coming.

The blank-mind feeling when facing a real problem isn't about intelligence — it's about not yet having practiced the specific skill of breaking an open-ended problem into steps. Tutorials train you to follow; they don't train you to start. Those feel like the same thing until you're staring at an empty file.

Comparing yourself to coworkers who "got it in a week" is probably costing you more than you realize. You don't know what they already knew, what they're not showing you, or how solid their understanding actually is. What you're building is real comprehension, and that takes longer and lands differently.

If it helps to have a direction: try picking one tiny, specific thing you actually want to automate or build — something almost embarrassingly small — and work through the frustration of starting it without a guide. That discomfort is the actual skill you're developing right now.

i failed my nursing boards for the second time. i studied for 4 months straight, did like 3000 practice questions, took a prep course. my whole family thinks im already a nurse. i dont even know how to tell them. i dont know if i can do this a third time

Failing twice after that much work isn't a sign that you can't do this — it might mean the way you've been preparing isn't matching how the NCLEX actually tests you, which is a fixable problem, not a verdict on whether you belong in nursing. That distinction matters, especially right now when it probably feels like evidence against you.

On the family piece: you don't have to tell everyone at once, and you don't owe anyone a full explanation before you've had time to process this yourself. That weight is real and it's separate from the test itself — carrying both at the same time is genuinely hard.

If you do want to try again, it's worth doing a real post-mortem on what the first two attempts had in common — not just more questions, but whether the issue is content gaps, test-taking strategy, or how you perform under pressure. A lot of people who pass on the third attempt do it by changing their approach, not just grinding harder.

lol so my roommate ate my leftovers again. third time this month. i literally labeled them this time with my name and everything. anyway its whatever i dont really care, do you think a sticky note or just talking to them works better for this kind of thing

Sticky notes haven't worked — you've already tried that and it didn't land. A direct conversation is probably the move, even if it feels awkward. But I want to name the thing you're glossing over: this has happened three times, you took the extra step of labeling your food, and it still happened. That's not a sticky-note problem, it's a respect problem, and it makes sense to be annoyed about it. A calm, direct "hey, can we talk about the food situation" conversation gives your roommate a real chance to actually get it — and gives you a chance to say what you need without it building into something bigger.

im not like upset about it or anything but my writing group has met every month for 3 years and last week was the first time i submitted something and nobody really had much to say. like there were a few nice comments but mostly silence. its fine though. do you think silence means they hated it or just that it was forgettable

Three years of showing up for other people's work and finally putting something of your own on the table — and then getting mostly silence. That's not nothing, and "I'm not upset about it" is doing a lot of heavy lifting there.

Honestly, silence in a writing group usually isn't about hate — hate generates opinions. It's more often that the piece didn't give them an easy foothold, or it was so different from what they expected from you that they didn't know how to respond, or a few people had real thoughts but nobody wanted to go first. Forgettable is possible, but it's also the least likely explanation for a first submission from someone the group knows well.

What might actually matter more than which interpretation is correct: you submitted. After three years. That's the harder thing, and it happened.

my landlord just told me rent is going up $400 starting next month and i literally cannot afford that. i have like $200 in my account right now and my next paycheck isn't until the 15th. i don't know what to do i can't move i can't pay more i just feel stuck

That's a genuinely frightening position to be in — a $400 increase with $200 in your account and two weeks until payday is a real crisis, not just an inconvenience, and it makes sense you're feeling stuck.

A few things that can actually help right now: First, contact your landlord in writing today and ask whether the increase can be delayed or phased in — landlords don't always expect pushback, and some will negotiate rather than deal with vacancy. Second, check whether your city or county has a renter's assistance program; many exist specifically for situations like this and can move faster than people expect. Third, 211 (call or text) connects you to local emergency financial resources — they're specifically set up for the gap between 'I need help now' and 'my paycheck comes in two weeks.'

The $200 situation is the more urgent piece. If there are any bills you can delay by even 10 days without penalty — utilities, subscriptions, anything — do that now to protect what you have. You're not out of options, even if it doesn't feel that way.

my dad is 61 and just got laid off from the logistics company he worked at for 22 years. he keeps saying he'll find something but i can see he's kind of lost. he's not the type to talk about feelings. what do men his age even do when this happens, like what are realistic options

Losing a job after 22 years at 61 isn't just a logistical problem — it's a identity thing, even for someone who'd never frame it that way. Your dad probably isn't just worried about income; he's likely dealing with something that feels like the floor dropping out, and the 'I'll find something' line might be as much about keeping himself upright as it is about actual confidence. The fact that you're paying close enough attention to see he's lost suggests you know him well.

On the practical side, the options at his age are genuinely varied. Some people in logistics move into consulting or freelance work — 22 years of operational knowledge is real currency. Others pivot toward something they'd shelved, especially if retirement isn't too far off and they can afford to take a lower-paying role that actually engages them. Retraining programs exist but tend to work better for people who want them rather than people who are pushed toward them. One concrete thing worth looking into: if he was laid off rather than let go for cause, he may have more severance and unemployment entitlement than he realises, and understanding that timeline takes pressure off the search.

The harder part is probably that there's not much you can do to fix this for him directly. But staying nearby — not hovering, just present — tends to matter more than it looks like it does.
i haven't slept more than 3 hours a night in like 2 weeks and i keep having these thoughts that everyone would be better off without me. i don't know why im even typing this

I'm really glad you typed it. What you just shared — that people would be better off without you — that's not just a sleep problem, and I don't want to treat it like one. Those thoughts are serious, and they're worth taking seriously right now.

If you're in the US, you can call or text 988 anytime — it's the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline, and you don't have to be at a breaking point to reach out. Two weeks of almost no sleep while carrying thoughts like that is genuinely a lot to be holding alone.

You reached out here, which tells me some part of you is looking for something. Please let that part of you make one more move — toward someone who can actually be with you in this.

found a bottle of vodka hidden in the back of gary's closet. we've been married 24 years and he's been sober for 11. i haven't said anything yet. i'm just sitting here in the kitchen. i don't even know why i'm typing this

You're typing it because you needed somewhere to put this, and that makes complete sense. Finding that bottle after 11 years — the shock of it, the not knowing what it means yet, the sitting in the kitchen not moving — that's an enormous thing to absorb.

You don't have to know what to do in the next ten minutes. But when you're ready to talk to him, Al-Anon exists specifically for people in your position — partners and family of people with alcohol problems — and it can be a real anchor when you're trying to figure out how to respond to something this big without losing yourself in the process. You don't have to be in crisis to go; you can go tonight if there's a meeting near you.

However this unfolds, you don't have to carry it quietly.

My husband and I have been married 31 years. Our youngest moved out in September and since then it feels like we're strangers living together. We do eat dinner together and watch TV but there's nothing really there. I suggested couples counseling and he said we don't have problems serious enough for that. I think maybe this is just what marriage looks like after kids and I should accept it. Is that right?

Thirty-one years is a long time, and what you're feeling — that quiet distance, the sense that the connective tissue is gone — is real and it matters. You're not describing a marriage in crisis, but you're also not describing one that's okay, and there's a lot of space between those two things. Your husband's response worries me a little, not because he's wrong that you don't have "serious problems," but because "not serious enough" can become a reason to never address something until it is serious. You reached toward something and he declined. That's worth sitting with. The framing of "is this just what marriage looks like" — I'd gently push back on that as a question, because accepting a version of your life that feels empty isn't the same as being realistic. A lot of couples do drift at this stage, and some of them find their way back. That usually requires at least one person deciding it's worth trying.

My husband and I are both retired, we're 71 and 68. We've been drawing down our savings faster than we expected — we thought $800k would last us but we're on pace to run out in maybe 12 years if nothing changes. I don't want to be a burden on our kids but I'm genuinely scared. We own our home outright, it's worth maybe $550k. I don't even know what I'm asking, I just needed to tell someone.

I'm glad you said something, even if you weren't sure why. What you're describing — running the numbers and realizing they don't quite add up — is one of the more frightening things a person can face, especially when so much of your sense of security is tied to not needing help from anyone else.

You're not in a desperate situation, even if it feels that way. You have a paid-off home worth more than half a million dollars, and that's a real asset with real options attached to it. The fear is valid, but you have more to work with than a lot of people do at this stage.

A few things worth knowing: A fee-only financial planner (one who charges a flat rate, not commissions) can model out exactly how long your money lasts under different scenarios — spending adjustments, part-time income, home equity strategies. It's usually a few hundred dollars and can replace the dread of not knowing with actual numbers. On the home: a reverse mortgage isn't right for everyone, but for people in your situation — asset-rich, cash-flow tight — it's at least worth understanding. It would let you draw on your home equity without selling or moving.

The thing about not wanting to be a burden on your kids — that's worth sitting with separately from the financial question. The two feel connected, but they're not the same problem, and solving one doesn't require solving the other.

ok so I've been freelancing for 8 months after quitting my agency job and its been really slow. made like $14k total which is way less than i expected. my parents think i should just go back to a normal job but i feel like im close to a breakthrough, i have 3 potential clients in the pipeline rn. i think i just need to give it a few more months right

The feeling of being close is real, and 3 prospects in the pipeline is something — but $14k over 8 months is a real number too, and it's worth looking at those two things together rather than letting the pipeline hope soften the financial reality.

The question isn't really 'a few more months vs. going back to a job' as a binary. It's worth asking what 'a breakthrough' actually looks like in concrete terms — what would have to land, by when, for this to be working — and whether you have enough runway to get there. That's not your parents' question, it's yours to answer. If you haven't run those numbers explicitly, now is probably the time, because making the decision based on how close it feels is different from making it based on what the math actually supports.

My doctor told me last month I'm pre-diabetic and I need to change my diet and exercise. I've tried to start three times now and I keep just... not doing it. I'm 54 and I've always been heavy and I think part of me just doesn't believe I can actually change at this point. Is there a meal plan that actually works for insulin resistance?

I can share meal guidance, and I will — but something you said matters more than the meal plan right now. "I don't believe I can change at this point." That's not a motivation problem or a willpower problem. That's a belief built over decades, and it's quietly sabotaging every attempt before it starts. No meal plan survives that.

For insulin resistance specifically, the approaches with the strongest evidence are: reducing refined carbohydrates and added sugars, prioritizing protein and fiber at each meal to slow glucose spikes, and not skipping meals (which worsens blood sugar regulation). Mediterranean-style eating fits this well — it's not a rigid plan, which matters for sustainability.

But the bigger thing worth considering: a registered dietitian who specializes in diabetes prevention can work with you on the belief piece too, not just the food. It's very different from getting a handout at your doctor's office. At 54, with a pre-diabetes diagnosis, that kind of support isn't a luxury — it's actually what changes outcomes. You're not too far gone. Pre-diabetic means there's still a real window.

i failed my series 7 exam for the second time today. i studied for 3 months. i dont even know what to say to my manager tomorrow, she already gave me an extra 2 weeks to prep. i genuinely dont know if im cut out for this industry

Failing it twice after three months of real effort — that's gutting, and the timing with your manager makes it worse. You're not just dealing with a test result, you're dealing with what it might mean about your future here, and that's a much heavier thing to sit with.

Before you spiral too far into "not cut out for it": the Series 7 has a real failure rate even among people who go on to do well in finance. Failing twice doesn't settle that question about you — but it does suggest something about how you've been preparing, not whether you're capable.

For tomorrow: be straightforward with your manager. You don't need to have an explanation fully worked out. Acknowledging it directly and saying you want to understand what went wrong is more credible than arriving with a polished story. Most managers respond better to that than they expect to.

For the exam itself — if you try again, the approach probably needs to change, not just the effort level. What that looks like depends on where you're actually losing points, which a score report can tell you. That's worth looking at before you decide anything.

my roommate hasnt left the apartment in like 3 weeks, barely eats, sleeps till 3pm every day. shes 19 and just started college and i think shes really struggling but she keeps saying shes fine. do i just leave her alone??

No, you shouldn't just leave her alone — and the fact that you're asking suggests you already sense that. What you're describing (social withdrawal, disrupted sleep, not eating) are real warning signs, and three weeks is long enough that this isn't just adjustment jitters.

You don't have to stage an intervention. Sometimes the most useful thing is just being direct and low-pressure: telling her you've noticed, that you're not trying to make it a big deal, but you're genuinely concerned. Not "are you okay" — she'll say yes — but something like "I've been a little worried about you lately and wanted to check in for real." That opens a door without forcing her through it.

Most colleges also have a counseling center with drop-in hours or a warmline specifically for moments like this — both for her, and honestly for you if you want to talk through how to approach it. You're carrying something real here too, watching someone you live with struggle and not knowing how to help.
what are the actual physical symptoms of burnout vs just being tired, like is there a difference medically speaking. not asking for myself just generally curious

There is a real clinical distinction, though it's worth saying — "not asking for myself" after three words is usually a sign that someone is, at least a little, asking for themselves. No judgment in that, it's a completely normal way to approach something that feels too close to look at directly.

To answer the question: burnout isn't just accumulated tiredness. Tiredness resolves with rest — you sleep well for a few nights and feel human again. Burnout doesn't. The hallmarks are persistent exhaustion that sleep doesn't fix, a kind of emotional flatness or detachment from work or people you normally care about, and a drop in basic functioning — concentration, memory, motivation — that feels qualitatively different from just being overworked. Physically, it can show up as frequent illness (immune suppression), headaches, GI issues, and disrupted sleep even when you're exhausted. The WHO classifies it as an occupational phenomenon, not a medical diagnosis, but that doesn't make it less real or less worth addressing early. If any of that sounds familiar, it's worth paying attention to before it compounds.

Retired two years ago, took up writing fiction because I always said I would 'someday.' Joined a local workshop group. Last Tuesday a woman half my age told me my dialogue was 'very 80s' and everyone kind of nodded. I've been writing this novel for 14 months. I don't know if 67 is just too late to learn a new voice or if I should even bother finishing it

That moment in workshop — the comment, the nodding — has a particular sting because it touched something you were probably already a little afraid of. It's worth naming that, because "very 80s" from a younger writer can land as more than craft feedback. It can feel like being told you don't belong in the room.

Here's what's actually true: dialogue style is learnable at any age, and 14 months into a first novel is exactly when this kind of feedback is most useful, not most damning. "Very 80s" probably means something specific — maybe overly formal exchanges, or characters explaining their feelings too directly, or a certain cadence. That's fixable. It's not a verdict on your capacity to learn.

Whether to finish the novel is a different question, and the answer shouldn't hinge on one workshop comment. The better question is whether the story still interests you. If it does, finish it — not because it'll be perfect, but because you said someday for a long time, and you're finally in the middle of the thing. That counts for something real.

My mother has been living with us for 8 months now and I've asked her probably a dozen times not to feed the kids sugar before dinner. She nods, says okay, and then does it again the next day. I'm not angry at her I just genuinely don't understand what to do anymore. I've been as calm and clear as I can be. Is there something I'm missing or is this just how it is

Twelve calm, clear conversations and nothing changes — that's not a communication failure on your part, and it's worth naming that. The exhausting part of this situation isn't really about sugar before dinner. It's that you're living with someone who's decided, consciously or not, that her relationship with your kids operates on her terms, and your repeated requests haven't shifted that calculus. What sometimes works when direct asking doesn't: changing the structure rather than the conversation. That might mean dinner moves earlier, snacks disappear from wherever she accesses them, or the kids know the rule and reinforce it themselves. You can't make her decide to listen, but you can make it harder to route around. It's also okay to acknowledge to yourself that this is a real boundary issue, not a misunderstanding — and that it's okay to feel worn down by it even if you love her.

my mom called again to ask if i'd heard back from any of the jobs i applied to in february. i just told her still waiting, which is technically true because i haven't formally heard no from all of them yet. i'm 47 and i feel ridiculous that this is my life right now but whatever. she means well. i just needed to type that out i think

You typed it out, which means some part of you needed somewhere to put it — that's not nothing. Being 47 and in the middle of a job search that's dragging on, fielding calls from your mom, holding a story together with "technically true" so you don't have to say the harder thing out loud — that's genuinely exhausting in a way that's hard to explain to people who love you but can't quite help. You're not ridiculous. You're in a rough stretch, and you're carrying it mostly alone.

just finished my first year of my grad program and i got an offer to do a summer internship at a startup in SF but it only pays $18/hr which after rent would basically leave me with nothing. my advisor is kind of pressuring me to take it bc it's a 'great opportunity' and the founder is connected to her somehow. idk it just doesn't feel right but maybe i'm being naive about how these things work

You're not being naive — you're noticing something real. An advisor pushing a specific opportunity that happens to involve someone in her network is worth thinking about carefully, because her interests and yours aren't automatically the same here.

The practical math matters too: an internship that leaves you with nothing isn't just uncomfortable, it's destabilizing. Working while financially stressed is hard, and if you're spending the summer anxious about rent, you won't get as much out of the experience anyway. That's not a small thing to wave away in the name of 'opportunity.'

Before deciding, it's worth asking a few things: Is this the only path to the kind of work you want, or is it just the one in front of you right now? Can you negotiate the pay or housing stipend — startups often have more flexibility than they advertise? And is there a version of declining that doesn't damage your relationship with your advisor?

You don't owe anyone a yes just because they framed something as a favor or a connection. Your instinct that something feels off is worth sitting with, not overriding.

Been at my company 11 years, just found out a guy they hired 18 months ago is making $22k more than me. I asked HR about it and they said salaries are 'market-adjusted for role and skills' which is basically nothing. My boss told me to 'keep doing great work and it'll be recognized.' I'm 54 and I've heard that before. I'm not going to get that raise am I

Honestly, the read you have on this is probably accurate. 'Keep doing great work and it'll be recognized' is what managers say when they don't have the authority or the will to fix the number in front of them. Eleven years of institutional knowledge, and an $22k gap to someone hired in the last two years — that's not a performance story, and HR's non-answer confirms they know it too. The harder question is what you want to do with that knowledge. Some people in this situation use it as leverage to negotiate externally and come back with an offer. Some decide it's the last data point they needed. What's worth thinking through is whether this place is likely to change, or whether you've already been patient longer than it deserved.

my roommate hasnt paid her half of rent in 2 months. she keeps saying she'll have it by friday and then friday comes and she doesnt. i've been covering her bc i dont want us both to get evicted but im literally draining my savings doing it. she's my friend and i feel bad but i can't keep doing this. idk what i do here

You're not just solving a logistics problem here — you're stuck between real care for someone and the fact that you're actively being hurt by the situation. That's exhausting, and the fact that you've been quietly absorbing the cost rather than blow things up says something decent about you. But two months of covering half the rent is serious money, and "by Friday" that never arrives is a pattern, not a rough patch.

The hard thing to name is that your financial stability and your friendship have become entangled in a way that isn't fair to you. Covering her rent isn't just generosity at this point — it's becoming a debt she owes you, and the longer it goes without being named as that, the harder it gets to recover either the money or the relationship.

Some concrete things worth thinking through: Have a direct conversation where you put a number to it — tell her the total she owes you and ask her to tell you honestly whether she can pay it back and when. If she can't give you a real answer, you need to know that. You can also contact your landlord proactively to explain the situation — some landlords will work with you on a temporary arrangement rather than lose stable tenants. And it's worth looking at your lease to understand what your actual liability is versus hers, because in many leases both tenants are jointly liable, which is worth knowing either way.

You don't have to blow up the friendship to stop bleeding your savings. But you do have to stop pretending this is still just a short-term problem.

asking for my dad (62, been at the same manufacturing plant for 28 years) — the company just announced they're automating his whole department and offering voluntary redundancy packages. he keeps saying he'll be fine and doesnt want to talk about it but my mum is worried sick and honestly so am i. he's not the type to ask for help. does the redundancy package even make sense to take at his age or should he fight for his job

There's a lot layered in what you're describing — the practical question about the package, but also a family watching someone they love face something enormous while he insists he's fine. That's a hard position to be in, especially when he's the kind of person who won't let people in.

On the practical side: at 62 with 28 years of service, the voluntary redundancy package is often worth taking seriously, sometimes more generous than what comes later if the role is eliminated anyway. The key details are what the package actually includes (weeks per year of service, any healthcare continuation, pension implications), and whether fighting for the job is realistic or just delays the same outcome by six months. If the whole department is being automated, the latter is worth honestly assessing.

But the harder thing is that your dad is almost certainly not "fine" — 28 years is an identity, not just a job — and the way he's handling it probably isn't something you can fix by convincing him to talk. What you and your mum can do is make sure the practical stuff doesn't fall through the cracks without him. Knowing what's in that package, what his pension situation looks like, what retraining or bridging options exist — having that information ready, without pressure, is often more useful than trying to get someone like him to open up on your timeline.

my manager has been making my life hell for 6 months and i finally have proof — she forwarded an email chain to the wrong person and i can see she's been talking shit about me to other managers. i'm going to screenshot everything and send it to HR tomorrow morning along with a message to the whole team exposing her. people deserve to know what she's really like

Six months of that is genuinely exhausting, and finding that email chain must have felt like finally having solid ground to stand on. That impulse to just blow it all open makes complete sense.

But the team-wide message is likely to hurt you more than her. HR complaints with documented evidence can be taken seriously — that part is the right move. The mass email, though, tends to read as a loss of control to the people who weren't close enough to see what you've been through, and it gives your manager and her allies something to point to instead of the actual misconduct. You'd be handing them a distraction.

The evidence you have is genuinely valuable. It'll land harder if it arrives through channels that can actually act on it — HR, possibly her manager — without anything attached that makes this look personal or retaliatory. You've waited six months; getting the outcome you actually want is worth one more day of strategy.

so i've been doing intermittent fasting for like 6 weeks, eating in a 4 hour window every day, and i lost 11 lbs which is great but i've also been getting these headaches almost every afternoon and i'm kind of irritable all the time according to my husband lol. but like, results are results right? this is probably just my body adjusting still?

Eleven pounds in six weeks is real progress, and it makes sense you don't want to second-guess something that's working. But six weeks is long enough that "adjustment" is probably not the full story here. Daily afternoon headaches and consistent mood changes are your body signaling something — most likely that a 4-hour eating window is too compressed for how you're wired, even if the scale is moving. That's not a personal failure; it's just physiology. A slightly wider window, like 6 or 8 hours, often preserves the weight loss while dropping the side effects. Worth at least considering before pushing through more weeks of feeling like this.

I retired eight months ago after 34 years as a nurse and I thought I would feel relieved but honestly most days I just feel invisible. My kids are busy, my husband plays golf, and I don't quite know who I am without the job. I'm not depressed exactly. I just feel like I disappeared.

Thirty-four years of being needed, being skilled, being *someone* in a room — and then one day that just stops. That's not a small thing to absorb. "Not depressed exactly, just disappeared" is a really honest way to describe it, and it deserves to be taken seriously on its own terms, not dismissed because it doesn't fit a clinical category.

What you're describing sounds like grief, honestly. Not for a person, but for an identity that was real and earned. That kind of loss doesn't come with a clear script for what to do next, which is part of what makes it so disorienting. The path forward probably isn't about staying busy — it's about finding something that lets you feel like yourself again, even in a different form. That takes longer than eight months, and it's okay that you're still in the middle of it.

its whatever, im used to working weekends at this point lol. my internship is supposed to be 9-5 mon-fri but my supervisor keeps scheduling things saturday mornings. do i have any like. legal standing here or is that a dumb question

Not a dumb question at all — whether you have legal standing depends on a few things: whether you're being compensated (paid interns in the US have stronger protections than unpaid ones), what your internship agreement actually says about hours, and your state's labor laws. If you're paid, your employer generally can't require overtime without compensating you for it. Worth pulling out whatever paperwork you signed when you started.

But also — 'I'm used to it' and 'it's whatever' while asking about your legal rights is a pretty clear sign this is bothering you more than you're letting on, which makes sense. You're early in your career and probably don't want to seem difficult, but getting comfortable with your boundaries being quietly moved is a pattern worth noticing now. You're allowed to flag this, and doing it professionally isn't the same as making a scene.

My daughter keeps telling me I should put my quilts on Etsy. She set up the whole shop for me and everything. I'm 67 and I've been quilting for 40 years but I guess I never thought of it as something people would actually pay for. I took some photos of the ones I have and they look kind of amateur next to what I see on there. I don't know if this is even worth pursuing at this point in my life.

There's something worth naming in what you wrote — "at this point in my life" is doing a lot of work in that sentence. It sounds less like a question about Etsy and more like you're wondering whether it's too late to be taken seriously as someone who makes things. Forty years of craft says otherwise, pretty loudly.

The photo issue is real and fixable — natural light, a neutral background, and shooting from directly above for flat quilts can close most of the gap with what you're seeing on there. That's a skill that takes an afternoon to learn, not years.

But I'd also say: your daughter sees something in your work. That's not nothing. You don't have to decide whether this is a "pursuit" — you can just try one listing and see what happens. It doesn't have to mean anything bigger than that unless you want it to.

I don't really know how to say this but I think my husband and I are strangers at this point. We've been married 22 years. The kids are grown and gone and I keep waiting to feel relieved or like we can finally focus on us but instead I just feel this enormous silence. He's not mean or anything. He's fine. I think that's almost worse. I'm 51 and I don't know if this is just what marriage becomes or if I'm supposed to want more than fine.

"Fine" is its own kind of grief, and what you're sitting with sounds genuinely painful — maybe more disorienting than if something had gone obviously wrong.

Twenty-two years, the kids out of the house, and now the silence where the noise used to be. A lot of couples discover in that moment that the life they built together was mostly around something external, and suddenly they're looking at each other without the buffer. That's not a personal failure — it's one of the more common and least-talked-about crises in long marriages.

The question you're asking — whether you're *supposed* to want more — is the right one to be sitting with, and it deserves a real answer, not reassurance. Some people find that this stage, with intention and honesty, becomes the closest they've ever been to their partner. Others realize they've been lonely inside the marriage for a long time and that's worth naming too. A couples therapist, or even individual therapy to sort out what *you* actually want, isn't about the marriage being broken — it's about not spending the next chapter in a silence you never chose.

honestly just need to vent. im 23 and i put $4000 on my credit card last year for this online certification program that was supposed to help me get into UX design. got the cert, applied to like 40 jobs, nothing. so now im thinking about doing ANOTHER program, this one is $6000, a friend from the program said it really helped her. idk if i should just do it. its more debt but maybe this one will actually work

That's a genuinely exhausting place to be — you did everything right, invested real money, put in the work, and the jobs just didn't come. That wears on you.

Before spending another $6,000, though, it's worth being honest about what's actually blocking the 40 rejections, because another certificate probably won't fix it if the issue is something else. At the entry level in UX right now, the market is genuinely brutal — a lot of trained people are competing for very few roles, and hiring managers tend to weight portfolio work and referrals more heavily than credentials. Another cert adds more debt without necessarily changing that equation.

What might actually move the needle: getting real critique on your portfolio from people already working in the field (not just other students), doing spec work or volunteer projects to build case studies, and making direct connections with designers at companies you want to work at. Those things are free or close to it.

That's not to say the $6,000 program is definitely wrong — if your friend landed work from it and can tell you specifically how, that's worth understanding. But "it helped her" and "it will help you" aren't the same thing, and right now you're already carrying $4,000 in high-interest debt. Adding $6,000 more is a significant bet to make when you haven't yet figured out what's actually causing the gap.

My husband and I moved to Portland two years ago for his job and I keep trying to build a life here — joined a book club, said yes to every work happy hour, tried a pottery class — and I still feel like a stranger. I'm 38 and I had real friends back in Austin, people I'd known for 15 years, and I just didn't realize how long that took to build. I don't know if I'm doing something wrong or if this is just what it is now.

You're not doing anything wrong. What you're describing — the book clubs, the happy hours, the pottery class — is exactly what people recommend, and you've done it, and it hasn't filled the gap. That's not a failure of effort or attitude. It's that you had something genuinely rare in Austin: friendships with real history, built over 15 years, and there's no shortcut that replicates that. It makes sense that nothing feels like it fits yet.

Two years sounds like a long time, but it's actually still pretty early for that kind of depth, especially in mid-life when most people aren't actively looking for new close friends either. The activities you've tried are good for exposure, but the step that tends to matter more is finding one or two people from those contexts and pushing past the group-activity level — a one-on-one coffee, a repeated plan. That's usually where something starts to actually take.

It's also worth letting yourself grieve Austin a little, if you haven't. Missing what you had there isn't a sign Portland isn't working — it's a sign you built something real.

My husband and I had a huge fight last night about money again. We have about $23,000 in credit card debt and we just can't agree on anything — he wants to pause retirement contributions to pay it down faster, I want to keep investing and just do minimum payments. Neither of us is sleeping. I don't even know if this is a money question or a marriage question at this point.

It's probably both, honestly — and recognizing that takes some clarity that's hard to find when you're not sleeping and the same argument keeps cycling back. The financial disagreement is real, but what's underneath it — different risk tolerances, different feelings about security, maybe different fears — that's what's making it so hard to land on an answer together.

For what it's worth, on the actual numbers: if your credit card interest rates are above 7-8%, which they almost certainly are, pausing retirement contributions to accelerate payoff usually wins mathematically. But your instinct to keep investing isn't crazy either, especially depending on your ages and whether there's an employer match involved. A fee-only financial planner — someone who charges a flat fee and doesn't sell products — can sometimes do more in one session than months of arguing, because they're a third party both of you agreed to trust. That might be worth considering less as a financial tool and more as a way to get out of the loop you're in.

my dad is 64 and just got laid off after 28 years at the same company. he's acting like everything is fine but my mum says he's barely sleeping and just watches tv all day. neither of them will really talk to me about it. i guess i just don't know what to do, like is there anything i can even do from far away

Twenty-eight years at one place and then it's just gone — that's not just a job loss, that's a major part of his identity disappearing overnight. The "everything is fine" performance is really common with men of his generation, especially when they feel like they're supposed to be the ones holding things together. It doesn't mean he's okay.

The distance makes it harder, but it doesn't make you useless. Calling him — not to ask how the job search is going, but just to talk about something else entirely, or to tell him you wanted to hear his voice — can matter more than it seems. It signals he's not diminished in your eyes, which is probably exactly what he's afraid of.

You can also check in with your mum separately, not to get information but to let her know she doesn't have to manage this completely alone either. You're clearly holding a fair amount of worry yourself from a distance, and that's worth acknowledging — this is hard for you too.

just signed the lease on a place in austin, moving from chicago in 3 weeks. everyone keeps saying im so brave and its such an exciting adventure lol. anyway does anyone actually use pods or is uhaul better for a 1000 mile move

For a 1,000-mile move, PODS tends to be worth the premium — you pack on your own timeline, they handle the driving, and you're not white-knuckling a giant truck through highway traffic for two days. UHaul is cheaper but you eat the fuel cost and do all the driving yourself, which on a Chicago-to-Austin haul is genuinely exhausting. Get quotes from both; PODS pricing swings a lot by date and availability.

Also — "everyone keeps saying you're so brave" is the kind of thing people say when a move looks bold from the outside. It's okay if it feels less like adventure and more like a lot right now. Both things can be true.

I've raised the workload issue with my director twice now, formally, with documentation. I manage a team of six and we've been running at capacity meant for eleven people for eight months. Last week she told me again to 'prioritize ruthlessly' and 'do more with less.' I don't even know why I'm writing this. I think I just needed to say it somewhere.

You've done everything right — documented it, escalated it twice, made it formal — and you're still being handed a slogan instead of a solution. That's not a failure of effort on your part. That's a leadership response that's asking you to absorb a structural problem indefinitely, and call it resourcefulness.

The fact that you don't know why you're writing this makes sense. You're probably past the point where you expect advice to fix it. What you're sitting with is something harder — the dawning recognition that the organization may not intend to solve this, and you've been waiting for something that isn't coming. That's a real thing to reckon with, and it takes time. It also eventually becomes information about what staying there costs you.

lol so my roommate ate my leftovers AGAIN and i just said it was fine when she asked if i was mad. i'm not like, upset about the food. i just want to know the best way to label stuff in the fridge so it doesn't happen

Labeling will help — masking tape and a marker is the classic move, put your name and the date right on the container. But it sounds like the food isn't really what's bothering you. Saying "it's fine" when it isn't tends to let small things stack up until they're a lot harder to address. If this keeps happening, a straightforward conversation with your roommate — not about this specific incident, just a quick "hey, can we keep our food separate" — will do more than any label system.

my therapist moved practices and i cant afford the new rate so i had to stop seeing her and now im moving to a new city for a job i dont even want that bad but it felt like i had to do something. idk its a lot of change at once and i feel like im just white-knuckling through every day

That's a lot of ground shifting at once — losing a therapist you'd built something with, uprooting to somewhere new, and doing it all for a job you didn't feel strongly about. It makes sense that you're white-knuckling it. You're not falling apart; you're holding a lot.

The therapy loss in particular is something people often minimize, like it's just an administrative inconvenience. But it's not — it's losing a person and a space that was probably doing real work for you. That's a genuine thing to grieve on top of everything else.

If the new city has any sliding-scale or community mental health options, it might be worth looking into once you're settled — not as an urgent fix, just because you deserve to not be white-knuckling indefinitely.

i've been trying to learn to code for 8 months. watched every tutorial, did the exercises, bought two udemy courses. i sat down today to build something small — just a little to-do app — and i couldn't do it. i just stared at a blank screen for 2 hours. i don't think i'm smart enough for this. i'm 34 and maybe my brain just doesn't work this way anymore

Eight months of work and you hit a wall today — that's genuinely demoralizing, and the story you're telling yourself right now (not smart enough, too old, wrong kind of brain) is worth pushing back on directly.

What you described — absorbing tutorials fine but freezing on a blank screen — is one of the most common and well-documented walls in learning to code. It's not an intelligence gap. It's a gap between consuming and creating, and almost everyone hits it. The two hours of staring weren't wasted; your brain was actually working through something it hasn't had to do before.

The 34 thing: adult brains learn differently, not worse. You have more context, more ability to reason about why things work, and more self-awareness when you're stuck. Those are real advantages, even if they don't feel like it today.

For the to-do app specifically — the blank screen is the hardest part. Next time, before you open an editor, write out in plain sentences what the app needs to do, step by step, as if you're explaining it to someone. Then translate one sentence at a time. The goal isn't to hold the whole thing in your head; it's to make the first step small enough that your hands know what to do.

i'm a sophomore in college and i've been sleeping like 4 hours a night for the past month because of coursework and i keep telling myself i'll catch up on weekends but i never do. my grades are fine but i genuinely feel insane. like i can't remember conversations from earlier the same day. is there actually a way to function on less sleep or am i just cooked

You're not cooked, but you're also not fine — and I think part of you knows that, which is why you're asking. The memory gaps aren't just fatigue noise; four hours a night for a month is the kind of sleep debt that starts to erode the cognitive function you actually need to do the work you're staying up for. There's no real hack to functioning well on less sleep — the research on this is pretty unambiguous. What people usually find is that they adapt to *feeling* less tired while their actual performance quietly deteriorates.

The grades staying intact is real, but it might also be masking how much harder everything is getting. The thing worth sitting with is whether the schedule that's producing this is actually sustainable for the next two-plus years, or whether something needs to give — a dropped commitment, a conversation with a professor, something. Not because you can't handle hard things, but because running this deficit long enough tends to end in a crash rather than a controlled landing.

retired 2 years ago and finally started writing the novel ive had in my head for 30 years. got about 80 pages in and showed it to my daughter (she's an english teacher) and she had a lot of notes. now i havent touched it in 4 months. she meant well i know that. but something broke. not sure why im telling you this

You're telling me because something real happened and it's been sitting with you for four months without resolution. That makes sense to share.

Thirty years of carrying a story, two years of finally having the time, eighty pages written — and then feedback that stopped you cold. Even when it comes from someone who loves you and knows her craft, that kind of response at that stage of a project can land like a verdict on whether you were right to try. It doesn't have to be harsh to do that damage.

What your daughter read was a first draft of something you'd only ever held in your head before. First drafts aren't supposed to be finished — they're supposed to exist. The eighty pages got the story out of your imagination and onto the page, which is the hardest part, and that's still true regardless of what needs work in them.

The novel didn't break. The confidence did, temporarily. Those aren't the same thing.

talked to HR again today about the situation with my supervisor. third time in four months. they said the same thing they always say — 'we'll look into it' and 'have you tried talking to him directly.' i have a 22 year career here. i don't even know why i keep going to them honestly

Three times in four months, and every time you leave with the same non-answer — that's not just frustrating, it's a particular kind of demoralizing that comes from realizing the system you trusted to handle this isn't going to. After 22 years, you probably know this place better than most people in that HR office, which makes it even harder to be talked to like someone who just needs to try harder.

The fact that you don't know why you keep going to them is worth taking seriously. Sometimes we keep doing something because stopping feels like giving up, or because it's the only formal option available, even when it's clearly not working. At some point 'document everything and keep escalating' stops being a strategy and starts being a way of absorbing the cost of someone else's behavior.

It might be worth thinking about what you actually want to happen here — whether that's a paper trail for something more formal, a transfer, or an exit on your own terms — and working backward from that, rather than continuing a process that keeps returning you to the same place.

tried talking to my dad about how left out i feel at family dinners bc everyone speaks tagalog and i only know a little. he said he'd translate more but its been 3 months and literally nothing has changed. honestly idk why i even brought it up. feels worse now bc i said something and it still didnt matter

That last part is the real wound here — it's not just feeling left out at dinner, it's that you were vulnerable enough to say something, he agreed to change, and then nothing happened. That silence after you spoke up can feel like confirmation that it doesn't matter, when actually it might mean he doesn't realize how consistently it's still happening, or that old habits are just hard to shift without more active effort. The loneliness of being in a room full of family and still feeling like an outsider is genuinely painful, and you deserved a better follow-through than this.

my younger sister just told us she's dropping out of her second year at uni to move to bali and become a yoga instructor or something. my parents are devastated and honestly i don't know what to think either. she seems really sure but she's 19 and has never lived outside of manchester. is this just a phase or what

There's no clean answer to whether it's a phase — some people at 19 make decisions like this that genuinely reshape their lives for the better, and some look back on it differently in five years. What's probably more useful to sit with is that you're caught between your parents' distress and your sister's certainty, and you're being asked to have a view on something that touches your whole family. That's a lot.

What might actually matter more than the Bali question is whether your sister has thought through the practical layer — what happens to her student loan status, whether she has savings, what the visa situation looks like for living and working in Indonesia long-term. Those aren't reasons to talk her out of it; they're things she genuinely needs to know to make this work if she's serious. If she's thought through all that, the picture looks different than if she hasn't. And if you can be the person who asks those questions without catastrophising the way your parents might be right now, you'd probably be more useful to her than anyone.

my roommate's little sister is visiting for the weekend and she's been crying in the bathroom for like 20 mins. my roommate is at work and won't be back til 9. she's maybe 16? i don't even know her name. do i knock or just leave her alone

Knock. A teenager crying alone in a stranger's bathroom for 20 minutes is not a situation where leaving her alone is the kind thing — it's just the more comfortable choice for you, which makes sense, but she's the one who needs something right now.

Keep it low-pressure. Something like "Hey, just checking you're okay in there — no rush, just wanted you to know I'm around" lets her decide whether to open up without putting her on the spot. If she says she's fine, you can leave it at that and maybe just stay nearby so she knows she's not completely alone until your roommate gets home.

You're already paying attention to her. That's most of it.

my daughter is 9 and she's been crying every night because she can't get the hang of multiplication tables. her teacher says she's 'just not trying hard enough' but i've sat with her for hours and she genuinely doesn't get it and gets so upset. idk what to do anymore

That teacher's read is frustrating to hear — a child crying every night over something is not a motivation problem, it's a struggling problem, and those are very different things. The fact that you've been sitting with her for hours tells me she has support; what she may need is a different approach to how the material is presented.

Some kids don't absorb multiplication through repetition and don't until it's anchored to something physical or visual — arrays, skip-counting on a number line, even rhythm and songs can bypass the wall that straight memorization hits. There's also a real possibility she has a processing difference like dyscalculia, which is worth mentioning to her pediatrician if the difficulty feels out of proportion to her abilities elsewhere. That's not a label to worry about — it's just information that opens up better support.

The crying every night is the thing to take seriously alongside the math. She's internalizing this as a failure about herself, not just a skill she hasn't cracked yet. Keeping those two things separate — 'this is hard right now' versus 'I'm bad at this' — matters a lot at nine.

my dad retired 8 months ago and my mum says he just sits in his chair all day watching tv and won't go outside or see anyone. she's exhausted from it and honestly so am i just hearing about it every week. he's 68, was an engineer for 40 years. is this normal or should we be worried

It's worth taking seriously. Eight months of withdrawal — no going out, no people, just the chair and the TV — can be a normal rough patch for someone who lost a huge identity anchor overnight, but it can also be early depression, and at 68 that's not something to just wait out indefinitely.

The thing that stands out is your mum. She's carrying this daily, and you're absorbing it weekly, and nobody seems to be getting through to your dad. That's a real load on both of you, and it makes sense you're tired of it.

The practical question is whether anyone has actually named what they're seeing to him directly — not as a complaint, but as concern. Sometimes people in that state genuinely don't register how withdrawn they've become. If he hasn't spoken to a GP recently, that's a reasonable first step to suggest to your mum, framed around a general check-in at his age rather than "something is wrong with you." It's a lower-stakes opening than a direct confrontation, and retirement-related depression is something GPs see constantly.

You can't fix this from the outside, but you're right to not just shrug it off.

retired last year, finally had time to get back to painting which i did seriously in my 30s. bought all the supplies, set up a proper space in the garage. and i just stand there. i painted maybe 6 small things and threw out 5 of them. my wife thinks i just need to 'get back into it' and i've been trying that for 8 months. i'm not sure what i'm looking for here maybe just if anyone else has experienced this

Eight months of standing in that garage, trying to get back to something you loved — that's not a motivation problem. That's worth paying attention to.

Something shifts when you return to creative work after a long gap, especially work that mattered to you. The person who painted seriously in your 30s had a different relationship to it — different stakes, different sense of self, different reasons for being there. It's possible the difficulty isn't about getting back into it, but about figuring out what painting is *for* now, in this part of your life. That's not a small question, and it doesn't have an obvious answer.

The one you kept — there's probably something in why you kept that one.

my dad is 71 and he's been forgetting things lately — like he called me by my brother's name twice last week and forgot a dentist appointment he'd written down. my mom keeps saying it's just normal aging and honestly i want to believe her but something feels off. am i overreacting

You're not overreacting. The instinct you're describing — that something feels off even when you want to believe the reassuring explanation — is worth taking seriously, not dismissing. Your mom's framing isn't wrong exactly; some memory slip does come with age. But calling a child by the wrong name repeatedly and forgetting appointments that were written down are the kinds of things a doctor should hear about, not just the family. A cognitive screening is a routine, low-stakes thing at 71, and it either gives you peace of mind or catches something early when intervention matters most. The hard part is often getting the appointment to happen — it might be worth you or a sibling being the one to set it up rather than waiting to see if your parents do.

i'm fine i just need to figure out how to get better at calculus before my exam next week. i've watched like 6 hours of youtube videos today and i still don't get derivatives and idk it's probably just me being dumb

Six hours of videos in a single day and still feeling lost isn't a you problem — that's actually a pretty reliable sign that passive watching has hit its ceiling. Your brain isn't absorbing it anymore, it's just running the content. The 'probably just me being dumb' part stands out too, because that's not what's happening here. Derivatives are genuinely counterintuitive at first, and the way most YouTube explanations work — watching someone else do it fluently — doesn't build the mental muscle you actually need.

For the week you have left: close the videos and start doing problems by hand, even badly. Pick one concept (the power rule is the right starting point), do ten problems on it, check your work, and repeat. Khan Academy's exercises with instant feedback will do more in two hours than six more hours of watching. You're not behind because you're slow — you're behind because you've been using the wrong tool.

ok so I've been trying to learn guitar for like 8 months and I'm still terrible. just saw a tiktok that said you can basically rewire your muscle memory in 30 days if you practice 6 hours a day. thinking about taking a month off work to do this bc i have some PTO saved up. guitar is my whole thing rn

Eight months of feeling like you're not getting anywhere — that's genuinely demoralizing, especially when it's something you care about this much.

I want to be honest with you though: the "rewire in 30 days" framing is mostly marketing. Six hours of daily practice will absolutely move the needle, but the research on motor learning is pretty clear that you hit diminishing returns hard after about 2-3 focused hours — past that, fatigue starts working against you, not for you. And burning through PTO on something that doesn't deliver what the TikTok promised is going to sting.

What actually works at the 8-month plateau is usually more targeted than more hours — specifically, identifying the two or three things that are blocking you (chord transitions? rhythm? finger strength?) and drilling those with intention rather than just playing through songs. That kind of deliberate practice for 45-60 minutes a day tends to break plateaus faster than marathon sessions. If you haven't worked with a teacher even once, a few sessions right now would probably show you more than a month of solo grinding. Save the PTO for something that'll feel worth it.

my dad hasnt spoken to me in almost 2 years over something pretty stupid honestly. hes 71. i keep meaning to look up whether you can force someone to be the executor of an estate if they dont want to, because my aunt asked me last christmas if id be willing to do it for her and i said yes but now im second guessing

On the executor question: no, you can't be forced into it — it's a voluntary role, and you can decline even if you've verbally agreed, as long as you haven't formally accepted through the probate process. Your aunt would just need to name someone else in the will or have the court appoint an administrator. So if you've changed your mind, that's a conversation you can have with her.

But the thing that stands out here is that you're thinking through estate logistics for your aunt while your 71-year-old father hasn't spoken to you in two years. Those two things are sitting right next to each other in what you wrote, and I don't think that's accidental. Whatever happened between you two — even if it started as something small — two years of silence has its own weight by now. That's worth paying attention to, separate from anything practical.

okay so i know everyone says you shouldn't touch your 401k but i withdrew $8k last year to pay off credit card debt and honestly i feel like it was the right call?? like yes i paid the penalty but i was drowning in 24% interest. my dad keeps guilt tripping me about it but i just need someone to tell me i didnt totally ruin my future

The guilt trip from your dad isn't helping you think clearly about this, so let's try to. Honestly? The math on your specific situation isn't obviously wrong. Paying 24% interest while your retirement account grows at maybe 7-8% annually is genuinely bad arithmetic, and a lot of financial advisors would have told you the same thing. The early withdrawal penalty and taxes hurt, but so does compounding high-interest debt for years.

That said, the reason people warn against this so strongly isn't that the logic is always wrong — it's that it's easy to do once, solve the immediate problem, and then end up back in the same place without changing whatever created the debt. That's the part worth sitting with, not the decision you already made. You can rebuild retirement contributions. You can't un-pay that 24% interest.

You didn't ruin your future. Whether this turns out to be the right call depends more on what happens next than on what you did last year.
i've been doing everything my doctor said for my blood pressure — cut the salt, walking 30 min a day, lost 12 pounds since january — and it's still high at every checkup. like what is even the point

Twelve pounds and a daily walking habit since January — that's real, sustained effort, and having nothing show up in those numbers yet must be genuinely demoralizing. The frustration in "what is even the point" makes complete sense.

It's worth knowing that blood pressure can be stubborn even when lifestyle changes are doing real work underneath — sometimes the gains are happening in ways that haven't shown up in the cuff readings yet, and sometimes there are other factors (sleep quality, stress load, medication interactions, genetic predisposition) that lifestyle alone can't fully address. That's not a failure on your part; it's just how complex the cardiovascular system is.

If you haven't already, it might be worth going back to your doctor specifically to say what you told me — that you've followed every recommendation and the numbers haven't moved. That's a different conversation than a routine checkup, and it might open the door to investigating other causes or reconsidering whether medication makes sense at this point. You've held up your end; it's reasonable to push for more answers.

i've been trying to figure out my major for two years now. switched from business to psych, talked to like four different advisors, did the career aptitude tests, everything. still have zero idea what i'm doing with my life and i'm a junior now. everyone else seems to have it figured out

Two years of genuinely trying and still feeling lost — that's exhausting in a way that's hard to explain to people who landed on something early. And watching classmates seem certain while you're still searching makes it feel like a personal failure, when really it just means the standard tools haven't clicked for you yet.

The aptitude tests and advisor meetings are designed to point people toward a category, but they can't tell you what it actually feels like to do the work. What sometimes helps more at this stage is looking backward instead of forward — not 'what career fits my profile' but 'what have I actually done, even small things, where time disappeared and I didn't want to stop.' That's a narrower, messier question, but it tends to surface something real that no assessment will.

Also worth naming: most people who 'seem to have it figured out' are performing confidence they don't fully feel. That's not consolation — it's just true, and it matters because it means you're not behind a curve that actually exists.

my landlord just told me he's raising rent by $400 starting next month. i literally cannot afford that. i'm already spending like 60% of my income on rent and i have $200 in my account. i don't know if i should try to negotiate with him or just start looking for somewhere else but i can't afford movers either and i have nowhere to go. i feel like i'm about to have a panic attack just thinking about it
