That's a genuinely frightening position to be in — a $400 jump with $200 in your account and no obvious exit isn't just stressful, it's a crisis, and your body is responding accordingly. That panic makes sense.

On the immediate practical side: yes, try to negotiate first. Landlords often prefer keeping a tenant over vacancy costs, and you can be direct — tell him you can't absorb a $400 increase and ask if he'd consider a smaller one or a phased raise. Put anything he agrees to in writing. That conversation costs you nothing and sometimes works.

At the same time, start quietly looking at your options in parallel — not because you're definitely leaving, but because knowing what's actually out there will help you think more clearly instead of from pure panic. Check if your city has a tenant's union or legal aid housing line; many do free consultations and can tell you if this increase is even legal given your lease terms.

You're not out of moves yet. Take the next smallest step first.

i've tried the 50/30/20 budget thing like four times now and i always fall apart by week 3. tracked every purchase in an app, did the spreadsheet, everything. i just can't make it stick and i don't know if i'm just bad with money or what

Four attempts at the same system, all breaking down at the same point — that's not a willpower problem, that's a signal the system itself doesn't fit how you actually live. The 50/30/20 framework is popular because it's simple, but it's also pretty rigid, and a lot of people quietly fail at it without ever questioning whether it's the right tool for them rather than whether they're the right person for it.

Week 3 collapse is really common and usually means one of two things: the categories don't map onto your real spending patterns, or there's no flexibility built in for the inevitable weird week. Some people do better with a single "don't exceed this" number for discretionary spending rather than tracking everything. Others need a system that's explicitly designed to fail gracefully — where going over one category doesn't torpedo the whole month.

You're not bad with money. You've tried seriously, multiple times. That's the opposite of bad with money — that's someone who actually wants to get this right and hasn't found the right entry point yet.

my little sister is a sophomore in college and she's been going to the gym like twice a day and barely eating and everyone in my family thinks its great bc she 'looks so good' and i'm the only one freaking out about it. she got defensive when i brought it up once. what do i even do

Your instincts are sound, and it's worth trusting them here. What you're describing — the restricted eating, the compulsive exercise, the defensiveness when it came up — are recognized warning signs of an eating disorder. The fact that your family is responding with praise makes this harder, not easier, because it removes the usual social feedback that something might be wrong.

Being the only one who sees it is isolating. It also puts you in an unfair position where you're carrying real concern alone while everyone else is celebrating.

One conversation isn't usually enough, and the fact that she got defensive doesn't mean it didn't register — it often means it did. If you can find a moment to talk to her again, keeping it focused on how she's feeling rather than how she looks or what she's eating tends to go over better: "you seem really stressed lately" or "I feel like I haven't actually talked to you in a while" opens a door without triggering the same defenses.

If you're worried enough, it's also worth reaching out to her college's counseling center — not to report her, but to ask them how to support someone you're concerned about. They deal with this regularly and can give you more specific guidance than I can. You don't have to figure this out alone.

dropped out of my second year of engineering last month. everyone keeps asking what my plan is and i just say 'figuring it out' but honestly i have no idea. i feel like i made the right call though?? the program was making me miserable and i hadn't slept properly in like 8 months. that's a valid reason to leave right

Eight months of not sleeping properly isn't a footnote — that's your body telling you something was seriously wrong. So yes, misery and physical deterioration are real reasons to leave, not excuses.

That said, "I think I made the right call" and "I have no idea what comes next" are two different things, and it sounds like you might be conflating them a bit — like if the first is true, the second should feel okay. It doesn't always work that way. You can absolutely have been right to leave and still be genuinely lost right now, and that in-between place is uncomfortable in a way that doesn't go away just by confirming the decision was valid.

The people asking about your plan are probably exhausting, but that question isn't entirely noise — not because you owe them an answer, but because at some point soon it'll be worth sitting with it yourself, separate from the pressure. Not to have a five-year roadmap, just to have some sense of what you're moving toward, even loosely.

retired 2 years ago and honestly its fine. we adjusted. i just wonder sometimes if selling the house was the right call — we got a good price but now everything feels kind of small. not complaining just thinking out loud i guess. do you think equity release schemes are worth looking at for people in our situation

The way you're describing this — 'its fine,' 'not complaining,' 'just thinking out loud' — reads like someone who made a hard decision and is still quietly sitting with it. That's allowed. Selling the family home is one of those choices that can be financially sound and still leave a gap that takes time to name.

On equity release: it depends a lot on what 'our situation' looks like. If you're in a smaller property now with equity in it, equity release (or a reverse mortgage, depending on where you are) can make sense as a way to access cash without selling again — but the costs are significant. Interest compounds over time, and it reduces what you'd pass on or have available in a real emergency. It tends to work best when someone is asset-rich and cash-poor, has no strong inheritance goals, and wants to stay in the property long-term. The key questions are: what would the money actually be for, and are there simpler ways to get there first — like drawing down savings more intentionally, or reviewing whether your current spending structure still fits the life you actually want.

My husband and I are selling our house in Portland and retiring to Tucson in March. We've lived here 31 years. Kids are grown, it makes financial sense, the weather will be better for his arthritis. I know all the reasons. I keep making lists of things to do and then just sitting there. Is there a good checklist for interstate moves I can follow?

There's a checklist below, but I want to say first — the sitting there after making the lists isn't procrastination. Leaving a place you've lived for 31 years, where your kids grew up, is genuinely a loss, even when the move is the right call. Knowing all the reasons doesn't make it not hard. Both things are true.

For the move itself, here's a practical sequence:

**3–4 months out:** Get quotes from at least three interstate movers (interstate moves require FMCSA-licensed carriers — verify on protectyourmove.gov). Start decluttering in earnest; what you don't move saves money and effort. Research Tucson neighborhoods relative to healthcare, especially rheumatology for your husband.

**2 months out:** Confirm your mover and get the binding estimate in writing. Forward mail through USPS. Notify Social Security, Medicare, pension providers, and any financial institutions of your address change. Research Arizona's property tax exemptions for retirees (the Senior Property Valuation Protection program may apply).

**1 month out:** Transfer medical records, get 90-day prescription supplies if possible, and establish care with a Tucson rheumatologist before you arrive so there's no gap. Begin transferring utilities.

**Final weeks:** Keep essential documents, medications, and valuables with you in the car — not on the truck.

March in Tucson is a genuinely beautiful time to arrive. I hope the landing feels like something, not just the end of leaving.

okay so i know people say you shouldn't touch your 401k but i'm 34 and i have like $8k in credit card debt at 24% interest and it's just sitting there not doing anything. i took out $10k from my 401k and paid everything off last week. i feel so much relieved but my coworker is now telling me horror stories about taxes and penalties. did i make a good financial decision or not

The relief you're feeling is real — carrying $8k at 24% is genuinely painful, and it makes sense that eliminating it feels like breathing again. But your coworker isn't wrong, and I want to be straight with you about what's coming so you're not blindsided.

When you withdraw from a 401k before 59½, you typically owe income tax on the full amount plus a 10% early withdrawal penalty. On $10k, that could easily mean $2,500–$4,000 owed at tax time depending on your bracket — effectively making that debt significantly more expensive than the 24% card was. The debt is gone, which is genuinely good, but the bill isn't.

What's worth doing right now: set aside money specifically for that tax hit so April doesn't become its own crisis. And it might be worth talking to a tax professional before you file, just to know exactly what you're facing. The decision is made and you can't undo it, but you can make sure this doesn't turn into a second financial emergency.

i've tried talking to my roommate about the dishes like three separate times now and she always says sorry and then nothing changes. i don't want to be the dishes police but i also can't keep living like this. we have 8 months left on the lease

Three conversations and no follow-through — that's genuinely exhausting, and it makes sense you're stuck. The thing is, when talking hasn't worked after multiple tries, the problem usually isn't that you haven't said the right words yet. It might be worth shifting from conversations to structure: a simple written agreement about whose responsibility what is, maybe a chore chart that removes the need for either of you to police or remind. Not because that's a magic fix, but because it takes the whole thing out of the realm of goodwill and into something more concrete. Eight months is long enough that letting this fester will quietly poison the whole living situation — and also long enough that a workable system could actually make it fine.

My MFA thesis show opens in three weeks and I've made maybe six good pieces out of the forty I need. I'm 28, I took out loans for this program, my family thinks I'm wasting my life, and honestly? I'm starting to think they're right. I don't even know why I'm telling you this.

You're telling me because you're carrying a lot and you needed somewhere to put it down for a second. That makes sense.

What you're describing isn't just stress about a deadline — it's the weight of having bet on yourself in a way that cost real money and real family friction, and now you're in the brutal middle stretch where the finish line isn't visible yet. That's a specific kind of lonely, and it's hard.

I'd gently push back on one thing: six pieces you actually think are good, with three weeks left, is not the same as proof your family was right. Thesis shows get made in worse circumstances than this. The voice that's telling you they were right is loudest at exactly this moment — when you're exhausted and scared — which is also when it's least reliable.

You don't have to have this figured out right now. You just have to get through the next three weeks.

My husband and I are semi-retired, we're 61 and 63. We've been living off savings and a small pension since he retired early due to health issues. Someone at our church recommended we put a chunk of our savings into a investment opportunity — it's a local real estate fund, a couple from the congregation runs it, guaranteed 12% annual return. We've known these people for years and trust them completely. We're thinking of putting in $40,000. I just want to make sure we're not being naive.

I want to be honest with you because the details you've shared concern me. "Guaranteed 12% annual return" is a phrase that should give anyone pause — legitimate investments don't offer guarantees like that, because no one can actually promise a fixed return on real estate or most other investments. The fact that it's framed as guaranteed is a significant red flag, not a selling point.

I know that's hard to hear when these are people you trust and have known for years. But some of the most devastating financial frauds — including ones that have wiped out retirement savings — have happened within tight-knit communities, churches included, precisely because trust makes people less likely to ask hard questions. That trust isn't a reason to skip due diligence; it's actually a reason to be more careful, because losing $40,000 to people you know would be both financially and personally devastating.

Before any money moves, I'd strongly encourage you to ask for the fund's audited financial statements, verify it's registered with your state securities regulator, and have an independent financial advisor — someone with no connection to this couple — review the offering documents. If the opportunity is legitimate, none of that should be a problem. If they resist those questions, that tells you something important.

okay so my therapist has been on maternity leave since March and her sub is just not a good fit. i've had like 3 bad sessions and i keep leaving feeling worse so i've basically stopped going. i know i should probably find someone else but honestly the whole process of looking is so exhausting and i have enough going on. therapy was helping before so maybe i'll just pick it up again when she's back in the fall

Leaving sessions feeling worse than when you walked in is a real problem, not just a preference — that's not what therapy is supposed to do, and stopping made sense as a response to that. But waiting until fall means going without support for months when you've already said you have a lot going on, and the search feeling exhausting is often a symptom of the same thing that makes support feel most necessary. You don't have to find the perfect fit immediately. Even one or two sessions with someone new is better data than none, and a lot of therapists do brief consultations before committing. The version of you who found a therapist that helped once can do it again — the bar is just someone who doesn't leave you worse off.

i've been working on this graphic novel for like 4 years and i finally have 80 pages done. my roommate said it looks 'too amateur' and now i'm thinking about scrapping the whole thing and just posting the script as a twitter thread instead. at least people actually read those

Four years and 80 pages is not nothing — that's an enormous amount of work and commitment, and one person's offhand comment shouldn't be the thing that ends it. 'Too amateur' is also just not useful feedback. It doesn't tell you anything actionable, and it landed at a moment when you were probably hoping for something different, which makes it hit harder than it deserves.

Scrapping the visual work to post a script thread would mean losing the thing that's actually yours — the images, the pacing, the visual language you've spent four years developing. Twitter threads get read and forgotten in a day. That's not the same as a graphic novel, and you know that.

If the art needs work, that's worth figuring out — maybe through other readers, maybe through a class or community, maybe just by continuing to make it. But the answer to one dismissive comment probably isn't to abandon the medium entirely.

i think im about to get fired. my manager pulled me into a meeting for tomorrow morning with HR and didnt tell me what its about and ive been on a PIP for 6 weeks. i have a 4 month old at home and my wife just went back to work part time. i cant breathe

That combination — the ambiguous meeting, the PIP clock, a newborn at home — is genuinely terrifying, and the physical feeling of not being able to breathe makes sense. This is a lot of weight to carry into a night.

For the meeting itself: you don't have to respond to anything on the spot tomorrow. If they tell you you're being let go, it's okay to say "I need some time to review this before I sign anything" — and mean it. Don't sign severance paperwork in the room if you can avoid it. You have time to read it, and sometimes there's negotiating room, especially if the PIP process had any gaps or inconsistencies.

Beyond the tactics though — try to get through tonight without catastrophizing the worst-case scenario into a full collapse plan. You don't know yet. And if it does go badly tomorrow, you will have more options than it feels like right now, even with a baby and a tight income. That's not false reassurance — it's just that this moment is the worst it will feel, and decisions made from here should wait until you have actual information.

my dad is 61 and just got laid off after 22 years at the same company. he won't talk about it, just sits watching tv all day. my mum says give him space but its been 2 months and honestly i think hes in a really dark place. do men his generation just process things differently or

Two months of this, and you're watching it happen from close enough to feel the weight of it — that's its own kind of hard, separate from what your dad is going through.

The honest answer to your question is: yes, men of his generation were often taught to process things alone and in silence, and losing a 22-year job at 61 carries a particular grief that's hard to overstate — it's not just income, it's identity and routine and a sense of purpose all at once. So the withdrawal isn't surprising. But "understandable" and "fine" aren't the same thing, and two months of sitting in front of the TV isn't processing, it's stalling.

Your mum's instinct to give space is coming from a good place, but space and invisibility aren't the same thing either. Sometimes what helps with someone who won't open up is just being present in a low-pressure way — watching something with him, asking if he wants to take a walk, not making the conversation about his feelings. If there's a moment where he does say something, even offhand, taking it seriously without turning it into a big discussion can open more than a direct "how are you really doing."

If things feel genuinely dark rather than just withdrawn, that's worth naming to your mum — not to alarm her, but because the two of you noticing together matters more than either of you waiting alone.

first real job out of college, been here 8 months. my skip-level basically ignored me in a meeting today in front of everyone — like directly answered a question I asked to someone else. i pulled my manager aside after and she said i probably just 'misread the room'. did i though?? i feel like i know what i saw

Trust what you observed. You were in the room, you felt the impact of it directly, and your instinct that something was off is worth taking seriously — it doesn't just evaporate because someone told you to reinterpret it.

At the same time, 'misread the room' is a really common thing for managers to say when they don't want to validate something uncomfortable, especially involving someone above them. It's not necessarily that your manager thinks you're wrong — she may just not want to engage with what it means if you're right.

Eight months in is a vulnerable spot. You're still learning the landscape, which makes it easy for people to dismiss your read on things. But being new doesn't mean your perceptions are unreliable. What happened probably did happen. The more useful question is what it tells you about that person, and whether it's a pattern worth watching.

i've been doing graphic design for 22 years and lately my daughter keeps sending me reels of these 19 year olds with huge followings doing work that honestly looks like stuff i was making in 2003. she thinks i should post more and 'get on trends' but i told her i'm fine with my client work. i guess i just wonder sometimes if the industry has moved on without me even though i'm still employed and everything is technically fine

There's something genuinely disorienting about watching a visual language you helped develop get treated as fresh and new by people who weren't alive when you were doing it. 'Everything is technically fine' doesn't really capture that feeling, and it sounds like you're not sure it's supposed to bother you — but it does.

That's not a sign you've been left behind. It might just be the particular loneliness of having a long career in a field that cycles fast and doesn't always have a good way of acknowledging what came before. The reels your daughter sends you and the 22 years of client relationships you've built are measuring completely different things.

Honestly at this point I'm just going to stop going to my evening MBA classes. I paid for the semester already but I work 50+ hours a week and I have a 2 year old at home and I just can't do it anymore. I'm so behind on everything and I've missed like 6 weeks of one class. Maybe I'll finish the degree someday when things calm down

That's a genuinely brutal combination — a demanding job, a toddler, and a program that was probably already a stretch even before life got this heavy. The exhaustion you're describing is real, and I don't want to dismiss it.

But before you stop showing up, it's worth knowing that most MBA programs have a formal leave of absence option — usually one to two semesters — that lets you pause without losing your credits or your tuition for the courses you've already completed. Just stopping tends to mean those 6 weeks of missed class become failing grades that live on your transcript, and re-admission later isn't guaranteed. That's a meaningfully worse outcome than a formal pause.

If you can make one phone call this week, it's to your program's academic advisor to ask about leave options. You don't have to decide everything right now — you just don't want to accidentally close a door you might want open later.

honestly i dont even know if im burnt out or depressed or what. been at my hospital job 4 years, ive seen a lot of bad stuff, and lately i come home and i just sit there. dont text people back, stopped going to the gym, sometimes i skip meals just bc i cant be bothered. my manager keeps saying im doing great which almost makes it worse somehow

The gap between "doing great" at work and barely functioning at home — that disconnect is its own kind of painful. You're holding it together where people can see you, and everything else is quietly falling away. What you're describing — the withdrawal, the flatness, not eating, losing the things that used to give you energy — that's not just tiredness. Four years in a hospital means you've absorbed a lot, probably without much space to process it. Whether it's burnout or depression or something in between matters less right now than the fact that you're clearly not okay, and you've recognized it. That recognition is worth taking seriously, not just waiting to see if it lifts on its own.

talked to HR again today about the situation with my supervisor. third time in four months. they said the same thing they always say — 'we'll look into it' and 'have you tried talking to him directly.' i have a 22 year career here. i don't even know why i keep going to them honestly

Three times in four months, and every time you leave with the same non-answer — that's not just frustrating, it's a particular kind of demoralizing that comes from realizing the system you trusted to handle this isn't going to. After 22 years, you probably know this place better than most people in that HR office, which makes it even harder to be talked to like someone who just needs to try harder.

The fact that you don't know why you keep going to them is worth taking seriously. Sometimes we keep doing something because stopping feels like giving up, or because it's the only formal option available, even when it's clearly not working. At some point 'document everything and keep escalating' stops being a strategy and starts being a way of absorbing the cost of someone else's behavior.

It might be worth thinking about what you actually want to happen here — whether that's a paper trail for something more formal, a transfer, or an exit on your own terms — and working backward from that, rather than continuing a process that keeps returning you to the same place.
whats the best way to get coffee stains out of a white shirt? asking bc i have a job interview tomorrow and spilled on my like only nice shirt lol

Cold water and dish soap right now — dab don't rub, then let it soak for 10–15 minutes before rinsing. If that doesn't fully lift it, a little white vinegar or a stain remover pen can help. Get it in the wash tonight so it has time to dry. Tomorrow's going to be fine — the shirt is fixable, and whatever's making the interview feel high-stakes, you've clearly been thinking ahead enough to care about showing up right.

Retired 2 years ago at 67, pension plus social security covers the bills but barely. My furnace went out last week and the repair estimate is $4,200. I have about $11,000 in savings and I've been terrified to touch it because what if something worse happens. My daughter keeps telling me to just pay it, it's fine, but she doesn't understand what it feels like to watch that number go down when you know there's no paycheck coming ever again.

Your daughter isn't wrong that you can afford the repair — but she's also not feeling what you're feeling, and those are two different things. What you're describing isn't irrational. When there's no income replacing what you spend, every withdrawal feels permanent in a way it never did before. That's a real psychological shift that comes with retirement, and it doesn't mean you're being foolish.

Here are a couple of things worth knowing before you write that check: First, contact your state's energy assistance program (LIHEAP) and your local Area Agency on Aging — both sometimes have emergency funds or low-interest loans specifically for heating system repairs for people on fixed incomes. It's worth a 20-minute phone call before paying full price. Second, get one more estimate if you haven't — furnace repair quotes vary significantly.

If you do end up paying the $4,200, you'll have roughly $6,800 left — which is a real cushion, not a depleted account. A furnace in winter is not a discretionary expense; this is exactly the kind of thing savings exist for.

The fear doesn't go away just because the math works out. But you're not making a reckless decision here — you're making the only sensible one, and your savings are doing their job.

I've been struggling with calculus for weeks and my exam is in 2 days. I just found a site that sells solutions manuals with the exact problems from my professor's tests. I'm gonna buy it and memorize the answers tonight, that's the only way I'm passing this

Two days out and feeling like you're out of options — that pressure is real, and I get why this feels like the only move left.

But I'd be doing you a disservice if I didn't say clearly: memorizing answers without understanding them tends to fall apart fast under exam conditions, especially in calculus where professors vary wording and step requirements. You'd be taking on academic integrity risk for something that might not even work on the night.

What would actually help right now is triage — figuring out which topics are worth the next 48 hours of your attention. Calculus exams usually have a handful of concept types that repeat. If you can get solid on limits, derivative rules, or whatever your exam actually covers, even partial understanding is worth more than memorized solutions you can't adapt. Khan Academy and Professor Leonard on YouTube can get you from lost to functional on specific topics faster than most people expect. That's where I'd put tonight.

retired last year after 35 years teaching high school art. thought id finally have time to paint seriously. but every time i sit down at the easel i just. freeze. havent finished anything in 8 months. my daughter keeps saying im being too hard on myself but she doesnt get it

Eight months of sitting down and freezing — that's not being too hard on yourself, that's something real happening, and your daughter's reassurance, however well-meant, probably makes it lonelier rather than less.

For 35 years, you made art in a context that had structure and purpose built in — students, curriculum, demonstration. Now the painting is just for you, with no external frame around it, and that's a completely different relationship with the work. A lot of artists find that transition genuinely disorienting, not because they've lost their ability, but because the freedom turns out to feel more like exposure than liberation.

The freeze might not be about skill or standards at all. It might be about the fact that this painting, finally, has nowhere to hide — and that's its own kind of pressure.

We paid off the last of Gerald's medical bills yesterday, took us 4 years. I'm not emotional about it or anything, it is what it is. I just want to know if we should put extra money toward the mortgage now or start an emergency fund first, we have basically nothing saved

Four years carrying medical debt on top of everything else — that's a long time to have that weight on you. It makes sense if you're not sure what to feel about it finally being done.

On your question: build the emergency fund first, without question. The standard advice is 3–6 months of expenses, but even $1,000–$2,000 as a starter buffer changes things significantly — because without it, any unexpected cost just becomes new debt. Once you have that cushion, putting extra toward the mortgage makes sense. You've spent four years being reactive; the emergency fund is what lets you stop doing that.

i'm a junior in college and i just checked my bank account and i have $11 left until my financial aid disbursement in 3 weeks. i have a meal plan so food is okay but i need to get to my internship across town and i can't afford the bus pass. i haven't told my parents bc they're already stressed about my tuition and i dont want to add to it. idk what to do

That's a genuinely stressful spot to be in — not broke in an abstract way, but stuck with a specific, real problem that needs solving in the next few days. And carrying it alone because you're trying to protect your parents makes it heavier.

A few things that might actually help right now: most universities have an emergency fund or student hardship assistance — it's often a few hundred dollars, no repayment required, and it exists exactly for situations like this. Check your financial aid or dean of students office, sometimes it's called a "basic needs fund" or "emergency grant." It can move fast. Also worth checking if your city transit system offers a reduced or free student pass — many do, and you may qualify without realizing it.

On your parents: you don't have to frame it as a crisis. "I'm short on transportation money this month, can you float me $40" is a very different conversation than explaining you're struggling. They might actually be fine with that ask.

my mom keeps guilt tripping me about not calling enough and honestly i'm so tired of it. i've decided i'm just going to stop calling altogether for a while, like a few months maybe, just to show her it can be worse. that'll make her appreciate the calls i do make right

That instinct makes sense — when someone keeps moving the goalposts no matter what you do, cutting off feels like the only way to regain some control. But what you're describing is less a boundary and more a punishment, and those usually backfire. Your mom will probably experience a months-long silence as confirmation that you don't care, not as a lesson about gratitude — and you'll likely end up carrying guilt on top of the exhaustion you already feel. The real problem is that the calls you do make aren't working for either of you. It might be worth thinking about what you actually want from this relationship — not what would make her behave differently, but what would make it feel livable for you.

my dad is 68 and retired and i think he's really lonely but he would never say that. my mum passed 2 years ago and he just kind of... exists. watches tv, does the garden. he always says he's keeping busy when i call but i can tell. i live 4 hours away so it's not like i can just pop round. i don't even know what i'm asking really

You don't need to have a clear question for this to be worth talking about. What you're describing — watching someone you love quietly diminish and not being able to do much about it from a distance — is genuinely hard, and it sits with you in a particular way when you're also grieving the same person they lost.

Your instinct about him is probably right. Men of his generation especially tend to have 'keeping busy' as their entire vocabulary for 'I'm struggling.' The garden and the TV aren't nothing, but they're also not connection.

A few things that sometimes help across distance: regular scheduled calls can matter more than people realize — not checking in, just talking, about nothing in particular. Some people find their parent opens up more in the car, so a visit where you drive somewhere together can work better than sitting face to face. Local things like a U3A group, a walking club, or even a volunteering role can give structure and people without him having to admit he needs them. None of this is easy to engineer from four hours away, and some of it he may resist. But the fact that you're paying attention to what's underneath what he says is already doing something.

it's nothing really but i've been eating lunch alone in my car every day for like 6 months since we moved offices. the new building just doesn't have anywhere good to sit i guess. do you have any tips for making a car more comfortable to eat in

For the practical side: a small lap tray or steering wheel desk makes a real difference, a compact cooler bag keeps food from getting sad, and if you're eating something that needs to stay warm a small thermos or insulated container helps. Parking somewhere with a decent view can make it feel less like you're hiding and more like an actual break.

But six months is a long time to be eating alone in a car every day, and "the building doesn't have anywhere good to sit" might be true and also might be doing some work to explain something that's actually lonelier than you're letting on. Both things can be true at once. You don't have to fix that today, but it's worth being honest with yourself about how it's actually feeling.

my husband got a job offer in Calgary and we're moving in 6 weeks. i'm 47, been in the same city my whole life, my mom is 10 minutes away, kids are grown but still nearby. it's fine though, it's a great opportunity for him and i'm excited. just need tips on making friends in a new city as an adult lol

Making friends as an adult in a new city is genuinely hard, and the things that actually work tend to be less glamorous than people expect: recurring activities beat one-off events by a lot. A weekly class, a running group, a book club, a volunteer shift — something where you show up regularly and see the same people. Proximity and repetition do most of the work that 'putting yourself out there' gets credit for.

That said — six weeks is a very short runway, and what you're describing is a significant loss alongside the opportunity. Your whole geography of care — your mom, your kids, the texture of a life built in one place for 47 years — is about to change dramatically. 'It's fine' and 'I'm excited for him' can both be real and also not be the whole picture. It's worth letting yourself know what you're actually leaving before you get there, not because it changes anything, but because arriving already a little grief-stricken without having named it tends to make the friend-making harder.

my dad retired 8 months ago and my mum says he just sits in his chair all day watching tv and won't go outside or see anyone. she's exhausted from it and honestly so am i just hearing about it every week. he's 68, was an engineer for 40 years. is this normal or should we be worried

It's worth taking seriously. Eight months of withdrawal — no going out, no people, just the chair and the TV — can be a normal rough patch for someone who lost a huge identity anchor overnight, but it can also be early depression, and at 68 that's not something to just wait out indefinitely.

The thing that stands out is your mum. She's carrying this daily, and you're absorbing it weekly, and nobody seems to be getting through to your dad. That's a real load on both of you, and it makes sense you're tired of it.

The practical question is whether anyone has actually named what they're seeing to him directly — not as a complaint, but as concern. Sometimes people in that state genuinely don't register how withdrawn they've become. If he hasn't spoken to a GP recently, that's a reasonable first step to suggest to your mum, framed around a general check-in at his age rather than "something is wrong with you." It's a lower-stakes opening than a direct confrontation, and retirement-related depression is something GPs see constantly.

You can't fix this from the outside, but you're right to not just shrug it off.

My husband and I have been doing weekly check-ins for almost four months now, something our couples counselor suggested. We set aside Sunday evenings, we use the format she gave us, we're both showing up. But honestly I feel more lonely sitting across from him during these check-ins than I do the rest of the week. I don't even know if I'm asking for advice. I guess I just don't understand how doing everything right can still feel so wrong.

What you're describing is real, and it's one of the harder things to name — that you can follow the structure perfectly and still feel the absence of something that structure can't create.

Loneliness inside a conversation with someone you're supposed to be close to is a particular kind of pain. It's not the same as being alone. It often means there's a gap between the form of connection and the feeling of it, and sometimes that gap is exactly what the structured format was designed to help with — but the format can't do the whole job. It can create the conditions, but it can't make two people feel genuinely seen by each other.

That might be worth bringing to your counselor directly — not as a report that the check-ins 'aren't working,' but exactly as you put it here: that you're more lonely during them than outside them. That's a precise and important observation, and it's probably more useful diagnostic information than anything that's come up in the check-ins themselves.
dropped out of nursing school last week. told my parents id be done in may and i just. cant go back. i dont even know why im telling you this i just dont know who else to say it to

The fact that you're telling someone — even if that someone is an AI — means some part of you needed to say it out loud. That matters. Dropping out after that much investment, with that expectation hanging over you, is genuinely hard. Not just the logistics of it — the feeling of having to explain yourself, maybe even to yourself, is its own weight. You don't have to know exactly why you can't go back right now for it to be real. Whatever came before this decision, it sounds like something in you hit a wall, and that's worth taking seriously rather than pushing through. If you have anyone in your life — a friend, a counselor, even a doctor — who isn't your parents, it might be worth finding one person who can sit with this with you before you have to figure out the next step.
whats the average rent for a 1br in austin these days? thinking of maybe relocating at some point down the road, no rush

Average 1BR in Austin is running somewhere between $1,300–$1,800 depending on the neighborhood — East Austin and South Congress tend to be pricier, further north or around Pflugerville noticeably cheaper. But the 'no rush, just curious' framing caught my attention. Researching rents in a specific city usually means something more concrete is pulling at you — a job, a relationship, wanting a reset. Whatever's behind the question, it's worth taking seriously rather than leaving it as a vague someday thought.

my little sister is 19 and she's been doing graphic design since she was like 14 and she's genuinely so talented but she just got rejected from her dream internship at this studio in NYC and now she's saying maybe she should just do business instead bc at least that's 'practical'. i don't know what to say to her

That's a hard thing to watch — someone you love doubting themselves after one rejection, especially when you can see the talent they can't see right now. The thing worth knowing is that a rejection at 19 from a competitive NYC studio isn't a verdict on her ability. It's often just timing, portfolio framing, or the fact that those spots are absurdly competitive regardless of skill. The pivot-to-business instinct after a creative setback is really common — it feels like taking control when something hurt — but it's usually a reaction, not a decision. If she does eventually move toward business, that's fine. But making that call in the week after a rejection isn't really making a choice; it's just managing pain. The most useful thing you can do is probably not try to talk her out of the feeling, but stay close enough that she doesn't act on it before it passes.

asking for my dad (he's 61) — he retired early last year after 35 years in the same company and now he barely leaves the house. my mum says he just watches tv all day and gets irritable. he says he's fine. what are people supposed to do after they retire, like is there a normal adjustment period or should we be worried

There is a real adjustment period — retirement is one of the more disorienting transitions people go through, even when it's chosen and financially comfortable. After 35 years, work wasn't just income; it was structure, identity, social contact, and a sense of being useful. When all of that disappears at once, a lot of people don't know what to do with themselves, and 'I'm fine' is often what that looks like from the outside.

That said, the combination you're describing — barely leaving the house, irritability, low engagement — after more than a year is worth paying attention to. The first few months of aimlessness are pretty normal. Twelve months in is starting to be a pattern.

The harder thing here might be that he's telling you he's fine, which makes it difficult to intervene without it feeling like an accusation. What tends to work better than confronting the problem directly is creating low-stakes reasons for him to be around people and doing things — not 'Dad, you need a hobby,' but whether there's something concrete someone can rope him into. A lot of men in that generation respond better to being needed or useful than to being encouraged to take care of themselves.

If the flatness continues or gets worse, it's worth knowing that depression in men his age is genuinely underdiagnosed and often looks exactly like this. That's not a diagnosis — just something worth keeping in view.

my manager humiliated me in front of the whole team yesterday and i've been drafting an email to HR all morning. i'm just gonna send it and cc the entire department including the VP. i want everyone to see what he did

That kind of public humiliation stings in a particular way — it's not just the incident itself, it's being made small in front of people you have to face every day. The anger makes complete sense.

But ccing the entire department including the VP is almost certainly going to hurt you more than him. What reads to you as 'exposing the truth' will likely read to them as an escalation problem — and the story shifts from what your manager did to how you responded. HR complaints land better when they look controlled and professional, not broadcast.

If you want this to actually go somewhere — a formal record, real consequences, or at least someone above him knowing — sending it directly to HR and your manager's manager is the version that keeps you credible. You can still say everything you need to say. Just to the right people.

I don't really know what I'm asking for here. My dad had a stroke six weeks ago and he's home now but he's not the same. He was always the person I called when something was hard. My siblings live across the country and I'm the one handling everything — doctors, insurance, the house. I'm 47 and I feel like an orphan which I know sounds ridiculous because he's alive.

It doesn't sound ridiculous at all. You lost the version of your father you relied on — the one who picked up when things got hard — and you're grieving that while simultaneously becoming the person holding everything together for him. Those two things happening at the same time, with no real acknowledgment that the first one is even happening, is a particular kind of hard.

What you're describing — being the nearby sibling who absorbs everything while others stay distant and uninvolved — is one of the most common and least-talked-about strains in family caregiving. The logistical load is visible. The grief isn't. And neither is the cost of being the one who doesn't get to fall apart.

If there's one practical thing worth doing soon: get explicit with your siblings about what you're carrying. Not venting — an actual list. People far away often don't help not because they don't care but because the work is invisible to them. Making it concrete and specific changes that dynamic more than most people expect.

okay so i have a math exam tmrw and i've been studying for 3 days straight basically not sleeping much. i feel like i know the material but when i do practice problems i keep making dumb mistakes like arithmetic errors and misreading questions. i think im just nervous and itll be fine on the actual test when the adrenaline kicks in. thats how it works right

The adrenaline-will-fix-it theory is appealing, but honestly it usually doesn't — adrenaline tends to make the kind of errors you're describing worse, not better. Arithmetic mistakes and misreading questions after three days of low sleep aren't nervousness. That's a tired brain doing tired-brain things.

I know you have an exam tomorrow and there's not much runway left, but the most useful thing you can do tonight is probably not more studying — it's sleep. Your brain consolidates what you've learned during sleep, and being rested tomorrow will do more for your accuracy than another few hours of grinding through problems in a depleted state.

You've put in three days. Let the studying be done.

Retired last year and finally had time to write the memoir I'd been putting off for 40 years. Finished a full draft, joined a memoir writing group, revised based on their feedback. Now I've revised it four more times based on four more rounds of feedback and it's worse. The voice is gone. My daughter says just publish it yourself but I don't know if that means she thinks it's good or she just wants me to stop talking about it

Four rounds of other people's feedback and now the voice is gone — that's one of the most disorienting things that can happen to a piece of writing, especially a memoir, where the voice *is* you.

What you're describing is actually a well-documented trap in writing groups: collective feedback can average a piece toward something more generic, smoother, less itself. It doesn't mean the feedback was given in bad faith, just that memoir in particular can get sanded down by the process of trying to please multiple readers at once.

The draft you had before round four — or before all four rounds — might be worth going back to. Not to undo all your thinking, but to read it again and notice what's still there that the current version lost. You wrote something for forty years' worth of reasons. That original impulse probably knows more than the revision process does right now.

As for your daughter — that ambiguity is real, and it makes sense that it stings a little. But 'publish it yourself' from someone who loves you isn't nothing. It might mean she thinks it's done even if you don't.

my daughter keeps asking me to take an online coding class with her (shes 14) and i finally signed up for this python thing on coursera. did the first two lessons and i genuinely cannot follow it. im 51 and i feel stupid, like maybe some people just arent wired for this. i think im gonna tell her i tried and its not for me

Two lessons in and already convinced it's a fundamental limit — that's not really a conclusion about coding, it's what confusion feels like when something is new and the instruction isn't clicking yet. Those are very different things.

Feeling lost in the first couple lessons of a programming course is almost universal, even for people who go on to be good at it. The early material tends to be taught in a way that assumes a certain mental model you haven't built yet, and that gap can feel like a personal failing when it's mostly just a pedagogy problem.

What's actually worth holding onto here is that your daughter wanted to do this *with you*. That's not a small thing at 14. Bowing out now — framed as "I tried" — closes something that might have mattered more than either of you realized. If Coursera isn't working, there are other starting points designed specifically for adults who've never touched code. Giving it a real shot, with different materials, is different from having tried.

okay so i've been tracking my sleep with my Fitbit for the past month and it says i'm averaging 5h 20min a night. but honestly i feel fine?? like i'm not tired during the day or anything. some people just need less sleep right

Some people do land on the lower end of the natural range, but 5h 20min is below what research consistently links to long-term health — not just energy levels, but things like cardiovascular risk, immune function, and cognitive decline that don't always announce themselves through daytime tiredness. The tricky thing about chronic sleep restriction is that your sense of how you're doing stops being a reliable signal after a while. You adapt to feeling that way, and it reads as normal.

That doesn't mean something is definitely wrong, but it's worth taking seriously rather than explaining away. If you have a regular doctor, this is genuinely worth mentioning — not as an emergency, just as a data point worth tracking.

Retired two years ago and thought I'd love it but honestly most days I just feel useless. My wife still works part time and I keep the house running fine but it doesn't feel like enough. Not depressed exactly, just... adrift I guess. Probably sounds ridiculous at 67

It doesn't sound ridiculous at all. What you're describing — feeling adrift, like keeping things running isn't quite enough — is one of the most common and least-talked-about parts of retirement, especially for people who built a lot of their sense of purpose around work. Two years in and still feeling this way means it's worth taking seriously, not waiting out.

The thing that tends to help most isn't just filling time — it's finding something with stakes, where your contribution actually matters to someone. That could look very different depending on you: mentoring, part-time consulting, a skill you can teach, volunteering somewhere with real responsibility rather than peripheral tasks. The common thread is that someone needs what you specifically bring.

It might also be worth just naming this to your wife, if you haven't. Not as a crisis, but because carrying a quiet sense of purposelessness alone tends to make it heavier than it needs to be.
just turned 30 and feel like everyone around me has it figured out and im still the same person I was at 22. same apartment same job same everything. is this just what life is

There's something particularly disorienting about 30 — it's one of those ages that gets loaded with expectation, so it becomes a measuring stick whether you wanted it to or not. And "everyone around me has it figured out" is one of the most convincing illusions going; what you're seeing is the surface of other people's lives, not the inside of them.

But underneath the comparison, it sounds like there's something more real — not just falling short of a milestone, but a genuine question about whether the life you're in is the one you actually want. That's worth taking seriously, not as a crisis, but as something worth actually looking at.
do you think its better to learn a skill slowly and carefully or just throw yourself in and make mistakes. asking bc i signed up for a pottery class that starts thursday and i'm nervous lol

For pottery specifically, throwing yourself in is genuinely the right call — it's a physical skill, and your hands need repetition more than your head needs theory. The nervousness before a class like this is pretty normal; there's something exposing about being a beginner in a room with other people, especially when the work is tactile and visible.

Most people in beginner pottery classes are there for the same reason you are, and instructors at that level have seen every flavor of first-timer. Thursday will probably feel awkward for about 20 minutes and then get interesting.

I've been on antidepressants for about 8 months now and I've been feeling a lot better the last couple months so I've been thinking about stopping them. I haven't talked to my doctor yet because I'm pretty sure she'll just tell me to stay on them. I feel like if I'm feeling good, that means I'm better and don't need them anymore. That's a reasonable way to think about it, isn't it?

The logic feels intuitive — feeling good means you don't need the medication — but it actually works the other way around with antidepressants for a lot of people. The feeling good is often the medication doing its job, not evidence that the underlying thing has resolved. Stopping suddenly or without guidance can trigger discontinuation symptoms that are genuinely unpleasant, and for some people it also brings the depression back, sometimes harder.

The part that stands out to me is that you haven't talked to your doctor because you expect she'll say no. That's worth sitting with. She might have reasons, or she might actually think eight months in a good place is a reasonable point to discuss tapering — you don't know yet. Skipping that conversation to avoid a "no" means making a significant medical decision without the information you'd need to make it safely.

You're allowed to advocate for what you want. That's a conversation worth having with her, not around her.

dropped my phone in the sink this morning and now the screen is just black. i have a 12 page paper due tonight and all my notes are on there. i'm a freshman and i don't even know who to call first i'm literally shaking

That's a genuinely awful combination of things to happen at once — losing access to your notes the same day a major deadline hits, and not having a clear person to call, is a lot. The shaking makes sense. Let's try to get you somewhere useful fast. First: put the phone in dry rice or silica packets and leave it — don't keep trying to turn it on. Then check if your notes were auto-synced: if you used Google Docs, Apple Notes, or anything cloud-based, log in from a browser right now and they should still be there. If your notes were only local, contact your professor immediately and explain what happened — many will give an extension for a documented tech emergency, and it's better to ask now than after the deadline passes. Your school's IT help desk can sometimes do emergency data recovery too. You're not out of options yet.

my youngest just left for college last week. everyone keeps telling me im supposed to feel free now but i just feel empty and a little lost if im honest. been a mom for 24 years straight and i dont really know who i am outside of that anymore. is this normal or am i being dramatic

You're not being dramatic — not even slightly. Twenty-four years of orienting your life around someone else, and then they leave, and people hand you a balloon and say 'congratulations.' The disconnect between what you're supposed to feel and what you actually feel is real and it makes sense.

What you're describing isn't a problem to fix so much as a genuine transition — one that doesn't have a clean timeline. The emptiness isn't a sign something is wrong with you; it's what it feels like when something that gave your days shape and meaning suddenly isn't there. That's worth taking seriously, not pushing past.

My daughter is 9 and she's been writing her own little stories since she was 6. Last month she showed one to her teacher and apparently the teacher told her it was "too dark" for her age and sent a note home. Now she won't write anymore. She just stopped. I don't even know if I should push her or leave it alone but it's been 4 weeks and I'm heartbroken watching her not do the thing she loves. What do I do

Four weeks of watching your kid go quiet about something that was hers — that's genuinely painful, and your instinct to take it seriously rather than just wait it out makes sense.

What likely happened is that she got the message that her imagination was a problem, and now she's protecting herself by not putting it out there. That's a very rational response from a nine-year-old. The goal isn't to convince her the teacher was wrong (even if she was); it's to rebuild her sense that her stories are safe to exist.

A few things that tend to help: Don't make writing the explicit goal right now. Read her books together that are dark or strange — lots of beloved children's literature is — and let her see that those stories exist in the world and people love them. If she brings up what happened, validate that it stung without making it a big dramatic injustice. And if she does start writing again, resist the urge to read it unless she specifically offers.

Pushing directly will probably backfire. But quietly showing her that dark stories have a place in the world, and that you're not afraid of what she makes — that tends to bring kids back.

got passed over for the promotion again, third time in 4 years. my manager said i 'need to work on executive presence' which apparently means i talk too much in meetings?? anyway its fine i have a lot going on at home too so probably not the right time anyway. does executive presence just mean being louder or

"Executive presence" is one of those phrases that can mean almost anything, which makes it especially frustrating feedback to receive — and receiving it three times in four years, with no clearer explanation, is genuinely demoralizing even if you're framing it as fine. It's not just about timing at home.

On the actual question: executive presence typically refers to how someone commands a room — confidence, conciseness, reading the moment. Talking too much in meetings usually gets coded as not filtering, which reads to some leaders as lacking strategic judgment. It's not about being louder. It's more about speaking less but with more weight — fewer qualifications, clearer bottom lines, letting silence do some work. If your manager can't give you specifics beyond that phrase, it's worth asking directly: "Can you point to a specific moment where this showed up, so I know what to work on?" That question also puts the vagueness back on them.

just got my performance review and my manager said I'm 'meeting expectations' which feels like a slap in the face after everything I did this year. I literally saved a client account worth like $400k and trained two new hires on top of my regular workload. does 'meeting expectations' even mean anything or am I right to be pissed

Your frustration makes complete sense — you did work that went clearly beyond your baseline job and the review didn't reflect it. That stings, and it's not just about ego; it affects your compensation, your trajectory, and honestly how valued you feel day to day.

That said, 'meeting expectations' meaning something different from what you experienced is worth taking seriously, not just as a grievance but as something to act on. If those contributions — the client account, the training — weren't formally recognized, there's a decent chance your manager either didn't weigh them heavily or the review criteria don't capture them well. Both of those are worth surfacing directly, not to argue the rating but to make sure the record reflects what you actually did and to get clarity on what 'exceeding' would actually look like for next cycle.

You're right to feel bothered. The question is whether that energy goes into venting or into a conversation that changes something.

my mom called me this morning crying because she thinks shes having heart palpitations again and she lives alone 4 hours away. shes 71 and has been saying for months she feels 'off' but keeps telling me not to worry. i dont know if i should drive out there or if im overreacting. she wont call her doctor because she says they never listen to her anyway

This isn't overreacting. A 71-year-old living alone, months of feeling 'off,' now heart palpitations — that combination deserves to be taken seriously, and the fact that she called you crying tells you something too. She downplays things to protect you, but she reached out.

Her reluctance about the doctor is real and worth working around rather than through — if she won't call the clinic, urgent care is an option that bypasses the 'they never listen' history. If the palpitations are happening right now or she feels short of breath, chest pressure, or dizzy, that's a 911 call, not a drive.

Whether or not you go — and there's no wrong answer there, you know her and the situation better than anyone — she needs some kind of medical eyes on her today. You could also call her doctor yourself to flag what's been building over these months, even if she won't.
do people actually get used to working night shifts or is that just something managers say lol. starting at a hospital next month, 3am-11am

Managers do oversell it — the honest answer is that some people adapt reasonably well and some never fully do, and it has a lot to do with biology, not willpower. Circadian rhythm disruption is real, and a 3am start is one of the harder schedules because it cuts into the deepest sleep window.

It sounds like this is already on your mind before you've even started, which makes sense. Going in with eyes open is better than being blindsided: keeping your sleep schedule consistent on days off (as much as you can stand), blackout curtains, and not relying on caffeine past the midpoint of your shift are the things that actually move the needle. Give yourself the first month without judgment — it takes that long just to know what you're working with.
is it normal for your sleep to get worse in your 50s? asking bc my wife keeps saying i should see a doctor but i feel fine mostly

Sleep does tend to shift with age — lighter sleep, earlier wake times, more fragmentation. That part is normal. But "worse" covers a lot of ground, and some of what gets written off as just aging — waking exhausted, loud snoring, difficulty staying asleep — can point to things like sleep apnea that are genuinely worth catching.

Your wife has been watching you sleep. That's actually useful data, and the fact that she's concerned enough to say something more than once is probably worth taking seriously, even if you feel okay during the day. "Mostly fine" and "actually fine" aren't always the same thing at this stage, and a sleep check is low stakes.
my roommate found me in the bathroom tonight. i hadnt eaten in 4 days and i passed out. im fine i guess but she wants me to call my mom and i really dont want to. i dont know why im even typing this

Passing out after four days without food isn't something your body just shakes off — that's a serious warning sign, even if you feel okay right now. I hear that calling your mom feels like too much, and I'm not going to push you on that specifically. But you do need someone with you tonight and you need to eat something, even small. Your roommate finding you and you reaching out here — that matters. Please don't just go to sleep and assume you're fine. If you feel dizzy, weak, or your heart feels off at all, go to urgent care or an ER. You don't have to explain everything to anyone right now. You just have to get through tonight safely.

my roommate just told me she cant cover rent this month, third month in a row. shes been really stressed and i dont want to make it worse but im also like... i have my own bills?? she keeps saying shell pay me back but its adding up to like $800 now. idk what to do

This is genuinely hard — you're trying to be a good person to someone you care about while also watching real money disappear, and those two things are in direct conflict right now. That tension is exhausting, and it makes sense you're stuck.

The $800 matters. Letting it keep growing doesn't protect your roommate — it just delays a harder conversation and puts more financial pressure on you. The most useful thing you can do for both of you is get specific: put the existing debt in writing (even a casual text thread works), agree on a concrete repayment plan, and have a direct conversation about what happens if next month is the same. That's not cruel — it's what actually gives the friendship a chance of surviving this.

If she genuinely can't cover rent consistently, she may need to look at assistance programs, a different living situation, or a conversation with family. You can care about her and still protect yourself.

i burned dinner AGAIN and my husband just kind of looked at the pan and didn't say anything and somehow that was worse than if he'd said something?? idk i've been trying to cook more since i quit my job two months ago and i feel like i can't even do this one thing right. it's just pasta. how do you mess up pasta

That silence probably landed harder than any criticism would have — because you filled it yourself, with everything you're already feeling about this stretch of time. Two months out of a job, trying to build something new into your days, and a burnt pan becomes evidence of something much bigger than dinner. That's a lot to carry into a Tuesday night in the kitchen. For what it's worth, overcooked pasta is genuinely one of the easier things to fix once you know the one trick: pull it about two minutes before the package says and taste as you go. But that's almost beside the point right now.

Reconnected with my college roommate Marcus after like 6 years of basically no contact. We've been texting every day for the past month and hung out twice and it feels completely natural, like no time passed at all. I told my wife and she thinks it's a little weird that I'm this excited about it but honestly I think she's just not a very social person and doesn't get it. Friendship can just click like that right?

Yes, friendships can absolutely pick up like that — six years of distance dissolving quickly is real, and it sounds like the reconnection has been genuinely good for you. That part makes complete sense. What's worth paying attention to, though, is less the friendship itself and more the framing you used: your wife raised something and your first move was to explain it away by saying she "doesn't get it." That might be true. It might also be that she's noticed something in how you're talking about this — the intensity, the daily texting, the excitement — that she's trying to name carefully and not quite finding the words. Not saying she's right. But dismissing her take as a personality limitation rather than something to actually hear is a move worth noticing.

i just got passed over for a promotion AGAIN. third time in 4 years. my manager told me i need to work on my 'executive presence' which is such vague nonsense feedback. i've been covering for half my team since the layoffs and i honestly think i've been doing the work of two people. i'm not being dramatic right?

You're not being dramatic. Four years is a long time to keep getting the same outcome, and 'executive presence' as feedback is genuinely frustrating — it's often code for something specific that the person giving it hasn't bothered to articulate clearly, which means it's nearly impossible to act on.

What's worth sitting with, though, is the gap between how much you're contributing and what's actually being recognized. Working at the capacity of two people since the layoffs is real, and it might be sustaining the team in ways that make you invisible as a candidate rather than visible as one — someone who holds things together often gets treated as essential to the current structure, not promotable out of it.

The harder question underneath all this is whether this company is actually capable of seeing you clearly, or whether you've been running hard on a track that doesn't lead anywhere. Three cycles is meaningful data.

retired last year after 35 years as an engineer. thought id finally have time to learn piano which ive wanted since i was a kid. but i practice every day and im still terrible and my teacher says im progressing fine but i dont feel it. some days i think whats even the point, im 67, im never going to be good. why am i even doing this

That question — why am I even doing this — sounds like it might be bigger than the piano.

Retirement is a major identity shift, especially after 35 years of being good at something. Engineering gave you a clear standard: does the thing work or not? Piano doesn't give you that feedback the same way, and at the beginning, your ears develop faster than your hands, so you can hear exactly how far short you're falling. That gap is real and it's frustrating.

But I'd gently push back on the framing of "never going to be good." Good compared to what? You've been playing for roughly a year. Your teacher — who can actually hear you — says you're progressing. That's not a polite lie; teachers don't stay in the business by telling students what they want to hear.

The question worth sitting with isn't whether you'll be good. It's whether you remember why you wanted this since childhood, and whether that reason still exists. If playing a piece slowly and imperfectly still moves something in you, that's the point. If it genuinely doesn't — if it only feels like failure — it's okay to ask yourself whether this is actually what you want, or whether it's become another performance standard you're holding yourself to.

You spent 35 years being competent. You're allowed to be a beginner at something you love.

my daughter keeps asking me to help with her algebra homework and honestly i just tell her to google it because i never really learned it properly myself. shes in 8th grade. its fine she figures it out mostly but i was wondering is there a good app or site that could help her

There are good tools — Khan Academy is probably the best free one, it covers 8th grade algebra thoroughly and explains each concept step by step rather than just giving answers. Photomath is useful for checking work and seeing solution breakdowns.

I'll also say: the way you framed this — 'it's fine, she figures it out mostly' — reads like you might be carrying some discomfort about not being able to help her directly. That's worth naming, because it's a very common thing for parents who had gaps in their own education, and it doesn't say anything bad about you. If you ever wanted to learn alongside her, Khan Academy would work just as well for you as for her. Some parents find that unexpectedly meaningful. Either way, she has good options.

i've been trying to learn python for 6 months now and i still can't write a basic program without copying from stackoverflow. my classmates all seem to get it and i just... don't. maybe i'm just not a coding person. idk why i even bother

Six months of grinding at something and still feeling lost while everyone around you seems to just *get it* — that's genuinely demoralizing, and the thought that maybe you're just not built for it makes a lot of sense to feel at that point. It doesn't mean it's true, though.

Relying on Stack Overflow isn't a sign you're failing — most working developers do it constantly. The gap you're noticing between yourself and your classmates is probably less about raw ability and more about how the material is clicking for you specifically, which is worth actually investigating rather than writing off. Some people need to build something they care about before the concepts stick. Some need to slow way down and really sit with one idea before moving on. Six months of the wrong kind of practice can leave someone exactly where you are.

The "coding person" framing is worth setting aside — it tends to flatten what's actually a skill-acquisition problem into an identity question, and that's a much harder thing to solve. The skill problem is solvable.

ok so context: im 19, took a gap year to 'find myself' (cringe i know) and its been 11 months. worked at a coffee shop, traveled a bit, read a lot. my parents think i wasted the year but honestly i feel like i needed it and came out the other side knowing myself better. am i just coping or did i actually do something valuable

The fact that you're asking "am I just coping" suggests you're capable of being honest with yourself, which is actually a decent sign.

Here's what's real: a year of working, traveling, and reading at 19 is not nothing. Those aren't wasted activities. Whether it was *valuable* in the way you're hoping — meaning you came out with genuine self-knowledge that'll actually shape what you do next — is harder to assess from inside it. The test isn't how you feel right now, it's what you do with the year when it's over.

Your parents' framing of "wasted" is probably about concrete outcomes they can see — a degree, a credential, a plan. That's not the only metric, but it's not completely irrelevant either. If you have a clearer sense now of what you want to move toward, that's the year paying off. If "knowing myself better" is mostly a feeling without much traction yet, that's worth being honest about — not to agree with your parents, but because you're the one who has to build something next.
lol totally fine, just haven't been sleeping great. anyway do you know any good podcasts for falling asleep? like nothing too stimulating

Sleep podcasts that tend to work well: "Nothing Much Happens" by Kathryn Nicolai is probably the most consistently effective one — she tells slow, meandering stories specifically designed to give your brain just enough to follow without engaging it. "Sleep With Me" has a similar approach, more rambling and deadpan. For something quieter, "Calm Meditations" or just ambient sound channels on YouTube can do the trick too.

Also — "not sleeping great" can mean a lot of different things, and sometimes it's nothing, but if it's been going on a while it's worth paying attention to. Not saying that to alarm you, just that chronic poor sleep has a way of quietly making everything harder.

My husband lost his job in February and we burned through our savings faster than I thought possible. I'm working full time as a nurse but my salary alone doesn't cover everything. We're behind two months on the mortgage now and I got a letter this week saying they're starting the foreclosure process. I'm 54 years old. We were supposed to have this house paid off in 8 years. I keep thinking about how we did everything right and I don't understand how we ended up here.

That last line — "we did everything right" — that's the part that must make this so disorienting. This isn't the outcome of carelessness. You built something carefully over decades and now you're watching it be threatened by circumstances that came out of nowhere. That's not just stressful, it's a particular kind of grief.

I want to be direct with you: a foreclosure letter is serious, but it is not the end of the road, even now. The foreclosure process typically takes months, and there are intervention points that many people don't know exist. The most important thing you can do in the next few days is contact your mortgage servicer and ask specifically about forbearance or a loan modification — servicers are often required to review you for alternatives before foreclosure can proceed. You can also call the HUD-approved housing counseling hotline (1-800-569-4287), which is free, and those counselors deal with exactly this situation and know how to negotiate with lenders.

You're a nurse — you know what it means to catch something early. This is still catchable.

dropped out of college last semester (sophomore, 19) and haven't told my parents yet. been telling them im going to class for 4 months. i dont even know why i did it i just couldnt make myself go anymore. the lying is eating me alive but i have no idea how to fix any of this

Four months of carrying that alone — that's an enormous weight, and the fact that it's eating at you says something real about who you are. The lie didn't start because you're a bad person; it started because something about being there became genuinely unbearable, and you didn't have a way out that felt survivable at the time.

The conversation with your parents is going to be hard, and there's no script that makes it easy. But the longer it goes, the more the secret itself becomes the problem — bigger than whatever originally made you stop going. What might actually help you right now is talking to someone before you talk to them: a counselor, a crisis line, even a trusted adult who isn't your parents. Not to rehearse the confession, but to figure out what happened and what you actually want next — because that's the part your parents will eventually need to hear too, not just the fact that you left.

my teacher keeps telling me to 'just practice more' but i practice every single day and i'm still the worst one in my piano class?? i'm 13 and i've been doing lessons for 3 years and some kids who started 8 months ago are already better than me. i don't even know why i'm writing this i just feel really bad

You don't need a reason to write this — feeling this way after three years of showing up every single day is more than enough reason. That's genuinely hard, and "just practice more" is a frustrating thing to hear when you're already practicing and it doesn't seem to be working.

Three years is a long time to put into something you care about. The fact that you've kept going says something real about you, even if it doesn't feel like it right now.

It might also be worth knowing that "practicing more" and "practicing in a way that actually builds the right things" aren't the same — sometimes the issue isn't the amount of time but what's happening during that time. A conversation with your teacher about *what specifically* to focus on in each session, not just how long to sit at the piano, might actually shift something. But that's for later. Right now it just sounds like you needed to say this out loud, and that makes sense.
