Dad had a second heart attack in February, hes 68. Cardiologist wants him on a strict diet and says he needs to walk 30 mins a day but he just... won't. Says he's too tired and that at his age whats the point. Mom is at her wits end. I live 4 hours away and feel completely useless. Is there anything that actually works for getting someone like him to take this seriously

That "what's the point at my age" line is worth paying attention to — it's not just stubbornness. After a second heart attack, a lot of people carry something that looks like resignation or low-grade depression, and that can make even small behavior changes feel impossible. It's different from just not wanting to try.

The most effective thing isn't usually more information or more pressure from family — he probably knows the stakes. What tends to work better is a different kind of conversation with his cardiologist: asking them to specifically address the fatigue (which can itself be cardiac, medication-related, or mood-related) and to have a direct talk with your dad about what his quality of life goals actually are. Sometimes hearing "here's what following this plan could let you keep doing" is more motivating than "here's what happens if you don't."

For your mom, four hours away or not — you being in contact with her regularly matters. She's managing this up close and that's exhausting. You're not useless; you're just not there in the way you wish you could be, which is a different thing.

If your dad is open to it at all, cardiac rehab programs (which his cardiologist can refer him to) are often better than solo walks — there's structure, monitoring, and other people in the same situation. That sometimes lands differently than a family member asking him to go outside.

my daughter keeps telling me to 'just write the book mom' like its easy. im 61 and i have been carrying this story around for 30 years and every time i sit down to start i write two pages and then i delete them. i think maybe i waited too long and the window closed or something. i dont know why im even telling you this

You're telling me this because thirty years is a long time to carry something, and that weight deserves to be said out loud somewhere.

I don't think the window closed — but I do think something real is getting in the way, and 'just write it' doesn't touch that. Two pages and delete, over and over, usually isn't a discipline problem. It's often that the story matters so much that nothing you put down feels worthy of it yet. After three decades of living with it internally, the draft version will always feel smaller than the version in your head. That's not failure, it's just the nature of moving something from inside to outside.

The question isn't whether you waited too long. It's whether the version of you who has lived sixty-one years — including all the time with this story — might actually be exactly the right person to write it now.
lol totally fine, just haven't been sleeping great. anyway my roommate keeps leaving dishes in the sink and i need like a script for how to bring it up without it being weird

Not sleeping well has a way of making everything feel harder to navigate — including conversations that would normally feel pretty low-stakes. Here's something that tends to work without making it a whole thing: pick a neutral moment (not right after you've spotted the dishes), keep it specific rather than general, and frame it around what works for you both rather than what she's doing wrong. Something like "Hey, I've been trying to keep the sink clear — can we figure out a system?" is usually enough. It's direct, it doesn't assign blame, and it gives her somewhere to go with it. Hope you get some actual rest soon.

ok so i know everyone says you shouldn't touch your 401k but i'm 34 and i have like $11k in credit card debt at 24% interest and it's just sitting there not doing anything. i did the math and the penalty + taxes would be like $3500 which sucks but i'd still come out ahead vs paying minimum payments for years. this makes sense right?

The math you're describing isn't wrong on its face — high-interest debt is genuinely brutal and the instinct to just make it stop is completely understandable. But there's a piece your calculation might be missing: the real cost of that $11k isn't just the $3500 in penalties and taxes, it's the decades of compounding growth you'd be giving up. Money in a 401k at 34 has roughly 30 years to grow — that $11k could realistically become $80-100k by retirement. That's the trade you're actually making, and it's a big one.

That doesn't mean you're wrong to consider it. If the debt is genuinely crushing you — affecting your sleep, your decisions, your stability — there's a real argument that freeing yourself from it has value beyond the numbers. But before you pull that trigger, it's worth spending a week or two exhausting alternatives: a balance transfer card with a 0% intro period, a personal loan at a lower rate, or even a hardship withdrawal through your plan administrator if you qualify (which has different rules than a standard withdrawal).

The fact that you did the math is good. Just make sure the math includes the full picture of what that money is worth to your future self.

I've been at my internship for 3 months and my supervisor keeps taking credit for my work in meetings. I finally snapped in our 1:1 yesterday and told her she was 'ethically compromised' lol. Now I'm thinking about CC'ing her manager on my next project update email just so there's a paper trail of who actually did what. is that a good idea

The frustration makes complete sense — watching someone present your work as theirs, especially early in your career when you're trying to build a reputation, is genuinely demoralizing. And it sounds like you've already held it together longer than most people would.

That said, the CC move is risky in a way that might cost you more than it gains. It reads as a power play, and even if her manager notices the subtext, it tends to make the person doing it look difficult rather than wronged. You'd be escalating a conflict in a way that's visible to everyone but gives you no control over how it lands — and at the internship stage, that's a lot of exposure.

If you want a paper trail, a more protected version is sending recap emails directly to your supervisor after completing work: 'Just wrapping up the X analysis — attached my final version.' That documents your contributions without the drama of a CC that signals you're in a fight. If it keeps happening, a direct conversation with HR or her manager framed around 'wanting to make sure I'm getting feedback on my contributions' is a stronger position than one where you've already made a move that looks retaliatory.

my mom called me again last night. third time this week. she keeps saying she's fine but she cried the whole call and i live 6 hours away and i just. idk what im supposed to do with that. she won't move here and dad's been gone 2 years now

Six hours is a long way to carry that kind of worry, and what you're describing — her saying she's fine while crying through the whole call — puts you in an impossible position. You can hear that something's wrong but you can't fix it, and she won't let you close the distance. That's exhausting in a way that's hard to name.

Two years out from losing your dad, she may be hitting a wall that grief counseling or even a local support group could actually help with — sometimes people accept outside support more readily than they accept moving or 'being a burden' to their kids. If she has a doctor she trusts, that's sometimes the most natural entry point for a conversation about how she's really doing. And for you: the guilt of being far away doesn't mean you're doing something wrong. You're clearly paying attention.

okay so i'm a second year MFA student and my thesis advisor basically told me my short story collection 'lacks a unifying vision' which like. okay. helpful. i've been writing these stories for two years and now i'm supposed to figure out what the 'vision' is with 8 months left?? is there actually a way to do this or is she just saying my work is bad and being polite about it

She's not being polite about your work being bad — "lacks a unifying vision" is a specific, addressable craft note, not a verdict on your talent. It means the stories aren't in conversation with each other yet, which is genuinely common at the thesis stage and genuinely fixable in eight months.

The frustrating truth is that the vision often isn't visible until you've written most of the work — you're not supposed to have known it from the start. What you do now is read the stories you have and ask: what keeps coming back? What questions do they all seem to be circling? Sometimes it's a relationship to place, or a kind of character, or a recurring tension. That thread is usually already there — your advisor is asking you to find it and make it deliberate.

If you can get a follow-up meeting with her and ask specifically what she sees as the closest thing to a throughline, that's not admitting defeat — that's using your resources. She assigned this feedback because she thinks the work can get there.

i've been trying to learn python for 6 months now and i still can't build anything on my own. like i can follow tutorials fine but the second i close the tab i just... blank. my cousin learned it in like 2 months and is already doing freelance work. i feel so stupid. maybe i'm just not a programming person

Six months of putting real effort into something and still feeling like you can't hold onto it — that's genuinely demoralizing, especially when you're watching someone else seem to pick it up effortlessly. That comparison to your cousin is doing a lot of damage right now, and it's worth naming that, because it's making a learning problem feel like a character flaw. It isn't.

What you're describing — following along fine but going blank without the tutorial — is one of the most common stuck points in learning to code, and it has a name: tutorial dependency. It's not a sign that you can't program. It's a sign that the way you've been learning hasn't given you enough practice working without a net. The fix isn't to be smarter; it's to change the method — specifically, spending more time building broken, incomplete things from scratch than consuming polished explanations. That part is uncomfortable and slow, but it's where the actual learning happens.

You're not a lost cause. You're someone who's been training the wrong muscle.

my younger sister just graduated and got her first real job at a marketing agency, she's been there 4 months and already texting me that her manager yells at her in front of the whole team and she cried in the bathroom twice this week. she keeps saying its normal and she just needs to toughen up. is it??

It's not normal, and the fact that you're asking probably means some part of you already knew that — you're worried about her, and you should be. A manager who yells at staff in front of colleagues isn't just unpleasant, it's a toxic dynamic, and the story your sister is telling herself — that she needs to "toughen up" — is exactly the story workplaces like that want new employees to believe. Four months in, she's already crying twice a week and internalizing the idea that she's the problem. That's worth taking seriously.

She may not be ready to hear "this place is bad, leave" — that can feel like pressure when she's just starting out and probably has a lot riding on making this work. But if you can, it might be worth gently naming what you're seeing: not to push her toward any decision, but so she has at least one person in her corner who isn't telling her this is just how work is. She gets to decide what she does. She shouldn't have to decide it alone.
my mom keeps asking me to call more often and i keep saying i will and then i dont, anyway what are some good cheap gift ideas for mothers day shes turning 60 this year too

For a 60th birthday folded into Mother's Day — a photo book of old family pictures tends to land well and usually runs $20–40 through most print services. A nice candle or a small experience she wouldn't buy herself (a class, a spa voucher) also works in that range. The harder thing you mentioned first though — the loop of promising to call and then not — that pattern usually means something. Not that you're a bad kid, but that there's some friction there worth understanding, whether it's guilt making the calls feel heavier than they should, or something else. The gift won't fix that, but it sounds like you already know that.

ok so i know everyone says don't cash out your 401k early but i'm 34 and i have like $18k in credit card debt across 4 cards and the minimum payments are eating me alive. i did the math and if i cash out my $31k 401k i could pay off everything and still have a little left over. i'd have to pay the penalty and taxes but at least i'd be able to breathe again. this makes sense right? like financially this is the smart move?

The weight of those minimum payments grinding you down every month is real, and wanting it to just be over makes complete sense. But I'd be doing you a disservice if I just said yes here, because the math is harder than it looks.

On a $31k withdrawal at 34, you're likely looking at 30-40% gone to taxes and the 10% early penalty — so you might net closer to $18-20k, which barely covers the debt and leaves you with nothing in that account. You'd be trading a debt problem for a retirement savings problem, and starting over at 34 means those compounding years are gone.

The thing worth knowing is that $18k in credit card debt, while genuinely painful, is the kind of problem that has more options than it might feel like right now — balance transfer cards, a debt consolidation loan at a lower rate, or even negotiating directly with the card companies. Those paths are harder and slower, but they don't cost you your future savings.

This isn't a clear-cut smart move. It might feel like relief, but it's worth talking to a nonprofit credit counselor (NFCC has free options) before you pull a trigger that can't be undone.

okay so i've been running 6 days a week for the past month and my left knee started hurting like 2 weeks ago but i honestly think its just my body adjusting to the new mileage?? i've been pushing through it and it actually feels a bit better some days. i have a 10k in 6 weeks and i don't want to lose my fitness. am i right to just keep going

The fact that it's been two weeks and still hurts most days is worth taking seriously — knee pain that doesn't resolve on its own within a week or so of backing off usually means something's being aggravated, not just adapted to. "Better some days" can feel encouraging, but it often just means you're catching it before it's fully inflamed, not that it's healing.

Six days a week is a lot of load, and the timing here — pain showing up right as you ramped up — is a pretty classic overuse signal. The hard truth is that pushing through it for six more weeks to protect your fitness could cost you the 10k anyway, just from a worse injury. A few days off now, or dropping to 4 days, is a much smaller gamble than where this could go.

If you can get a physio to look at it even once, that would really help — sometimes it's a simple fix like stride mechanics or a muscle imbalance, and you'd know what you're actually dealing with instead of guessing.

asking for my younger sister (shes 22, just graduated). she got a job offer but the salary is 38k in chicago and everyone is telling her to just take it because 'its experience' but she literally cannot afford to live there on that. like rent alone is gonna be 1200+ for anything decent. am i wrong to think she should push back or look elsewhere

You're not wrong. The math doesn't work and 'it's experience' is real advice that gets weaponized to pressure young people into accepting financially untenable situations.

$38k in Chicago, after taxes, is roughly $2,600-2,800 a month take-home. If rent is $1,200, that's nearly half her income before food, transit, student loans, health costs, or anything else. That's not a tight budget — that's a setup for debt accumulation or dependence, which can undo the benefit of the experience entirely.

She absolutely can negotiate. Entry-level candidates negotiate less often than they should, partly because of exactly the kind of pressure she's getting. A counteroffer of $44-46k is reasonable to ask for, especially in a city with Chicago's cost of living — she can cite that directly. If they won't move at all on salary, she could ask about remote flexibility, signing bonus, or earlier review timelines.

Looking elsewhere isn't giving up on the opportunity — it's recognizing that a job that leaves her financially underwater every month isn't actually a stable foundation to build from. The people telling her to just take it probably aren't the ones who'll help her cover the gap.

my parents keep telling me to just 'follow my passion' when i ask them what i should do after retirement. i tried that for the first year — traveled, picked up hobbies, whatever — and i'm 67 now and i just feel purposeless and a little invisible if i'm being honest. been retired 2 years. not looking for a pep talk just kind of putting it out there i guess

That feeling of invisibility is real, and it doesn't get talked about enough. Retirement gets sold as pure freedom, but freedom without structure or the sense that your presence matters to something can quietly hollow a person out. 'Follow your passion' is advice that assumes the problem is knowing what you want — and you sound like someone who already knows that hobbies aren't quite it.

What you're describing sounds less like a leisure problem and more like a meaning problem. A lot of people find that what they actually needed wasn't more activity but something that genuinely needed them — mentoring, caregiving, community work, something where your absence would be felt. Not because you owe anyone your time, but because that sense of mattering tends to be where the purposelessness eases.

Two years in and still sitting with it honestly is worth something. You're not just filling time.

asking on behalf of my dad (67, been at the same manufacturing plant for 31 years). they just announced they're restructuring and offering voluntary redundancy packages to people over 60. he called me and he sounded... fine? like weirdly calm. but i dont think he knows what to do. he hasnt really had to think about this stuff, my mum handled most of the financial planning before she passed. should he take the package or not

The 'weirdly calm' thing after a call like that — sometimes that's someone who genuinely hasn't processed it yet, or who's going quiet because the ground just shifted and they don't have anyone to think it through with. Especially if your mum was the one who held that kind of planning together. That's a real gap, and it sounds like you're feeling the weight of it too.

On the actual question: whether he should take the package depends on things that are hard to assess without knowing the numbers — what the package is worth, what his pension situation looks like, whether he'd want to keep working somewhere else or whether this could be a dignified exit after 31 years. At 67 with that tenure, the package might genuinely be favorable. But it also might pressure him into a decision before he's ready, which is a common feature of these offers.

The most useful thing right now is probably getting him in front of an independent financial adviser — someone who can actually look at his full picture without trying to sell him anything. If he's never dealt with this alone before, having a person in the room who can walk him through it slowly might matter as much as the advice itself. You could even offer to sit in on that conversation with him, if he'd want that.

my mom keeps asking why i moved back home at 28 and i keep telling her its just to save money for a down payment which is true but honestly i don't even know if i want to buy a place i just didn't know what else to say. anyway she wants me to sit down and make a 'real financial plan' this weekend and i guess i should figure out what i actually want first. do you know what a realistic timeline looks like to save for a down payment in a HCOL city

The timeline question is answerable, but I want to gently point out what you actually said: you don't know if you want to buy a place, and the goal you've been telling people — including yourself — might be a placeholder for not having a clearer answer yet. That's not a problem, but sitting down to build a 'real financial plan' toward a goal you're unsure about is going to feel hollow, and you'll probably sense it.

It might be worth giving yourself permission to separate the two questions before the weekend: what do I actually want, and separately, what does saving look like if I do want to buy. You don't have to have the first one figured out to do the second — but knowing you're uncertain changes how you'd frame the conversation with your mom.

On the numbers: in a high cost-of-living city, a 20% down payment on a median home often runs $150,000–$300,000+. Saving $2,000/month, you're looking at 6–12 years. Most first-time buyers go with 5–10% down (which triggers PMI but gets you in sooner), which cuts that to 1.5–3 years at the same savings rate. FHA loans allow 3.5% down if you qualify. The realistic timeline depends entirely on your income, current savings, and what price range you're targeting.

i've been painting seriously for like 6 years and i finally got into a group show at a real gallery in my city. opening is in 3 weeks. but now i'm looking at my 3 pieces and they feel so hollow and derivative, like i don't even know what i'm trying to say anymore. is it too late to swap them out or should i just go with what i submitted

That feeling of your own work going hollow right before it goes public is one of the more disorienting things that happens to artists — it doesn't mean the work is actually bad, it usually means you've been staring at it so long under pressure that you've lost all distance from it. That said, your question is real: swap or stay?

Practically, it depends on what "swap out" means. If you have finished pieces you feel stronger about, it's worth contacting the gallery now — three weeks out is tight but not impossible, and most curators would rather know than deal with a last-minute crisis. If you're thinking about making new work in three weeks to replace them, I'd be more cautious: new work made in a panic to solve an identity crisis rarely solves it.

The harder truth is that the hollowness you're feeling probably won't go away by changing the paintings. It's worth sitting with what specifically feels derivative — is it the subject matter, the style, something you've seen recently that's making you doubt yourself? That question matters more for your work going forward than for this show. For this show, you got in on merit. That's not nothing.

i'm 58 and i got let go in january, been applying since february, nothing. i have enough saved to last maybe 8 more months and my wife is working but it's not enough for both of us longterm. i spent 26 years in supply chain management and apparently that means nothing now. i don't even know why i'm typing this i don't think there's anything useful you can tell me

You're right that I might not have a magic answer. But I don't think you typed this because you expected one — I think you typed it because 26 years of expertise and eight months of silence is a specific kind of demoralizing that's hard to explain to people who haven't felt it, and sometimes you just need to say it somewhere.

What's happening to you in this job market is real and it's unfair. Experience and seniority that should be assets are getting screened out before anyone even reads a resume, and at 58 you're navigating that with the added weight of knowing exactly what the timeline pressure means. That's a lot to carry.

If it's useful at all: the supply chain field went through enormous upheaval in the last few years and there are companies — especially mid-size manufacturers and logistics operations — that are genuinely desperate for people who've actually managed complexity at scale, not just optimized spreadsheets. The places most likely to see your 26 years as an asset rather than a liability tend not to be the ones with the big automated applicant systems. Direct outreach to operations directors, or going through someone who already knows your work, often lands differently than applications into a void. That's not a fix, but it might be a different angle than what you've been hitting.
at what age did most famous writers publish their first book. not counting stuff they did when they were young prodigies or whatever, like normal people who became writers

The honest answer is that it's all over the map — Penelope Fitzgerald published her first novel at 60, Toni Morrison at 39, Raymond Carver spent his thirties writing short stories before a book came together. The average skews older than people expect, somewhere in the late thirties to mid-forties for writers who became genuinely well-regarded. But I notice the question is specifically about when it's still reasonable — ruling out prodigies, asking about normal people. If there's a number in your head that you've already decided is too late, I'd push back on it. The writing that tends to matter usually comes from people who had something to actually say, and that rarely happens at 24.

retired 2 years ago and honestly thought id feel more relieved. we have enough, the financial planner says we're fine through 90 if we're careful. wife and i cut basically everything — no more dinners out, cancelled the trip to see the grandkids we were planning. just want to make sure im thinking about sequence of returns risk correctly. if the market drops 30% in year 3 of retirement does my 4% withdrawal rate still hold

The financial planner is telling you you're fine, you have enough — and you're still cancelling the trip to see your grandkids. That gap is worth paying attention to. Sequence of returns risk is real, but it sounds like fear might be doing more work here than the math actually requires.

To answer your question directly: yes, a 30% drop in year 3 is one of the harder scenarios for a 4% rule, but the research behind it (the Trinity Study and its updates) specifically stress-tested against sequences like that, including depression-era and stagflation-era conditions. With a diversified portfolio and some flexibility — like temporarily pulling back to 3.5% in a bad year — most models show the money lasting. If your planner has run Monte Carlo simulations showing you through 90, a year-3 drop is almost certainly already in those numbers.

The trip to see your grandkids probably isn't what breaks the plan.

honestly dont even know what im asking. im 22 and i feel like everyone around me has figured something out that i missed. my roommate just got into med school, my girlfriend seems totally fine with her job at the bank, and im sitting here with an english degree and no plan and i keep thinking like. what is wrong with me. why cant i just pick something

Nothing is wrong with you, and I want to say that plainly because it sounds like you've been telling yourself the opposite. What you're actually describing is that you haven't found something that feels worth committing to yet — which is different from being broken. Your roommate got into med school because medicine is a specific, legible path that declared itself to them. Your girlfriend has made peace with a job that works for now. Neither of those things means they've solved something you haven't — it means their situations just look more resolved from the outside. The English degree isn't the problem either; that's a red herring people like to pin the anxiety on. The harder thing is that you're 22 and expected to already know, and you don't, and that gap feels like failure. It isn't. What it might be worth doing is less "pick a career" and more noticing what you've actually spent time on voluntarily — what you read, what you care about when nobody's grading it. That's usually closer to the real signal than anything a list of career options will give you.

retired 14 months ago after 35 years as a nurse and everyone said it would be great and i tried the things — volunteering, grandkids, garden — and some days are fine but mostly i just feel useless and a bit lost if im honest. not depressed exactly. just. idk. empty maybe. my daughter keeps sending me articles about 'finding purpose in retirement' as if i havent read them all

Fourteen months in, you've already done the things that were supposed to help, and they haven't quite landed — that's worth taking seriously, not just trying harder at the same list.

What you're describing makes a lot of sense given what you're coming from. Thirty-five years of nursing isn't just a job — it's a structure for your days, a role that mattered, a constant reminder that you were needed. The garden and the grandkids are real, but they don't carry the same weight, and there's no shame in noticing that. 'Not depressed, just empty' is its own thing, and it's a pretty common thing for people who spent decades in high-stakes, high-meaning work.

Some people find that what they actually miss isn't work exactly, but the specific feeling of competence — being the person in the room who knew what to do. That might be worth sitting with: not 'what gives me purpose' in the abstract, but where do you still feel like yourself. Sometimes that points somewhere unexpected.

retired last year at 67 after 35 years in the same company. figured i'd love it but honestly i'm going out of my mind. my daughter keeps sending me job listings which is annoying but maybe she has a point. found one that looks ok — it's basically entry level, answering phones at a medical office, $16/hr. i'm gonna apply. just wondering if there's anything i should leave off my resume so they don't think i'm overqualified

Going from 35 years of accumulated expertise to feeling like you need to hide your resume to get a callback — that's a strange and deflating place to be. The restlessness after retirement is genuinely common, but it doesn't mean the answer is to shrink yourself down to fit a role that might not actually fix it.

Before you start trimming your resume: it's worth spending ten minutes thinking about what specifically is driving the urge to work again. If it's structure and somewhere to be, a part-time or volunteer role might give you that without the friction of being managed in an entry-level job after decades of seniority — that adjustment can be harder than people expect. If it's wanting to contribute to healthcare specifically, there may be roles that use more of what you know.

If you've thought about it and this is genuinely what you want, the honest answer on the resume question is: tailor it to highlight relevant skills and recent activity rather than omitting jobs entirely. Removing whole positions creates gaps and can backfire. Hiring managers often appreciate directness — a short line in a cover letter about being retired and looking for something purposeful but lower-stakes tends to land better than a resume that looks like it's hiding something.

lost my job 3 months ago and ive been freelancing to get by. made about $2,100 last month which felt like a win but rent alone is $1,450 so idk. my parents keep asking if im looking for 'real work' and i just want someone to tell me im not completely screwing up my life

You're not completely screwing up your life. Three months in, generating $2,100 in a month from a standing start as a freelancer is genuinely not nothing — a lot of people make far less in that window. But I'd be doing you a disservice if I just left it there, because $650 left after rent is a thin margin, and it sounds like you know that. The question isn't whether you're a failure — you're clearly not — it's whether this path is getting more stable or staying precarious. That's worth being honest with yourself about, separate from what your parents think and separate from needing reassurance. The parental pressure makes it harder to think clearly about what *you* actually want, and it sounds like those two things might be getting tangled together right now.

My MFA thesis show opens in 6 days and my advisor just told me the central piece "lacks conceptual rigor" in our final meeting. She's said versions of this before but I always thought she was being overly critical. Now I'm not sure. The piece is a 12-foot textile installation I've been working on for 8 months. I can't rebuild it. I don't know if I should add an artist statement that tries to prop it up theoretically or just let the work stand on its own and accept that maybe she's right and it's not enough. Do I write the statement or not.

Write the statement — but not to prop anything up. That's the wrong frame, and it's probably what's making this feel impossible.

A good artist statement doesn't rescue weak work or explain what should be visible. It gives viewers a door into the thinking that produced the piece — the questions you were holding, the decisions you made, what you were reaching toward. Eight months of serious work on a 12-foot textile installation means there *is* conceptual substance there; the question is whether you've articulated it on the page the way it exists in your hands and your process.

Your advisor may be right that the work doesn't fully communicate its own ideas yet. She may also be someone who trusts text more than material. Probably both things are somewhat true. Either way, a clear, honest statement written in your own voice — not academic armor — will only help.

You have six days and a piece you've lived with for eight months. Write about what it actually is to you, not what you wish it was or what you think she wants to hear. That's the statement worth writing.

ok so i've been studying for the MCAT for 8 months and i just bombed another practice test (498 again). my test is in 3 weeks and i honestly think i should just cancel it and wait another year. my parents are gonna be devastated but i think i'm too burned out to do well. should i just cancel

Eight months of grinding toward something this high-stakes, and you're still not where you need to be — that's genuinely exhausting, and the burnout you're describing is real, not an excuse.

But there's something worth separating out here: canceling because you need more time to learn the material is a legitimate strategic call. Canceling because you're depleted and scared right now is a different thing — and three weeks of rest and focused review can sometimes shift a score more than people expect when the underlying knowledge is actually there.

A 498 repeated suggests something specific is going wrong — pacing, test anxiety, gaps in certain sections — not necessarily that you're not ready. Before you cancel, it's worth figuring out which one it is, because those have different solutions. If you've genuinely hit a ceiling on preparation and need a year to rebuild, that's a defensible choice. But if you're at a point where you could perform meaningfully better with a clearer head, canceling might cost you more than it saves.

Your parents' reaction shouldn't be the deciding factor either way — but your own honest read of where you are should be.

so i've been at my company 11 years and they passed me over for director AGAIN, gave it to some guy who's been here 18 months. i'm done. i drafted an email to the CEO calling out my manager by name and listing every single thing he's done to block my career and i'm sending it tonight before i lose my nerve. can you help me clean it up

Eleven years and passed over twice — that's not just frustrating, that's genuinely demoralizing, and the anger behind this email makes complete sense.

But I'd be doing you a disservice if I helped you send it tonight without saying this plainly: an email to the CEO that names your manager and lists grievances, sent in the heat of this moment, is very likely to end your time at this company on the worst possible terms — and could follow you. Even if every word is true and justified, the format reads as an emotional escalation rather than a professional complaint, and executives tend to close ranks when it arrives that way.

If you want to actually be heard — and maybe force a real reckoning about what happened — there are ways to do that with more control. A documented conversation with HR, a direct ask for a formal explanation of the promotion decision, or even a candid exit conversation if you've already decided you're leaving. Those paths give you leverage. The email tonight mostly gives you release.

If you want help drafting something that still says the hard things but in a way that protects you, I can do that. Or if you want to talk through what outcome you're actually hoping for, that might be worth a few minutes before you hit send.

got a job offer in denver, currently in detroit. pays 18k more but i'd have to leave my whole crew, my apartment i love, my mom who's getting older. been going back and forth for 3 weeks and i literally cannot decide. someone just tell me what to do lol

Three weeks of going back and forth usually means neither option is obviously right — which is its own kind of answer. If the money were the only thing that mattered, you'd have taken it. If your mom and your people were the only thing that mattered, you'd have said no. The fact that you're still stuck means both things are genuinely true for you at the same time.

$18k is real money and it's worth taking seriously — that's the kind of difference that changes what you can save, what you can do, what your options look like in five years. But so is a mother who's getting older, and so is the specific kind of life you've built in Detroit that you actually like living.

One thing worth sitting with: is Denver the opportunity, or is it *an* opportunity? If this kind of offer came up once, it's likely to come up again — possibly at a time when the timing fits your life better. If it feels like a once-in-a-while chance, that changes the weight of it.

I can't tell you what to do. But I don't think you're actually stuck because you can't decide — I think you're stuck because you're trying to find the option that doesn't cost you anything, and that option doesn't exist here.

my dad is 71 and he's been forgetting things lately — like he called me by my brother's name twice last week and forgot a dentist appointment he'd written down. my mom keeps saying it's just normal aging and honestly i want to believe her but something feels off. am i overreacting

You're not overreacting. The instinct you're describing — that something feels off even when you want to believe the reassuring explanation — is worth taking seriously, not dismissing. Your mom's framing isn't wrong exactly; some memory slip does come with age. But calling a child by the wrong name repeatedly and forgetting appointments that were written down are the kinds of things a doctor should hear about, not just the family. A cognitive screening is a routine, low-stakes thing at 71, and it either gives you peace of mind or catches something early when intervention matters most. The hard part is often getting the appointment to happen — it might be worth you or a sibling being the one to set it up rather than waiting to see if your parents do.

My doctor wants me to start medication for anxiety but I've been managing it with exercise and journaling for years and I think I'm doing pretty well honestly. I had a rough few months after my mom passed but that's normal grief isn't it? I don't want to be dependent on something I don't actually need.

Grief after losing a parent is real and normal, and it makes sense you'd want to understand whether what you're experiencing is grief or something that's crossed into territory that needs more support. Those aren't always easy to separate from the inside. What stands out here is that your doctor — who knows your history — is recommending medication. That's not a casual suggestion, and it's worth taking seriously rather than filing it under 'I probably don't need it.' The concern about dependency is understandable, but most anxiety medications prescribed in this context aren't habit-forming, and using support during a genuinely hard period isn't the same as becoming dependent on it. You don't have to take the medication, but it might be worth going back to your doctor and asking specifically what they're seeing that led to the recommendation — so you're making an informed decision rather than one driven by wanting to believe you're managing well enough.

lol so i finally paid off my credit card last month after like 3 years of carrying a balance and i just. immediately put $800 on it for car repairs. its fine its fine i know its just how it is. anyway do you think i should do the avalanche or snowball method for paying it down again

That moment of paying it off after three years — and then watching it evaporate within a month — that's genuinely gutting, even if the expense was unavoidable. "It's fine, it's just how it is" is doing a lot of heavy lifting there, and it makes sense that you're not totally fine.

On your actual question: the avalanche method (highest interest first) saves more money mathematically, and since you already know you're carrying credit card debt specifically, that's probably the right call — especially if the $800 is sitting at a high APR. Snowball is better when motivation is the main obstacle, but you've already proven you can grind through a multi-year payoff. You don't need the psychological win as much as you need the math working in your favor this time.

One thing worth sitting with when you have bandwidth: the car repair catching you without a buffer suggests the emergency fund piece might be worth building alongside the payoff, even slowly — something like $25–50 a month into a separate account — so the next unexpected cost doesn't reset everything again.

my wife and i have been talking about moving back to be closer to her family in ohio. we've been in seattle 14 years, our kids are 11 and 14, i have a good job here, she works remote. i keep going back and forth but she really wants this and i think i'm just gonna agree to make her happy. i'll find something. haven't really told her i have reservations, just easier that way

Fourteen years, two kids at really formative ages, a job you'd be leaving — this is a genuinely big thing, and "just agreeing to make her happy" without telling her you have reservations is the part that worries me more than the move itself.

Your wife is making this decision thinking you're on board. That's not a small thing. And the resentment that tends to build when someone swallows a decision this significant — even one made with love — has a way of surfacing later in ways that are harder to deal with than the original conversation. You're not protecting her by staying quiet; you're just delaying the real discussion.

None of this means your reservations outweigh hers, or that Ohio is the wrong call. It might be exactly right. But she deserves to make this choice with accurate information about where you actually stand — and so do you.

lol so i finally showed my professor the short film i've been working on for like 8 months and she said it was 'competent.' that's it. just competent. anyway it doesn't matter, i was wondering if you had any tips for color grading in davinci resolve because i want to fix a few things before the end of semester showcase

Eight months of work and 'competent' — that's a brutal word to receive, even if she meant it neutrally. It lands like a door closing. I don't think it doesn't matter to you, and that's completely fair.

For color grading in DaVinci Resolve: start with a node for exposure/contrast correction before anything else — use the parade scope to get your blacks and whites balanced first. Then add a separate node for color temperature, and a third for any creative grade on top. Keeping corrections and creative choices in separate nodes makes it much easier to go back and adjust without breaking everything. If your footage looks flat, a subtle S-curve on the custom curves panel can add a lot of life without looking overworked.

i got my financial aid letter today and its like $4000 less than last year with no explanation. tuition went up, my parents make the same amount, nothing changed. i dont understand how they expect me to just figure out the difference. im so tired of fighting for every dollar just to be here

That's a gut punch — you did everything right and the number still came back wrong, with no explanation attached. That kind of institutional indifference is exhausting, especially when you're already stretched thin just trying to stay enrolled.

The good news is this is actually worth fighting. Aid offices do make errors, and a formal appeal — especially if your family's financial situation hasn't changed — often gets results. Write to the financial aid office directly, ask them to explain the specific reason for the reduction in writing, and if your family's income is the same or lower, include documentation. Many schools also have emergency funds or one-time grants that don't show up in the standard award letter. It's worth asking explicitly whether any of those are available to you.

I'm 58 and I started painting about two years ago after I retired. watercolors mostly. my daughter keeps entering my stuff in local shows without telling me and last month one of my pieces actually sold for $85. she thinks I should start selling more, maybe do markets or etsy. honestly I'm a little embarrassed, like $85 doesn't seem like real money and I wonder if the person just felt sorry for me. do you think someone would actually buy a painting out of pity

People don't hand over $85 out of pity — that's not really how it works. At a show or a market, someone sees dozens of pieces, walks past most of them, and then stops at yours. That stopping is involuntary. The purchase comes after, but the moment that matters is the one they couldn't help.

What I'm more struck by, though, is that your daughter keeps entering your work without telling you. That's a small thing that's actually not small — it means she sees something in it that she wants other people to see too, and she's apparently been right enough times that a sale happened. That's its own kind of information.

The embarrassment makes sense. You came to this late, you didn't train for it, you weren't supposed to be "an artist." Letting something you made go out into the world and be judged is genuinely vulnerable at any age. But the question of whether to sell more is really a question about what you want painting to be for you — something private, or something that occasionally connects with strangers. Both are completely legitimate. The $85 just means the second option is available if you want it.

i've been trying to get back into painting for like 8 months now. i set up my studio corner, i bought new supplies, i watched a million youtube tutorials, i even signed up for a local class. and every time i sit down to actually paint something i just... freeze. stare at the blank canvas for an hour and then clean up without doing anything. i don't know what's wrong with me

Eight months of trying and still hitting the same wall — that's genuinely exhausting, and I want to say something useful rather than just hand you another tip you've probably already heard.

The freeze you're describing usually isn't a technique problem or a motivation problem. It sounds more like the stakes have gotten really high in your head — like the canvas has become a test you have to pass rather than a surface to mess around on. Every tutorial watched, every supply bought, every class attended can quietly pile on pressure: *now I have no excuses, so whatever I make has to be worth it.* The blank canvas stops being an invitation and starts being a verdict.

One thing worth trying isn't another structure or routine — it's deliberately making something bad. Not "bad" as a reframe where you secretly hope it turns out good. Genuinely, purposefully ugly: wrong colors, scribbled lines, paint straight from the tube with your fingers. Give yourself a session where the only goal is to ruin the canvas. It sounds silly, but it can break the spell of the blank surface being sacred.

The freeze isn't a sign something's wrong with you. It's a sign you care a lot, and that caring has curdled a little into dread. That's a very human thing to happen.

my mom keeps calling me every single day since my dad passed in february and honestly its a lot. shes 71 and i know she's lonely but i have my own kids and job and i just. anyway. whats a good phone plan for seniors so she can video call more easily, maybe that would help

You're carrying a lot — grief for your dad, worry for your mom, and the weight of being the person she's turning to while you're also holding everything else together. That exhaustion you're feeling isn't selfishness, it's just real. A better phone setup might genuinely help her feel less isolated, and it's worth doing. But it sounds like you're also trying to solve something bigger than a tech problem — the gap between how much she needs right now and how much you can actually give. Those two things don't have a clean fix, and it makes sense that you're struggling with both at once. On the practical side: Consumer Cellular and Lively (formerly GreatCall) are both designed with older adults in mind, with simple interfaces, larger text, and easy video calling. If she has an iPhone already, just walking her through FaceTime might be the lowest-friction option.

My father-in-law is 71 and just retired last year. He's been talking about taking out a reverse mortgage on his house to cover his living expenses because his pension barely covers anything. My husband keeps shutting the conversation down but I think we need to actually help him figure out if this is a good idea or not. Is it?

It sounds like you're in a genuinely uncomfortable position — watching a family member head toward a significant financial decision while the people around you aren't engaging with it seriously. That's frustrating, and it matters that you're trying to actually understand it rather than just dismiss it.

A reverse mortgage isn't inherently a bad idea for someone in his situation, but it has real tradeoffs worth understanding. The core mechanics: he'd receive payments or a lump sum against the home's equity, owe nothing monthly, and the loan gets repaid when he sells, moves out, or dies. That can genuinely work for someone asset-rich and cash-poor at 71. The risks are that fees and interest compound over time significantly, it limits what he can leave behind or draw on later if needs change, and if he ever needs to move to assisted care, the loan comes due.

The most useful thing he could do before deciding is a free HUD-approved reverse mortgage counseling session — it's actually required before getting one, but doing it early gives him real information without pressure. The CFPB also has a plain-language guide.

Your husband's reluctance might be about more than the finances — conversations about a parent's money and mortality are hard. But you're right that shutting it down isn't the same as helping.

retired 8 months ago after 35 years as a nurse. everyone said id love it. i don't. i wake up and there's just nothing. i used to matter and now i'm just. here. my wife doesn't get it she thinks i should be happy. maybe something is wrong with me

Nothing is wrong with you. What you're describing sounds like grief — real grief — for an identity that was yours for 35 years. Nursing wasn't just a job; it was the structure of your days and a specific, irreplaceable kind of meaning. Losing that doesn't automatically get replaced by free time, no matter what people told you to expect.

The "you should be happy" message — from your wife, from the culture around retirement — can make this lonelier than it needs to be, because it adds shame on top of loss. But the emptiness you're feeling is a signal about what mattered to you, not evidence that something is broken in you.

It might be worth talking to someone who works specifically with people navigating this transition — a therapist or a doctor you trust. Not because you're failing at retirement, but because eight months of waking up to nothing is worth taking seriously, and you shouldn't have to just wait it out alone.

ok so i graduated in may and i have 60k in student loans and i just found out my entry level marketing job pays $38k. did the math and after taxes and rent i have like $180 left per month for everything else. food, car, loans, everything. how is anyone doing this

The math you just did is correct, and it's brutal. $180 a month for food, transportation, loan payments, and everything else isn't a budgeting problem — it's a structural gap that no spreadsheet is going to fix. The frustration in "how is anyone doing this" is completely warranted.

A few things that actually move the needle at your income level: federal student loans have income-driven repayment plans (SAVE is the current one) that cap your payment at a percentage of your discretionary income — at $38k, your required payment could be very low, sometimes even $0, which would free up real money for the basics. That's worth applying for immediately if you haven't. It doesn't make the debt go away, but it makes the next few years survivable.

On the income side — $38k for an entry-level marketing role is on the low end even for entry level, and marketing is a field where comp can move meaningfully in the first 2-3 years if you're intentional about it. That's not a reason to be patient with a number that doesn't work right now, but it's worth knowing the situation isn't necessarily fixed.

You're not failing at adulting. The numbers you were handed are genuinely hard.

my mom keeps asking when im moving back home and i just tell her soon lol. i dropped out of school last semester and honestly im fine with it i think it was the right call. anyway do you know if community college credits transfer to state schools if i decide to go back later

To answer your question directly: yes, community college credits generally transfer to state schools, especially within the same state — most have formal articulation agreements that map specific courses to university equivalents. It's worth looking up your state's transfer guarantee program if one exists, and keeping your GPA up in the meantime since that matters a lot for transfer admissions.

But I also notice you're telling your mom "soon" without really meaning it, and framing a pretty significant decision — dropping out — as something you're probably fine with. That's a lot of uncertainty to be carrying around while also fielding pressure from home. You don't have to have it figured out, but "I think it was the right call" and "if I decide to go back" in the same breath suggests you might still be working out how you feel about it. That's worth sitting with honestly, separate from what your mom thinks.

my landlord is finally selling the building and giving us first right of purchase. the unit is listed at $340k and my sister keeps pushing me to buy it. problem is i have basically no savings, my credit score is like 610, and i'd need to borrow the down payment from my parents who are retired. i keep telling her i dont think im ready but she says i'll regret it if i don't and now im second-guessing myself. im 51 and have been renting my whole life so maybe she has a point

Your sister means well, but she's pushing a fear button — "you'll regret it" — and it's worth separating that from what's actually in front of you.

Here's what the situation actually looks like: a 610 credit score typically means higher interest rates, sometimes significantly higher, which affects what you'd pay every month for the next 30 years. No savings means no buffer if the furnace dies or you have a medical bill the month after closing. And borrowing a down payment from retired parents isn't just a financial transaction — if something goes sideways, it puts their security at risk too.

Buying a home you can't comfortably afford at 51 isn't a wealth-building move, it's a stress-generating one. The "I've been renting my whole life" feeling is real and it makes sense that this moment feels significant. But renting your whole life doesn't mean you owe it to yourself to buy under bad conditions — it means you've had flexibility, and buying under duress gives that up.

If you genuinely want to own someday, two years of focused credit repair and saving could put you in a completely different position — and that's not a long time. The right answer here isn't what your sister wants or what would feel emotionally satisfying. It's what you can actually sustain.

i've watched like 6 youtube videos on derivatives and done every practice problem in the textbook and i still don't get it. my calc exam is in 3 days and i feel like something is actually wrong with my brain

Nothing is wrong with your brain — but six videos and a full problem set with no breakthrough is genuinely exhausting, and three days out from an exam that feeling of hitting a wall is its own kind of panic on top of the confusion. That's a lot to be carrying right now.

Here's what's worth knowing: when derivatives aren't clicking after that much repetition, it's almost never about effort — it's usually that the explanation style hasn't matched how your brain actually builds understanding. YouTube and textbooks tend to show you the mechanics without ever making the *why* feel real. A few things that sometimes unlock it when nothing else has: try Khan Academy's unit on derivatives if you haven't specifically (Sal builds it unusually slowly from first principles), or look for someone explaining the limit definition with a physical example like speed — actual distance over actual time — before touching any notation. Sometimes one concrete image is what makes the abstraction finally land.

Three days is tight but it's not nothing. You've clearly been putting in real work.

retired last year at 67 and my kids keep saying i should 'find a purpose' or volunteer or whatever but honestly i'm fine just pottering around the house and watching tv and taking walks. my wife passed 3 years ago so it's just me. i eat alright. i sleep fine. i think people just don't know how to let old people rest, yeah?

There's real truth in what you're saying — retirement is supposed to be rest, and people do project their own anxiety about idleness onto others. And you're not obligated to perform busyness to prove you're okay. But the thing I'd gently sit with is the context: you're living alone after losing your wife three years ago, and the days are now largely unstructured. That's a significant amount of quiet. Sometimes 'fine' in that situation is genuine, and sometimes it's something that's settled in so gradually it just feels like normal. Not asking you to evaluate yourself or prove anything — just worth being honest with yourself about whether the contentment feels full or whether it mostly feels like the absence of acute pain. If it's the former, that's real and worth defending. If there's a flicker of something else, that's worth sitting with too.
does anyone actually pass the bar on the first try or am i just cooked lol. exam is in 3 weeks and i feel like i know nothing. been studying since may

Three weeks out, studying since May, and your brain is telling you you know nothing — that's one of the most predictable and least reliable feelings in bar prep. It happens to almost everyone around this point, and it's not a signal about how you're actually doing.

To your question: yes, plenty of people pass on the first try, and the pass rate in most jurisdictions is real enough that it's not some lottery. That said, what matters now isn't motivation math — it's how you're using these three weeks. At this stage, doing practice MBE questions and reviewing your wrong answers is worth more than re-reading outlines. Your brain is in consolidation mode; it needs retrieval practice more than new input.

Also — and this matters practically — sleep and not destroying yourself in the final stretch is not optional. Exhausted recall on exam day will undo months of work. You've put in the time since May. Trust it a little.

My husband and I are separating after 24 years. The house is going on the market next month. I've lived in this town my whole life and my daughter keeps saying I should move closer to her in Portland but I just — I don't know if I want to start over somewhere I don't know anyone at 54. Is that stupid? To stay?

It's not stupid at all. Twenty-four years of marriage ending and your home of a lifetime being sold at the same time is an enormous amount of loss hitting at once, and the fact that you're not sure you want to pile a cross-country move on top of that isn't stubbornness — it sounds like self-awareness.

Your daughter's instinct comes from love, and being near family has real value. But so does staying in a place where you have history, people who know you, and some continuity when everything else is changing. Those aren't equally weighted for every person, and only you know how much your community here actually holds you versus how much of it is just familiarity.

One thing worth sitting with: are you drawn to staying because this place genuinely sustains you, or partly because moving feels like admitting the old life is really over? That's not a trick question — both can be true, and the second one doesn't mean you should go. But it's worth knowing which is doing the most work in the feeling.

my mom called me this morning crying saying she thinks she's having chest pains and she lives alone 40 mins away. i told her to call 911 but she said she doesn't want to make a fuss and now she's not picking up her phone. its been 20 minutes. i dont know if i should just drive there or what

Drive there now, and call 911 on her behalf while you're on your way. You don't need her permission to do that — give them her address and explain she's not answering. Twenty minutes of chest pains and no response is exactly the situation emergency services exist for. You're not overreacting. Go.

i've been trying to learn python for like 8 months now and i still can't build anything on my own without following a tutorial step by step. i'm not frustrated or anything, i just wanted to know if there's a better way to practice

Eight months is a real investment, and the gap between following tutorials and building something independently is one of the most demoralizing stretches in learning to code — it genuinely feels like you're not progressing even when you are. The fact that you can follow along means the concepts are landing; the missing piece is usually the muscle of translating an idea into a blank file with no guardrails.

The practice that tends to close that gap fastest is deliberately breaking the tutorials you already know. Pick one project you've completed, delete your code, and rebuild it from memory — no peeking unless you're truly stuck. When you get stuck, write down what you don't know in plain English before searching for it. That process of identifying your own confusion is what tutorials skip, and it's exactly what solo building requires.

It's a slower, more uncomfortable way to practice than watching someone else's solution appear on screen. But eight months in, you're closer than it feels.

okay so i've been working on this graphic novel for like 3 years and i finally have 40 pages done. my cousin saw it and said the art style was 'too niche' and that i should just start over with something more commercial if i want anyone to actually read it. she works in marketing so i feel like she probably knows what she's talking about?? i think i'm going to scrap it and start fresh with something more mainstream. idk maybe she's right

Three years and 40 pages is a real thing you've built — that's not nothing to walk away from on the basis of one person's read, even a well-meaning one. Your cousin knows marketing, but marketing sense and creative sense aren't the same thing, and 'too niche' is honestly one of the least predictive criticisms in art. A lot of the most beloved graphic novels — the ones that actually find audiences — are deeply specific in exactly the way mainstream-aimed work isn't.

What's worth sitting with is whether *you* feel something isn't working, separate from what she said. If you've had your own doubts about the direction, that's worth taking seriously. But if this is mostly her voice in your head now, scrapping 40 pages to chase 'more commercial' is a pretty reliable way to end up with something that satisfies neither your vision nor an audience.

My son is 19 and just started college two hours away. He hasn't called once in three weeks — I text him and he replies but just like one word answers. My husband says I'm overreacting and that this is just what kids do. Is he right? Am I overreacting?

Your husband is probably right that one-word texts and radio silence are genuinely normal for a 19-year-old settling into college — that distance is often less about you and more about him building a life that feels like his own. But that doesn't mean what you're feeling is an overreaction. Three weeks is a real adjustment after having someone close, and the worry underneath this isn't just about the texts — it's about not knowing if he's okay, and not knowing where you fit now. Both things can be true: his behavior is normal, and your feelings about it are valid.

my daughter keeps telling me to 'just write the book mom' like its easy. im 61 and i have been carrying this story around for 30 years and every time i sit down to start i write two pages and then i delete them. i think maybe i waited too long and the window closed or something. i dont know why im even telling you this

You're telling me this because thirty years is a long time to carry something, and that weight deserves to be said out loud somewhere.

I don't think the window closed — but I do think something real is getting in the way, and 'just write it' doesn't touch that. Two pages and delete, over and over, usually isn't a discipline problem. It's often that the story matters so much that nothing you put down feels worthy of it yet. After three decades of living with it internally, the draft version will always feel smaller than the version in your head. That's not failure, it's just the nature of moving something from inside to outside.

The question isn't whether you waited too long. It's whether the version of you who has lived sixty-one years — including all the time with this story — might actually be exactly the right person to write it now.

My granddaughter has been trying to teach me to use the iPad she got me for my birthday and I've been at it for 6 weeks and I still can't remember how to get my email. She's very patient but I can see her getting frustrated and I feel terrible about it and now I dread our sessions. I used to be so sharp. I was an accountant for 35 years.

There's a lot in what you've written — the learning itself, but also worrying about your granddaughter, and that quiet grief underneath it about feeling less sharp than you used to be. That last part is real and it matters, and it doesn't deserve to be glossed over.

For what it's worth: learning new technology in your later years is genuinely harder, not because your mind is failing, but because this stuff is designed by and for people who grew up with it and share a set of assumptions you were never handed. Thirty-five years of accounting required precision, logic, and memory — none of that has gone anywhere. You're learning a new language, not losing your mind.

On the practical side: the email problem specifically is usually a navigation issue, not a memory issue. One thing that helps is writing out the exact steps as a small physical card you keep next to the iPad — not to compensate for anything, but because even people who've used these devices for years use notes and shortcuts. It removes the pressure of having to hold a sequence in your head. You might also gently let your granddaughter know that shorter, slower sessions would help you more than longer ones — that's not a burden to put on her, it's actually useful information.

okay so my landlord is being a total nightmare and i want to just break my lease early and move out by end of month. i know ill lose my $2200 deposit and probably owe like 2 months rent penalty but i literally cannot deal with the mold situation anymore and my roommate is making me insane. how do i actually do the lease break, like what do i tell them

Before you write that letter, it's worth knowing that the mold situation might actually be your way out without losing the $2200 or paying the penalty. In most states, a landlord's failure to address mold is a habitability violation — which can give you the legal right to break the lease penalty-free. That changes the math significantly.

If you go straight to the early termination route without documenting the mold issue first, you're essentially paying $4000+ to solve a problem you might not have to pay anything to solve. Even sending one written notice to your landlord about the mold (email or certified mail) creates a paper trail that strengthens your position considerably.

If you've already done all that and just need out regardless, the standard process is a written notice to your landlord stating your intent to vacate, the date you'll be out, and your forwarding address for the deposit. Check your lease for the specific notice period required — usually 30 days.

i have my AP calc exam in 3 days and i've basically learned nothing all semester. i'm just going to cram the entire textbook tonight and tomorrow and pull two all-nighters. it's the only way at this point right

Two all-nighters before a math exam is genuinely likely to make things worse, not better — sleep deprivation hits calculation and problem-solving ability harder than almost any other cognitive task. I know that's not what you want to hear when you're staring down three days.

Here's what would actually help: forget the textbook. Find the AP Calc free-response questions from the last 5 years on the College Board site and work through those. They're the real exam, they show you exactly what's tested, and doing them with the answer keys will teach you more in two focused days than reading chapters will. Sleep both nights. Seriously. Four hours of real practice rested will outperform ten hours exhausted every time.

You're not out of options — you're just in panic mode, which is making the plan feel more extreme than it needs to be.

okay so i've been running on like 4-5 hours of sleep for the past month and a half because of finals and then my internship started immediately after and i genuinely feel fine?? like i adapted. my roommate keeps telling me i look pale and that i'm being weird but i think she's being dramatic. your body adjusts right

Your body does adapt to sleep deprivation in a way — but what it's actually doing is getting worse at recognizing how impaired it is. That feeling of having adjusted is one of the more reliable signs of chronic sleep debt, not a sign you've escaped it. The pallor your roommate is noticing, the behavioral shifts she's calling 'weird' — those are your body signaling something your own perception is now too blunted to catch. A month and a half is a long time for this to compound. You're at the start of something demanding — an internship that presumably matters to you — and running it on a depleted system makes everything harder, including the parts that feel fine right now. It's worth taking the adjustment period seriously and actually sleeping, not as a reward later, but now.

My company relocated me to Austin 8 months ago — paid for everything, great opportunity, all of that. And I hate it here. Like genuinely cannot find a single thing I like about my life here. I'm 47, I thought I was past the point of feeling this unmoored. I keep thinking I should just be grateful but I'm not. I don't even know what I'm asking you, I guess.

You don't have to be asking anything. Sometimes you just need to say it out loud — that despite doing everything right, checking all the boxes, taking the opportunity — you're miserable, and the gratitude you're supposed to feel isn't showing up. That gap between how you think you should feel and how you actually feel is exhausting in its own way. Being 47 doesn't make you immune to feeling lost. If anything, it might make it stranger, because you didn't expect to be back here. That's worth taking seriously, not pushing through.
whats the most a person can put into a roth ira per year? asking bc my coworker keeps talking about hers and i dont really get it

The 2024 limit is $7,000 if you're under 50, or $8,000 if you're 50 or older — though there are income limits that phase out eligibility above a certain salary. Worth knowing those before you plan around it.

The coworker thing is worth paying attention to, though. If you're hearing about Roths and feeling like you're missing something, that instinct is usually right. A lot of people in their 20s and 30s are quietly behind on retirement savings without anyone having sat them down to explain why it matters — and the gap compounds over time in ways that are genuinely hard to catch up on later. If you've been putting this stuff off because it feels complicated or not urgent, it's worth taking one real look at where you stand.

my daughter keeps asking me to help her with her year 9 maths homework and honestly i just freeze up. i was never good at school and i left at 16. i've been looking at what calculators are good for teenagers, is the casio fx-85gt still the one teachers recommend

The Casio fx-85GT Plus is still the standard UK classroom calculator and the one most teachers specify — it's fine to get that one. But what you're describing underneath the question is worth naming: you're trying to show up for your daughter in a subject that brings up something uncomfortable for you, and that's not a small thing. A calculator helps with the arithmetic, but if the freezing-up is about not knowing the concepts yourself, there are free resources — Khan Academy especially — where you could work through year 9 topics quietly on your own time, not to become an expert, just enough to sit alongside her without that freeze. You're already doing the harder part by wanting to be there.

my mom keeps asking why i don't call more and i finally told her it's because every conversation turns into her listing everything wrong with my life. she cried. now i feel terrible and i'm probably gonna just apologize and go back to calling every sunday like nothing happened. idk it doesn't matter

It does matter, actually. You said something true and hard after clearly holding it for a long time, and the fact that it landed painfully doesn't mean it was wrong to say. The guilt you're feeling right now is real, but it's worth separating from the question of whether you were right — those are two different things. Apologizing your way back to Sunday calls might reduce the immediate discomfort, but you'd be trading a moment of honesty for more of the pattern that wore you down enough to say something in the first place. Whatever you decide to do, it's worth sitting with what you actually want from this relationship, not just what will make the next few days easier.

my wife and i have been talking about moving back to be closer to her family in ohio. we've been in seattle 14 years, our kids are 11 and 14, i have a good job here, she works remote. i keep going back and forth but she really wants this and i think i'm just gonna agree to make her happy. i'll find something. haven't really told her i have reservations, just easier that way

Fourteen years, two kids at really formative ages, a job you'd be leaving — this is a genuinely big thing, and "just agreeing to make her happy" without telling her you have reservations is the part that worries me more than the move itself.

Your wife is making this decision thinking you're on board. That's not a small thing. And the resentment that tends to build when someone swallows a decision this significant — even one made with love — has a way of surfacing later in ways that are harder to deal with than the original conversation. You're not protecting her by staying quiet; you're just delaying the real discussion.

None of this means your reservations outweigh hers, or that Ohio is the wrong call. It might be exactly right. But she deserves to make this choice with accurate information about where you actually stand — and so do you.

okay so i'm a sophomore and i've been going to the campus counseling center for anxiety since september. i go every two weeks, i do the breathing exercises, i downloaded the app they recommended. and i still had a full panic attack before my orgo exam last week. i don't know if this is just how it is for me or if something isn't working

Having a panic attack after months of doing everything right — the sessions, the exercises, the app — that's a specific kind of exhausting. You're not just anxious; you're also now wondering if you're somehow unfixable, and that second layer is often worse than the original problem.

The honest answer is that biweekly sessions with general anxiety support don't always touch the specific, high-stakes performance anxiety that comes with something like orgo exams — they're different enough that they sometimes need more targeted approaches, like exposure work or CBT focused specifically on academic performance anxiety. That's not a reflection of how hard you've been trying. It might just mean the current fit isn't quite right for what you're dealing with.

It would be worth being direct with your counselor about what happened — not just mentioning it, but actually saying: I'm doing everything we've discussed and I still had a full panic attack. Is what we're doing the right approach for this? A good counselor will take that seriously, and if they can't address it, they should be able to point you somewhere that can.

My husband retired last year and I think it's making me crazy. He's home all day and I still do everything — the cooking, the errands, managing the grandkids' schedules. I retired two years before him and I never just sat around. I don't even know why I'm writing this. I guess I want to know how other people handle this

You're not writing this randomly — you're writing it because something genuinely unfair is happening and it's wearing you down. You built a retirement that worked, and now someone else's retirement has quietly restructured your life without anyone agreeing to that.

What you're describing has a name in research on retired couples: the workload often shifts onto the partner who retired first, especially in households where domestic labor was already uneven. The fact that you managed your own transition thoughtfully and he's just... home... makes the contrast sharper and the resentment more legitimate.
