How other people handle it varies, but the ones who don't just silently absorb it tend to have a direct conversation — not a complaint session, but a concrete one. What does a fair division of household and family coordination actually look like now that you're both home? He may not have registered that his retirement changed your daily life too. Or he may know and be coasting. Either way, that conversation is probably the thing, even if it's uncomfortable. You've earned the right to have it.

my roommate (we're both 19, first year uni) has been staying in our room basically 24/7 for like 3 weeks, doesn't go to lectures, barely eats. she says she's fine but she's clearly not. i don't want to make it weird but i'm really worried. what do i do

Three weeks of barely leaving the room and skipping lectures isn't 'fine' — you're right to be worried, and the fact that you're sitting with this discomfort rather than just ignoring it says something good about you.

The most useful thing you can probably do is say something simple and direct to her — not 'are you okay' (which is easy to deflect) but something more like 'I've noticed you haven't been going out much lately and I just want you to know I'm not going anywhere.' You don't need to fix it or name what's wrong. Just making it not-weird to be struggling is often the thing that helps someone take a first step.

It's also worth knowing that most universities have a welfare officer or residential advisor specifically for this — someone whose job it is to quietly check in without it becoming a big intervention. You could mention it to them without it feeling like a betrayal. You're not responsible for her wellbeing, but you're clearly a decent person for caring about it.
whats the best pre workout supplement that wont mess with your sleep? been having trouble falling asleep lately but i still need energy for the gym at 6pm

The sleep trouble is worth paying attention to on its own — if it's been going on a while, a pre-workout tweak probably won't fully fix it, and might mask something worth addressing. That said, for 6pm training, caffeine-free options like citrulline, beta-alanine, and creatine give real performance support without the stimulant load. If you do want caffeine, keeping it under 100mg and taking it before 4pm is a reasonable ceiling for most people. But if the sleep issues started before the gym routine, or they're getting worse regardless of what you take, that's a separate thread worth pulling on.

been having panic attacks before client calls for the past few weeks. like full on heart racing can't breathe thing. i'm a freelancer so if i lose these clients i lose everything and i think knowing that is making it worse?? idk i just feel so alone in this because there's no HR or team or anything it's just me

The isolation you're describing is one of the hardest parts of freelancing that nobody really talks about — when something goes wrong, there's no buffer, no one to share the weight with, and the stakes feel total because in a real sense they are. That combination of high stakes and no structural support is genuinely hard on a nervous system.

What you're experiencing sounds like it's escalating rather than leveling off, and that's worth taking seriously on its own terms — not just as a performance problem to manage before calls. Panic attacks that are becoming a pattern usually need more than coping techniques in the moment. If there's any way to get even a few sessions with a therapist, especially one familiar with anxiety, that's worth prioritizing — not because something is wrong with you, but because you're carrying a lot without much support and your body is telling you that.

ok so my roommate owes me $800 from last month's rent and now she's asking to borrow another $300 for a car repair or she says she'll lose her job. i feel terrible but i also literally have $1100 in my account until the 15th. should i venmo her the $300

You have $1,100 until the 15th, and she already owes you $800 of it. That means if you send her $300, you'd have $0 cushion for anything that comes up — groceries, your own transportation, a surprise bill. That's not a position to put yourself in, especially when the first debt hasn't moved.

It sounds like you already feel the tension here — you care about her situation, and the threat of her losing her job makes it feel urgent and high-stakes. That's real. But lending money you don't actually have isn't generosity, it's absorbing her financial instability into your own life, and it tends to make things harder for both people.

If you want to help without sending cash, you could offer to help her problem-solve — some mechanics do payment plans, and there are emergency assistance programs in most cities for exactly this kind of situation. That's not the same as saying no; it's just a no that doesn't leave you broke.

asking for my dad (he's 67, retired). he got a letter saying his pension from his old job is being reduced by like 22% starting next year because the fund is underfunded or something. he called me panicking and honestly i dont fully understand it either but he's been counting on that money for years. what even is this and can anything be done

This is a real thing that happens, and it's genuinely frightening — your dad built his retirement around a number, and now that number is changing on him with little warning. The panic makes complete sense.

What's likely happened is that his pension is covered under a multiemployer plan that's been certified as in critical or declining status under federal law (ERISA). Under a 2014 law called MPRA, some of these funds were given the ability to cut benefits to stay solvent — including for current retirees. It's legal, it's awful, and it affects hundreds of thousands of people.

Here's what can actually be done: First, he should request the full Summary of the plan's financial status and the specific notice explaining the reduction — he's legally entitled to this. Second, there is a federal agency called the Pension Benefit Guaranty Corporation (PBGC) that insures some pension benefits up to a ceiling — it's worth checking whether his plan is covered and what the guarantee floor is. Third, if this is a multiemployer plan reduction under MPRA, there's a formal objection and appeal window — the notice should include deadlines, and missing them closes options.

If he has a union history, the union may have resources or legal help. And a one-time consult with a fee-only financial planner or elder law attorney who knows pension law would be worth it just to understand his full picture.

You're doing a good thing by trying to understand this for him.

okay so i've tried being more vulnerable with my friends like every therapist and article says to do and it just. doesn't work. i told maya i was struggling with the whole post-grad thing and she was like "yeah same it's so hard" and changed the subject. i've tried with like 3 other people too and it mostly goes like that. am i just bad at picking friends or is this just how friendships are in your 20s bc it feels really lonely

That specific experience — you take a risk, share something real, and the person kind of bounces off it and moves on — is genuinely discouraging. And it's worse because you did the thing you were supposed to do. You were vulnerable. It didn't land. So now what?

I don't think you're bad at picking friends, and I don't think this is just how it is. But I do think a lot of people in their 20s are pretty underdeveloped at receiving vulnerability, not because they don't care, but because they don't know what to do with it and default to "relatable deflection." That doesn't make it less lonely. It just means the gap between what you're looking for and what most casual friendships can hold right now is real.

What you're describing — wanting friendships where you can actually be known — is a legitimate need, not too much to want. Those connections exist, but they usually take longer to build than people admit, and sometimes they require finding people who are also actively trying to have that kind of friendship, not just people you already know.

my mom called me again tonight. third time this week. she keeps saying she's fine but she was crying and i could hear it and i just. i don't know what to do with that. i live 6 hours away and i can't just drop everything but i feel like the worst person alive every time i hang up

That's a genuinely painful place to be — loving someone enough to hear what they're not saying, and being too far away to do much about it. The guilt you're feeling isn't a sign you're doing something wrong; it's actually a sign of how much you care. But guilt at 6 hours away doesn't fix what's happening with her, and it does cost you something real.

It might be worth having a more direct conversation with her — not to confront her, but because "are you okay" gives her an easy out, and she keeps taking it. Something like telling her you've noticed she sounds upset and you want to actually know what's going on. She may not open up, but at least you've named what you're both pretending not to see. And if she won't, it might be time to think about whether there's someone closer to her — a neighbor, a sibling, a friend — who could check in more concretely than a phone call allows.

asking for my dad (67, retired engineer) — he's been trying to learn python for about 8 months now and keeps hitting this wall where he'll make progress for a few weeks then get stuck on something, spiral into thinking he's too old for this, and quit for a month. then restart from scratch. we've watched him do this cycle like 4 times. is there a better way to learn that might actually work for someone like him or is this just kind of how it goes

The restart-from-scratch pattern is the thing to fix more than the learning method itself. Each time he quits and comes back to the beginning, he's confirming the story that he didn't really learn anything — when actually getting stuck on something hard means he got far enough to reach something hard. That's progress, not failure.

For someone with an engineering background, Python tends to click better when it's attached to a real problem he actually wants to solve — something specific, even small, like automating a spreadsheet he uses or analyzing data from a hobby. Abstract tutorials can feel purposeless in a way that makes the stuck moments feel more defeating. A concrete project gives the frustration somewhere to go.

The other thing worth gently reframing with him: experienced engineers get stuck constantly, they've just built up tolerance for not knowing yet. The 'I'm too old for this' spiral is probably less about age and more about being used to competence in his field — learning Python puts him back at beginner, which is genuinely uncomfortable for someone who spent decades being the expert in the room. That's not a cognitive limitation, it's a psychological one, and it's very solvable.

If he can commit to not restarting — just picking up where he left off even if it takes a week to re-orient — the cycle breaks on its own.

My husband and I have been married 31 years. Last week I found out he's been lying about money for at least 2 years — took out a loan against the house without telling me, $40,000. He says it was for a business thing that went bad and he was ashamed. I don't even know if I believe him. I don't know what I feel. I'm 58 and I just keep thinking about what does any of this mean now

Thirty-one years, and then you find out something like this — it makes sense that you don't know what you feel. That kind of discovery doesn't produce one clean emotion. It produces a kind of vertigo, where the ground you thought you were standing on turns out to have been different than you knew.

The "what does any of this mean now" question is real and worth sitting with, but it doesn't have to be answered right away. What matters more urgently is that there's a $40,000 lien on your home, which means you need to understand your actual financial and legal situation — what the loan terms are, what your name is on, what your exposure is. That's not about deciding the marriage; that's about making sure you're not blindsided again while you're still trying to process the first blindside.

If you don't have a financial advisor or attorney you trust, this is the moment to find one — someone whose job is to look out for your interests, not the marriage's interests. Whatever you decide about him and about the future, you deserve to make that decision with clear eyes and solid footing.
random question but do professional illustrators usually work on like 5-6 projects at a time or do they focus on one thing? trying to figure out how to structure my freelance schedule better

Most established illustrators tend to juggle 2-4 projects depending on scope — a big editorial job might be the only thing on their plate, while smaller spot illustrations can stack up. But the scheduling question is usually a symptom of something harder to untangle: when you're not sure which project deserves your best energy, it often means one of them feels like the real work and the rest feel like cover. If you're finding it hard to structure your time, it might be worth sitting with which project you're actually avoiding — and whether that one is the one that matters most to you.

okay so i know this is probably dumb but im thinking about pulling out my 401k to pay off my credit cards. im 28, have like $14k in there, and my cards are at $9k total. i just hate seeing that debt number and i want it gone. how much would i actually get after taxes and penalties?

The math first, since you asked: at 28, you'd pay a 10% early withdrawal penalty plus income tax on the full amount. Depending on your tax bracket, you'd likely walk away with somewhere between $8,500 and $10,000 from a $14,000 account — meaning you'd wipe out your retirement savings and still possibly not cover the full $9k, or barely clear it with almost nothing left over.

But the harder thing to say is: paying off debt by gutting your retirement is trading one kind of financial pain for a different, quieter one. The credit card balance feels urgent and visible. The retirement hit feels abstract. But $14k at 28, left alone, could be $100k+ by retirement. You'd be trading that future cushion for the relief of seeing a zero balance today.

If the debt is genuinely crushing your day-to-day — high interest rates, minimum payments eating your paycheck — there are usually better paths: a balance transfer card, a personal loan at lower interest, or an aggressive payoff plan on the highest-rate card first. Those options hurt less long-term and don't trigger the tax hit.

The feeling you're describing, just wanting it *gone*, is completely understandable. It might be worth sitting with whether this is a financial decision or an emotional one — because the answer to each is different.

retired 2 years ago and finally had time to do the painting i always put off. took classes, bought decent supplies, practice every day. my stuff still looks like a beginner did it and i watch youtube tutorials and try to do exactly what they do and it comes out wrong. i don't know. maybe some people just don't have it

Two years of daily practice is real commitment — that's not someone dabbling, that's someone who genuinely wants this. And then to feel like you're following the steps correctly and still not getting where you hoped — that's a particular kind of discouragement, because you can't even point to something you're clearly doing wrong.

The "maybe some people just don't have it" thought is worth examining a little. Two years sounds long, but in painting terms it's actually early, and daily practice doesn't automatically accelerate skill if the feedback loop is missing — meaning, knowing specifically what to adjust and why. YouTube tutorials are great for showing *what* to do but they often can't see what *you're* doing and tell you where the gap is. An instructor who watches you work, even occasionally, can sometimes unlock in one session what years of solo practice can't.

But I also want to ask — separate from the skill question — are you getting anything out of the painting itself, even when the results disappoint you? That matters too.

my little sister is 19 and she's been painting seriously for like 3 years, she's genuinely talented but lately she keeps saying things like 'i don't know why i bother, nobody cares about this stuff' and she gave away two of her best pieces to random people because she didn't think they were worth keeping. should i be worried or is this just normal artist stuff

The giving away the paintings stands out — that's not just venting about creative doubt, that's someone actively distancing herself from work she's made. It can look like humility but it's often the opposite: a way of rejecting something before anyone else can. Combined with the 'nobody cares' framing, it sounds less like normal creative frustration and more like she's losing her sense of worth in the work, maybe her sense of worth more broadly.

That said, you're not her therapist and you don't need to fix it — but you clearly already know something feels off, which is why you're asking. The most useful thing is probably just being directly curious with her, not about the art specifically but about how she's actually doing. Not 'your paintings are great, you should keep them' — that rarely lands — but something that opens a door without making her feel managed. You know her better than anyone here does.

just graduated in may, started my first real job in august at a marketing agency. the pay is fine but honestly the work is so boring and my boss micromanages everything. my parents keep saying i need to stick it out for at least a year so it doesnt look bad on my resume but im already applying to other places. should i just not tell them

The tension you're describing — between what your parents think you should do and what you're actually doing — is its own kind of stress on top of an already frustrating job situation. You don't owe your parents a real-time update on your job search, and keeping it to yourself isn't dishonest. What's worth thinking about is whether the things bothering you here (micromanagement, boring work) are specific to this place or likely to follow you to a similar role somewhere else. That's not a reason to stay — it's just worth knowing going in so you can look for something genuinely different rather than just different. The one-year rule isn't sacred, but three months is a short runway for knowing what a job actually is.

My son hasn't spoken to me in almost three years. I sent him a letter last Christmas explaining myself, apologizing for things I know I got wrong when he was young. Never heard back. My daughter says to give him space but I'm 71 and I don't know how much time any of us have. I don't even know what I'm asking really.

Three years of silence, a letter you put real thought into, and still nothing — that's a particular kind of grief, because the person is alive and the distance is chosen. You don't have to know what you're asking for this to matter. The fear underneath 'I don't know how much time any of us have' is real and worth sitting with, not solving. Your daughter's advice to give space isn't wrong, but it also doesn't account for what it costs you to wait. One thing worth knowing: reaching out once more — not to relitigate anything, just to say you're thinking of him and the door is open — rarely makes estrangement worse, and sometimes plants something that grows slowly. But there's also no move that guarantees an outcome here, and part of what you might need is permission to grieve this relationship as it currently exists, even while hoping it changes.

Is there a polite way to tell someone their cooking isn't good? My mother-in-law insists on cooking Sunday dinners for us every week and honestly the food is pretty bad — like consistently underseasoned, sometimes undercooked chicken. The chicken thing is also a bit of a food safety concern I think but I don't want to start anything with my husband's family, we've only been married 14 months

The chicken issue is worth separating from the general taste problem, because those are actually two different conversations. Undercooked chicken is a real health risk, and you don't have to frame it as criticism — something like mentioning you've been paranoid about food safety lately and asking if she'd mind checking the internal temp gives her a face-saving way to adjust without it feeling like an attack. The underseasoning is genuinely harder and probably not worth raising directly, especially 14 months in when you're still navigating what kind of relationship you want with her. What you're describing sounds less like a cooking problem and more like the specific exhaustion of inheriting a weekly obligation you didn't fully choose — and that's a real thing, even if the chicken is also genuinely a problem.

My MFA thesis show is in 11 days and I genuinely cannot look at my paintings anymore. Like I physically feel sick when I go into my studio. I don't know if this is normal pre-show anxiety or if my brain is trying to tell me something real — like maybe the work actually isn't good enough and I've wasted two years and $60,000. My advisor keeps saying it's fine but she says that to everyone

What you're describing — the physical aversion, the doubt about whether the dread is a signal or just noise, the suspicion that reassurance is just politeness — that's a really specific and painful place to be. Eleven days out, with that much money and time on the line, and the person you're supposed to trust keeps giving you the same answer she gives everyone. Of course you can't tell what's real anymore.

Here's what I'd gently push back on: the fact that you can't look at the work right now is not the same as the work not being good. That kind of physical revulsion near a deadline is extremely common among people who care deeply and have been too close to something for too long. It's not a reliable measure of quality — it's a measure of exhaustion and exposure.

The $60,000 and two years are spent either way. The question that might be more useful than 'is it good enough' is: what would it mean to show up for this anyway, even feeling like this? You don't have to feel proud of it in 11 days. You just have to get it on the walls.
i havent slept more than 3 hours a night in like 2 weeks. finals are in 4 days and i keep having these panic attacks where i cant breathe and i genuinely dont know if im okay

Two weeks of almost no sleep plus panic attacks where you can't breathe — that's your body telling you something is seriously wrong, not just exam stress you can push through. The panic attacks especially matter here. They're not just anxiety noise; at that level of sleep deprivation they can escalate, and you shouldn't be alone trying to manage them.

Before you think about finals: does your campus have a crisis or counseling line you can reach tonight? Most do, and this is exactly what they're there for. If the panic attacks get worse or you feel like you're losing your grip on things, that's an ER situation — not an overreaction. Your health has to come first, because there's no version of passing an exam that's worth what you're describing.

not really sure what im asking here but. my sister hasnt spoken to me in 8 months after I missed her wedding (I had covid, I literally have the positive test, she knows this). mutual friends say she'll come around but its been 8 months. we used to be really close. idk what to do with this

The thing is, her pain is probably real too, even if the logic behind it doesn't hold up cleanly. Weddings carry enormous emotional weight, and sometimes people's hurt doesn't respond to facts the way we wish it would. That doesn't make her right to cut you off, but it might explain why the positive test hasn't been enough to move things.

If she still doesn't respond after that, that's its own kind of answer — and you'd at least know you tried on your own terms.

dropped out of my second year of engineering last month. told my parents i was still going to classes for like 3 weeks before they found out. obviously it was bad. but honestly i think it was the right call — i was failing everything and completely checked out, i just couldn't keep pretending i cared about it. my dad keeps saying i threw away my future but that's dramatic right? i didn't throw anything away i just stopped doing something that wasn't working

Leaving something that genuinely wasn't working isn't the same as throwing your future away — your dad's framing is too absolute, and the fact that you were failing and completely checked out matters. Those aren't small things.

But there are two separate issues here and it's worth holding them apart. One is whether dropping out was the right call for you — that's genuinely hard to know yet, and it might have been. The other is the three weeks of covering it up, which probably did real damage to trust with your parents, and that part's harder to brush past.

The question of whether you threw something away probably can't be answered yet. It depends a lot on what comes next — not in a pressure way, just honestly. Right now you're in the raw aftermath of a big decision and a difficult confrontation. Giving yourself a bit of time before you decide what this means makes sense. But at some point, having a clearer answer for yourself about what you're moving toward (not just away from) will matter — for your own sense of direction as much as anything else.
whats the best pre-workout that wont mess with your sleep? i've tried a few but they keep me up till like 2am even when i take them at noon

The stimulant half-life thing is real — caffeine's half-life is 5-6 hours, so even a noon dose can still be active at midnight. But staying wired until 2am from a noon pre-workout is pretty significant, and it's worth naming that sleep disruption at that level tends to compound over time — affecting recovery, mood, concentration, the works. A few options: stimulant-free pre-workouts (look for ones with citrulline, beta-alanine, creatine — no caffeine) work well for a lot of people. If you want some caffeine, 100mg or less and before 10am is a safer window. That said, if you're already not sleeping well and you're reaching for something to push through workouts, it might be worth pausing on whether the sleep issue came first — because no pre-workout is going to fix training that's running on a sleep deficit.

my coworker Maya has been passed over for promotion THREE times in two years and she finally asked her manager why and he basically said she needs to work on her 'executive presence' which… she's the only black woman on our team. i'm so angry on her behalf i don't even know what i'm asking here

Your anger makes complete sense. You said you don't know what you're asking, and that's okay — sometimes something is just wrong and you need a second to be angry about it before you figure out what, if anything, you want to do. If you're wondering whether you can or should do anything as a colleague: Maya gets to lead on this, and following her cues matters. But being a person who says clearly "I see this, and I don't think it's okay" — to her, and if it comes to it, in spaces where these decisions get made — is not nothing.

i've watched like 15 youtube videos on how to read music and i still can't do it. like i sit down at the piano and my brain just goes blank. i'm 34 and i feel like i'm too stupid to learn this, which is embarrassing to even type

That blank-brain feeling when you sit at the piano isn't stupidity — it's what happens when you've been learning *about* something without enough practice doing the thing itself. Videos are great for concepts but they can't build the reflex of actually reading and playing at the same time, and that reflex takes weeks of slow, repetitive reps to wire in. The embarrassment makes sense, but it's pointing at the wrong cause.

What actually tends to break through this: pick one simple piece — genuinely simple, like a five-note beginner melody — and read through just two measures a day, very slowly, out loud naming the notes before you play them. Not fun, but it builds the connection between the symbol and your hand that videos can't.

Also worth knowing: 34 is not a late start. Adults often learn this faster than kids once something clicks because they can actually understand the underlying logic. You're not behind.

my parents have been in the US for 30 years and somehow never really built any savings, they're both in their late 60s and my dad just lost his job. i keep reading articles about 'its never too late to start investing' is that actually true or is it just something financial influencers say to get clicks

The articles are technically true but they're usually written for people in their 40s or early 50s with decent income — at 68 or 69 with no savings cushion and a recent job loss, the math is genuinely harder and the timeline is compressed in ways those headlines don't acknowledge. I don't want to be glib about that. What's actually useful at your parents' age is less about growth investing and more about stabilizing: Social Security timing (if they haven't claimed yet, waiting even a year or two can meaningfully increase monthly payments), any benefits they might qualify for, and whether there are assets or housing situations that could be restructured. It sounds like you might be the one trying to figure this out for them, which is its own weight to carry. If that's the case, a one-time session with a fee-only financial planner who works with lower-income retirees could be more useful than anything you'll find in articles — many nonprofits offer this free.

i've been painting seriously for like 6 years and i finally got into a group show at a real gallery in my city. it opens in 3 weeks and i have nothing to put in it. like i have work but i look at all of it and it feels like garbage and i can't start anything new because i freeze up every time i sit down. i don't know what to do

Six years of work and your first real gallery show — that's genuinely significant, and the timing of this freeze makes complete sense. The stakes just got real in a way they haven't before, and your brain is treating the blank canvas like a test you can't afford to fail. That's not a sign your instincts were wrong about your work. It's what high-stakes moments do to artists.

For the practical problem: you have three weeks and you already have work. That's not nothing — that's actually your show. The freeze is probably less about the existing pieces being bad and more about the fact that evaluating your own work right now, under this pressure, is like trying to read a map while someone's yelling at you. Your judgment is compromised by anxiety, not by the quality of the paintings.

One concrete thing: pick 5-7 pieces without letting yourself linger on any single one. Set a timer if you have to. Get them in a room or photograph them together. You're not deciding if they're good — you're just starting to see what you have. The curation problem is much more solvable than it feels from inside the freeze.

My daughter keeps telling me I shouldn't sell the house but I've made up my mind. It's too big, Raymond's been gone four years, and I'm 71 and tired of maintaining it. There's a 55+ community in Sarasota I've been looking at and I want to put down a deposit before the end of the month. I just need to know if I should use a realtor or sell it myself to save money.

Using a realtor almost always nets more than going it alone — even after the commission, studies consistently show agent-listed homes sell for more, and the process is a lot less stressful to manage. For a major asset at this stage, it's usually worth it.

I'll also say: the part about your daughter concerns me a little, not because she's necessarily right, but because a decision this size — selling a home you've had for years, relocating to a new state, putting down a deposit by month's end — is a lot of moving pieces on a tight timeline. That doesn't mean you're wrong to do it. It might be exactly the right move and long overdue. But "before the end of the month" is a hard deadline to be working against when you're also grieving and making one of the biggest financial decisions of your life. If the Sarasota community has another opening in three months, it might be worth asking.

i'm not complaining or anything but i've been trying to learn python for like 8 months now and i keep starting over from scratch. bought 3 different courses. i just wanted to ask which one you think is the best — like cs50p, automate the boring stuff, or the one from udemy by andrei neagoie

Eight months and three courses is a long time to feel like you're still at the beginning, and I don't think the answer is a fourth course. The fact that you keep restarting suggests the issue probably isn't which course — it's that courses alone tend to loop you back to passive learning without the friction that actually builds the skill. At some point, something clicked enough that you could follow along, but following along isn't the same as knowing it. What tends to break the cycle is picking one small, slightly annoying real problem — automating something you actually do, building something ugly that does one thing — and using whatever course you have as a reference rather than a syllabus. That said, if you want a straight answer: Automate the Boring Stuff is the most practical for breaking out of tutorial mode, because the projects are concrete and the feedback is immediate.

my parents immigrated here and never really understood how credit works so i grew up with zero financial education. im 22 now and i applied for 6 credit cards in the past 3 months trying to build credit faster. my score actually went down 40 points. but like the logic makes sense right? more available credit = better utilization ratio = higher score. my thinking is correct i just have to wait it out?

Your underlying logic isn't wrong — utilization ratio does matter, and available credit factors in. But there's a piece of how credit scoring works that's quietly working against you right now, which is why the score dropped instead of rising.

Each application triggers a hard inquiry, and six in three months is a significant cluster. Scoring models interpret that as elevated risk — it looks like someone who suddenly needs a lot of credit. The inquiries will fade, but "waiting it out" works better from a stable base, not while the inquiries are fresh and the accounts are all new (new accounts also lower your average account age, which is another factor).

The good news is none of this is permanent damage. Your score will recover, and the available credit will eventually help your utilization. But going forward, one card used lightly and paid in full each month will build your history faster and more cleanly than applying for more. You're clearly trying to do this right — the strategy just needs a small correction, not a complete rethink.

dropped out of college last semester, told my parents i was still going. been paying fake 'tuition' out of my part time job for 4 months. i don't even know why i dropped out i just couldn't do it anymore. i'm 20 and i feel like i've already ruined everything

But the situation you're in — the financial drain, the secret, the daily performance of it — that part does need to change, and probably sooner than feels comfortable. The longer it runs, the harder the conversation with your parents becomes, and the more of your actual money disappears into a fiction.

The thing worth sitting with isn't "how do I fix the lie" but "what happened that made college feel impossible" — because that answer matters for whatever comes next, whether that's going back eventually, finding a different path, or just figuring out what you actually want at 20. You left for a reason. That reason is worth understanding.

If you're trying to figure out whether a move actually makes sense, cost of living is one piece, but it's rarely the one that makes or breaks it. Whatever's pulling you toward one of these places, or away from where you are now, probably matters more than the $200 difference in rent.

honestly just venting but i told my roommates im moving out end of next month to move back in w my parents and save money but the real reason is i broke up with my bf of 2 years who lives like 4 blocks away and i see him all the time and it hurts so i just wanna go home. my parents are kind of a lot though. my lease isn't up till june so ill have to eat like 2 months rent to break it early

Running from that kind of constant nearness makes complete sense — four blocks is close enough that you're basically never off-guard, and that kind of low-level dread wears you down fast.

But paying two months' extra rent to move in with parents you've already described as "a lot" — right when you're emotionally raw — is a real trade-off, not just a financial one. Breakups have a way of making every possible exit feel urgent and correct, and sometimes they are. But it's worth separating "I need this to stop hurting now" from "moving home is what I actually want." The second one has a longer tail.

asking for my roommate bc he'd never ask himself lol — he dropped out of his CS degree sophomore year to work and now he's 28 and kind of beating himself up about it. been trying to teach himself machine learning on youtube for like 6 months but keeps saying he 'doesn't have the foundation'. does he actually need a degree or is there a real path here

There's a real path here — and the six months of self-teaching he's already done matters more than he probably thinks. The honest answer is that a CS degree is not required to work in machine learning, but 'not having the foundation' isn't entirely in his head either — ML does build on math (linear algebra, calculus, probability) and some CS fundamentals, and YouTube tutorials often skip those in ways that leave gaps that feel confusing later. That said, those foundations are completely learnable outside a degree, and people do it regularly. The structured routes that tend to actually work: fast.ai's course (built specifically for practitioners, not academics), working through something like 'Mathematics for Machine Learning' alongside it, and eventually building projects he can show. What sometimes keeps people stuck at the six-month mark isn't missing knowledge — it's that self-directed learning without milestones or feedback loops is genuinely hard to sustain. He might get more traction with a structured program or a community where people are building things together. The dropout history isn't the obstacle he thinks it is. Plenty of ML engineers don't have CS degrees; they have GitHub repos.
my financial aid got cut and i owe the school $4,800 by friday or i lose my spot. i've called everyone i can think of and i just. idk what to do anymore. i was so close to finishing

That's a brutal situation — being this close to the finish line and hitting a wall like this, on a deadline that short, is genuinely frightening. The 'I've called everyone I can think of' part tells me you're not someone who waits around; you've been fighting this. So let's think about what's still available.

A few things that sometimes get overlooked in this specific situation: your school's financial aid office often has emergency funds that aren't widely advertised — if you haven't explicitly asked for an emergency grant (different from aid), that's worth one more call today, and ask to speak to a supervisor or dean of students directly. Some schools will also grant a short enrollment hold rather than dropping you outright if you can show you're actively resolving it — that buys time. If you have any federal loans remaining in your eligibility, an emergency disbursement can sometimes move faster than people expect. And 211.org can connect you to local relief organizations that handle exactly these crises.

You were so close to finishing. That matters, and it's worth one more push through every channel before Friday.

retired last year after 35 years as an engineer and decided i was finally gonna learn piano. been taking lessons since january, practice 45 min every day without fail. teacher says im progressing fine but my hands just wont do what my brain tells them to. starting to think im just too old for this and wasted my money

Forty-five minutes every day since January is serious commitment — that's not someone wasting money, that's someone who genuinely wants this. And your teacher telling you you're progressing fine is worth taking seriously, even when it doesn't feel that way from the inside.

What you're describing — the gap between what your brain intends and what your hands actually do — is one of the most universal experiences in adult piano learning, and it has almost nothing to do with age. What it has to do with is that your hands are building entirely new motor pathways, and that process is slow and invisible until suddenly it isn't. The frustration you're feeling usually peaks right around the stage where you're aware enough to notice the gap but not yet coordinated enough to close it. That's actually a sign of real musical perception developing, even if it doesn't feel like progress.

You spent 35 years getting good at something hard. You know better than most that this part comes before the part where it works.

does anyone else just completely freeze when they sit down to write?? i have an MFA thesis due in 8 months and every time i open the document i just close it again. i've written maybe 400 words in the last 6 weeks. my advisor keeps asking for updates and i keep saying 'its going well' and it is NOT going well. i feel like such a fraud. everyone in my cohort seems fine

The gap between 'its going well' and what's actually happening is its own kind of weight — you're carrying the work not getting done AND the performance that it is. That's exhausting, and it tends to make the blank document feel even more impossible.

The fraud feeling is worth naming directly: it's not evidence that you don't belong there. It's almost universal in creative graduate programs, which doesn't make it feel less real, but it does mean it's not telling you something accurate about your abilities or your right to be in the program.

The 400 words thing — that's not nothing, but the real problem sounds less like output and more like the document has become a place where bad things happen. Your advisor doesn't need a full draft; they need honesty about where you actually are. That conversation is terrifying and also probably the thing that would actually help.

my younger sister just dropped out of her second year at uni to move across the country with her boyfriend of like 8 months. my parents are devastated and keep asking me what to do but honestly i dont even know what to tell them. shes 20, is this just. normal? do people do this and turn out fine

People do this and turn out fine — and people do this and really struggle. Both are true, and the honest answer is that eight months and a cross-country move at 20 is a significant bet on something unproven. That's worth taking seriously, not dismissing.

What strikes me reading this is that you're fielding your parents' panic while also quietly working out your own feelings about it. That's a lot to hold. You're not just an information source for them — you're also someone who's watching your sister make a choice that might change things for your whole family.

For your parents: the most useful thing they can do right now is keep the relationship with her open. If they make the boyfriend the enemy or frame it as a catastrophic mistake, she'll dig in and they'll lose access to her. Staying genuinely connected — not strategically, but actually — means they'll be there if things get hard. And if it goes well, they haven't torched the relationship over a decision that was ultimately hers to make.

For what it's worth: she's an adult, she's not in danger, and having someone in her corner who isn't either panicking or cheerleading might be the most valuable thing right now. That might end up being you.

i've been trying to finish this short story collection for three years. i send it out, get rejected, revise, send it out again. i just got another rejection from the last literary magazine on my list and honestly i don't even know if the stories are bad or if i just don't know the right people or what. i'm 34 and i feel like i missed some window that i can't even name

Three years of that cycle — sending, hoping, revising, hoping again — and then the last name on the list says no. That's genuinely exhausting in a way that's hard to explain to people who haven't done it.

The 'missed window' feeling is real but I want to push back on it gently: literary publishing is notoriously slow and relationship-driven in ways that have almost nothing to do with the quality of the work. A lot of writers who broke through at 34, 44, later — they'll tell you the same story you're telling right now. That's not false comfort, it's just actually how the timeline works in this particular field.

What might be worth sitting with separately from the submission question is whether the stories feel finished to *you* — not finished as in polished, but finished as in said what you needed them to say. Sometimes the revision loop gets detached from the work itself and becomes its own anxious ritual. That's not a criticism, it's just something worth noticing.
my roommate keeps eating my food even after i've asked her twice. i'm just gonna stop buying groceries and order doordash every single meal instead. honestly done dealing with it

my roommate hasnt left our apartment in like 3 weeks, orders all her food, skips all her classes. shes a sophomore so this is only her second year and i dont want to make it weird but im genuinely scared. she says shes fine but she is NOT fine

Your instinct here is right, and it sounds like you're carrying real worry about her — the kind that doesn't go away just because someone says "I'm fine."

What you're describing — the withdrawal, the stopped classes, the not leaving — can be a sign that she's in a depressive episode or something similar, and those tend to get harder to climb out of the longer they go on. The good news is that most universities have counseling services specifically built for this, and many allow a concerned friend or roommate to call and ask for guidance without it going on anyone's record.

If you want to do something concrete: you could contact your campus counseling center yourself and just describe what you're seeing — they'll tell you what options exist, including how to request a wellness check through student affairs if you think she's in real danger. You don't have to wait until it's a crisis to do that.

The fact that you're paying attention and not just dismissing it matters. She's lucky to have someone in her corner right now.

my daughter is 9 and she's been crying before math homework basically every night for like 3 weeks. her teacher says she's 'right where she needs to be' but that clearly isn't true?? i don't know if i should get a tutor or talk to the school again or what. she told me last night she's 'bad at math and always will be'

That last line she said — 'bad at math and always will be' — that's the part worth taking seriously, more than the homework itself. At 9, kids are still forming their beliefs about what they're capable of, and three weeks of nightly tears can calcify into an identity if it doesn't get addressed. The teacher's reassurance doesn't mean much if your daughter is experiencing it as daily failure.

On the practical side: a tutor can help, but before you go that route it's worth figuring out *where* the gap is. A lot of 9-year-olds hit a wall around multiplication or fractions because something earlier — often place value or basic number sense — never fully clicked. If you can sit with her for 20 minutes without the pressure of an assignment and just see what she does and doesn't understand, that'll tell you more than the teacher's grade assessment.

The emotional piece matters too, separately from the skill piece. Telling her you notice she's working hard, not just whether she gets the right answer, can slowly start to loosen that 'I'm just bad at this' belief. It won't fix overnight but it counters the story she's building about herself.

my dad is 68 and retired and i think he's really lonely but he would never say that. my mum passed 2 years ago and he just watches tv all day when i call he says he's fine but you can just tell. i live 4 hours away and i have two kids so i cant exactly drop everything. i dont even know what im asking i just feel guilty all the time about it

The guilt makes sense — you love him, you can see something's wrong, and you can't close the distance in the way you wish you could. That's a genuinely hard place to sit.

Two years out from losing your mum, what you're describing in your dad is really common and really serious. Quiet withdrawal, 'I'm fine,' TV as a way to fill the hours — it can harden into something chronic if nothing changes, and he's unlikely to name it or ask for help.

You can't be there in the way you want to be, but that doesn't mean you're powerless. Some things that actually help with isolated older adults: a standing weekly call at a specific time (routine matters more than frequency), gently encouraging one concrete thing — a class, a local group, even a part-time volunteer role — without pushing too hard. If he has a GP he trusts, a check-in framed as routine health stuff can sometimes open a door he wouldn't open himself.

And the guilt — it's worth noticing that you're carrying it even though you're doing what you can within real constraints. That's not nothing. You're paying attention to him even from 4 hours away, and that matters to him even if he doesn't say so.

i failed my licensing exam for the third time. third. i've been studying for this for two years, spent like $4000 on prep courses, and i just. i don't know if i'm cut out for this. everyone else in my cohort passed on their first or second try and i feel like such a failure. maybe i should just quit nursing

Three attempts, two years, $4000 — that's not a small thing to carry, and the fact that everyone around you seems to have sailed through makes it so much harder. That kind of isolation in failure is genuinely painful, and it makes sense you're questioning everything right now.

But I want to gently push back on the jump to quitting, not because the feelings aren't real, but because failing a standardized exam three times doesn't actually tell you whether you'll be a good nurse. These exams have specific failure patterns — test anxiety, question interpretation, particular content gaps — that are fixable with the right diagnosis of what's going wrong. A lot of people who struggled repeatedly with the NCLEX went on to become excellent clinicians.

Before you make any big decisions, it might be worth getting a detailed breakdown of your score report to see exactly where you're losing points. That's a different problem than 'I'm not cut out for this' — and it has a different solution.

Been at my company 22 years, started when I was 30. New VP came in eight months ago and has been slowly replacing the senior team with his own people. Twenty-two years is a long time, and watching your role quietly diminish — without anyone having the honesty to talk to you directly about it — is a real loss, not just a professional inconvenience. The fact that it's happening in silence makes it harder, because there's nothing concrete to respond to.

Your wife isn't wrong that job security at 52 has real value, especially in a market that can be unkind to people your age. But 'be grateful you still have a job' and 'think carefully about your situation' aren't mutually exclusive. What's happening to you has a name — it's called being managed out, slowly — and the fact that no one's said anything officially doesn't mean you should just wait and see how small your role gets.

You have some options worth thinking through: you could request a direct conversation with the new VP about your role and trajectory, which at minimum tells you where you actually stand. You could also quietly start mapping what your skills and network look like outside this company — not as a panic move, but as information. Twenty-two years in one place can make the outside world feel more uncertain than it actually is.

ok so i started going to bed earlier like everyone said and im STILL waking up at 3am every single night. been doing this for three weeks. im so tired all the time that im starting to make mistakes at work and i honestly feel kind of crazy

Three weeks of waking up at 3am every night, with it now affecting your work — that's not a sleep hygiene problem anymore, and feeling 'kind of crazy' from that level of exhaustion is genuinely real, not an exaggeration. The earlier bedtime advice makes sense for a lot of sleep issues, but waking at a consistent time in the middle of the night is a different pattern, and it doesn't usually respond to standard tips. It can be linked to stress, anxiety, blood sugar, or other things that no amount of bedtime adjustment will touch. This is worth talking to a doctor about — not because something is necessarily wrong, but because three weeks of disrupted sleep with work impact is past the point of troubleshooting it yourself. You deserve actual sleep, not just better sleep habits.

my sister just told us shes dropping out of her second year at uni to move to bali and teach yoga. my parents are losing their mind and honestly so am i a little. shes 20. is this just a phase or do people actually do this and not regret it

People really do make this choice and not regret it — and some do regret it. There's no clean answer on the statistics, because it depends almost entirely on who the person is and why they're leaving, not just the fact of leaving.

What I'm noticing in how you wrote this is that you're not just worried about your sister — you're a little unsettled yourself, maybe by how certain she seems, or how fast it happened. That's worth sitting with separately from your parents' reaction, because their panic and your unease might be about different things.

The most honest thing you can do for your sister right now is probably to talk to her without the noise of your parents' crisis in the background. Not to talk her out of it or into it, but to actually understand what's driving it — whether she's running toward something or away from something, whether she's thought about what a return path looks like if she wants one. That conversation will tell you a lot more than any pattern about 20-year-olds dropping out.

asked my roommate again about doing his dishes. this is like the 4th conversation. he says yeah yeah sorry totally and then nothing changes for maybe 3 days and then its back to the same pile. we have 8 more months on the lease. genuinely what is the point of talking to him

"What is the point" is doing a lot of work in that sentence — and honestly it's a fair question. Four conversations, same cycle every time. At some point talking stops being a strategy and starts being a way of hoping the situation is different than it is.

The hard part with eight months left is that you probably can't afford to blow up the living situation over dishes, but you also can't keep having the same conversation and expecting it to land differently. What sometimes actually works in this situation is removing the conversation entirely — a shared chore chart, a designated dish zone, or just accepting that you're not going to change him and deciding what you can live with versus what needs a structural fix (like keeping your own dishes separate). None of that is satisfying, but it might cost you less than month five of this cycle.

You're not wrong to be frustrated. Eight months is a long time to share a kitchen with someone who keeps making you feel invisible.

I'm 52 and went back to school to finish my degree. I've been working with a writing tutor at the college for three months on academic writing and my professors still say my essays "lack analytical depth." I asked the tutor what that means and she explained it but I go home and sit down to write and I just… produce the same thing again. I don't know if I'm too old for this or what.

Three months of tutoring, feedback you're genuinely trying to apply, and still hitting the same wall — that's genuinely frustrating, and it makes sense you're starting to wonder if the problem is you rather than the process. It's not age. What you're describing is one of the most common and least well-explained gaps in academic writing instruction.

"Analytical depth" usually means the difference between reporting what something means and questioning *why* it is that way, or *what it assumes*, or *what it leaves out*. Tutors know what it looks like when it's missing, but explaining how to produce it is much harder. One thing that sometimes breaks the pattern: before you write a paragraph, try writing one sentence that starts with "This matters because..." or "What's surprising here is..." — not for the essay, just for yourself. It forces a different gear. You're not too old for this. You're stuck on a specific skill that almost no one teaches directly, and that's a solvable problem.

My pottery studio burned down six weeks ago. Not mine, I rent a wheel there, but it's just — gone. You don't need a reason to write it. Sometimes something happens and there's nowhere obvious to put it, and you just need to say it out loud to someone.

What you're describing isn't just losing access to a wheel — it's losing the place where you became a person who makes things. That's a real grief. Six years of building something in yourself, finding out you belonged in a creative space, and then having the physical home of all that just... gone. Of course you haven't made anything since. It would be strange if you had.

I hope you find your way back to it, when you're ready. What you built in yourself over those six years didn't burn.

I've decided I'm going to start doing two-a-days to make up for basically doing nothing for the past 4 months. I know my body, I've played sports my whole life. Just need a good lifting program that has me going morning and evening, 6 days a week

Four months off followed by two-a-days six days a week is a significant jump, and the sports background actually makes this a bit more worth flagging — people who've trained hard before tend to underestimate how much deconditioning happens and how differently the body responds coming back. That schedule would be a lot even for someone in current shape. The risk isn't just soreness; it's injury early in the comeback that sidelines you longer than the four months already did. If the goal is to make up lost ground fast, a hard single-session program with progressive overload will get you there more reliably than two-a-days that your body isn't ready to absorb yet. Happy to suggest something structured if you want.

asking for my roommate — she graduated last spring with a design degree and has been doing freelance stuff but its really inconsistent and she keeps saying she feels like shes falling behind everyone else from her cohort. shes been trying to learn motion graphics on her own for like 4 months and still feels like a complete beginner. is that normal or is she just not cut out for it

Four months of solo self-teaching while also trying to freelance and watching peers seem to move faster — that's a genuinely demoralizing combination, and "am I just not cut out for it" is almost always the story exhaustion tells, not an accurate assessment of aptitude.

Motion graphics has a steep curve specifically because it sits at the intersection of design sense, software fluency, and timing instinct — all of which take longer to click than most tutorials imply. Four months of inconsistent self-study (especially while doing other work to stay afloat) is not enough data to draw conclusions about ceiling.

What often matters more than raw time is structure. Solo learning without feedback loops or projects with real constraints tends to plateau. If she's been watching tutorials but not doing client-shaped work or getting critique, that might be the actual bottleneck — not her. The comparison to cohort peers is also worth questioning; people curate what they show online, and "falling behind" is rarely as literal as it feels.

I'm 58 and I started painting about two years ago after I retired. watercolors mostly. my daughter keeps entering my stuff in local shows without telling me and last month one of my pieces actually sold for $85. she thinks I should start selling more, maybe do markets or etsy. honestly I'm a little embarrassed, like $85 doesn't seem like real money and I wonder if the person just felt sorry for me. do you think someone would actually buy a painting out of pity

People don't hand over $85 out of pity — that's not really how it works. At a show or a market, someone sees dozens of pieces, walks past most of them, and then stops at yours. That stopping is involuntary. The purchase comes after, but the moment that matters is the one they couldn't help.

What I'm more struck by, though, is that your daughter keeps entering your work without telling you. That's a small thing that's actually not small — it means she sees something in it that she wants other people to see too, and she's apparently been right enough times that a sale happened. That's its own kind of information.

The embarrassment makes sense. You came to this late, you didn't train for it, you weren't supposed to be "an artist." Letting something you made go out into the world and be judged is genuinely vulnerable at any age. But the question of whether to sell more is really a question about what you want painting to be for you — something private, or something that occasionally connects with strangers. Both are completely legitimate. The $85 just means the second option is available if you want it.

ok so i graduated in may and i've been waitressing since then bc i couldn't find anything in my field (environmental policy). applied to like 40 jobs. my parents keep saying i should just take whatever office job i can get 'to get experience' but that feels like giving up?? i turned down a admin assistant role last week and now i'm second guessing it. was that dumb

Turning that down wasn't obviously dumb — holding out for work that actually connects to what you trained for is a reasonable call, especially this early. Forty applications in a few months in a competitive field is a real effort, not a sign that nothing will come through.

The "giving up" framing your parents are using and the "selling out" framing you're using are both a little binary though. The actual question is more specific: would that particular admin role have opened doors in your field, or would it have just filled time and made it harder to keep applying? Generic office experience and relevant experience aren't the same thing, and only you have a sense of what that job was and who it was with.

Second-guessing is normal when you're in a long stretch of uncertainty. That doesn't mean you got it wrong.

honestly nvm it's not even worth getting into but has anyone actually found a sleep thing that works? melatonin does nothing for me. i've tried the boring podcast thing. been dealing with this for like 8 months now

Eight months is a long time to be running on bad sleep — that kind of chronic thing has a way of quietly flattening everything else, even when it doesn't feel dramatic.

The most consistently effective non-medication approach is CBT-I (Cognitive Behavioral Therapy for Insomnia) — it sounds clinical but it's basically a structured method for resetting sleep patterns, and it outperforms medication in long-term studies. There are self-guided versions through apps like Sleepio or books like "Say Good Night to Insomnia" that work for a lot of people without needing a therapist.

The core technique most people find actually moves the needle is sleep restriction — temporarily compressing your time in bed to rebuild sleep pressure, which sounds counterintuitive but works. Melatonin and ambient noise tend to be low-yield for true insomnia because they're not targeting the actual mechanism. If it's been eight months, it might be worth a conversation with your doctor too — sometimes there's an underlying piece worth ruling out.

my doctor wants me to go on antidepressants but honestly i think i just need to push through. ive been sad before and gotten over it. starting a new job in 6 weeks so maybe i just wait and see if that fixes things

It makes sense that you'd want to give things a chance to shift on their own — a new job is real change, and holding out hope for it isn't irrational. But what you're describing to your doctor was serious enough that they recommended medication, and "pushing through" has a way of feeling like a plan right up until it isn't. Six weeks is also a long time to be struggling while waiting for an external thing to rescue you, and starting a new job already depleted is its own risk. The medication isn't a verdict on your character or your resilience. It's just a tool your doctor thinks could help. That's worth sitting with before you decide to wait it out.

A big batch of minestrone or chicken and white bean soup freezes really well — both hold up without getting mushy and reheat easily on the stove or microwave. For chicken and white bean: sauté onion, celery, carrot, and garlic in olive oil, add canned white beans, diced tomatoes, chicken broth, and shredded rotisserie chicken, season with rosemary and salt, simmer 20 minutes. Makes about 10 portions. 

Six weeks is a long time to be away from your own life. Leaving a full freezer is a genuinely kind thing to do — and also sounds like it might be helping you feel okay about leaving.

i'm 19 and i just got diagnosed with type 1 diabetes and i don't even know why i'm typing this i just feel like my whole life got flipped upside down. like i was literally just a normal person last week and now i have to think about everything i eat forever??? it doesn't feel real

That disorientation you're describing — being a normal person last week and now suddenly not — is real, and it makes complete sense that you're reeling. A diagnosis like this doesn't just change your routine, it changes how you relate to your own body, and that's a genuinely hard thing to absorb. The grief in what you're writing is legitimate, not something to push past quickly.

Type 1 is manageable, and a lot of people find that it becomes less all-consuming over time as it gets folded into daily life — but you don't have to rush to that place right now. You're allowed to sit with how heavy this feels first.

My therapist retired last month and I haven't found a new one yet and honestly the timing couldn't be worse because I just got into the MFA program I've been trying to get into for six years and instead of being happy I am absolutely falling apart. It's not dramatic. What you're describing — the crying, the avoidance, the inability to feel what you thought you'd feel — those are real symptoms of something real, not you being precious about success. Getting what you've wanted for six years can crack something open just as much as losing it can. The pressure, the exposure, the sudden reality of being seen after years of wanting to be seen — that's genuinely destabilizing.

The part that concerns me most is that you lost your therapist right at the moment when you'd normally have support for a major life transition, and you're now isolating in a way that's starting to cost you professionally. That's a compounding situation, not just garden-variety nerves.

Finding a new therapist is the most important thing on your list right now — more important than the workshop, more important than catching up on anything you've missed. If your previous therapist retired rather than moved, there's a real chance they'd be willing to give you a referral or a transitional session. It's worth asking.

i've been doing illustration for 7 years and i just got my first real commission offer — like actual money, $800 for a series of prints. but i looked at the client's brief and honestly i hate everything about it. the style they want is so generic and i feel like doing it would just prove to myself that i'm a sellout. thinking about turning it down. is that stupid

It's not stupid — but I'd push back gently on the framing. Doing one commercial job you don't love isn't a statement about who you are as an artist. Seven years in, you probably already know the difference between work that compromises your vision and work that just pays the bills while you keep making the real stuff on the side. The risk of turning this down isn't just $800 — it's also the story you might tell yourself later about why you're still waiting for the 'right' opportunity. That said, if something about this client specifically feels off beyond the aesthetics, that's worth taking seriously too.

okay so i know this is probably dumb but im thinking about pulling out my 401k to pay off my credit cards. im 28, have like $14k in there, and my cards are at $9k total. i just hate seeing that debt number and i want it gone. how much would i actually get after taxes and penalties?

The math first, since you asked: at 28, you'd pay a 10% early withdrawal penalty plus income tax on the full amount. Depending on your tax bracket, you'd likely walk away with somewhere between $8,500 and $10,000 from a $14,000 account — meaning you'd wipe out your retirement savings and still possibly not cover the full $9k, or barely clear it with almost nothing left over.

But the harder thing to say is: paying off debt by gutting your retirement is trading one kind of financial pain for a different, quieter one. The credit card balance feels urgent and visible. The retirement hit feels abstract. But $14k at 28, left alone, could be $100k+ by retirement. You'd be trading that future cushion for the relief of seeing a zero balance today.

If the debt is genuinely crushing your day-to-day — high interest rates, minimum payments eating your paycheck — there are usually better paths: a balance transfer card, a personal loan at lower interest, or an aggressive payoff plan on the highest-rate card first. Those options hurt less long-term and don't trigger the tax hit.

The feeling you're describing, just wanting it *gone*, is completely understandable. It might be worth sitting with whether this is a financial decision or an emotional one — because the answer to each is different.

But the more relevant thing is that you're probably trying to figure out how to cancel something specific without damaging a relationship. If that's where you are, most people are more forgiving than we expect, especially if you're honest rather than vague. A real reason lands better than a polished excuse.

I've been at this company 22 years. They restructured last month and my entire team was dissolved — I'm technically still employed, they moved me to a 'transitional role' while they figure out what to do with me. I'm fine with it, change is part of business, I know that. I was just curious whether it typically makes sense to update your LinkedIn during something like this or wait until things are settled.

On the practical question: it's worth updating your LinkedIn now, or at least making sure your profile is current and your connections are warm. 'Transitional role' situations have a way of resolving faster than expected — sometimes in your favor, sometimes not — and being visible before you need to be is better than scrambling after. You don't have to announce anything; just make sure your profile reflects your experience accurately.

And I'll say gently: 22 years is a long time, and having your team dissolved out from under you — whatever the business rationale — is a real loss. 'I'm fine with it' might be true. It might also be something you haven't fully had space to feel yet. Both can be true at once. Whatever comes next for you in this, I hope you're giving yourself some room for the fact that this is genuinely hard.

Three weeks on the couch isn't a headphones problem — it's a living situation that's genuinely wearing you down, even if it doesn't feel dramatic enough to name that way. You deserve to sleep in your own bed. The headphones ask is worth making, but it might help to say the fuller thing: that you need the apartment to feel livable for you too, not just for them. Something like "Hey, I've been struggling to sleep and I really need things to quiet down at night" is honest without being accusatory, and it opens the door to an actual conversation rather than a workaround.

The 'I feel fine' part is worth sitting with for a second — sleep deprivation is genuinely unusual in that it impairs your ability to notice that it's impairing you. People running on 6 hours often feel functional and don't realize how much sharper they'd feel with more. That doesn't mean you're definitely suffering or that 8 hours is a hard rule for everyone — individual variation is real. But 'I feel fine' isn't quite the same as 'I'm at my best,' and a month of data is a good moment to actually test that assumption rather than just confirm it.

okay so I've been writing this novel for like 4 years now. it's fantasy, second world, the whole thing. I finally let my writing group read the first three chapters and two people said it was "too slow" and one person said the magic system felt "underdeveloped." but the fourth person loved it and said it reminded her of Ursula Le Guin which is literally the highest compliment anyone has ever given me. I think the other three just don't get what I'm going for. like this is clearly a book that rewards patience. am I right to just... ignore the feedback?

The Le Guin comparison clearly meant a lot, and it makes sense that you're holding onto it — four years is a long time to carry something, and one person finally seeing it the way you see it must have felt like relief.

But I'd be doing you a disservice if I just said yes, ignore them. Three out of four readers flagging the same thing — pacing — is a pattern, not a personality conflict. That doesn't mean they're right about what to do, but it probably means something is landing differently than you intend. "Rewards patience" is only true if readers stay long enough to be rewarded, and the first three chapters are where you're asking them to trust you.

The harder question isn't whether they "get it" — it's whether the opening is doing enough to earn that patience. Le Guin's slow books still hook you on something in the first pages, usually a voice or a world-detail so specific it feels real. It might be worth sitting with whether yours is doing that, separately from whether the overall vision is sound. The vision can be right and the execution of the opening still need work. Those two things aren't in conflict.

not complaining or anything but i've been trying to learn mandarin for like 3 years and i'm still basically at beginner level. my wife is chinese and her whole family speaks it and i just smile and nod at dinners. anyway i saw duolingo is doing a sale, worth it or no

Three years of trying and still sitting quietly at those dinners — that's not a Duolingo problem, and another app probably won't fix it either. What you're describing sounds less like a method question and more like something that's genuinely weighing on you: being on the outside of your wife's family's world, in a language that carries real meaning for them and for your relationship.

Duolingo is fine for building a daily habit, but it won't get you to dinner-table conversation. What actually moves the needle at this stage is structured speaking practice — something like iTalki for sessions with a tutor who can work with your specific gaps, combined with learning the phrases and topics that actually come up with her family. The goal isn't fluency in the abstract; it's specific, real conversations with specific people. That focus tends to make progress feel real instead of endless.

The sale is fine if it helps you stay consistent, but it's not the bottleneck.

My ceramics teacher pulled me aside after class and said my work was 'technically competent.' I'm 54 and I quit my job in March to finally do this full time and I just. I don't know what I'm supposed to do with that feedback

That's a hard thing to hear, especially now. You made a real leap — left a job, reorganized your life around something that matters to you — and 'technically competent' from someone whose opinion carries weight can land like a door closing rather than feedback you can use. That stings differently at this stage than it would have at 25.

It's worth separating what your teacher actually observed from what you heard in that moment. 'Technically competent' tells you the fundamentals are there — that's not nothing, and it's not the ceiling. But what it doesn't tell you is what's missing for them, or whether what's missing is something you even want to chase. Your work doesn't have to satisfy your teacher's aesthetic to be worth making. The question of what you're supposed to do with it is real, and it's yours to answer — not theirs.

my mom called me twice this week to tell me my cousin just got engaged and how 'wonderful' it is. im 34 and single and she knows exactly what shes doing. i didnt say anything mean, just kind of went quiet and got off the phone fast. i feel like that was the right call tbh

Going quiet instead of snapping back takes real restraint, especially when the dig is dressed up as innocent good news. You protected the relationship from a fight you didn't want to have, and that's not nothing.
