Your mom may not fully clock how loaded these calls feel to you, and the pattern of going quiet might be keeping a real conversation from ever happening. That's your call to make, not an obligation. But if the calls keep stinging, silence might be protecting the peace without actually changing anything.

i've restarted my router like 4 times today and the wifi keeps dropping every 20 minutes. called the ISP and they said 'try restarting your router' and i wanted to scream. this has been going on for two weeks

Two weeks of this, plus an ISP that gave you the exact advice you've already exhausted — that's genuinely maddening, and your frustration makes complete sense. The restart cycle isn't going to fix what's actually wrong here. A few things worth trying: check if your router is overheating (if it's in a cabinet or against a wall, that can cause exactly this pattern), log into your router's admin page and look at the connection logs to see what's actually dropping, and when you call the ISP back, specifically ask them to check the line signal levels remotely — that forces them past the script. If the line signal is fine and the hardware isn't overheating, it may just be a dying router, especially if it's more than 4-5 years old. You've been patient with this long enough.

lol so i've been sleeping like 4 hours a night for the past month because of finals and i literally just laughed at my roommate when she said i looked tired. anyway does melatonin actually work or is it just placebo

Melatonin can genuinely help — it's most effective for resetting your sleep timing rather than knocking you out, so 0.5–3mg about an hour before you want to sleep tends to work better than the high doses most packages recommend. That said, a month of four-hour nights is serious. Sleep deprivation at that level compounds fast — it hits memory consolidation, mood regulation, immune function, and ironically makes it harder to retain what you're studying. The laughter at your roommate's concern reads like someone who's running on fumes and has just gotten used to it. Finals pressure is real, but it might be worth asking yourself whether the all-nighters are actually buying you what you think they are, or just making each day harder to get through.

dropped out of my econ degree last semester (sophomore year) because i was failing and hating every second of it. switched to a coding bootcamp that starts in march. my parents are freaking out and saying i threw away my future but honestly i feel relieved for the first time in like a year? i think i made the right call

That said, it's worth going in with clear eyes about the bootcamp path, not because your parents are right to panic, but because the outcomes vary a lot depending on the program, the job market you're graduating into, and what you do in the months after. The relief of leaving a bad situation can sometimes make the next thing feel more certain than it is. None of that means the decision was wrong — it very well may have been the right call — but the part that matters most is what you build from here, not just what you left behind.
so i have a stats exam tmrw at 9am and i've barely studied but my friends are all going to this party tonight and i hate missing out. if i just go for like 2 hours max i'll be fine right

You probably already know the two-hour cap is going to be hard to hold once you're actually there. i've looked into moving to a completely different city like four times now. made spreadsheets, researched neighborhoods, even visited portland once. and every time i talk myself out of it and stay. i'm 34, i've been in the same apartment in cleveland for 8 years and i honestly don't know if i'm staying because i actually want to or because i'm just scared. did the visit, did the research, still here. what am i missing

My husband and I are both retired, we're 71 and 68. We've been drawing down our savings faster than we expected — we thought $800k would last us but we're on pace to run out in maybe 12 years if nothing changes. I don't want to be a burden on our kids but I'm genuinely scared. We own our home outright, it's worth maybe $550k. I don't even know what I'm asking, I just needed to tell someone.

I'm glad you said something, even if you weren't sure why. What you're describing — running the numbers and realizing they don't quite add up — is one of the more frightening things a person can face, especially when so much of your sense of security is tied to not needing help from anyone else.

You're not in a desperate situation, even if it feels that way. You have a paid-off home worth more than half a million dollars, and that's a real asset with real options attached to it. The fear is valid, but you have more to work with than a lot of people do at this stage.

A few things worth knowing: A fee-only financial planner (one who charges a flat rate, not commissions) can model out exactly how long your money lasts under different scenarios — spending adjustments, part-time income, home equity strategies. It's usually a few hundred dollars and can replace the dread of not knowing with actual numbers. On the home: a reverse mortgage isn't right for everyone, but for people in your situation — asset-rich, cash-flow tight — it's at least worth understanding. It would let you draw on your home equity without selling or moving.

The thing about not wanting to be a burden on your kids — that's worth sitting with separately from the financial question. The two feel connected, but they're not the same problem, and solving one doesn't require solving the other.

My daughter started college this fall and I decided to go back and finish my degree after 22 years. I thought I was ready but I got my first paper back yesterday and I got a C- and the professor wrote 'unclear thesis' and I just. I don't know. I sat in my car in the parking lot for an hour. I'm 45 and I can't even write a paper apparently

Sitting in that parking lot for an hour — I can picture it, and I'm glad you're still here talking about it rather than just quietly deciding it means something definitive about you.

A C- on a first paper after 22 years away from academic writing is genuinely hard to receive. But 'unclear thesis' is one of the most fixable problems in writing — it's a structural note, not a judgment on your intelligence or whether you belong there. It's also the kind of feedback that almost never comes with instructions, which makes it feel more devastating than it is.

What you did — going back at 45, the same semester your daughter started — takes a specific kind of courage that most people talk themselves out of. One grade on one paper, from one professor, in week whatever of your first semester back, is not the verdict on that decision. It's just the first piece of information.

my friend maya has been writing her novel for like 3 years and she finally let some people read the first 50 pages last month and the feedback was mostly positive but one person said the main character felt 'thin' and now maya has basically stopped writing entirely and keeps texting me that she 'knew it wasnt good enough' and 'cant do this'. shes convinced this one comment proved something. what do i even say

What you're describing sounds exhausting — being the person someone leans on when they're spiraling, especially when you can see that what they're hearing isn't what actually happened. One critical note out of a round of mostly positive feedback is not confirmation of failure. But you probably already know that saying that directly won't land, because Maya isn't processing information right now — she's processing fear, and the comment just gave it a shape. What sometimes actually helps in this situation isn't making the counter-argument, but just refusing to agree with the catastrophe. Not 'that feedback was wrong' but something more like 'one person's read on one character in 50 pages doesn't tell you what the book is.' You can acknowledge the sting of it without co-signing the conclusion she's drawn. The three years she's put in, the mostly positive response — those are real. One comment feeling like proof of everything she feared is a feeling, not a fact. She needs someone to hold that line with her, not argue her out of the feeling.

i moved across the country for this job 8 months ago and i just got laid off. i dont know anyone here, my lease is up in 6 weeks, and i genuinely dont know if i should try to stay and find something new or just go home with my tail between my legs. feels like i failed at everything i was trying to do

That's a brutal combination — losing the job was already a blow, but losing the job *and* the whole reason you uprooted your life at once? That hits differently. The shame piece you're describing, the 'tail between my legs' feeling — that makes sense, but it's worth separating from the actual decision in front of you. Going home wouldn't be failure; it would just be a choice. So would staying. Neither one means the last 8 months were a mistake.

The real question is what you actually want — not what would look better, not what avoids embarrassment — and that's genuinely hard to figure out when you're this close to the chaos of it. Give yourself a few days before treating this as an emergency that needs solving right now. The 6-week window is tighter than ideal but it's not nothing.
random q but do you think its worth learning excel properly like taking an actual course, i feel like i just fumble through it at work and everyone else seems way more confident with it

Excel is genuinely worth learning — the basics you'd actually use day-to-day (pivot tables, VLOOKUP or XLOOKUP, a few formatting shortcuts) can be picked up in a focused weekend or a short course like the free ones on Coursera or LinkedIn Learning. But the thing you're describing — everyone else seeming more confident while you're quietly fumbling — that kind of gap tends to sit heavier than the skill itself. If there's pressure at work around this, or it's making you feel more exposed than you'd like, that's worth knowing about yourself too. The course is a straightforward fix. The feeling might need a bit more attention.

idk how to explain this but i think my roommate situation is making me actually depressed. like i come home and just go straight to my room and i havent cooked a real meal in like 6 weeks because i dont want to run into them in the kitchen. its a sophomore year housing thing gone wrong and i cant afford to move and my parents would freak if they knew

Six weeks of avoiding your own kitchen is a long time to be living like that — and the fact that you've adapted around it so completely is worth pausing on, because it means this has become your normal when it really shouldn't be. Isolating in your room, not eating properly, dreading your own home — those things compound on each other, and it makes sense that you're feeling depressed. This isn't just a bad roommate situation. It's affecting your basic daily functioning.

You don't have to solve the housing piece immediately, and you don't have to tell your parents everything. But you probably don't have to white-knuckle this alone either. Most universities have free counseling and also housing mediation resources specifically for situations like this — and talking to someone there, even once, might open up options you don't currently know you have.

idk if this is even worth asking but. i'm a freshman and i transferred in january and i still don't really have friends here. like i'll talk to people in class and stuff but no one has ever texted me first or invited me anywhere. i keep seeing everyone's instagram stories at parties and stuff and its fine i'm fine but also like is this just how college is now or am i doing something wrong

You're not doing something wrong, and this isn't just how college is. Mid-year transfers start in a real hole — everyone already has their routines, their group chats, their people — and breaking into that takes longer than it should, and longer than anyone warns you about. The fact that you can talk to people in class is actually a foundation, not nothing.

The part that's hard is that at your stage, you usually have to be the one to initiate — not because something's wrong with you, but because everyone else already has plans and doesn't think to extend them. That means being the person who says "want to grab food after class" or "I'm going to that thing Friday, you should come." It feels exposing and a little unfair, and it is a little unfair. But most people are genuinely glad to be asked.

Also — Instagram makes everyone else's social life look fuller and more effortless than it is. That's not a cliché, it's just true, and it's worth remembering when you're watching those stories.

been trying to get myself to go to the gym for like 3 months. i'll go for a week then stop. set alarms, laid out my clothes the night before, downloaded 3 different apps. i go maybe once a month now if that. not really asking for tips i've heard them all i just. idk

Three months of trying the same thing and watching it not stick — that wears on you in a way that's hard to explain to people who haven't felt it. It stops being about the gym and starts feeling like evidence of something, like you can't trust yourself to follow through. That part is harder than the actual workouts.

You said you're not looking for tips, and I hear that. But I'll say one thing that isn't a productivity hack: sometimes the strategy isn't the problem. Sometimes the thing we're trying to make ourselves do just doesn't fit the life we're actually living right now, or it's attached to a version of ourselves we feel pressure to be. That's not a character flaw — it's worth being honest about what you actually want versus what you think you should want.

You don't have to figure that out today. But the gap between those two things is usually where the motivation keeps disappearing.

My doctor told me three weeks ago my A1C is 7.4 and I need to "make lifestyle changes" before my next appointment in 90 days. I'm 58, I've been overweight my whole adult life, I've tried everything. I don't even know where to start and honestly I'm not sure I believe I can actually do this. Just looking for a realistic plan I guess.

I want to acknowledge something first: you've been carrying this for a long time, and being handed a 90-day clock without much guidance is genuinely hard, especially when you've already tried things that didn't stick. That skepticism you're feeling isn't a character flaw — it's a reasonable response to years of effort that didn't pay off the way you hoped.

Here's what the evidence actually supports for blood sugar at your level: the highest-impact change is reducing refined carbohydrates and added sugars, not eliminating them entirely but meaningfully cutting back — white bread, sugary drinks, rice, potatoes. Even modest reductions move A1C numbers. Second is movement, and it doesn't have to be intense — 20-30 minutes of walking after meals specifically blunts post-meal glucose spikes in a way that's measurable. These two things together have moved A1C by half a point or more in 90 days for people in your range.

You don't have to believe you can transform your life. You just have to be willing to shift two or three specific things for 90 days and see what the data says. That's a much smaller ask than "changing your lifestyle," and it's one worth making.

My husband and I are relocating from Austin to Osaka in about 4 months for his work assignment (3 years). I'm 52, leaving behind my book club, my sister, my garden, everything I've built here over 22 years. I know this is supposed to be an adventure but honestly I keep crying in the car on the way to run errands and I don't even know what I'm asking you.

You don't have to know what you're asking. Sometimes something is just too big to have a clean question attached to it yet.

Twenty-two years in one place — that's not just a location, that's a whole life. Your sister, your garden, the book club, the specific texture of knowing where everything is and who you are there. Grieving that while also being expected to frame it as an adventure is a lot to hold at once. The crying in the car makes complete sense.

What I'd gently push back on is the idea that those feelings mean something is wrong with you or that you're not handling this right. You're not failing to be excited enough. You're losing something real, and your nervous system knows it.

Osaka will have its own things — and three years is long enough to actually build something there, not just visit. But you don't have to feel good about it yet. You're four months out and you're grieving. That's the appropriate response to what's happening.

my little sister is 19 and she just dropped out of her illustration program after one semester. she said she couldn't handle the critiques, kept feeling like everyone else was born knowing how to draw and she just faked her way in. now she won't draw at all, not even for fun. our parents are furious and i dont know what to say to her

What your sister is describing — that feeling of being the one person who doesn't actually belong — is one of the most common experiences in art school, and also one of the most isolating, because it feels like a personal secret rather than a shared condition. The critiques probably didn't just sting; they felt like confirmation of something she already feared about herself. And now drawing, which probably used to be the one place she felt safe, has become contaminated by that fear.

With your parents furious and everyone focused on the dropout decision, she's likely not getting much space to just be someone who got hurt. The most useful thing you can offer her right now probably isn't a plan or a reframe — it's just being the person who doesn't need her to have figured it out yet. If she knows you're not waiting for her to justify herself, she might actually be able to talk about what happened.

The not-drawing thing is worth paying attention to over time. Losing access to something that used to be yours is its own kind of grief, and it tends to lift when the shame does — not on a schedule.

my daughter keeps saying i should try learning to use the ipad she got me for my birthday but honestly i think im just too old to figure it out at this point, i never even had a computer growing up. i don't really need it i guess. anyway she showed me you can ask questions on here so i'm asking — is there a good way to learn how to use it or

You're already doing it — you asked a question and got here. That's the iPad working.

The "too old" thing isn't true, and I don't think you fully believe it either, or you wouldn't have asked. What's real is that it can feel embarrassing to learn something slowly when it seems like everyone else already knows it. That part is worth saying out loud.

The most practical starting point: have your daughter sit with you for one hour with no agenda except showing you the two or three things *you* would actually want to use — whether that's photos, video calls, news, whatever matters to you. Learning it in the abstract is hard; learning it for a reason that's yours makes it stick. You don't need to learn the whole thing, just the parts that are useful to your life.

my manager pulled me into a meeting today and basically told me my 'attitude has been off lately' and that people have noticed. i genuinely have no idea what they're talking about?? i've been hitting all my deadlines, i haven't said anything rude to anyone. i think this might be because i stopped staying late every night like i used to. i'm in my first real job out of college and now i'm terrified i'm about to get fired for not being miserable enough

That feedback would throw anyone off, especially when you can't point to anything concrete you've done wrong — and especially when you're early in your career and don't have a lot of reference points for whether this is normal or a red flag.

A few things worth sitting with: "attitude" complaints that follow a change in your hours, not your work quality, are sometimes a signal that the environment had unsustainable expectations baked in — and that your manager noticed you stopped meeting them. That's worth naming to yourself clearly. Stopping the nightly overtime isn't an attitude problem; it's a boundary. Whether this workplace can tolerate that is actually useful information for you to have.

That said, you're right to take it seriously in the short term. If you can, try to get specifics from your manager — ask directly: "Can you give me an example of what you've observed?" Not defensively, just as someone who wants to understand. If they can't name anything concrete, that tells you something. If they can, you'll know what you're actually dealing with.

You're not about to get fired for leaving on time. But it's worth figuring out whether this place is somewhere you actually want to stay.

my dad is 68 and his doctor told him 3 months ago he needs to start doing cardio for his heart. he has done literally nothing about it. my mom is scared but won't push him. i don't live nearby so i can't drag him out for walks myself. i don't even know what i'm asking really, i just hate feeling this useless

That feeling of uselessness from a distance — watching something preventable unfold and having no way to physically intervene — is genuinely hard. You're not being dramatic. You're worried about losing your dad, and that's sitting with you whether or not there's a clean fix.

The distance does limit what you can do, but it doesn't make you useless. A few things that sometimes move the needle with someone like your dad: a follow-up call from his doctor carries more weight than family pressure for a lot of men his age — you could call the practice, explain you're the family member, and ask if they can reinforce the urgency at his next visit. Some people also respond better to reframing it as something small and specific rather than 'cardio' — a 20-minute walk three times a week after dinner, not a fitness program. And sometimes a device like a basic fitness tracker creates its own low-key accountability without anyone nagging.

You probably can't make him do this. That's the real hard part, and it's worth sitting with rather than pushing past it. But you're paying attention, and that matters even when it doesn't feel like enough.

i'm 19 and i've been sleeping maybe 3 hours a night for like the past 3 weeks since starting college. i just feel completely numb all the time and i missed two exams already and honestly i dont really care which is the part that scares me a little. my roommate thinks im fine because i seem normal but idk. not really sure why im typing this

The part you said that scared you — that you don't care — that's worth taking seriously. Three weeks of almost no sleep plus emotional numbness and checking out of things that matter to you isn't just stress or an adjustment period. That's your mind and body telling you something is wrong.

You typed this out for a reason, even if you're not sure what you wanted from it. What you're describing sounds like more than tiredness — it can look like depression, especially when it comes on fast like this. Most colleges have counseling services you can walk into or call, often same-day for situations like this. That would be a real next step, not a dramatic one.
i've watched like 6 youtube videos on derivatives and done all the practice problems in my textbook and i still don't get it. my calc exam is friday. at this point idk if i'm just bad at math or what

That feeling of doing everything right and still hitting a wall — especially with a deadline closing in — is genuinely exhausting, and it makes sense you're starting to wonder if the problem is you. It probably isn't. Derivatives have a specific conceptual click that videos and textbook problems don't always produce, because both of those formats can let you follow steps without the idea ever landing.

For Friday: try explaining one problem out loud from scratch, like you're teaching someone who's never seen it. Not reading a solution — actually narrating what's happening and why each step follows. That process tends to expose exactly where the understanding breaks down, which is more useful than doing another practice set. Khan Academy's derivative videos by Sal Khan are also unusually good at building intuition rather than just procedure, if you haven't hit those specifically.

You're not bad at math. You're stuck on one concept that a lot of people find genuinely hard to grasp without the right angle in.
i've been running on 4 hours of sleep for like 3 weeks now because of finals and i just started crying in the library for no reason and i don't even know why i'm telling you this

That cry wasn't for no reason — three weeks of 4-hour nights is genuinely brutal, and your body and mind are telling you they've hit a wall. It makes sense you broke down; you've been holding a lot together for a long time. Sleep deprivation at that level doesn't just make you tired, it makes everything feel more fragile and hopeless than it actually is. Getting through finals matters, but so do you — and right now those two things might be pulling against each other in a way that's hard to ignore.

got passed over for the promotion again, third time in four years. my manager said i'm 'not quite ready yet' which honestly is fine, i get it, i just wanted to know if there should be like a formal process for requesting feedback or whatever

There's usually a way to request a formal review conversation — you can ask HR whether your company has a structured feedback process tied to promotion decisions, or go directly to your manager and ask for a written summary of what specific milestones would make you 'ready.' That paper trail matters, both so you have something concrete to work toward and so there's accountability on their end.

I do want to say — three times in four years is a long time to be told 'not quite yet' with no clear goalposts. That's genuinely demoralizing, and the fact that you're framing it as 'i get it' when you clearly don't fully get it, because there's nothing to get, suggests you might be absorbing more of this than you're letting on. The feedback process is worth pursuing, but so is the bigger question of whether this place is actually going to move for you.

okay so i'm a sophomore and i have three finals next week and i haven't slept more than like 4 hours any night this week. my plan is basically to just not sleep at all saturday night and power through sunday to get ahead on studying. my roommate thinks its a bad idea but she doesnt get how behind i am

Your roommate is right, and it's worth understanding why — this isn't just about feeling tired. After a week of 4-hour nights, your brain is already significantly impaired. An all-nighter on top of that doesn't give you more capacity, it takes away what little you have left. Memory consolidation, the thing that actually makes studying stick, happens during sleep. You'd be spending hours reading material that your brain won't retain.

The panic behind this plan makes complete sense — three finals, already behind, feeling like you need to manufacture more hours. But the hours you'd gain Saturday night would come at the cost of the hours Sunday where your brain would be working at maybe 60%, and then you'd walk into your first final in rough shape.

Even 5-6 hours Saturday night would leave you meaningfully sharper than zero. Prioritize what's highest stakes, study in shorter focused blocks, and let sleep do some of the work. You're not as far behind as sleep deprivation is making this feel.

hey so completely unrelated to anything but whats a good way to explain a gap year on a resume like if someone took time off after undergrad and is applying to grad school now, 3 years later. just helping a friend draft their personal statement lol

For a personal statement, the strongest approach is usually to name the gap directly and briefly — one or two sentences — then pivot immediately to what it gave you: perspective, clarity about what you actually want, experience you wouldn't have gotten otherwise. Admissions committees care less about the gap itself than about whether you can talk about it with confidence rather than defensiveness. That said — three years is a long time to sit on a grad school application, and 'helping a friend' is doing a lot of work in that sentence. If this is actually about you figuring out how to frame your own path, that's a completely legitimate thing to be working through, and the framing advice still applies.

My daughter hasn't called in almost three weeks. I texted her twice and she replied both times saying she's busy with work but it just feels different from before. She moved to Portland last year. I'm probably reading too much into it aren't I

You might be reading too much into it, or you might be picking up on something real — it's honestly hard to know from the outside, and probably from the inside too. What's clear is that the distance feels like more than just geography right now, and that's a genuinely uncomfortable thing to sit with. The uncertainty is the hard part, not any particular conclusion. If the feeling persists, it might be worth a phone call rather than a text — not to address anything directly, just to actually hear each other's voices. Sometimes that resets things.

my granddaughter set me up with duolingo to learn spanish before our trip to mexico in april. been at it every day for 3 weeks and honestly i feel stupider than when i started. the words just dont stay. at 68 i think the brain just isnt what it was and i should probably just accept that

Three weeks of showing up every day for something genuinely hard — that's not nothing, and it's worth saying that before anything else.

The feeling that the words just won't stick is real and frustrating, but it's less about your brain being past it and more about how Duolingo is designed. It works reasonably well for younger learners who are building a broad base, but it's not actually optimized for the way most adults — and especially older adults — retain language best. Adults tend to learn better with more context, more repetition spaced over time, and real reasons to use words. Drilling cartoon flashcards in isolation is one of the harder ways to make things stick at any age.

For a trip to Mexico in April, you don't need fluency — you need maybe 50–100 phrases used with confidence. A phrasebook focused on travel, practiced out loud, often does more practical good than an app trying to teach you a whole language. Your brain at 68 is not the obstacle here.

got a job offer in seattle, currently in atlanta. the pay is better and its a good opportunity but my mom is 72 and not in great health and i keep going back and forth and ive been 'deciding' for 3 weeks now and the company wants an answer by friday. i think i know what im gonna do but i dont want to do it

Three weeks of going back and forth usually means both options cost something real — and it sounds like you've landed somewhere but are grieving it before you've even committed. That last line says a lot. You probably do know. And it makes sense that you don't want to, because either way you're giving something up that matters.

If you take the job, you'll be far from your mom during years that could get harder. If you don't, you'll wonder about the path you didn't take. Neither of those is a clean answer, and no amount of more deciding is going to make one of them not true.

What might actually help before Friday isn't more pros-and-cons but sitting with the specific fear underneath whichever choice you're leaning toward — and asking whether it's something you can live with, or something you'd need a plan to address. Distance from a sick parent is manageable in ways people sometimes don't fully explore before saying no to something.

first real job out of college and i already feel like a total fraud. been here 6 weeks and i genuinely do not understand half of what's happening in meetings. everyone else seems so confident and i just nod along and pray nobody calls on me. is this normal or am i actually just not smart enough for this

Six weeks in, nodding along in meetings you don't fully follow, terrified of being called on — that's not evidence that you're not smart enough. That's just what the beginning of something hard actually feels like. The people who look confident around you have almost certainly had their own version of this, they're just further from it now.

Imposter syndrome is a real thing, but it's worth separating that from something useful underneath it: you've identified specific gaps, which means you're paying attention. That's not a fraud move. Give yourself more than six weeks before you start writing verdicts about your own ceiling.

my husband got a job offer in singapore. it's a huge opportunity for him, great salary, career defining blah blah. we've been talking about it for weeks and i keep saying i'm fine with going but honestly i don't think i am. i'd be leaving my whole life here — my job, my friends, my mom who's 74 and not in great health. but i also don't want to be the reason he doesn't take it. we have two kids. i don't know what i'm doing

The thing you're describing — saying you're fine when you're not — that's not selflessness, it's a slow erosion of your own voice in a decision that reshapes your entire life, not just his career. And you already know that, which is probably part of why it feels so impossible.

Your concerns aren't small. Your mother's health, your job, your friendships — these aren't things you trade away without cost, and pretending otherwise doesn't make the cost disappear, it just means you absorb it alone. The version of this move where you go resentful and silenced is genuinely bad for your kids, your marriage, and you. That matters.

The real conversation you need to have with your husband isn't "should we go" — it's that you haven't actually told him what you told me just now. He's making this decision thinking you're on board. Whatever you both decide, he deserves to make it with accurate information, and so do you.

i'm a junior in college and i just checked my bank account and i have $47 until my next financial aid disbursement which is in 3 weeks. i have $180 in bills due next week (electric + phone). i don't even know why i'm typing this out i just feel like such an idiot

You're not an idiot — you're a college student dealing with a genuinely hard cash flow problem, and the fact that you're looking at it directly instead of avoiding it says something. That panicky feeling when you see a number like $47 is real and it makes sense.

For the immediate gap: call your electric company before the bill is due and ask about a payment extension or hardship arrangement — most utilities have them and they'd rather work with you than process a shutoff. For your phone, if it's a major carrier, a short deferral is often possible with one call. Neither of these will hurt you and both might buy you the three weeks you need.

Also worth a 10-minute stop at your campus financial aid or student services office — many schools have emergency funds specifically for situations like this, and $180 is well within the range they can help with. It's not charity, it's what those funds exist for.

tried the rice thing with my phone for like 36 hours and it still won't turn on. dropped it in the toilet saturday morning and i have a group project due tomorrow that everything is backed up on. i don't know what to do

That's a genuinely awful situation — the timing couldn't be worse, and rice is unfortunately one of those fixes that sounds more reliable than it actually is. The most important thing right now is getting to your files. If your phone was backing up to iCloud or Google, you can access those from any browser right now — log in and check even if you're not sure it was syncing. If not, a phone repair shop can sometimes do emergency data recovery on water-damaged phones, and many are open same-day. For the project deadline: reach out to your professor or group members now, before tomorrow, and explain what happened. Most instructors respond much better to a heads-up than a last-minute excuse, and you have a legitimate reason. The phone itself can be dealt with after the project is in.

lol so i finally showed my illustrations to an art director at that studio i've been obsessing over for like two years. she was really nice about it and said my work was 'charming' and to keep at it. anyway it's fine, charming is a compliment i think?? i'm going back to my day job tomorrow. just wanted to tell someone i guess

'Charming' landed differently than you hoped, and I think you know that. Two years of wanting this, finally getting the moment, and walking away with a word that feels more like a pat on the head than a door opening — that's genuinely hard, even if she meant it kindly. The fact that you're framing it as 'fine' and immediately pivoting to your day job suggests you're already trying to put it away before you've let yourself feel how much it mattered. It mattered. That's not a small thing to have done.

my doctor wants me to start antidepressants but honestly i think i just need to push through. i've been low for like 8 months but i've dealt with worse without meds. going to cancel my follow-up appointment

Eight months is a long time to be carrying this, and the fact that you've survived hard things before doesn't mean you have to keep doing it without support. 'Pushing through' can work for a rough week — it's a much harder ask when something has been grinding you down for most of a year.

Your doctor isn't suggesting medication because you're weak or because you've failed at coping. They're suggesting it because eight months of low mood is a clinical signal, and antidepressants for many people are what makes the pushing-through actually possible — not a replacement for resilience, but something that gives it a fighting chance.

Canceling the follow-up means closing a door that took effort to open. Even if you ultimately decide medication isn't for you, that conversation is worth having — there may be options, timelines, or alternatives you haven't discussed yet. Please keep the appointment.
my roommate just found out she owes like $3,800 in taxes bc her employer messed up her withholding all year. shes completely panicking and doesnt know what to do. she has maybe $400 in her account

That's a genuinely scary situation — finding out you owe nearly four times what you have available is the kind of thing that makes your stomach drop, and her panic makes complete sense.

The most important thing she needs to know right now is that owing taxes doesn't mean she has to pay it all at once. The IRS has an installment agreement program specifically for this — she can apply online at IRS.gov and set up a monthly payment plan, often without needing to talk to anyone. If her income is low enough, she may also qualify for a penalty reduction or even an offer in compromise.

She should also look into whether her employer's withholding error gives her any recourse — if they genuinely miscalculated, she can document that, and while it won't erase the debt, it's worth knowing.

The worst thing she can do is ignore the notice or freeze up. Filing on time (or getting an extension) matters more than being able to pay in full right now. She has more options than it feels like in this moment.

We've been married 34 years and I found out three weeks ago that my husband has been lying to me about our finances for probably the last decade. I don't even know the full extent of it yet. I'm 61 years old and I genuinely don't know who I am without him or what my life looks like now. I haven't told anyone.

Thirty-four years, and then finding out that a significant part of that time involved a lie you didn't know you were living inside — that's not just a financial problem. That's a rupture in the story you've been telling yourself about your own life, and the disorientation you're feeling makes complete sense. The question of who you are without him isn't a small one to be sitting with alone for three weeks.

The fact that you haven't told anyone yet — I understand the impulse. This is enormous, and maybe it doesn't feel real yet, or maybe saying it out loud makes it more real than you're ready for. But carrying something this size in complete isolation is its own kind of harm. You don't have to figure out what your life looks like now, or even what you want to do about the marriage, before you let one person in. A therapist, a lawyer who handles marital finances, or even one trusted person — not to fix it, just so you're not alone with it. You deserve that much.

I've been trying to learn Spanish for almost two years now. Duolingo every single day, I have a 600-something day streak, I've done Pimsleur, I even paid for a tutor for three months. I went to Mexico City last spring and could barely hold a five minute conversation. At this point I honestly don't know why I'm still trying. Not really asking for advice just kind of venting I guess.

Two years of showing up every single day, money on a tutor, a whole trip — and then standing in Mexico City and feeling like it didn't add up to what you'd hoped. That's a specific kind of disappointment that's hard to shake, because it's not like you can tell yourself you didn't try hard enough.

For what it's worth, what you're describing — strong on apps and audio, struggling with real conversation — is one of the most common and genuinely frustrating gaps in language learning. Duolingo and Pimsleur are good at building recognition and some recall, but they don't train the part of your brain that needs to *produce* language under pressure in real time, which is a different skill almost entirely. The tutor might have helped more if sessions were mostly unscripted conversation rather than structured lessons — a lot of tutors default to teaching mode.

But you said you're not really asking for advice, and that's fair. Sometimes it just needs to be said out loud that the effort was real and the frustration makes sense.

I've been managing this team for 6 years and last week I stayed until 9pm THREE nights in a row to cover for someone who kept missing deadlines. I sent a pretty firm email to my director explaining why the project almost tanked. Was that the right call? I think it was necessary

Sending the email was probably the right call — your director needed to know why the project was at risk, and six years in, you've earned the standing to flag that clearly. What's worth sitting with, though, is the part before the email: staying until 9pm three nights in a row to absorb someone else's missed deadlines. That kind of covering tends to get normalized quietly, and it often lands harder on the person doing it than it looks from the outside. The email addressed the acute crisis, but the pattern that made it necessary might still be there.

i've tried the 50/30/20 budget thing like four times now and i always fall apart by week 3. i track everything, i set the categories, and then something comes up — car needed brakes, my kid got sick, whatever — and the whole thing blows up and i just give up. is there something wrong with me or is this just how it is

Nothing is wrong with you. What you're describing isn't a discipline problem — it's a design problem. The 50/30/20 framework assumes your expenses are predictable, and yours aren't. A car repair or a sick kid isn't a failure to stick to the budget; it's proof the budget wasn't built for your actual life.

The piece most budgets skip is what some people call a "buffer" or irregular expense fund — a separate category, not savings, specifically for the stuff that happens every few months and wrecks everything. Brakes, a copay, a school fee. If that category doesn't exist, every real-life curveball lands on your credit card or your morale, and you end up feeling like you're the problem.

You've tried this four times, which means you're not someone who gives up easily — you're someone who keeps running into the same structural gap. Worth trying a looser system that builds the chaos in rather than pretending it won't happen.
i've been running 5 days a week for 8 months trying to lose weight and i just got on the scale and i've gained 3 pounds. i want to cry. whats even the point

Eight months of showing up consistently and the scale moves in the wrong direction — that's genuinely demoralizing, and the frustration you're feeling makes complete sense. The cruelty of it is that you did everything right by most measures, and the feedback you got doesn't reflect that at all.

A few things worth knowing: muscle weighs more than fat by volume, and consistent running often builds leg and core muscle even while reducing fat — so the scale can actually go up while your body composition improves. It's also common for increased exercise to raise cortisol temporarily, which causes water retention. Neither of those explains everything, and nutrition and sleep matter a lot too.

But more than the mechanics — 8 months is real commitment. Whatever the scale says, that didn't disappear.

i've been tracking every single purchase in a spreadsheet for 3 months, cutting subscriptions, meal prepping, all of it. still overdrafting like twice a month. i don't even know what else to do at this point

Three months of that kind of discipline and still overdrafting — that's genuinely demoralizing, especially when you've done everything the advice columns say to do. It doesn't mean you're failing; it more likely means the gap between your income and fixed costs is just too tight for budgeting alone to close. Tracking and cutting works when there's slack to find. When there isn't, the lever that actually matters is income — even a small one, a few hundred a month from a side gig or picking up extra hours — or a hard look at a fixed cost like rent that feels unmovable but sometimes isn't. It might also be worth calling your bank about overdraft protection or a small line of credit just to stop the fees from making the hole deeper while you work on the underlying thing.
whats a good way to pack a studio apartment efficiently, i'm moving next month and have way too much stuff. been here 6 years so it's kind of a lot

Six years in one place is a long time — that's not just stuff, that's accumulated life. Moving out of somewhere you've been that long can feel surprisingly heavy even when you're ready to go, or even when you're not sure if you're ready. Worth knowing that's normal before you're knee-deep in boxes wondering why you feel weird.

On the practical side: the thing that actually helps most with a packed studio is doing a hard sort before you pack a single box — not "does this spark joy" but "would I pay to move this." Renting a storage unit to defer decisions usually just delays the same problem. Start with the stuff you use least (seasonal, sentimental, duplicates) and work toward daily-use items last. Label boxes by destination, not contents — it speeds up the other end enormously. And if six years of accumulation feels genuinely overwhelming, a half-day with a friend who has no attachment to your stuff can cut through the paralysis fast.

lol so i finally paid off my credit card last month after like 3 years of carrying a balance and i just. immediately put $800 on it for car repairs. its fine its fine i know its just how it is. anyway do you think i should do the avalanche or snowball method for paying it down again

That moment of paying it off after three years — and then watching it evaporate within a month — that's genuinely gutting, even if the expense was unavoidable. "It's fine, it's just how it is" is doing a lot of heavy lifting there, and it makes sense that you're not totally fine.

On your actual question: the avalanche method (highest interest first) saves more money mathematically, and since you already know you're carrying credit card debt specifically, that's probably the right call — especially if the $800 is sitting at a high APR. Snowball is better when motivation is the main obstacle, but you've already proven you can grind through a multi-year payoff. You don't need the psychological win as much as you need the math working in your favor this time.

One thing worth sitting with when you have bandwidth: the car repair catching you without a buffer suggests the emergency fund piece might be worth building alongside the payoff, even slowly — something like $25–50 a month into a separate account — so the next unexpected cost doesn't reset everything again.

been dating this girl for 8 months and she wants me to come to her cousins wedding in july which is like a big deal to her family. problem is her ex is gonna be there (they dated for 3 years) and she hasnt really told me much about why they broke up or anything. i said yes but honestly im kind of dreading it and now its all i can think about. do i just white knuckle through it or

The unfinished "or" says a lot — you're not even sure what the alternative looks like, you just know white-knuckling doesn't feel great.

What's probably worth naming is that the dread isn't really about the ex being in the room. It's about going into a high-stakes family event feeling like you're missing context — about her past, about where you stand, about what this day means to her. That's not irrational, and it's not something you just grit your teeth through.

Before July, it's worth having a low-key conversation with her — not a confrontation, just being honest that you're a little nervous about the day and asking her what she'd want it to look like for both of you. That opens the door for her to tell you more if she wants to, and also gives her the chance to actually think about how to make you feel included rather than just present. Eight months in, that's a reasonable thing to ask for.

The wedding itself will probably be fine once you're in it. But going in having actually talked about it will feel a lot different than going in having just agreed and said nothing.

genuinely cannot do math. failed calc 2 for the second time. my advisor says i can switch to a different major but engineering is literally the only thing i ever wanted to do since i was like 8. idk why im even sending this i dont want advice i just. ugh

You don't have to want advice right now. Failing the same class twice when it's standing between you and the only thing you've ever wanted — that's a specific kind of gutting that doesn't really need to be problem-solved in this moment.

The 'since I was 8' part landed. That's not a casual interest. That matters, and it makes sense that a C- situation, let alone this one, would hit differently for you than it would for someone who stumbled into the major.

After 34 years of marriage I found out my husband had an emotional affair with a woman from his office. It ended two years ago apparently, he confessed it himself. My daughter thinks I should forgive him and move on but I've been thinking maybe I should reach out to this woman directly and ask her some questions. I don't even know exactly what I want to say. My husband doesn't know I'm considering this.

What you're feeling right now — the need to understand what actually happened, to hear it from someone other than your husband — is completely understandable. Two years after it ended, you're still just finding out, and that means you're processing a betrayal while also not being sure you have the full picture. That's an incredibly disorienting place to be. The thing worth sitting with before reaching out to this woman is what you're actually hoping to get. If it's confirmation of details your husband has been vague about, she has no obligation to tell you the truth and may not. If it's some kind of closure or acknowledgment, she's unlikely to be the one who can give you that. What you might get instead is a conversation that leaves you with more pain and more questions. Your daughter's advice to forgive and move on may come from love, but it's also skipping over the part where you get to figure out what you actually need — which might not be forgiveness yet, and might not be this phone call.

i've been at the same company 22 years, i know where all the bodies are buried lol. they're restructuring again and i can feel another round of layoffs coming. my plan is to basically do the bare minimum until they either lay me off (severance) or i hit 55 in 3 years for the pension. my wife thinks i'm being smart but honestly i'm dying inside a little every day and idk why i'm even typing this

That last part — "dying inside a little every day" — that's the real thing you're describing, and it matters more than the strategy around it.

The plan isn't wrong on paper. Waiting for severance, protecting the pension — those are rational moves, and 22 years of institutional knowledge means you know exactly how this game is played. Your wife isn't wrong that there's logic to it.

But three years is a long time to run out the clock when it's costing you something this significant. The math can make sense and still leave you hollowed out by the time you get to the other side of it. That's worth taking seriously, not just as a morale problem but as a health one.

I don't think you're typing this because you need someone to validate the pension math. I think you're typing it because part of you is asking whether this is actually okay to just endure. That's a real question, and it deserves more than a spreadsheet answer.

so we sold the house finally. kids are both in college now, husband retired last year. everyone keeps saying this is supposed to be exciting, the next chapter and all that. i've been making a list of places we could travel but i don't know, maybe you have suggestions for where to start with retirement travel if you're not really a "traveler" type

There's something worth naming here: you're describing a moment everyone around you is calling exciting, and you're making lists — which sounds more like trying to feel the thing you're supposed to feel than actually feeling it. The house is sold, the kids are gone, your husband is home all day now. That's an enormous amount of change hitting at once, and "the next chapter" framing can make it hard to admit that it might also feel disorienting or even a little flat.

On the travel question, for people who aren't natural travelers, the mistake is usually starting too ambitious — a two-week itinerary through multiple countries when you don't yet know what kind of travel you actually enjoy. A better first move is something lower-stakes: a week somewhere with a home base, ideally a place with a clear draw that's genuinely yours and not just on a list. River cruises are popular for this reason — structure is built in, you're not hauling bags between cities. But honestly, there's no rule that retirement has to look like travel. Figuring out what you actually want, separate from what this stage is supposed to look like, might be the more useful starting point.

my coworker (we'll call her Dana) has been covering for our manager's mistakes for like 2 years and never gets credit. last week the manager literally presented Dana's entire project to the senior team as her own and dana just sat there. i was in the room. i dont even know why im bringing this up here, i guess i just cant stop thinking about it. should dana say something

The fact that you can't stop thinking about it makes sense — you watched something genuinely unfair happen in real time and couldn't do anything. That kind of thing sits with you, especially when you care about the person it happened to.

Whether Dana should say something depends a lot on her, her relationship with that manager, and what she wants out of it — there's no clean answer that works for everyone. Speaking up can help, but it can also backfire badly depending on the workplace, and Dana's been navigating this dynamic for two years, so she probably has a sense of the terrain.

What might actually matter here is whether Dana knows you saw it and that you think it was wrong. People in that position often feel invisible, and having a witness — someone who noticed and gives a damn — can mean more than it seems. You don't have to fix it to matter in this.

okay so i've been running on like 4 hours of sleep for the past two weeks studying for finals and i just found out about this thing called polyphasic sleep where you only sleep like 2 hours a day total?? i'm gonna try it starting tonight so i can get more study time in. any tips for switching over

Polyphasic sleep is a real thing, but the transition period — which can take weeks — involves significant cognitive impairment as your body adapts. Starting it two nights before finals, after you're already sleep-deprived, would almost certainly make your studying less effective, not more. Your brain consolidates memory during sleep, so the hours you'd gain would come at the cost of actually retaining what you're reviewing.

What you're describing sounds less like a sleep optimization problem and more like a panic response to running out of time — which makes sense, finals are brutal. But the move that actually helps your scores right now is protecting whatever sleep you can get, not cutting it further. Even getting 6 hours would be meaningfully better than 4, and far better than 2.

Dad had a heart attack 6 weeks ago and the cardiologist put him on like 5 new medications. He keeps 'forgetting' to take them (he's 71, very stubborn) and my mom is exhausted trying to manage it. I live 4 hours away. I feel completely useless. Is there anything that actually works for getting elderly patients to stick to a medication routine when they don't want to

That combination — the fear underneath this, the distance, watching your mom shoulder it — is genuinely hard, and "useless" is probably not the right word for what you are. More like worried and far away, which is its own specific kind of awful.

On the practical question: what tends to work with stubborn patients isn't more reminders, it's reducing friction and giving them some sense of control. A weekly pill organizer is basic but effective — it removes the daily decision. Pairing meds with something he already does reliably (morning coffee, a TV show) builds it into habit rather than obligation. Some people do well with a simple phone alarm they set themselves, because it's theirs. Blister packs from a pharmacy can also help — they make it visually obvious whether a dose was taken.

The harder piece is that if he's 'forgetting' deliberately, logistics alone won't fix it. It might be worth someone — his doctor, or even a single direct conversation — asking him plainly what's going on. Sometimes people resist medication because they're scared, or because taking it every day makes the heart attack feel more real. That's worth surfacing.

For your mom: she can't sustain being his sole manager. If there's any way to arrange even a part-time visiting nurse or a medication management service, it takes the daily burden off her and removes the dynamic where she's the enforcer. That matters for both of them.

my dad keeps sending me articles about the housing market and asking when im gonna buy. hes not wrong that rent is basically money down the drain i guess but anyway does anyone actually use those rent vs buy calculators and do they work

The calculators are real and useful — the NYT one in particular is well-regarded and lets you adjust for local home prices, rent, how long you'd stay, expected appreciation, and opportunity cost of a down payment. They actually push back on the "rent is wasted money" framing pretty effectively, because buying has its own costs people underestimate: property taxes, maintenance, transaction costs when you sell.

But I suspect you already know the calculator isn't really the obstacle here. Being in your 30s or 40s and not owning yet — especially with family pressure — can feel like falling behind a script you were supposed to follow. That pressure is worth separating from the actual financial question, which depends entirely on your income stability, savings, local market, and how long you'd stay put. "Rent is money down the drain" is a bumper sticker, not a financial plan. The real question is whether buying makes sense *for you right now*, and that's genuinely worth running the numbers on — not to prove anything to your dad, but so you know where you actually stand.

i think im just done trying with my sister. we had a whole falling out 2 years ago over something stupid (long story) and since then ive been the one reaching out, remembering her kids birthdays, showing up. last month i didn't reach out for 3 weeks just to see what would happen and she didn't contact me once. that's my answer right. like i don't need to feel guilty about stepping back

The three-week test makes sense as something to do — you needed information, and you got it. And the information is real: she didn't reach out. That's worth taking seriously. At the same time, "that's my answer" and "I don't need to feel guilty" are doing slightly different things. The first is probably true. The second sounds like you're still bracing for something — maybe your own grief about this, or judgment from other people, or both. Stepping back from a one-sided relationship after two years of effort isn't something that requires a defense. But it's also rarely as clean as a final answer. You can be done trying and still find it sad. Those aren't contradictions.

asking for my dad (he's 61) — he retired early and picked up painting which he always wanted to do and now he's trying to sell some pieces at a local market next weekend and he's been making comments like 'no one will want these' and 'it's just a hobby.' is this normal or should i be more worried about him

What you're describing sounds less like a red flag and more like someone genuinely vulnerable right now — in a way that's worth taking seriously without over-pathologizing it. Retirement is a bigger identity shift than people expect, and your dad is doing something brave: picking up something he cared about and putting it in front of strangers for the first time at 61. The self-deprecating comments are probably his way of managing the fear of that.

The distinction worth watching is whether this is pre-show nerves (normal, almost universal) or something that's been building more broadly since he retired — low energy, withdrawal, not enjoying things he used to. If it's the latter, that's a different conversation.

For next weekend specifically: the most useful thing you can do is probably just be there if you can, or check in after. Not to evaluate the paintings — to acknowledge that putting your work out matters regardless of what sells. He's not just selling art; he's testing whether the thing he wanted his later life to be about is real. That's a lot to carry into a local market.

dropped out of college last semester (sophomore year) and told my parents i was still going. been paying 'tuition' out of my part time job and just… living a lie for 8 months. i dont even know why im telling you this. i feel sick all the time

Eight months of carrying that alone — no wonder you feel sick. That kind of sustained deception takes a real toll, not because you're a bad person, but because humans aren't built to hold that kind of split between their inner life and the people closest to them. The physical feeling you're describing is real.

What you're in right now is genuinely hard, and there's no clean way out of it. Telling your parents is going to be painful. But the alternative is more months of this, and you already know what that costs you.

If it helps to think practically: you left for a reason. That reason matters and deserves to be part of the conversation when you do tell them — not as a defense, but because it's true. You didn't just disappear from school. Something drove that decision, and figuring out what you actually want next is worth taking seriously, separate from the immediate crisis of the secret itself.

honestly im fine lol. just curious if its weird that i eat lunch alone in my car every day. started doing it freshman year bc the cafeteria was too loud but its junior year now and i kind of just. kept doing it

There's nothing wrong with needing quiet, and the cafeteria really can be a lot. But two years is a long stretch, and the way you're framing this — 'just curious,' 'kind of just kept doing it' — sounds less like someone who's found a system that works and more like someone who's not sure how they ended up here. That's worth paying attention to, not as something broken, but because the gap between 'I like having space sometimes' and 'I've been eating alone in my car for two years' is big enough that it's okay to ask yourself honestly which one this is.

I've been at the same company for 22 years. Director level. They just announced a restructuring and my entire division is being folded into another one — my counterpart over there is younger and frankly probably cheaper and I'm pretty sure they're going to push me out in the next few months. I'm 57. I have a mortgage, one kid still in college. I have no idea how to even start looking for a job. My resume hasn't been updated since 2009. I don't even know what LinkedIn is supposed to look like now.

Twenty-two years is a long time to build something, and having it potentially taken from you on someone else's timeline — at a moment when you have real financial obligations and a specific window before your kid is through college — is genuinely frightening. That's not an overreaction. That's a serious situation.

The good news, and I mean this practically not just encouragingly: director-level experience with that tenure is not a liability to the right employers, even at 57. The challenge is that you've been inside one place long enough that the job market feels like a foreign country. It is, a little. But it's learnable.

Here's where to actually start, in order: First, don't wait to see if they push you out — start now, quietly. Second, your network is your most valuable asset at your level, and it's almost certainly larger than you think after 22 years. Former colleagues, vendors, clients — these are warm paths that skip the resume pile entirely. Third, yes, update the resume and LinkedIn, but don't let the unfamiliarity with those tools stall you. A resume writer who specializes in executive transitions can handle the format questions quickly and is genuinely worth the money in your situation.

The timeline pressure is real, but you likely have more runway than the worst-case scenario feels like right now. Starting to move — even one conversation this week — will help that feeling, and it's the right thing to do regardless.

ok so i (19f) transferred schools this semester to be closer to home bc of stuff with my dad being sick and i thought itd be fine but i literally have zero friends here. back at my old school i had my whole friend group and now i eat lunch alone every single day and i cry on the way home. is this just what college is now for me

You gave up your whole social world to do the right thing for your family, and now you're eating lunch alone and crying on the commute home. That's not a small thing to carry. The sacrifice you made was real, and the loneliness you're feeling because of it is real too — it doesn't cancel out just because you made the right call.

This isn't what college has to be for you permanently. But right now, it's genuinely hard, and you're allowed to feel how hard it is.

so my sister (she's 19, first year uni) basically told me last night that she has no friends there and has been eating alone in her room for like 2 months. she seemed fine when i visited in october?? i live 4 hours away and idk what im supposed to do with this information. i cant exactly just fix it

You're right that you can't fix it — and it sounds like part of what you're sitting with is the weight of knowing and not being able to do much from four hours away. That's a particular kind of helplessness.

The fact that she told you is something. Nineteen, away from home, eating alone for two months — that takes a lot to admit out loud. She probably wasn't looking for a solution last night as much as she needed someone to know.

What matters most right now is that she doesn't feel like she has to manage this alone. You don't have to have answers. Staying in closer contact — texting more, even just dumb stuff, maybe a regular call — can matter more than you'd expect when someone is that isolated. And when the moment feels right, it's worth asking if her university has any support (most do — counseling, student wellbeing services), not as a fix but as something that's there if she wants it. You knowing is already doing something.

i'm a junior in college and i just checked my bank account and i have $11. eleven dollars. rent is due in 8 days and i don't know what to do. i haven't told my parents because they're already stressed about money and i just feel so stupid for letting it get this bad

Having $11 eight days before rent is a genuine crisis, and the fact that you've been carrying this alone — trying to protect your parents while quietly panicking — makes it heavier than it needs to be. You're not stupid. You're in a hard situation that a lot of people hit in college, and you caught it before the due date, which actually gives you something to work with.

Most colleges have emergency funds specifically for this — they're often called emergency grants or student hardship funds, and they don't need to be repaid. The financial aid office is the place to start, today if possible. Your landlord may also give you a short extension if you contact them now rather than the day rent is due; they'd rather hear from you early. If you have any income at all, apps like Earnin can advance small amounts against hours worked.

As for your parents — that's your call and only you know your family. But sometimes the thing we're most afraid to say out loud turns out to be less catastrophic than the silence around it.

My son is 34 and we haven't spoken in almost two years. I wrote him a letter last spring, poured my heart into it, never heard back. My daughter says to give him space but I don't know how much space is enough. I'm not even sure what I did. Does it ever just... fix itself

Two years of silence after pouring your heart into a letter — and still not knowing what you did. That particular uncertainty might be the hardest part, because it doesn't give you anything to fix or apologize for. The honest answer to your question is: sometimes estrangements do soften over time, especially when the parent has made a genuine, low-pressure gesture like a letter and then waited. But 'fix itself' usually means one or both people changing enough internally that the old wound matters differently — not that it disappears. What you're doing, staying open without chasing, is probably the right instinct. That doesn't make the waiting less painful, and it doesn't mean you have to feel okay about it.
